Yes, the game is still in early access. Yes, people have been very vocal about their dissatisfaction with how long the game has been in early access and development. I myself was very hesistant to buy it and the game just sort of sat on my wishlist for a long time. I have been pleasantly surprised and happy with what the game has to offer right now though.
At it's basic core it's a stat raising dating so, so if that's not your thing the game is probably not for you as stats seem to play a very vital role in the gameplay itself. I'm only about a month into the game itself but already have a to keep a close eye on certain stats. Thankfully the most annoying fatigue stat doesn't rise TOO terribly much with activities and it goes down by a lot when you have a successful rest.
The most recent addition has been the voice acting and while I'll admit it was a little jarring at first, I've gotten used to it. Most of the voices do really fit the characters and just give a little more life into the story itself. There are little things here and there like random lines that aren't voiced or times when the volume of the line is very loud or very soft, but it will definitely make the game that much better when Sian is voiced as well.
Speaking of Sian, she is an...interesting main character. At first she appears to have a little bit of that quintessential sort of wallflower trait of otome mcs have? Thankfully she has proven to be a more than one-dimensional in her character development so far so hopefully the opinon that I continue to form of her will be positive. I really enjoy the fact that she's sort of behind the scenes in the industry as well and the fact that she is confident in her talents as a make-up artist and knows she deserves to do what she's doing with it. Things could have gone very badly if she was doubtful in herself throughout the entire game. The other character introduced so far have been very charming and likeable, the four love interests have very different personalities and different ways they interact with Sian so that has been interesting to see so far.
If you're interested in the game at all and have been on the fence about buying it, I would highly reccomend picking it up. Yes it still has a fair amount of bugs and such to work out, but it really is a wonderful game so far. If you're not a fan of VNs with tedious stat raising then perhaps this isn't the game for you.

Not a bad game; I'd say it's worth it if you're into the whole stat raising thing and like to go through a bunch of trial and error to get different endings, considering this one has 16 endings for you to spend more or less 80 hours on, considering that at least two of the routes I've already finished took me about 5 hours to complete (or maybe I'm just very slow).
Getting straight to the point, it gets repetitive, expected out of a stat raising otome. I wouldn't say it's repetitive to the point you just want to bash your head into the computer screen though, seeing as there are certain events from time to time, depending on whether you accept an offer or not, on what you decided to do that week, and some specific things, which I accidentally did before looking at the guide and seeing that X thing would only trigger by doing Y and Z before.
The art also isn't bad; the backgrounds were nicely done, and the sprites for each character is "unique", I guess you could say. Many times I've seen otomes having some sort of same-face syndrome with their handsome men and cute girl sprites, after all. Considering this is the same artist that has worked on RE: Alistair, sakevisual's first project if I'm not mistaken, it's impressive how much they've improved (though I must also admit their other artworks are just as great). I guess my only problems with the sprites are Matthew's chin when in front view and Adam's palm tree hair, but other than that, they're all unique on their own ways.
Though speaking of the characters, relating to their personalities, I did find them to be unique and endearing as well, or maybe the proper word would be amusing. Some dialogue lines too made me smirk to myself, mainly Mr. Newton's there, though some things seemed a tad bit forced, like the fanboy tutor (though he is still a lovely character). Then again, as much as I'd like to say there are no people that act the way he does, I have a friend that's pretty much like he is, both online and offline. The heroine was also nicely done, and a fresh change from the, usually, meeks ones I tend to see, mainly because my main focus tends to be Eastern otomes though, and social values all differ, but anyways. Depending on your choices, you can make her out to be hardworking, teasing and flirty at times, or a lazy bum that can even get expelled out of college. Though I don't really think there was much room for development for her, from start to finish, since she seemed pretty much the same to me, but my views may change as I go through other routes.
Another system I enjoyed is the ability to change clothes depending on the season, something like Tokimeki Memorial, there being certain styles the boys prefer and may mention about when in a date. My only peeve is that you couldn't wear things bought during other seasons, because I mean, I have shirts that I'll wear from Spring to Winter and the cycle continues. I can understand not wearing a thick jacket and a pair of boots during Summer, but a skirt or shirt bought during Spring should also be alright once Summer rolls around.
As for the voice acting, I'm not so sure on whether I enjoyed them or not; there were some parts where the cast did a good job, and others that seemed a bit too superficial. The voice choice for each character wasn't bad, you see, but I guess it just didn't feel very natural to me at certain points.
Now finally, as for the story, I'd say it's pretty straightforward, though I don't have much to comment since I only finished two routes, at the moment. You raise your stats, you get job offers, get money to buy things, depending on your choices you may go for friendship or lover route, you can give them presents during Christmas or their birthdays, you can hang out, and in the end there's the usual life lesson one or both of the characters learn once their bond deepends enough. Though personally, at least the romantic endings, aren't so satisfying; you bone'em, and then that's it. It'd be interesting if there were some sort of after-story rather than just finishing it right at the moment, like showing how they're doing a few months after getting together. It just feels a little "incomplete" to me, as if the endings were done a bit on a rush.
Overall, it's not a perfect game, but it's enjoyable and has its own charms, like many other games, I'd say. Bonus points for getting Mili to compose the opening there though; they're one of my favourites.

Game: Backstage Pass
Type: Visual Novel, Slice of Life, Anime, Dating Sim
Hours Logged: 18
Since this visual novel was on sale on steam I had to give it a try. And I figured I’d write a quick review before it went off of sale. Check it here. It’s 45% off at the moment so: $16.50. This is the first time I’ve seen it on sale and I’ve had it on my wishlist for awhile. So, this may be the biggest discount we get. Or as it looks like they just recently added the voices it may be that as they move forward they are trying to garner more positive reviews. I skimmed through some of the negative reviews and some of the issues folks have with it appear to have been resolved. Also, it looks like they went a really LOOOOONNNGG time without updates. It’s an early access game and just BTW as it stands I wouldn’t necessarily recommend it for the $30 price tag.
Game Play
Pretty straightforward. You are in school so part of your day will be filled with that and you have to decide what you want to with your free time: work, blog, study,go running, sleep, tutoring, go out with friends, or go out on the town. Each choice will effect your stats and your stats impact your relationships with other characters. Certain stats appeal to certain potential romantic interests.
You have dialogue choices while interacting with characters which will effect your relationships and what jobs and parties you choose to go to will impact your relationships and career options. Choose wisely.
Art
The art in my view was in the plus column. It’s very well drawn and has a fair bit of variety. The opening video is animated (if you search backstage pass in my tags you will find a gif set of it). It’s cute. There is also an animated video at the end, but I don’t have it unlocked. Can’t wait to get it though.
Characters
There are several characters you can pursue. But as I haven’t successfully gotten them all....I can’t really talk about all the characters. My first playthrough I got  Benito as a romantic option. I didn’t find that route too difficult and didn’t need to go back to old saves to make it work. Benito is cute, younger than your character and has a backstory which you slowly uncover as you go along. Second playthrough I didn’t end up with anyone. But I was attempting at Adam. I can’t seem to figure him out. As I like to play games cold the first few times I may not figure him out until I find a walkthrough for assistance. I got John romantically pretty easily as well once I was focused. He’s cool headed, romantic and older. Honestly, my personal preference meant his interactions were the most fun. I also got to the romance option with Matthew. He is the most full in my opinion. He’s pretty and he’s social awkward. If that appeals....
There are also three side options to romance (at least I think so?). I haven’t managed to get any of them even though I did try. I think I may have gotten close with two of them as I did get additional scenes with them and phone number, but I haven’t been successful in in my pursuit yet.
Overall
There are some funny moments, you will probably like at least one of the romanceable characters, you need to save often to go back and fix what you did if you make a mistake, and the gameplay is a bit tricky and if you aren’t invested will probably be annoying. I did have some issues with responsiveness like delays in clicking a button or sometimes it not clicking which was irritating. Not sure if that is just me or what.
Anyway, I really enjoyed this game and I am excited to see what happens when we finally get a finished product!

I've played various Otome games for awhile now and backstage pass reminded me of Magical Diary if Magical Diary was done 10000000000000 times better.
Pros:
1. The story line is realistic and the micro variations you can make within it are aplenty. It isn't 100% linear once your "path" is chosen, you can sucessfully romance guy A to 3 levels of sucess and your own personal life can be different as well.
2. The game is much more interactive than a lot of other popular Otome titles, instead of a choice every 10 - 20 pages of dialogue you get one in stat collection every "week" of the 2ish year long story. The actual Dialogue choices are minimal though, your stats will weigh heavier in getting the best endings, even if you did all the dialogue correct you may not of gotten the right stats for example.
3. The main character for once isn't a totally push over. She has one "weakness" or "ailment" that I'm almost certain they could of left out and it would of been fine, it isnt like memory loss so you can only talk every week so the MC doesnt say anything *cough* Amnesia:Memories *cough*. This MC voices good opinions and logical ones, especially on the more mature routes the game offers.
4. The art work and English voice acting is great to be honest. I havn't had alot of english voice acted otome experiences, and at first Adam's voice annoyed me at the start but John's totally made up for it all.
Cons:
1. The developers are slow on finishing this game, they are still adding more content and routes, so if the 4 routes are not enough for you right now, wait to buy it, though I'm excited to revisit the game later.
2. There were moments in this game where I'd of died without the skip button, some of the stat stacking gets tedious as the game goes on and this puts you in a bit of a daze, then you might miss something ... like forgetting to check your emails for one week and then screwing yourself over on the romance because you missed something important and having to start over.
3. No. 2 leads me into No. 3: Most Otome games have a pretty extensive rewind on choices, like if you misclick or decide oh crap im going to get a game over, rewind now. This game does not, while it has a rewind feature, it's small, and once you make a choice you can't fix it, you can rewind and see the dialogue but the check points for this are not chapter by chapter but instead are MUCH closer together. I missclicked on the mall button when i had to go another shop for an xmas gift... couldn't rewind, ended up not filling the romance bar to the max and had to start all over. So i guess, suck less and this isn't a con.

Victoria 2 is a monster of a game and a very good one at that but it can be a bit off putting just like most of the other paradox grand strategy games. Every single time I boot it up, I find myself on the wiki trying to understand some complex feature that completely went over my head before but which could actually help me as I try and try to make a nation (usually Venezuela) into a great power.
How well your country is doing relative to others all depends on your ranking which is decided by a combination of your prestige, industrial strength and military power, all of which will grow as you research new techs and watch the industrial revolution happen in front of your eyes. To top it all off, crisis can start to bubble up which involve the most powerful nations and may end up with a WW1 style great war happening, where nations are called into battle who might not even want to but who basically must due to the complex politics of the time and potential ramifications.
At its heart, Vic2 is all about population management. You citizens all have ideologies which change over time and it is up to you to try to get them to support the best policies for your current situation. One moment you might find yourself trying to get reactionaries in power to bring about a social revolution to bring in immigrants while the next you might be desperately trying to keep the status quo to avoid more restrictive policies. It's all very engrossing and the fact that the game has this incredibly tightly designed economic and political system that doesn't exist in a vacuum is incredible.
The game however can be brutal though in a fun way if you are a masochist like me. Not all countries are the same and finding yourself under the watchful eyes of a much more powerful nation is madenning (I'm looking at you USA). These powerful nations already have a headstart on you and have tools to compete with one another to ensure first dibs on the resources produced by the small nations. As such,It is very easy to accidentally find yourself fighting an enormous monster like Britain, France or Russia because they decided to get involved in your minor spat with a tiny nation that produces some rare resource.
I really can't recommend this game enough. It is unforgiving but so enjoyable. Several times now I have noticed the time just fly by and have had to force myself to stop and head to bed at 4am.

I'm about 5 hours into the game and I haven't beaten the Adventure mode final boss yet, but I've come close. There is still a lot of content left to unlock at this point and I haven't even opened the Endless mode yet.
The premise of the game is that you are put into a confined level and you have to clear the level of enemies. Most levels only take a couple minutes, though they get longer and more challenging the higher the level. There are about 16 regular Adventure mode levels so far. You earn credits for every enemy you kill, and you use that currency to unlock things like better weapons, more ammo, shields, and even things like the additional Endless mode, as well as level skips so you can jump right into level 2 or 3 or 4 instead of having to go back through levels you've already cleared.
Oh, and on top of this there are "Relics" which is essentially loot that you find every few levels, which permanently unlocks perks, of which you can apply 3 at a time to your character before you play a level. Once you have cleared a level of the all its relics you probably won't bother to go back to it again and will want to unlock the level skip with credits.
If you die, and you will, probably a lot of times on the final boss level, you have to start over again, but if you have unlocked the level skips you can jump back into the late game action quickly. You spend your curreny inbetween levels in a shop with limited items which also unlocks them as starting items, so after a few hours of gameplay you will be able to jump into level 4 with a sniper rifle and a boosted shield perk and have high level play right away.
The actual gameplay mechanics are satisfying as well. You have three types of ammo and can carry two guns (I really wish it was 3, maybe this is something I will still unlock?), there are lots of gun drops during play, you have both run and dodge mechanics which use a stamina bar, there are multiple types of shields to purchase or find as drops and equip, the guns have laser sights which show distance of the proejctile so you can set up shots, most of the map is destructable, and probably other stuff I'm forgetting as well.
For a free game it is extremely impressive. I highly recommend it. Give it a few playthroughs to understand the economy and the systems though. I only hope they continue to add lots of content for quite awhile, as this game is a fanastic framework to build on.

Wipeout is a series I only recently discovered, but almost instantly fell head over heels in love with. Unfortunately, it's also a series that's been almost entirely confined to itself, with little in the way of similar games to be found on other platforms, and whose future looks incredibly bleak with the shutdown of its developer, Sony Liverpool. As such I've been clamoring to find something to fill this soon to be gap, and the unapologetic clone that is Flashout 2 seemed like a good stopgap while I waited for a more fleshed out experience. How very, very wrong I was to assume even that much.
If you've (sadly) never gotten the chance to play Wipeout, it's a futuristic racing game set at an absurd speed as you careen through gravity defying courses, shooting off missiles and hitting speed boosts along the way to fend off competitors. Flashout 2 recreates this almost exactly, but what it loses is everything that makes Wipeout such an addictive, visceral game in the first place.
First on the chopping block are the controls, which have the dubious honor of being among the most unnecessarily convoluted control schemes of any game I've ever played. Every pickup is tied to a different button (or direction on the analog stick), and these are explained through a horrendous button map screen and almost hilariously bad tutorial, which couldn't even be bothered to remove the "tap the screen" text from the original mobile version.
Secondly, the racing itself is plagued by extreme repetition and a noticeable lack of any sense of speed. Each of the games ten tracks are almost entirely indistinguishable from each other, and are so plainly designed that I was already tired of them the first time around, let along the hundreds you'll be seeing them throughout the campaign. The different ships you can pilot all feel more or less identical, with the only difference being each is slightly faster than the last and takes more to blow up, but even when you're flying at seemingly impossible speeds it doesn't
like you are. Flying through races in Flashout 2 is unbelievable dull and tame in what it attempts, which for a game that bills itself upon light-speed futuristic racing is a huge problem.
Further to this point, the handling is especially odd, with a bizarre alignment problem that feels halfway between an overly controlling assist and another person trying to steer your vehicle at the same time. It's awkward and I have no explanations for why it is how it is, or what reason the developer could have for making it this way (assuming it's not simply another of the many bugs of the game). Online multiplayer is a joke, lacking any way to invite friends, and opting to use your PC's name instead of your Steam handle.
Graphically there's a lot happening on screen, but none of it is particularly impressive. Textures are blurry and simple, and the color pallet virtually unchanged from every race in the game. Particle effects lack any power behind them, seeming more like excessive lens flare than explosions. If there is anything nice I can say about the game, it would be that the soundtrack is actually not half bad, and in another context I might actually enjoy listening to it.
I had high hopes for Flashout 2, despite its always questionable mobile origins, but it failed on a fundamental level to deliver even a small dose of the excitement I get whenever I play the series that "inspired" it. Even taken by itself, there's nothing fun or impressive about anything Jujubee S.A. has done, and the more I dug into it the lazier they seemed, with an abundance of bugs and mobile-port carryovers that have no business in a PC version.
At this point I guess it's time to make another sacrifice at Sony's altar and hope they bring Wipeout back, because this just isn't cutting it.

All right, I'm going to keep this fairly simple.
Cobalt is a blast. The singleplayer I found to be meh (there wasn't much there that was interesting - a lot of exploring environments that aren't particularly interesting, taking out a couple enemies here and there, maybe a miniboss or two . . . I dunno, I just wasn't very interested), but the multiplayer/arcade mode is phenomenal.
To be perfectly honest, there aren't a whole lot of people online at any given time. There are peak hours/days where you might get a full server, but my experience has mostly been starting a server and just playing against the bots until someone joins and you can play with one or two (sometimes three) other people for a little while. There's a variety of fun gamemodes, and while there's a bit of a steep learning curve (particularly because most of the people playing have been around for quite a while and are really good), the community has been very friendly. When I was still learning to play, this one guy switched to a different map and gamemode just to take the time to teach me what has proven to be the most valuable technique that I currently know.
The gameplay, though, is obviously the selling point. And oh, it sells. The fast-paced action, intense moments, slow-mo exchanges of gunfire, impressively challenging bots and phenomenal players, all make for a wonderful experience, and I cannot tell you how many times I've wished that I record whenever I play the game, not just for my own awesome moments, but ones that I've seen other people make.
Is $20 a reasonable price for this game? Yeah, I think it probably is. But I would absolutely recommend it to anyone interested when it's $10 or less - it's a lot of fun!

Vic2 has the best combination of features for a grand strategy game, apart from the battle system which is just as simplistic as for any Paradox game except the HoI series. The level of details you get to oversee for your faction are just amazing.
You'll control nation states and will have to manage your multi-national state, ideologies (religious or political) and parties that are allowed by law. You have to manage your government, army, diplomacy (Pdox style) and you can play whatever GS fantasy you want (let's be honest, most of us go for world domination) and you have to do it in a flavourfull rulset that is quite immersive in the victorian era context, imo (how fast and what tools do you have to expand and what happens when you break the rules, won't reveal too much to avoid spoilers). The things you can control at home depend on your government system.
The cherry on top is the most detailed economical simulation of any video game with multiple resources and things you can produce in the context of the industrial era and the beginning of capitalism, socialism that blends into a basic supply-demand economy sim. Add jingoism and nationalism to the mix. Stir it, don't shake it and take it with a pinch of salt.
There are obvious problems with gameplay. The economy system is so complex that it has some serious bugs to how things work and cash managing vanishing from your economy amplifying the inflation you experience in the game. But it is so huge and complex, you'll most probably won't notice and be bothered by it, it'll feel like part of the problem you have to stay on top of. Ultimately, it does a good enough job at letting you feel that you can control some things and if you think you like sims and haven't yet played Vicky2, what are you waiting for?

Otto von Bismark: The Game.
Victoria II is a game about careful economic planning, diplomatic maneuvering, colonial expansionism, and trying your very best to prevent Germany from forming.
You take control of a nation and guide them from 1836 to 1936, and your goal is to become the world's foremost economic and military power.
The control you exert over your nation is, however, indirect at best and tenuous at worst: you can't just "make" more factory workers, for instance. Instead you have to manipulate conditions - taxation, education, employment opportunities - to encourage people to go into that line of work. Similarly, you don't get to decide what form of government your nation adopts, but are often at the whims of revolution. All of this is underpinned by a detailed economic simulator based on supply and demand that acts in mysterious ways to dictate the fate of the powers. Coupled with a diplomatic system based around alliance blocs and the concept of influence, this makes Victoria II feel like a realistic simulation of the long nineteenth century. This doesn't mean that you have no control over your own fate: only terrible players get swept along with the simulation. Once you're able to see the way things tie together, you can spend hours carefully crafting your plans to then spring everything together as soon as an opportunity is presented - which is exactly how 19th century realpolitik functioned. Because of all this, the stories that come out of a game of Vicky often feel engaging and realistic, and you can actually imagine reading about them in a history book somewhere.
The game's not perfect, of course, and the simulations can often break down or be gamed around by clever players. As the oldest still-current Paradox title, it's also starting to show its age a bit, with launcher issues and the occasional silly bug. More subtly, because it's a strategy game about a historical period that had a very definite, very tragic and very recent ending, Vicky can be a little deterministic in its interpretations of history. Thus, for example, Prussia tends to industrialize rapidly, grow its military power, hammer Austria  and unify Germany - exactly as happened in reality. Only in reality, it happened as a result of specific actions taken by certain people in positions of power across the continent, so it would be natural to assume that those people acting differently would've created a different outcome. Yet because Paradox (and the rest of us) know how things turned out, the mechanics feel tipped in favour of that outcome.

Victoria 2 is easily one of the best games I have played to date. To begin, the military system is brilliant, bringing manpower in to the fold of the amazing population mechanic in the game brings an interesting and favourable change to the more generic systems that you would find in ck2 or eu4 and each unit is unique in it's own way, I love the names given to each unit, the fact that their stats change throughout the game and how eventually you can even recruit tanks and planes into your by then massing armies, this system also ties into trade requiring different materials to complete each and every unit, I would wish that you could sign trade agreements with individual countries like in other paradox games however Victoria 2 compensates for this by introducing an interesting and ever changing global economy. Research is also one of my favorite parts of this game as you must choose to sacrifice certain technologies for others and unlike eu4 with only 3 platforms to research on with 1 researchable item on each this has several platforms with several items on each. Your internal politics is again a great part of victoria 2 with parties forming coalitions and popularity largely based off of population. The party in power can often limit what you can do within the game, such as building factories and negative parties that limit your control can often come about if you extort you population. Even if you are lucky enough to have a government that allows you to choose the party in power, it may often fail to stop parties coming in power through revolution. In my opinion diplomacy can sometimes be lacking but again the choices you make internally and externally can bring about the birth of nations and the fall of others, perhaps even your own. Yet there are negatives. The world crisis mechanic can often fail to even create a large war, and often it can cause the same war to happen again and again if it does start a war. Moving on, the civil war mechanic used to kick off the american civil war is honestly wasted compaired to it's potential, this mechanic can only influence the american civil war not any other possible civil war meaning that any possible 'civil wars' will only come in the form of rebels. Lastly colonization is also somewhat bad, though it is fun to colonise much of africa and asia governing the new land can often  just be a hastle.
TLDR: This game is good, very good and you should play it. 10/10.

I'll start this review off by saying that I pre-ordered this game back on the 360 after my brother, a mate and I played the co-op demo in which you fight one of the monster bosses. We all thoroughly enjoyed it and I continued to enjoy it for a long time. I bought it on Steam recently because it was on sale for something in the region of £2.
The first impressions I got from the Steam version is "Games with windows live. Here we go, I'm sure this will run perfectly"(Sarcasm intended), followed by "The thing doesn't even start" but thankfully, I came across a guide to fix these issues and I don't have any problems anymore. (
)
The actual game itself is great in terms of replayability, there are a huge amount of unlocks for the game and none of them require money to "feel a sense of accomplishment". It can be a bit of a grind but if you enjoy fighting huge monsters or doing mini AI deathmatches then it's all good.
The player base is virtually non-existent but when you consider that the game is 7 years old and it wasn't that popular to begin with, it makes complete sense. It's a perfectly fine game to play by yourself but if you can gather up some friends to play with you I would recommend it as it only gets better with more people, also the AI are thoughtless so playing alone is pretty much playing alone even though you have 3 AI teammates.
The main storyline is absurd but that's the point of video games, suspend your disbelief and you're in a land of crazy action. What other game has a storyline that involves the end of the world, a bunch of Mexicans commandeering a battleship owned by a world military and a huge worm that chases a train carrying a monster railgun? Oh, did I mention that the planet is inhabited by giant monsters because I don't think I can stress that enough.
Playing through the game once means you can play as your custom character in the story mode. You technically have 5 different characters from five different factions and they all have their own levels, so if you get to level 40 with a certain faction character you unlock appearance parts for that character. The 5 factions are the army peeps, some mercenaries, angry snow pirates, weird snow pirates and girls (Side note: You want to unlock all character parts for the girls if you're a horny teen)
There are also weapon unlocks which can change your playstyle drastically (Or just let you spam the hand cannon), there are a great deal of title unlocks which can range from the professional to the absurd, there are even a ton of emotes you can unlock for your character including different dances (Again, take note horny teenagers)
Overall, this game is underrated and it's worth a look if you can sort out the GFWL issues at the start. You'll have plenty of hours of entertainment and it's worth the price if you get it in the winter sale (£2.59 at time of writing this)

Despite the protest, a LP2 (lost planet 2) using the steam doo-hickey system rather than GFWL (Games For Windows Live) will most likely not happen, but dont let that discourage you from buying the game. You see comments talking about how GFWL prevents the game from launching or doesnt work period.
Trust me, all it needs is a little fixin and it'll work. There's a helpful comment written by
. His comment should show up on the top list but if you cant find it, here's a copy&paste of the main part of his instructions to fix GFWL:
After installing GFWL and restarting your pc/relaunching the game a couple times, it works as intended. You may need to create an xbox profile if you haven't one yet.
Now there are not a huge number of people playing the game. It is possible to find people for co-op. Pvp....not so much.

Another and much more annoying issue. Keybinding. Holy cr*p is it terrible. IF you have a mouse with some macro keys (Logitech g700s or etc) this is an easy fix. if not...well you can still make it work. Keep in mind you cant, i repeat.
rebind the keys for VS and they also are tied to some of the keys for basic movements and action. I.E. the Grenade button (which is right mouse click) that is also the button to fire Right VS Weapon. Yup.
So some keys you might want to rebind or have a macro for:
.sprint
.dodge
.crouch (depends on your go-to key for crouching that you find most comfortable)
.Zoom
.Ascend&Descend for VS (i think ascend is f2 and descend is 4; its bad for when u need to move and do one of those 2 simultaneously so if you have macro keys, use em)
Also be mindful of the
. For some reason the default settings cause the Cursor/reticle to 'stick' occasionally when you start firing a gun so I recommend keeping the Sensitivity high (like 27) and mouse speed low (like 10).
Besides that. The game runs pretty ok. Campaign is the main selling point and strangly has a lot of replay value for me. Others may not find it appealing. You can customize your character and even bring your custom one into the campaign once you beat the entire thing once. I like the 'slot machine' mechanic to earn nicknames, guns, abilities, emotes, and eventually character parts. Probably one of the things that drives me to ply campaign other than lvl'ing up my current faction.
Difficulty ranges from Cakewalk difficutly to 'I know where anything and everything is, what enemies there are, where the snipers are (trust me, you'll know), how to kill anything I see reguardless of what it is, and despite all that even the game's hardest difficutly cant stop me.' difficutly. Well thats my interpretation of the Etreme mode difficutly.
The hardest dificutly mode prevents your harmonizer from sucking up energy to regen health which is a GOOD thing. Conserving Thermal Energy is a huge aspect to some levels where it becomes hard to replenish it. There are a few OP items that can heal you in a jiff and are a must have if you plan on running Extreme mode. That plus the Survival perk and you can basically get away with half health since anything that can one-shot you (headshots from sniper rifles not included), Survival will prevent it from actually killing you. Pair that with an Injection Gun II and you'll be cheating death more than A Superhero from Marvel. Plus you can heal
(which will prevent one shot's of any kind along with VS's except falls-of-death)as well with the injection gun II.
You will learn to hate snipers if you're the type of player who's soul burns with anger when you die. Basically dont stand still and kill them as fast as possible. Also keep moving when you're engaging them. Shotguns or gunblade are awesome for them. Tho if you wanna be safe, use a shotgun and knock their *sses to the floor.
Lastly, be careful of mechs that can hover. Some maps have a lot of "falls-of-deaths-doom" that youll want to avoid. Too many times have I died like this cause I was a dummy and didnt watch my sorroundings. That and having blowback weapons like shotguns or rocket launchers psuhing me off the edge as well.
Its a fun game. Its more fun to play with other people (but no one wants to play extreme :/ ) but solo with bots is good enough to make do *cough*free cannon fodder*cough*. After you fix GFWL and rebind a few keys, its pretty smooth sailing after. Again, the campaign may seem repetitive to some people. Im a kind of person that likes certain forms of grinding, hence why games like Borderlands 2 and Warframe tickle my fance ever so nicely.
Its a nice game and I enjoy playing it. As always, I encourage you to try it out within the 2 hour return policy and see how it fairs with you.
Thank you for reading and have a good one.

I normally don't care much for action games due to their inherent linearity and lack of depth. However, this is perhaps the first and only action game I've played and enjoyed in as long as I can remember. Ryse is an intensely cinematic action game with graphics so superb, you might forget you’re playing a game at all. Though short lived, the experience this game offers is an epic adventure on a scale perhaps akin to movies such as Braveheart or Gladiator -- it also had a semblance to the recent Spartacus show on Starz, which was among my all-time favorites.
The combat is also something to be praised. The finishing moves and dynamic strategy are enough to ensure you don't get bored with the endless hacking and slashing typical of a medieval based action game. The storyline, too, will keep you enthralled from start the finish.
Although this game will only last up to about 12 hours, and it is admittedly a linear experience offering little replayability, it is still one I must recommend with enthusiastic applause. I recommend it to anyone who's a fan of ancient roman lore and of the sort of action-adventure carnage which inevitably ensues between opposing armies wielding pointed blades.

introduction: this is a turn based tactical action, where you play as a sort of mercenary and do whatever you want.
Now the describtion:
The War came to our galaxy in the year 3000. The Clissan race (smart machines, that came from nowhere) attacks and destroys EVERYTHING on their way. They have no fear, they have no mercy, they take no prisoniers. The Union of 5 races is loosing solar system one by one...  When there's no hope left, the United Government decides to make a risky step and make a new army, army of SPACE RANGERS. The idea is a complete success and soon, the threat of Dominators has been forgotten. All the living creatures thought it is the end and they can sleep well from on those days....
Now it is year 3300 and galaxy faces new war. War with another machines. Who are they? What do they want? Maybe... they are connected with Clissan race somehow? Why did Pirates decided to  Unite their forces, make revolution and set a new goverment exactly now? WIll Rangers save the situation this time? Or will they help Pirates instead? All of these questions must be answered by you, young Ranger! Do what you want - grab, kill and destroy everything on your way, for the sake of victory! Or help poor, fight the bandits and complete awesome text quests! Hire other rangers and make a perfect team which will retake any captured solar system, work with both, pirates and government to get the best equipment and make diversions under enemy camouflage or... just stay away and watch... The universe has it's own forces and you aren't the only hope for it's survival. Custom difficulty level (you can change EVERY POSSIBLE ASPECT OF THE GAME), 5 sides of the conflict (you can join only pirates and the official government tho), open world sandbox game, meaning every game will have completely different result. The mobile Universe that is different with every new game you start... What else... Isn't it enough for a good game, eh?

I haven't gotten to the end yet, so I'm not sure if the ending is worth a change in my review. I'll edit this review when I get to the end, but for now I have to comment on this title's bizarre gameplay.
Other negative reviewers have basically taken the words out of my mouth... It's certainly not an intuitive game, it's difficult to manuever in and more times than not, it is frustrating instead of enjoyable. Trust me, I really tried to like this game. I would tell myself that the fun was in the exploration, and to an extent, it is. This game is gorgeous. If you accepted the notion that you weren't going to have much success in completing the tasks, you could enjoy it. But one can only do that for so long and for all this game's faults, it's very suspenseful, and you'll be frustrated by your lack of progression.
I've played a number of games where the game leaves very cryptic clues and you have to figure out what to do next. If you don't like these games, you'll absolutely hate this one, because it's even more cryptic than most. The clues disappear
or sometimes leave you searching for a long time, or perhaps if you don't follow the directions exactly so, you'll misstep and lose your direction entirely. I barely had the patience for it, and I was interested in the storyline! If the storyline seems too pretentious or you just don't care for it, you won't enjoy this game.
Pros:
-Beautiful graphics
-Suspenseful/compelling story
-Sometimes makes you think (a little)
Cons:
-Jittery camera
-Cryptic clues
-Excessive/nonsensical swearing (And I love to ♥♥♥♥ing swear!)
-Weird audio effects (hint: don't be too far from the radio or you won't be able to hear it anymore)
-Achievements don't work
Basically, if you like pretty graphics or maybe want to think a little out of the box, this game might be good for you. But there are other games that can accomplish this without being so broken. Instead, how about watching a decent walkthrough?

Don't let the price fool you,  it's insanely worth it if you are looking for a visual novel that is so story packed.  It's well thoughtout,  and the storylines are simply amazing.  It's not your average visual novel however,  this is taking you through an entire year of life through Sian's eyes.  there are four men within the story that you can build relationships with,  one of them you already have a backstory with,  the other three you do not.  As the year progresses you will learn that keeping in contact with these men is vital,  but also impressing them is twice as important.   The game comes with a feature where you can dress Sian in certain outfits for each season that passes by the year.   If you get a correct combination,  the man you are trying to impress,  or a man in general who you haven't tried to impress may compliment you on that outfit.  The other way is perhaps waiting for certain holidays to come by,  buying them things you think they would enjoy would be best so pay attention to what these men tell you.  You may even be invited to certain events with them if you play your cards correctly.  This will build up hearts in the statistics section when you reach the weekend.
There are other cute activities that you can do,  such as checking the message boards,  or checking your email for jobs to earn some of that extra cash.  All in the way to describe this game is you will not have a dull moment,  and you will not believe that it's an entire year of a makeup artists life.

I definitely reccomend this game, to whoever is reading this, it is definitely worth it, even if it isn't the best of ports, and you don't have a PS2, get it, and play it. There are very easy workarounds to get the resolution you want, and to fix the gamepad controls.
I never really got a chance to play this game on the PS2, since it didn't seem like a game I would really be interested in, however after a few years of being released on PC, it caught my attention, most noticeably, it's really, really high rating, and I thought to myself, is this game really that good? Short answer: YES.
Back in 2007 (with a 2004 Packard Bell PC) I was just glad I was running the game, I was new to PC gaming, so I didn't really have a clue what to expect. The visuals weren't really impressive, especially in 640x480 resolution, but I did manage to get it to full screen and a slightly higher res. The main problem was the keyboard controls, they were very unusual at first, and the game also was probably the hardest one I had played to date on PC (mind you, it was probably only the 10th game I played on PC) Just the second mission boss was owning me again and again, and probably went the same way about 10 more times before, I got fed up and stopped playing, and this was on normal difficulty.
A few days later picked it up again and started playing, this time I somehow managed to scrape by the first boss, and off I went, one of the best games I have ever played, and also gave me the mentality to never give up on a hard game, it's always more satisfying when the game is hard, unlike DmC. DMC 3 truly is an epic game, with cheesy (but funny) one liners and whole load of awesome action, the cinematics are awesomely done, the storyline (though confusing at times) is awesome.
It really disappoints me that there hasn't been a true continuation of the DMC storyline, even in DMC 4, the main focus was not on Dante. But I am getting ahead of myself, and there are spoilers if I keep going on, and someone is still yet to play DMC 4, so I'll just stop here.
Now that I have the game on steam, I had a few problems with the controls again, but this time for the gamepad, I was already used to the keyboard controls, since I played through this game before, and I also wanted to play it in 1080p this time, and with the help of the Steam community and a few mods, I got it to run as I wanted it to both the resolution and the gamepad, except for the quick weapon switches the triggers on the 360 controller are the only buttons that don't respond, it doesn't bother me much since my favourite weapons are the default ones anyway, Rebellion is just too good, and Ebony and Ivory are just the trademark guns you can't go anywhere without them. This game is a broken port of the console version. Very badly made without thinking from the perspective of the PC player control ergonomics either using keyboard or gamepad.
GRAPHICS
The graphics are typical of the older Play Station games (think of Resident Evil 2 and 3, except that background buildings are also in 3D). It's dated for 2015, but nothing sinful from when it was originally released.
But the sinful thing in here is that there is no fullscreen mode. It can only be viewed in windowed mode. Max resolution is at 1600x1200. (Even DOS games has fullscreen).
SOUND
It's ok. From the intro to the rock tunes of the (in-game) broken jukebox, it does fine. Positional audio was not used.
CONTROLS
It's a bad port mainly because the control scheme is unbearably bad... keyboard or XBox controller.
With the keyboard, you can configure the key map. The problem with using the keyboard is that [Jump] is reflected as [Style Action]. Pressing [Style Action] is still [Style Action]. I can't make Dante jump.
Buttons can also be configured with the XBox controller... except for the directional movement which is unfortunately placed to the Right analog stick. Forget about no rumble feature. I just want to move the character properly, which I can't.
GAMEPLAY
It has a lot of potential and I can feel that this could have been a good game. Camera control poorly done as well, though. I can only reset the camera view to it's default location. I can't do anything else with it.
OVERALL
I can't even play it, so I can't recommend it at all. The DMC franchise has gone a long way, but unless they've made the controls better, it is probably best to play the older parts of the franchise in the console rather than the PC.

A stylish fighting game classic. This may be considered the peak of the Devil May Cry series. It is also out for quite the while now, so it seems hardly necessary to go into too much detail that has already been covered over and over again.
Storywise, you battle your way through an ancient tower to face your brother Vergil and foil his sinister intentions... but whose plan is really in action here?
Gameplaywise, this game really shines. You can achieve mastery in four styles with different foci (Gunslinger, Swordmaster, Trickster and Royal Guard), plus two slightly more gimmick-like unlockables. You acquire an arsenal of five melee and five long range weapons, each category of which you can equip two and seamlessly switch between them. This is hardly astonishing nowadays, but it still blends together magnificently. There is also the bloody palace, an arena mode that provides slaughter aplenty.
This version comes with new difficulty modes (compared to the original on PS2), which may or may not be of interest to you, and with a playable Vergil. This is a fun variant of the fighting gameplay, but does not introduce a lot of new content otherwise - the levels are simply the campaign all over again, minus the story cutscenes.
One thing that should be mentioned is the optimization of the steam version. I bought the game in retail originally, and there were quite a few problems with it not recognizing gamepads correctly or at all - I ended up with a JoyToKey-workaround, which rather nullified the use of analog sticks, and still had trouble mapping the controller because some buttons were not registered, some double, and some of the in-game controls refused to be changed. The steam game comes with a controller configuration application, a nice little thing that took all this work away and actually succeeded in using both sticks and the various seemingly problematic buttons. This little addition increases playability a good deal for me.
If you do not have this game yet and care for action / (sword-) fighting games with a really well thought-through combat system, I highly recommend looking into this.

Nice, simple rogue-lite where both melee and ranged combat feels satisfying

UTOPIA 9 is a procedurally generated rogue-lite with plenty of flavor and excitement. Unique for its take on the nemesis system, this colorful twin-stick shooter provides loads of vengeance seeking fun. Even though the solo experience is praiseworthy, support for local coop with up to 2 total players raises the experience to a new level.
The traveling protagonist is allowed the use of two sets of primary and secondary attacks. The weapon or item in either hand can be switched with ease, creating a personalized playstyle with constant on-the-spot switching.
UTOPIA 9 employs the use of many different melee and projectile weapons, each with a unique style. The classifications are: bullet, energy, explosive, melee and shell weapon types. Some weapons will release a charged-up blast, others will shoot scattered, focused, explosive or rapid projectiles. Depending on the weapon or consumable item, two-hands may be required. This encourages the player to focus and improve on active weapon switching. Upon mouse-over, weapon stats are also provided, such as: cooldowns, damage, spread, etc.
The enemies in this game are extremely varied, although many of them will utilize the same character model. Some of the creatures are aggressively fast melee vanguards, while others are focused snipers. Some of them will even retreat to backup if the player is starting to dominate. When an enemy is killed, ammo, health, and soylent will be randomly dropped. These loot items will disappear after a period of time.
UTOPIA 9’s take on the nemesis system is what sets it apart from many other twin-stick shooters. Upon dying, the enemy that landed the death strike will: transform itself into a nemesis enemy, take your gear, and earn itself a place on the wanted list. It will also be given a name and profession to add flavor to the newly promoted target of revenge. Defeating the nemesis will allow the player to reclaim the previously lost gear. It's also possible to have multiple nemesis enemies on the map, but only one can be present in a single level.
Mutating is a major form of character progression in this game. Upon collecting soylent from downed enemies, the character may level up and choose a mutation (ability). The mutations are classified below, along with an example. The mutation options are also randomly generated each time/playthrough.
Upon clearing a location, the player then chooses where to go next by selecting another location on a map. The map is similar in design to a hopscotch court where travel occurs at specific nodes. The map also provides small bits of information to help the player choose a location, such as: health, weapons, armor, and shield indicators. If the player perishes, the death location is marked on the map and in the level itself. Upon death, statistics are provided – number of discovered items, score comparisons and leaderboard information (most soylent, most points, etc.). Although it is possible to progress by running through the level while bypassing enemies, doing so is not advisable as the character’s mutation level and gear will be severely lacking for future endeavors.
UTOPIA 9 does an outstanding job creating an immersive and colorful alien world. Its use of vibrant purple, blue and green color palettes help sell the extraterrestrial aspect. The aesthetics, art style, and projectile animations are very appealing from a visual standpoint. Taking a laser to the face is less agonizing when it looks so pretty.
UTOPIA 9 utilizes procedurally generated levels which help break up any monotony experienced from rogue-lites of lesser quality. A more in-depth explanation of the game’s level generation is explained by the developers
. An important point mentioned within details how a level takes into consideration the time of the day, and generates fauna and lighting effects accordingly.
Although there is full controller support, the game doesn’t seem to favor incorporating it. A few examples of what this means include:
Even though UTOPIA 9 was only released last month, there seems to be an active player base, as seen in the Discussions board and community content. Despite the lack of reviews, which are all positive at the time of publishing this review, player support seems to be relatively strong. The developers have officially responded in every thread with a directed question, and Whalegun is currently working on multi-lingual support for the game.
There are a few suggestions that may improve gameplay listed below.
UTOPIA 9 is an extremely light-hearted and immersive game, despite the plethora of alien guts spread all over the place. The game’s aesthetics and nemesis system earn it a recommendation for any fan of rogue-lites or twin-stick shooters. Unfortunately, I didn’t manage to experience this vibrant game with other couch buddies, but I will say that the solo experience is still a worthwhile one.

Endless Legend - The non-Civ player review!
So - I've never played Civilisation V. I know, approximately 75% of you are screaming at me for being an idiot etc. I just never got around to it, okay!
So, Endless Legend is a game for me without the obvious Benchmark. The learning curve is (in my humble opinion) pretty perfect, easing you gently into the finer mechanics of the game through the short tutorial, and then freeing you up to experiment in a live game. The different factions offer fantastic replay value - I've now completed the game with *counts on fingers* four of the ten playable factions available without purchasing any additional content. The factions are diverse enough that you're forced into different play styles - which ultimately adds to the replay value in trying to master the niche aspects of different factions.; Each faction has a series of unique attributes and abilities as a means of delivering this, for example - The Cultists only allow one city, so you make it the biggest badass city that sprawls across an entire region, heavily defended with so many population you can (by end game) build an entire army in a single turn. The game also offers an extremely diverse set of victory conditions, which ultimately facilitates consideration as to which victory condition to go after with which faction.
Anyway - TL;DR: Good game, worth the purchase. Great replay value.

The first was fine, even though I didn't really know what I was doing, and I couldn't finish the second one, totally lost it at some point. You press W and you go at your maximum speed, which will be rather slow at the start (you better fly over the speedboost). The ship felt responsive, and I could feel the speed, but the camera is bad. There has been quite a bit of negative reviews assocaited with this game. Everyone is entitled to their opinion. That is great.
For my opinion, I'd say this is the best game in recent years. However, I will say there are nuances that are annoying.
The match engine itself has had a massive upgrade and it's noticeable. However, with that massive upgrade, it created issues in the 3D match engine. They significantly tried to reduce the OP part of crossing from fullbacks/wingbacks generating 20-30 assists a season in FM16. To do this, they've changed the way wingbacks/fullbacks operate.
Wingbacks/fullbacks hold the ball way to long before crossing so nearly all crosses are blocked or honestly just poor crosses. The play looks choppy/unintelligent when the wingback/fullback is yards past the defender, but then holds the ball for 2-3 seconds and allows the defender to catch up so he can block the cross.
Goalkeepers are....interesting at the best of times, and just laughable at the worst of times. There's also still the weird issue (I'd say bug) where the opposition will score their 1st shot on goal on approximately 60% of the attempts. It won't be a clear cut or half chance, it'll just be a weird shot that goes in. It is what it is.
Also, it's much more difficult to use a plug and play tactic. That plug and play tactic will generally be successful for you I'm sure. But if you're truly looking for an unbeaten season without reloading, minor changes will occur during the season as the opposition will learn/adapt to your style, as well as in game, quirky things happen. This is similar to real life. At any time, some team can beat another team. It happens.
People also complain about injuries. Yes they are an issue; but I suggest you look at your the teams in the league you watch and see how many teams have 2-5 players injured at any given time, for small 5-15 day injuries plus the long term injuries too. Injuries are in part, down to your tactic, your training intensity, lack of rotation etc.
Another thing that loses it's useful/entertaining aspect of it, is the social media addition. It's great for 3-4 games. Then it's very repetitive and worthless.
All in all, the game is overly positive, I just wanted to lay out a few negative issues so that people are aware of them, and they know what to expect going in. I'd recommend the game.

I felt like Sian had more depth and personality than most other protagonists I’ve played with. She had distinct personality traits/quirks that were hinted at (or made obvious) at various points in the story rather than being a complete blank or only having those traits appear for certain routes (e.g., she’s got super good aim/excels at shooting games).
I’ve completed each of the main romance routes, two secret routes, and three of the four friendship routes (curse you, John), and I found each one enjoyable. Again, the characters are pretty well fleshed out and each has an interesting story and relatively complex personality. I also appreciate the fact that there are multiple “independent” endings you can achieve that still feel like successes rather than a “boohoo, I’m still sad and single” ending. I also like that you can continue interacting with all of the characters even after committing to a particular route rather than cutting off everyone but the main person.
I’ve seen some people complain about the stats building and/or the overall game being too hard. While I agree that there are some parts that got a little frustrating (the friendship routes in particular), I don’t think it’s overly difficult. For this game, it’s just a matter of figuring out how things work, who prefers what, and focusing on the ending you want. Then again, I like a little more strategy and challenge than a lot of these types of games typically offer.
Would I like to see a few things done differently? Sure (a dialogue option for John similar to Adam’s aquarium one, Rachel route, some stats related activities for the weekends…). But overall, I think the story is solid, the characters are interesting and likeable, and the general gameplay is both challenging and fun. With all of those endings, I think it’s got enough replayability (especially after the final version with voices gets updated) make it worth the $.

I must admit that before I contacted Whalegun in regards to UTOPIA 9 – A Volatile Vacation I had not heard much about their game at all. The game’s page on the Steam store did, however, did catch my attention and very eager to try this Early Access game out. Before I delve too much further I will admit ahead of time that I am very glad that I did and that I believe this is one that I’ll be returning to along its development journey and will complete once out of early access. UTOPIA 9 is a roguelike action shooter that is extremely polished for an early access game. I’m quickly becoming surprised at the quality of early access games lately. It seems that many developers have learned from the mistakes of others and many are putting genuinely gameplay ready titles up.
There was one problem that I immediately had with the game. It is not programmed to recognize the trigger buttons on the Xbox One controller. Instead, the game demands that I use the bumper buttons. This problem persists throughout attempts to configure the controller through the in game menu as it simply doesn’t recognize them at all. I much prefer to use the trigger buttons rather than the bumpers as it feels natural. This is a fairly significant annoyance in actual gameplay because these buttons are the primary attack buttons. On the plus side in regards to the controller I was a big fan of the twin stick nature of the game with the left thumbstick used to move and the right used to aim. Despite my complaint concerning the trigger buttons I have to admit that the game controls very smoothly already which I am impressed with given the game’s current state of development.
In regards to the weapons I enjoyed the range of them. You begin with a standard gun that shoots in a straight line and a suitcase looking weapon – which makes sense given that you’re supposed to be on vacation – that you can utilize to bludgeon your enemies to death. Before too long you find more weapons to add to your arsenal. You can switch among these weapons so that you always have options unless you run out of ammunition in which case you’re stuck with the suitcase. Lack of ammunition became an all too common occurrence for this trigger happy gamer thus an advantage to the game is to be ammo conscious and use it when you feel you have clean shots.
Arguably the best thing about UTOPIA 9 is that they’ve implemented something similar to the Nemesis System used in Middle-earth Shadow of Mordor. Whenever a mob kills you it will be promoted but it will also loot your corpse. This promoted mob becomes much larger and stronger than it previously was. From here you must restart the game and build up your character again in order to overcome the now more difficult beast. In theory this sounds harsh because you have to overcome something harder than what you originally died to and although this is true you will become better at the game because of it. Finally, in order to satiate the thirst of the techheads among us the game looks gorgeous and sounds almost as good. It is clear that Whalegun have concentrated on the entire picture when it comes to their game and that’s a good thing.
Whalegun have an early access gem on their hands. I really hope that the game’s development is smooth sailing from here on out. I urge those of you who like the idea behind the game to give it an opportunity to woo you over as I can almost guarantee that you will not forget it.

Overall Score from me: 5.5/10.
I realise that the game is not yet complete, if It ever gets updated and fully finished I'll adjust my review accordingly. Keep in mind, that I've played many many many Otome style visual novel games, and there are basically three main types that exist. Stat building, choice maker/visual novel, point and click/adventure.
This one is mainly a stat builder but also is reliant on choices you make in relation to the character you're pursuing.
First the numbers.
Gameplay 4/10. There is no option to skip the mini cutscenes during the classes/work week, or making cupcakes, so if you're going for doing things efficiently and making 20 or so cupcakes it takes forever. The email system is critical for some of the game paths and EXTREMELY EASY TO MISS. Which means unless you save often you could miss half of the requirements for some of the game paths. The game length is too long in the worst way because of how long it takes you to complete the actual week day planning, (A "save this schedule" option would be great as well) And it is very difficult to monitor your character's stress levels while paying attention to the email system, and go out on enough dates with the bachelor of your choice. There are also numerous bugs, such as one on Matthew's path that if you press the skip button it occasionally brings you back to the start menu, on loading a save. Another one is that if you have skip on, and you bake cupcakes it makes that faster but can be turned off if clicking in the general area as well. I've also had certain event flags not start when they're supposed to so there's a few kinks that need working out.
Music 6/10. The music in this game is fairly well done, but one thing that I personally believe is that the music cannot actually be turned down low enough without being fully mute. I'm thinking this will be fixed when they add voices and such to the game, but that's my only issue there.
Artwork 8/10 The art in this game is very beautiful. The only thing I would like to point out is that there are a few cutscene pictures that distort the character's faces in a way that it's not attractive, but overall it's really well done and the character design is really good.
My current viewpoints:
*All of the paths are EXTREMELY difficult. As in pedantic and overwhelmingly difficult. I have yet to unlock one perfect ending with any of the characters, despite following guides and doing everything in my power for this. This game needs a walkthrough more than a guide.  Matthew's path for example is a bit unclear as I'm not sure what you need to say to Nicole in order to make things work or what stats you need to focus, as even with maximum charisma, specialized cupcakes, dates and popularity I didn't get the complete ending. The game takes way too long to complete due to needing to re-input every single command into the schedule every day.
I think that a lot of the game could be made smoother/more user friendly just by making the email button flash red on recieving a new email, and having the option to choose what sian's main "ideas" are at the start of the game, such as wanting to start a blog for popularity or practice speaking for charisma. It'd also be a lot better to add more stress relief books to the stores, and to make it easier to access the arcade as raising your gpa for another date-spot, plus trying to balance stats is a bit pedantic and difficult. It's not a bad game, but this goes beyond challenging to a painful grind and a lot of work. I still haven't gotten one perfect ending, though i'm not sure if it is related to the game or something i'm doing wrong, and there are no full guides or walkthroughs that completely cover the exact things people need to do to get the endings.
I'd still reccommend this for the story, but until it's finished and some of the bugs are removed, it's not a full reccommendation from me.

Cobalt is a fast paced, shooter/platformer with a great variety of things in it; from disco dancing to cracking safes, from grenade punching to high speed time challenges, it has it all.
It's graphics are relatively simple tile-to-tile, but when tiles are added together, can create an elegant plethora of style.
The combat its self seems complex and hard at first, but once you get the hang of it, you will find it all flows naturally without much difficulty. You can bounce enemy's bullets off your head to either redirect the bullet away, or (if well timed) bounce it straight back to them, dealing damage or even killing them; you can also punch or shoot grenades, sending them away from you or again, back at your opponent. Another important fact is that it has a "bullet time" feature, where the time of the local area is slowed to allow more complicated maneuvers.
When it comes to single player, it features a complete campaign and challenges, with a scoreboard to compare yourself to other players.
The multiplayer is where this game truly shines though, you can team up in survival against wave after wave of enemies, or battle it out in one of the P.V.P. modes. It includes a deathmatch gametype,
a "team strike" in which you are put in teams, fight, and then spend points on a better loadout, first team to eleven rounds won wins,
and a "plug slam" which is what you get if you crossed football (soccer) rugby, or American football with their deathmatch gametype, their are two goals (one for each team) and a "plug" in the center, once you pick up the plug, you must throw it into the opposing teams goal, however, you cannot shoot when holding the plug, so you must avoid any confrontation with the other team that you can.
It also contains a bot feature, so if their are not enough players, AI can fill their place.
Any of these game types can also be played with just these bots and no other players if one so wishes to do so.
All in all, Cobalt is a game that you can, and will, spend many hours in, trying to shave the second off that one speed challenge you just can't seem to get under mountain hammer time, obtaining a higher score then your friends on one of the combat challenges, getting 100% on the campaign, or even just matches online.

I've been following this game since beta and holy ****. I'm proud of what it has become. It had potential back then and they surely used that potential.
Cobalt is a 2D Shooter-Platformer.
While those are fun by themselves, Cobalt overdid it and added a enormous amount of features to enhance that genre.
A few of these features are:
> The bullet-deflecting dodge-rolls, which also change the direction of the character as he rolls, allowing for incredible trick-shots or other fun things like using a high-powered weapon to roll and shoot the ground, launching you upwards or forwards, depending on where you are facing.
> Time-distorting "Reaction Enhancer" which automatically slows down time whenever an iminent threat is about to obliterate you. Sure, this may sound like something that would make a game way too easy... But that is not the case at all. The slow-mo surely allows you and others to decide what to do in life-or-death situations that would normally destroy you before one could even see what happened, but you are slowed too and often these situations are not evadeable.
> Semi-Open-world story mode. It's episodic, unlocking more areas as you progress in the history and "To the right" is usually the correct way to go. But there are always plenty of ways to go where you want, depending on what kind of character you are building for yourself. The worlds are also full of secrets to be found and the occasional side-quest that will give you rewards beyond money, like yet another way to approach the boss.
> Character and weapon customization is a very important thing is this. It allows you to choose if you'll be the kind of character that takes it in the face and laugh at their puny guns, the guy who snipes them from afar before they even see you, the ninja that causes the local guards to disappear misteriously even few seconds, etc. Weapons and equipment can also be upgraded to have bigger magazines, laser-sights, scopes, silencers, etc. For a 2D shooter, this is an impressive feat.
Multiplayer is also fantastic with friends, specially on lan-parties.
The bad? Maybe two things. The first one, which didn't bother me but can be a problem to some, is the learning-curve since Cobalt has odd button patterns for a first timer and can get confuzing, but once they are mastered, you'll get shot in the face less. The second is a minor problem, where if you TAB out of the game while in full-screen, it cuts the window and move it up, making it impossible to readjust without quitting the game and opening it again.
I would certainly give this game a 10/10.

Endless Legend is a game made by Amplitude Studios, the creators of the hit Endless Space. This game is centred around fantasy, or as the title of the game tells us, legends, you have cultists, dragon people, forest dwellers, nomads, and many others each with their own pros and cons. As someone who never really got into many turn-based games before (I love the Total War series, but mainly for the real-time battles), I was sceptical this would be a game I'd really enjoy, but I picked it up on sale after reading some great reviews for it. I wasn't disappointed however, and feel this game could be enjoyed by both veterans of other turn-based series and relative newbies to the genre like myself.
Firstly, it's a beautiful game. The landscapes you spread your civilisation out into are rendered with great craft; alluring 'anomalies', jagged cliffs of crystal, and sweeps of forest and desert wash across your screen. The symbols used by the game for various resources and actions are intuitive and clean. The interface prompts you gently if you have a city or army being unproductive, but leaves a lot for you to discover by yourself. (It is worth pointing out the introduction is a bit insufficient, not suggesting what might be useful strategies or techniques to get you started.) The designs of the various factions you can choose to play as are fantastic, wonderfully evocative and characterful.
These factions themselves are another major part of what makes the game so deep. Each faction (a variety of fantastical races that avoid fantasy clichés) not only has a unique playstyle (radically different in some cases, for example the Broken Lords ignore one of the central resources, food, so you have to fuel many of your empire's core processes with 'dust') but they each have a fleshed-out narrative that provides you with another victory condition - by completing a line of quests. There are RPG elements in heroes that your empire can recruit, whislt another layer is added in the 'Minor Factions' that your empire can assimilate by various means, another factor that means no 2 games will develop in the same way.
Overall one of the most fun games I've played in a while, one to get lost in!

It's tons of fun to be playing with friends, though the game may tend to drag on longer than expected sometimes, it's definitely not a dull game to be sitting through though, nor a dull game to be replaying over and over again. A great buy if you're into the previous endless game, and a strong addition to the library if you've never tried a 4x game, this game would be a treat!!

The bounce of walls mechanic is obscure to tell the least.

This game really has a lot going for it. It features some stunning yet cute graphics and some very addictive gameplay.
It sort of reminds me of Captain Keen meets Diablo, only with ragdoll physics, sick weapons and some great sound effects. One minute you're shooting easy dudes with your pistol, the next you're hammering away at a mini-boss with some crazy laser cannon. Then you're out of ammo and have to beat it with your suitcase. There is also some interesting customisation options with the mutation system. Basically you're turning into an ammo-grabbing juggernaut.
Oh, and did I mention. It's very VERY challenging. You start out in a short intro-level and you think "I got this." But wait, because you don't. Somehow even with the most high-powered weapons and body armour these mutants always get me. That's why I like to stun them one by one, just to feel like I'm pawning them for a change.
If you didn't already, you will definitely want to buy this must-have gem of a game. If this is early access I can't even imagine what the full release will be like. I didn't beat it yet, but I'm sure gonna keep trying!

Utopia 9 is a very fun 2d roguelite shooter. The shooting mechanics and controls are more like a game like Shadowgrounds than Binding of Isaac, the game I think most people think of when you say "roguelite 2d shooter".
You are a person who is going on vacation to Utopia 9. However you land to find that everyone on this paradise vacation planet has been infected with mutagenic pollen and you have to fight your way out. There are melee, projectile, energy and explosive weapons that you can pick up along the way. When you die, the enemy who killed you mutates, becomes stronger and also loots your corpse, so on your next run through you have the opportunity to exact revenge and get some of your equipment back.
As you kill enemies, you gather mutagenic pollen. Acquire enough pollen and you get a mutation, basically a level up where you get to pick an enhancement. Enemies dropping more ammo or "healing" liquor bottles and an automatic retaliation after you accumulate 10 points of damage are a few examples of mutations.
After you get to the end of each area you go to a map screen where you choose the next area to go to. The map screen contains information about the choices including weapon types available in the area and whether an npc who has killed you (called a "known murderer") is present.
Finally the devs are very active and responsive, committed to creating a game that players will enjoy. I posted a comment before I even bought the game and was responded to very quickly, with the developer going out of the way to add something to the game quickly based on my feedback. I am not saying that every request will be treated that way, just that the devs seem to be dilligent about responding to comments and eager to please even potential customers.
If you like 2d shooters and/or roguelite games this is yet another fine addition with its own unique take on the genre.
