Although the game is still in development I'd recommend supporting it. It's got a long road ahead of it. From what I played I'd be happy to see it through to the end.
Pros:
-Simplistic yet beautiful art style that does a good job of capturing the scale of things, especially when looking at scenery while zoomed out.
-The Gameplay is new and fresh, with a unique style and spin on tactics that makes you think on your toes and really makes having good tactics a necessary measure for success. I can't see myself being bored of it, kind of like Fire Emblem although very different in a lot of major ways.
-New mechanics are added quite frequently making each level more fresh and interesting especially when the stealth feature comes along.
-The soundtrack is amazing... A perfect blend of old and new, with undertones of pixely noises and an explosion of gushing fantasy adventure melodies that really speaks the game's nature without you even seeing it. The one track that really stands out is The Steppe which I might have to start listening to on a daily basis.
-Boss fights that are spectacular and really force you to use the mechanics of the game to your advantage.
Cons:
-The game of course, is still in development, I haven't encountered any game-breaking bugs but error messages do occasionally pop up on screen when dealing with a certain type of enemy. Which can get annoying.
-Again, it's in early access for a reason. I was able to complete it in two hours which is an incredibly short amount of time, but the game is not finished. There are only currently two sort-of chapters in the game, each ending with a boss fight. And while I enjoyed my time with it, I find myself only wishing there was more I could play.
-The story... This one is a bit in the middle I would say. At the beginning the story is a bit run-of-the-mill not really anything to get too excited over or really be invested in. But I can clearly see it picking up later on as at the end of the second boss fight I did find myself wanting to know what was going to happen.
Conclusion:
All and all, I'd urge you to put your money into this and support it. It's going somewhere, even though it was released two years ago it clearly has places that need to be visited and ideas that need exploring. I see myself coming back to this game each time they announce that something new is being added. I'm very saddened to see such an amazing work fall under the radar, this game really needs a spotlight, it's clearly something more than the usual thousands of games that get released each month. I want Flamberge to succeed and I think you should too.

A recommendation but through gritted teeth. Only If is a surreal and intriguing game, which given that it's free, can excuse some (but not all) of its flaws. Curmudgeonly and awkward to interact with, but also enjoyable and entertaining. Frustrating and irritating, not through cryptic puzzles or intense gameplay, but through glitchy game mechanics and chance. Derpy controls (with no way to adjust settings like mouse sensitivity, graphics, and button mappings), but nevertheless an interesting story/adventure given enough patience. Avoid like the plague if you don't like mystery and do like smooth gameplay.
Where Only If fails. A major game-stopping bug (in the “black pawn” path); poor menu selection; painfully awkward button-mashing; a few moments of poor diction from the voice acting (at crucial elements in game); and too much live-die-repeat. Unfortunately, these flaws seriously detract from a game that actually manages to achieve something a bit different.
Where Only If succeeds is in producing something that is a novel first attempt at game-making, that shows promise from Creability for the future. It's free. It's short. It's interesting. It's got foul language. And it has a great soundtrack from Steven O'Brien.

One more year, the same addiction.  I am one of the fans that buys the game each year no matter what. FM2017 continues to bring the best of what a football simulator can offer. A brilliant game.
It's always hard recommend the new editions of Football Manager to a beginner player. Why? Simple. The price is too high and in some editions the changes are minimal, for me are always important, but are minimal, and for some players don't justify the price.
The gameplay is always the "same", you control a team, you implement your game model, yours tactics and good luck, leads her to glory, or die trying.
The game is closest to be perfect. To me is perfect. Sometimes you can noticed some bugs like the stamina of players, some injuries, but are always minimal aspects. There is nothing really big that can influence badly your game.
As powerful features this year in my vision, in this FM, before and after each game you receive a report from your analyst in which you can find every information about the opponent. Despite in the editions before you could only have a report about the next opponent, but not one after the match. Now, in FM17 your analyst will compile a summary of the match after it's finished and you can see what went good/wrong. This saves you time of analysing each stat after a game.
Other new features: new e-dashboard, vanishing spray, entrance scene, pre-match scene, beautiful skies, social feeds, running smooth, best interface, better manager character 3D than FM2016.
To the beginners, when you start, you have a chance to choose if you are more like a manager of tracksuit, or a manager of apparel and tie. The difference is that the first is more directed to characteristics of a physical trainer, and the second is more directed to a characteristics that a human resources manager have or needs to had. Personally, I choose always the minimal license possible as manager. I love see the characteristics grow up as my career progresses, and I am a fan of a long save term too. Take attention, the license you choose will influence your "save" - if you choose a high license, the players will respect you more, the tactics will be assimilated faster, basically you will have a game easier; in other hand, a lowest license it will be harder, and sometimes will give you a lot of frustration. To me, the manager license is the key point of
.
Be careful in the beginnig of a "save", don't ignore your technical team and their weakness or just lackness of members. The staff is the success of a team. Inside your finances try pick the best people possible to guide your team. Scouts, physiotherapists, (physical) trainers, etc. The scouts are too important to give to you reports from potential players, the physiotherapists are important to care your team and possible injuries, the physical trainers are important to assimilate the tactics and work the offensive or defensive part of your team. Basically, all people are crucial. Don't just choose good players and put a tactic of fashion, FM is a lot more than this.
Graphically, the game is very fancy. Since the beginning of the game, graphics are being a lot improved. But, at least to me, FM isn't about graphics. FM have a massive database of players, technical team, the game have a depth knowledge of all leagues in world what is so impressive. Searching for the best scout or physiotherapist to my technical team is sometimes a real challenge, even more when finances of the team are very limited. Searching the best striker, the great regens or newgens, a lot of hours that I spend all years on this details, and I love it! It's no coincidence that the database of FM is used to recruit players by some clubs of Premier League. FM is an incredibly good game, is a pure management game and can't be called just a football simulator, no way.

This is one of those hidden gems on Steam, that is being buried under an avalanche of asset-flip crap and other low quality games.
I like tactical games, and Steam Tactics did not disappoint me. The basic gameplay is rather simple: different guns have different attack patterns and damage types, you choose an optimal loadout for your ships, and the combat is basically about positioning: place your ships so you can deal maximum damage while avoiding or minimizing damage from counterattacks. This makes for a surprisingly deep and engaging gameplay.
-Solid gameplay mechanics. Simple, yet clever and satisfying
-Does not mentally overburden you. You have to think to win, but you can play in a pretty relaxed manner and don't have to calculate a ton of numbers for every turn and action you perform
-Likeable characters
-Visuals are nice. There is nothing really special about graphics here, but overall Steam Tactics looks very nice, and character art is very good
-I liked the music, it is catchy and fits in the game pretty well
-Steampunk! Why are there so few games in that setting?
-The ending was not very spectacular, so I felt kinda disappointed
-Music can get repetetive if you play long enough
-$12 feels a bit overpriced? Though considering that you can spend quite a lot of time getting all achievements, that may not actually be the case
-The AI is not very consistent. Most of the time it plays pretty well, but sometimes enemy ships can get stuck or perform some obviously dumb actions
Overall the game is very enjoyable, so get it, especially if you see it on sale.

It's a honest game. Not really hard when you understand how to play but can be a bit grindy by moment.
The story is doable in 15 hours ( but I grinded a bit so it can be finished earlier ) and I still got a bunch of 2 and 3 stars levels to do to max everything, I suppose I would need less than 25 hours to completly finish it. Kind of honest for a 12 $ game and I think I could replay it later.
Battles takes place on a 8x6 grid, with random unpassable tiles and some bonus/malus tiles ( more/less damages or resistances ). Regularly a repair kit or a chest of gold can appear on the field.
Each ship has 6 different resistances to damages to counter the 6 different kind of weapon. All the weapons come with various range and fire direction ( either in line or in diagonal ). Flamers and acid-sprayers got the lowest range, missiles got the longest. There is no AOE or multi-hitting mechanics in this game. Each time you attack a ship it can counter-attack IF you are in range of one of his weapon and the same rule apply to your own counter-attacks.
Ships also have different " equip load ". This value represent how heavy your combined weapons load is and affect how many tiles your ship can travel per turn. The max is 4 and the min is 1. But the various weapons got different weight ( flamers and sprayers being the lighter ones and missiles/canons the heaviers ) which combined to the right ships allow you to use up to 3 weapons while still being able to move enough. It's possible to mix weapons ( using a flamers with a machine gun and a missile launcher ) but weapons damage and critical rate are affected by the pilote skills, so it's best to specialize the pilots and focus on 1 or 2 type of weapons only.
Overall some weapons works better than others. Missiles and canons feels a bit useless ( at least in the story part ) because the battlegrounds are only 8X6 with some clutter. So long ranged weapons aren't that good because it's too easy to get boxed and cornered by ships with short range weapons without being able to fire back. I will also add the fact that a lots of ennemy ships have huge resistance to canon attacks overall. Flamers and sprayers are way better choices BUT all levels always feature highly ( mostly immune ) resistant to one of these attack ships so you still need to mix and match the others weapons to win.
So yeah the battle feels balançed enough but the base tactic is always the same to win : Focus all your fire on one ennemy, destroy it then focus on another. So it make the game repetitive, bigger maps with more varied ships per battle would be better.

Solid, reliable, little turn based strategy game about anthropomorphic animals piloting steampunk planes against meaner animals. Very light in most respects, it's really just about the quick missions and surprisingly deep weapon type vs. resistance and upgrading systems.
The art is beautiful and static. The writing is brisk and jaunty but not impactful enough to have any weight. Who cares - it's not that kind of game; no dialogue options or branching. Mission, upgrade, mission, etc.
Combat takes place on cramped grids of squares. There's both not a lot to do (move or fire) but a lot to consider. It almost feels puzzly (because of the unique firing mechanism) but it's chaotic and unscripted enough to not be a problem.
Bonus points given for the flawless combat interface. Things couldn't be clearer. Slight deductions for the fiddly inventory system which is a shame because loadout optimizing is fun and I would have done more if it wasn't so clicky. Completely stable and silky smooth at 3440.
It took around 10 hours to finish the campaign. There's more available if you like getting perfect missions - I still had some room to progress with my weapons, ships and characters. Super polished, especially for a tiny team indie. Nice job. I'd totally play a multiplayer version of this.

I don't like leaving negative reviews, but this time, I have to.
I bought this game when it was still in Early Access because I really liked the concept of playing TheHunter with dinos. I stopped playing because the game was full of bugs and really boring. I've tried to play it again a few days ago, and it still is, even if they added new dinos and got rid of annoying things.
They tried to make something between a hunting game and a survival game. I would have loved this. Problem is : It's neither.
It's not a hunting game, because you have to spend a lot of time gathering ♥♥♥♥♥ons of weapons and ammo before being able to kill anything, especially if you have to track a wounded " Big " dino ( Triceratops or T-Rex ), because you'll probably be attacked while doing so and you have to be able to defend yourself.
It's not a survival game because it has nothing of a survival except the " Everything will try to kill you " concept. You can't build a base, you can't craft items, you don't have to eat/drink/sleep...
So, you just walk around for hours and hours, try to gather weapons and enough ammo and hope not to see a single dino before you have enough things to be able to defend yourself. It can take a lot of time, because weapons and ammo spawn randomly in boxes far from each other, and your character is f*cking slow ( Plus you can't really run because you don't want to alert dinos anyway ).
This game has potential, but at this moment, it's just boring...

I bought this game shortly after its release (It was discounted a bit, I think about 10% or so?). I had already watched the anime, so I knew a few things about the characters beforehand. I love how all of them are more than what you see at first glance, there's always another layer hidden underneath what you see immediately.
There's Shin, your kinda tsundere childhood friend,
Ikki, the flirty guy who seems to change girlfriends more often than he does his clothes.
Kent, a guy who studies math and seems almost emotionless.
Toma, your other childhood friend who's been almost like your older brother (Which he even calls himself in other routes).
And after finishing all others, you get access to Ukyo's route.
Every boy has several endings. One good, one normal and several bad, depending on your relationship with him (Although some choices get you immediate Bad Ends), so you have more than enough reason to play the game again and again, trying out the other choices. Since you can save at any time, there's nothing stopping you from especially trying out the ones you immediately know are bad.

This game is more than you can expect.
At first you may think this game is a classic MOBA, with the heavy farming, do's and don'ts and stuff, but with a side scrolling style. It isn't.
This game may sound simple, but you have action from the first second. You can have fast games under 10 minutes, or really hard and comeback games with 30+ minutes. You have different maps, with different layouts and different objectives. There's no meta like all the other MOBAs, and you win games where you can make a great team fight with the 3 members over and over again, or win games with a great sinergy on defense between 2 nauts alone, where the other is split pushing like crazy, or simply 1 naut defending, and the other 2 pushing their lanes, there's tons of ways to win.
But still, you have to think: when to attack, when to defend, when to get that healing orb, or when to farm that wave bot/top. And still, you can make some good coomps that will make you win on early/mid/late game for sure. It's a fastpaced action with tons of details you can't forget, and it's perfect.
Plus, it gives you this old school feeling with the 2D, it makes you laugh with the references, and the music stucks into your head (Leon's Music and Ayla's. Gosh, they are top class for me).
Best purchase so far. I'm going to get the expansion for sure.

Alex Hunter - Lord of the Mind is a Hidden Object/Adventure game with above average graphics, and voice acting for the genre. You play Alex Hunter, a private investigator tasked with locating a missing uncle who happens to a scientist and as you investigate, you uncover a deeper plot involving mind control and world domination.
The game is is longer than most HOGs and has a lengthy bonus chapter that surprisingly, I enjoyed more than the main storyline.
The only places the game falls down is that some of the HO scenes contain more than one object with the same name as the object you are being asked to find and only one is acceptable, and/or it asks you to find an object that describes multiple objects in the scene, i.e. find a "plane" ... is it the toy plane hanging from the ceiling, no, it's the wood workers "plane" tool over in the corner. Frustrating.
The other area where the game falls down is it takes an old school approach to problem solving that other modern HOGs have moved away from. An example would be where you have to get past a guard. You are behind him with a crowbar in your inventory, but you have to go to the kitchen, find a note where he has ordered coffee with milk, then you have to find a coffee maker, coffee, milk, light the stove, fix the dumb waiter, only to be told you need water, and even though you are in a kitchen, you have to find a bicycle horn, frighten a bird into dropping something into the long grass, find petrol for a lawn mower, mow the grass, find the object, use it to fix the fountain, complete a puzzle, collect the water, boil the coffee, add the milk, find sleeping pills, add them to the coffee, and finally, send to coffee to the guard. Each of the actions above may have required multiple steps to complete. It's a convoluted approach that thankfully most modern HOGs have moved away from.
Other than that, the puzzles ranged from easy to difficult, and the story, although nothing special, did enough to keep me interested. The game features fast travel and indications on the map where actions need to be completed, which was helpful. Overall, it's an above average HOG that's worth checking out if you are a fan of the genre.

First let me say that FM17 is my first FM game. I'm a Yank who fell in love with football during the 1994 WC in the U.S. and have been a big fan of international football first, but more and more I'm an EPL fan, especially since NBC now let's us see ALL EPL games. Anyway, I'd never really given FM any thought in the past because quite honestly, I was a bit intimidated by the depth of the game. However, I decided to give the FM16 demo a spin a month or so ago and then bought FM17 during beta release and I....CAN'T....QUIT.....PLAYING! While I'm still getting my head handed to me for the most part (although believe it or not, I did win the Champions League with Tottenham in one of my first seasons), especially trying to win with Swansea (yeah, I'm a Bradley fan), I have learned SO much about the game (both real football and this game) from lurking in the forums and reading user-created guides that have been stickied.
Anyway, from what I can tell, the bad reviews are basically in one of three camps: 1. I'm Chinese and don't like the fact it isn't ported to Chinese 2. It is too much like previous versions 3. I can't win because of bugs or I'm just bad and won't admit it. While I can't speak about item 1, what is wrong with a game that is similar to the game you love with just a few more features on an annual basis? I've played over 100 hours and put down $50 and am just getting started. If I quit tomorrow and enjoyed myself, $2/hour is pretty cheap entertainment. Jeez guys, developers have to eat too so throw them a bone once a year if you like the game even if it doesn't contain earthshaking changes. As for item 3, I love the fact that I'm getting my butt kicked most of the time. In this day and age, everyone wants to win, but no one wants to put the time in that it takes to be good at something. After doing hours of reading in the forum tips/guides section, I'm actually starting to improve quite a bit and hope to someday coach Swansea into the top 4 and while I don't know if that will ever happen, I'm sure enjoying trying!
If I was going to give a game bad reviews on steam, it would be due to stability issues, lack of replayability or just poor gameplay so it just boggles my mind that the major of reviews (about 66%) are negative? I'd like to give the developers a big thanks and tell them to keep up the good work because you've won a fan for life! If you are the analytical type who really wants to get a feel for what it must be like to be a real, football manager and are willing to put some time in to study up, this game is for you.

*** THIS GAME IS CURRENTLY VERY SHORT!  VERY, VERY, *VERY* SHORT! ***
Let's just get that out of the way.  Shortness aside, the tactical combat system is absolutely fantastic, and I don't think I ran into ANY bugs for the SHORT *ahem* time it took me to finish the current campaign, which is a rarity among early access games, so that's good.
FOR THOSE LOOKING TO BUY THE GAME: Expect to see something with a ton of potential, but something that has not reached 90% of that potential (as of when I wrote this).  The entirety of the game currently consists of a very short campaign (less than 10 levels, I think), and four class preview showcases (each is a single pre-made encounter with no story; for testing unit types).  THERE IS NOT CURRENTLY MULTIPLAYER...or if there is, it's very very well hidden.
MY REASON FOR A POSITIVE REVIEW: Even though the game is not in what I would call "active" development, the combat system is fantastic and unique.  Maybe it's just a fluke, but I haven't played even one other game with this type of battle system, and it's very well done.  The closest I've come to something like this is probably Growlanser Generations in one direction and Fire Emblem in the other...but IMO this game's combat system is more interesting than either of those at its core.  It just needs more added to it.
FOR THE DEVS: The game is absolutely fantastic so far.  I hope someday you manage to get a full campaign and a custom battle + level editor in there.  IMO, this game would shine brightest in squad-based pvp.  You may be avoiding a lot of publicity since you're busy and not actively developing, and don't want to disappoint people who expect the game to be done within a year, but if you decide you want more people to notice your game, consider showing it at conventions and events.  If I were judging it as a up-and-coming indie title (and to be fair, didn't know it had already been on the market for years), it would probably be my top pick.  I guess mostly something to keep in mind if at some point in the future you decide "ok, now we're going to start developing way more often", or after the game slowly reaches a point where it can be considered a "full game" even if you still plan to add to it.

One of my fondest games when I was younger was Dungeon Siege II. It was an amazing game; a seemingly wide-open world, amazing levels of customization, and tough, too.
This game is a console port. The inventory system is optimized for console controllers (ie no grid system any more), the controls are built for a controller (ie to my knowledge, there's no strafe functionality, so if you want to strafe, you've got to use your mouse and stop attacking), and the skill system is simplistic enough for console controllers (ie no depth).
The game quickly deviates from the Dungeon Siege format. Instead of being able to build a character that does what YOU want with the ability to mix and match abilities, you get to pick from four pre-made characters. If something doesn't fit your fancy, well you can go screw yourself. What do you think this is, Dungeon Siege? ... Wait... Combat is MUCH more focused on positioning and fast-paced movement, where in earlier games movement was much more tactical and positioning was a little less relevant. The skill system is bland and uninteresting, not really letting you build characters like you could before. Oh, and your character can only use three skills at a time. Two stance abilities and a guard one.
Speaking of the stances... The game has what I can only describe as a stance system. You hit "q" to switch between two stances per character. One of the characters switches between double pistols and... a rile? shotgun? It's been a while since I've played her. Another switches between using a staff and spitting out fireballs. There's no customizing that, either. Each stance has one ability tied to it, and you have to be in that stance to use that ability. The ability use button (1) is right above the stance change button (q), so I often found myself switching stances instad of using the ability I wanted to.
One last thing that I want to harp on: the bounding boxes for terrain do not match up with their visuals half the time. I often found myself trying to walk into completely open spaces only to find myself unable to, because the stairs that were four feet away really had a bounding box there, or the cliff that was behind me was wrapping around in from of me somehow, or I was anywhere near rocks. For a game that relies so much on quick movement, you want to go NOWHERE near the rocks. They're devious traps set by the enemies to trap you and leave you helpless.
Essentially, this game is not a DS game. It's a bad attempt at a third party of cashing in on the name brand, and a sloppy game even on its own. Stay away.

This game, ah, this game! It's not a bad game.
Dungeon Siege 3 is not like its predecessors. Overburdened with strange, clunky PC controls and a horrible interface, despite its shortcomings, DS3 is a really competent Action RPG that deviates from the mold of its two older siblings and does its own thing to its own fault, since it disappointed a lot of people by not being... well, too much like a Dungeon Siege game.
But isn't it? I believe it actually is. There's loot drops, there's plenty of places to go (though most of them consist of narrower hallways, something it got from Dungeon Siege 2), and its combat system, while strange and quirky, is fun and cathartic.
No, you can't customize your character as you could before, but the characters you can choose from are classic archetypes of the characters we used to use in previous games anyway, so I don't know what the issue is. You always just stuck with a single specialization anyway or your character would not have turned out very good...
Anyways, this game suffered a mixed reception because it carried the name Dungeon Siege, and it wasn't the same Dungeon Siege game that people remembered and thought this game would be. Instead, it is a relatively competent action RPG with clunky controls... but still, I think it's worthy of praise for what it has done - not worthy of scorn for what it could have been.

Not surprising, Oik 2 is similiar to Oik.  You remove blocks and planks to get your blue block on the home plank.  There are two differences other than the puzzles themselves between the two games.  There is the addition of balls, which I enjoyed.  The other difference I didn't enjoy.  Puzzles seemed to be the somewhat random in the movement of these new balls and maybe in all puzzles in general.
For the most part I was able to easily get through the puzzles with ease.  I got stuck a few times and what I found was doing the exact same thing on each reset would yield different results.  I would remove one block only triggering a plank to become inclined and start the ball rolling.  Where that ball ended up changed.  I didn't like that aspect of it, if it was intended or not.  One puzzle really had me getting frustrated because of this.  You had no idea if you were doing it right and just needed to keep repeating the pattern until you got the desired result or if you were wrong and had to try something else for 30 times until you got the desired result.  I went to the guides for help.  What I found was everyone seemed to do it differently.  Watching a playthrough showed someone else struggling to get it to work too.  I did his winninng combination and it took me 17 resets going through the same pattern to finish it and it finished in a different way.
Having said that, the vast majority of the puzzles were very easy and were relaxing and fun to do.  I still finished the game rather quickly.  Like Oik, there is no windowed mode which I would have favored.  The music was nice and I will replay it again at a later date for the fun aspects of it.
If you're considering only getting either Oik or Oik 2, then I'd go with the first because of that randomness frustration.  But I'd recommend both to anyone who likes those little puzzles.  Like, Oik, the achievements come with each level finish and when you finish them all you've completed your achievements.  No hidden random weird achievement to get.  There are guides and walkthroughs if you do get stuck.

A typical HOG that has all the things you’d expect: Short story/plot, hidden object scenes, inventory management and puzzles.
The graphics & artwork are well done. Hidden object scenes were crisp along with the actual environment. Music is repetitive but blended into the background so you don’t really notice much.
Inventory management was good and I really like how you can easily scroll horizontally through your items automatically by just moving the cursor left or right. No clicking left or right arrows, etc. One thing that was missing was a lock to keep the inventory bar up at all times. Most HOG’s have that feature, but the ability to quickly bring up the inventory bar made up for it.
The puzzles were generally ok. I would say most of them are intermediate difficulty and some will take a bit of thinking. A small handful seemed fairly illogical. One in particular (the one with the clocks) didn’t seem to have any logic and was a guessing game. That was the only puzzle I had to use the built-in walkthrough for.

+The puzzle description doesn’t show up automatically. You have to click “description” first.
+The description box disappears too fast and should be on a toggle instead of a time.

I wanted to like this game, but couldn't.  The graphics are fine if a bit dated.  Cutscenes are often wasted - I don't need a cutscene of crossing a river, and then crossing part of a lake.  I have no idea what the story was about.  Something to do with a villain and a mind...machine?  The point-and-click parts of the game were generally not that bad for the genre.  But, in some cases I found myself with 4 (or 5?) areas requiring keys and no keys.  So each key I turned up after that was a guessing game about what it unlocked.  HOP areas were generally ok, but as others have said you have to revisit them a second time usually not having anything to do with where you are and were you are going.  So it comes across as randomly revisiting areas to do another HOPA scene.  Some of the HOP scenes are plagued with multiple items which could satisfy the list.  And on your second visit the items you removed the first time are mysteriously back again.
Then there are the puzzles.  They were generally more difficult than your average HOPA.  Often the rules of the puzzle weren't in the instructions or the underlying logic (if there was any) was difficult to decipher.  One puzzle (I think it was in the bonus chapter) seemed to have incorrect instructions.  The instructions said to arrange things in columns.  Intuitively you'd think to arrange them in rows.  But the instructions said columns, so that's what I did.  When my solution didn't work I just skipped the puzzle since my solution satisfied the instructions.  I actually skipped quite a few puzzles after struggling with them for too long and not getting anywhere.  There's little fun, or challenge, in brute forcing a solution but that seemed to be the main approach to many of them.
If you want a casual HOPA game, look elsewhere.  If you want a game with more challenging puzzles and don't care about the story too much, then you might like this one.

ARK: Survival Of The Fittest is a very fun spin off game of the new early access game Ark:Survival Evolved. It is based off the hunger games and with dinosaurs. I normally dont do reviews but im going to make an exception with this game. I like to think I have a somewhat unique perspective for the Early Access system as a programmer myself who develops apps for various companies. As this is an early access I tend to compare it to Alphas that I write and test. As for that it is a very well polished game. This does however have some problems along with it. Because it is an alpha there are missing features. For instance the only map is not really suited for the small 30 min for ffa. its too large and most of the map is just cut off. There are also bugs through the game. I have crashed a few times when I have a high end pc. As for optimization it is far better than the main game. I run around 60 fps while on the main game I could keep around 30 fps. There are a few problems with the ranking system as well but it is improving quickly. I do not recamend the game if you have a mid-low pc, as this being an early access it could cause you issues. There is also the problem that the free to play model brings, there are many rude 12 year olds in the game. I would like to see a mute button implemented some time in the future. There are many areas where the game can improve and many balance issues but compared to the old mod this is based on, this is a far greater improvement.... and plus its free so who can complain about that?

Let's flash forward a bit now. The game was released fully with like three to four more primary additions from early access. That' it. OVERVIEW:
This game has been a pleasant surprise even in its current Early Access incarnation. To me, it plays like a more open (and less tedious) version of Fire Emblem. The mechanics are simple and the difficulty is ramped up in a really intuitive way that slowly offers the player new ways to see situations and learn the mechanics.
GAMEPLAY:
As said by others, the strategy plays out a lot like futbol plays where both the player and the enemy are positioning characters and using the proper skill (parry/disarm/attack/dodge/etc.) that will put the player in a stronger position for the next turn.
You start getting accustomed to about how far parries and dodges will put the enemy and you start stacking plays to do some real strategical damage. When your plays work out you just feel so boss!
ART/MUSIC:
The game is beautiful in both art and sound and you'll find yourself zoning out to the ambient piano tracks.
VERDICT:
Overall a really solid game even in Early Access. Can't wait to see how it grows.

There aren't really that many games in the  turn-based, tactical rpg genre(tactical rpg for short, or "simulation rpg" in Japan), and even fewer that do it right imo. And that's a shame, since tactical rpgs are among my favorite types of games. Now  here comes Flamberge walking in, adding another adjective to an already long genre name, claiming to be a "simultaneous turn-based tactics RPG," which sounds like it must be oxymoronic. But oxymoron or not, Flamberge's combat works, and it works well. It's a fun and fairly unique combat system, and I'm happy to add Flamberge to my "Turnbased tactics rpg" shelf.
There's a demo on the developer website if you want to try the game out first.
However, as of right now, there isn't all that much content. The story isn't there, there's no customization and you'll probably finish all the single player missions in under an hour. That will all change of course, it's an early access game after all, but as of the date of this review, the single player component might not last you long, so if you're on a tight gaming budget, you might consider waiting a while before getting this one. You'll probably get a good bit of mileage if you play muliplayer though.
So, anyway, I think Flamberge is a very promising title, I look forward to it's future, and I trust the developer will deliver.

Flamberge, A challenging turn based strategy delight.
So In my first 30 minutes with 'Flamberge' I have to say it was so awesome. The pixel art is well done and the music is spot on.
However, what makes this game shine imo is the blend of tactical turn based combat and strategy.
Both you and the enemies turns are taken at the same time. You must strategically move your party around the battlefield and try to set up "plays" and dodge, parry, shield smash, charge, face stab(I'm assuming, I mean where else would you stab the guy?) your opponent.
This makes for such a different turn based strategy experience. Each turn you're looking at what the enemy can do, which abilities are on cool down and whether or not they're out thinking your dash to the right or your retreat.
I haven't tried multiplayer yet, but I can only imagine playing against a human counter-part would be incredibly challenging.
This is a game you have to support, if not for you then do it for me so I can get more content.

This was an excellent game. Were there routes that I didn't enjoy very much, sure. But this didn't take away from my over all enjoyment of the game itself. There were times that I found myself frustrated with the heroine and my lack of ability to answer the way I felt I would (there we a good few "Oh hell no's" that I would have liked to slap down now and then but couldn't). But an otome game cannot reasonably encompass any and all possible reactions that a person would have to a situation and still tell a cohesive story. On that note the story here is, in my opinion, a good one. It is also a rather expansive amount of content for the price. While a good deal of my hours logged were spent leaving the game on while I did other things, I still spent several hours playing through this game and getting each end.
There's also a bit of a culture gap for this game. It's not severe (and by no means a reason to over look the game) but it's definitely there. This occationally frustrated me as well, the way the males act with the heroine at times and the meek way that she reacts probably stems from a culture thing more then her being a "weak character" as some are prone to describe. I try to remind myself when playing games that originate somewhere so different that in certain cultures it is seen as attractive or appropriete for a man to tell a woman she shouldn't let other men look at her, or to grab her and roughly drag her away and then yell. This is seen as being "manly" and "protective", it is considered a good trait in a partner. Though I may strongly disagree with that conclusion, my culture is different.
TLDR: It's a really good game and if you like otome games you should play it. I mean grab it on sale if you're hesitant but grab it. It's worth it.

“A dark adventure about a boy with a prosthetic face and a mysterious past.” That is Steam’s synopsis for Sally Face by developer Steve Gabry, a new 2D side-scrolling episodic game, and much like the game’s first episode itself, it leaves you with more questions than answers. To say that the game is bizarre would be an understatement. The titular Sally Face, or Sal, wears his blue hair in pigtails and wears a prosthetic face mask for an unknown reason. The apartment building he and his father have just moved into may or may not be haunted. One of the neighbors is obsessed with a toy line (one that is clearly intended to represent a certain franchise targeted toward young girls but is infamously successful with men). Its music doesn’t sound “bad,” but it supports the overall tone in that everything feels…off. The art style is unique – very cartoony in a slightly grotesque way. (It makes me think of the YouTube series “Salad Fingers.”) Nearly everything about this game is designed to make you uncomfortable.

Brickochet is pretty challenging. It takes a good amount of skill/experience as well as some luck to be able to get through all 50 levels in one go. In a way, it has a strategic element depending where you initially direct your first few ball bounces -- can make an impact if you lose a life in some levels. I recommend experiencing every level at least once, likely through level select, just so you can be mentally prepared for some of the more tougher levels.
While the game is quite tough at some points, it also can be rather relaxing watching the ball hit bricks, blowing up stuff, and grabbing some pretty neat power-ups. The gameplay is solid, especially the accuracy of the various angles the ball can hit off the paddle. I’ve played a few other brick breaker games over the years, and I’ve yet to experience such high precision until now.
The only place I’d say is a minor downside is the music. For the most part the music fits with the “brick breaking theme,” but I find some tracks fall short and can get a tad annoying. But the music can be changed with the push of a button, or be turned off entirely.
In the end, this game is highly enjoyable and has a pretty good amount of replayability. For $2.99, you can’t go wrong with this one.

Ok HOG. Decent but forgetable storyline. Good if you like these types of games.

You are a private detective (of course) in turn of the century England, contracted to find a missing scientist. You explore his home / laboratory, follow the trail through the London sewers, break into an insane asylum, confront the mad asylum director on top of a lighthouse, get blasted with his mind control ray and sent into an illusory dimension / state of consciousness, then
, triggering the most epic confrontation / Tommy Wiseau-esque underacted temper tantrum ever.
That’s a downright coherent plot by HOG standards, that could work just as well for a proper adventure game. Actually, the coherence works against it. You spend the entire game in gloomy night-time London – gloomy laboratory, dark sewers, totally not creepy insane asylum (seriously, they don’t even try to do anything interesting with it)… compared to House of 1000 Doors 2, where you jump through portals into colorful Tibet or India at a moment’s notice, it’s kinda samey.
The plot’s relative coherence also makes you note the genre conventions, and strains your suspension of disbelief. I’ve spent a full chapter of House of 1000 Doors brewing rose-tea for a ghost, and I was fine with that because the game was just a collection of random scenes. Spending half a chapter in Alex Hunter trying to brew a cup of coffee is a bit more annoying.
When Kate (the protagonist of House) finds a portal to a spooky ghost train in the closet of a child’s bedroom, she just shrugs and jumps in, because there’s a pinecone to be retrieved aboard that train. When Alex finds a working robot in a professor’s basement (!) he just shrugs and gets to work trying to retrieve the gear the robot is clutching – which is the full extent of our interaction with a freaking steampunk robot. (In related news, I really want to see an HOG protagonist actually phased by all the weird♥♥♥♥♥♥they keep encountering)
The game feels a lot less polished than House in all kinds of relatively objective ways:
The “description” part of each puzzle (aka “what the hell am I trying to do here”) isn’t on screen by default, but rather briefly summoned by clicking the “description” button. Every time someone talks to you, you have to listen to or skip the whole spiel, as you cannot skip individual lines. When you try to use the wrong object to solve a puzzle, you get an obtuse “this doesn’t work here” message instead of a hint restating what kind of object you DO need. Entering certain rooms plays a 5 second animation every single time. The characters are 3d models rather than semi-static sprites, which means they have more freedom to move around and do stuff, but also means they are hella ugly. I cannot stop staring at the Inspector’s weird neck folds.
I actually prefer it when each puzzle gives you an item that allows you to overcome an arbitrary obstacle and move on to the next puzzle ad infinitum. When you get reusable items, you really do get something like adventure-game-lite. For a brief period, I was playing Alex Hunter: Guy with crowbar. (As Richard Cobbett aptly noted, about 60% of obstacles faced by the common adventurer could be easily solved with a quick trip to the hardware store).
There were some improvements compared to House though – besides the semi-reasonable storyline (arguable as to whether that’s an actual improvement, see above) there were little things like making sure the “exit this screen” button does not overlap with the things you have to click to solve the puzzle. Which helped a great deal, since the puzzle controls were kinda draggy in general. My mouse being on the brink of death probably didn’t help though. Also, random interactable objects that don't solve puzzles but do liven up random screens. Neat.
In conclusion – meh. Are you seriously playing an HOG for the story? Just get a proper adventure game instead.
Edit - oh yeah. The puzzles are harder than in the House series, and if you skip a puzzle you don't get to see how it's solved, which is kinda spiteful.

I'm finding more and more often that the best games to play are games that throw you into a situation, and then let you try to make your own way out of it. Only If takes that principle and multiplies on it tenfold. I want to review this game like how I normally review games, but with games like this, I simply can't. So I'll break it down. NO spoilers will be found ahead.
You start off the game with a small first-person cinematic. You're entering a house where there is a racous party happening. How the party was is anyone's guess, because the game starts immediately after. From there on out, this masterpiece unfolds into a crazy (and what i expect) drug inspired journey.
The voice acting is absolutely incredible, although difficult to discern at times. The best part of this game was the atmosphere, and the short length of the game only adds to it's brilliance. It doesn't overstay it's welcome, and it constantly keeps you progressing simply because you WANT to know what the hell is going on.
Apart from that, it's difficult to say too much without giving an awful lot away. It's a tough call to just say, "It's a puzzle game with good atmosphere." and leave it at that, because it's just not that simple. Parts of the game had me literally scratching my head, while other parts had me pounding it against a wall. It's not the the puzzles are difficult; they're not. At times the game seems to be antagonizing you (which ends up being pretty fitting), while at other points, it seems to be deliberately asinine.
Is it worth it? Currently the game is FTP, although with it's length and very limited replayability, I'd say that's what the game should stay. The graphics and visuals are perfect for the game, the voice acting is unbelievably good (on par with games like The Fall and The Walking Dead) and though there are few controls, it makes good use of what it has.
As for the storyline... I've just beaten the game, and I'm incredibly confused. I plan to go look up what the hell just happened as soon as I finish this review, so I can't say that the whole story is clear. There's a moment where a character remarks about giving you anxiety, and if that's what this game seeks to do, it does it with flourish right up until the end.
I genuinely don't know what else to say about it. It's good. Try it. It's short enough to be sat through in under an hour, and rewarding enough (if not confusing) to keep you wanting more. I look forward to future releases by this studio.

Sally Face Episode 1 is an impressive first installment in what I hope to be a long series.
Strange Neighbors introduces us to Sally Face, a fearless kid with a prosthetic mask, rad blue pig-tails, and a dark and mysterious past. His story slowly begins to unravel as you explore your new apartment and meet your peculiar neighbors. You soon learn of a murder in the building and with your new heavy metal loving friend, Larry, you decide to investigate. Who is the murderer? Is the building haunted? What happened in Sal's past and why is he shown incarcerated and being aided by a psychiatrist in the future?
The game not only has an intriguing storyline but is also fueled by a great soundtrack and sharp artistic style. I love the throwback art and animation combined with its dark sense of humor.
Players should be sure to unlock all achievements as they really open up the storyline (get the batteries for the game system and find the game).
In all, I can't recommend this game highly enough and I can't wait until the next episode is released.

Dungeon Siege 3 is actually a GOOD game, and you´ll enjoy it quite enough once you get past the 2 biggest problems of this game:

Let´s see: unlike the other 2 DS, this is NOT a HACK´N´SLASH RPG, it´s a (quite good, actually) ACTION RPG, with very pretty graphics (even now, considering its age), good acting voices, a deep and intriguing storyline full of lore.
2) A good controller is MANDATORY for this game become playable (and fun). Once you get the hang of it you´ll discover a whole different game than the one described by most of the reviews.
So, my advice, coming form a HUGE Dungeon Siege fan, that spent hundreds of hours on the previous titles, is to give this game a chance, making an effort to completely forget this is called Dungeon Siege 3, and after the initial hate ends, you´ll be surprised.

You already know reeally well what you bought this game for, and it's the achievements. I won't lie, I bought this game purely because of the alphabetical achievements as well, so let me just sweep over that topic first.
The basic achievements that are alphabetical/numeric and symbols, (which most of the people that are buying this game are after anyway) come in four different background colors. The font style is the type you see on american college movies, you know, that font. There are also some special achievements, like flags, which there are a whole lot as well.
The levels go A, B, C, D and so on... pretty straight forward.
Now a bit about the gameplay.
It's about completing physics puzzles, in which you try to get the blue square onto the landing zone, most typically. Completing a level itself feels satisfying, and then the achievements come raining in, it's nice.
Now about the minuses.
The game doesn't really have replay value, and is pretty quickly completed (I'm not the best with puzzles and still with a bit of help completed the game in just over an hour), but then again, you don't buy this game necessarily to play it over and over again, but for the achievements.
Another minus (not really about the game but the community) is that when I struggled, I tried to look at a walkthrough, and there are few walkthrough videos on Youtube. The most popular video was a guy who didn't even cut the fails most of the time, and made looking for answers really frustrating, as you could probably manage the level yourself before the guy in the video gets it done (happened a couple of times).
If you are, again, buying it to make your profile look cool etc. by the achievements, the 2€ price tag is not too bad for over 300 achievements to use. However, some are just random japanese (?) characters, so if you're not into those, or aren't trying to get 100% (as I wanted to do), just leave the last levels as they are.
In conclusion, 6/10 for the game as a game, but 7/10 as a whole (+1 for the achievements).

Clean and intuitive interface: 10/10
Rich and beautiful models, if garish: 8/10
Refreshing yet familiar game mechanics: 9/10
Sporadic density of content: 6/10
An inspired yet frustrating combat system with an acquired taste.
This game will take you out of your comfort zone and introduce you to new possibilities in the 4x genre, and you will be glad of it. Worth the money 83% of the time but doesn't get the recognition it deserves.
A note on the pros: the best interface I've ever had the pleasure of interacting with, and it really makes the game satisfying and simple to play. The game mechanics are familiar enough to get going but often take a twist or go off on a tangent completely, making for an exciting experience.
A note on the cons: I would have hoped for more unit customization options, but the wealth of customization in other areas allows this to be put on the back bench. Until affordable dlc comes along. The combat system is... interesting. Relinquishing absolute control on the field of battle is a hard pill to swallow and the pay off doesn't necessarily come through. This may, in part, be due to a lack of unit customization, or to an uncomfortable design decision, or it may be entirely due to my own reservations. Being introduced to something new, however, is usually a good thing.
In conclusion: as above. Despite the uncomfortable combat system and the minor customization niggle, this game is brilliant and really delivers a fun time.

This proved a pleasant return to HO/puzzle games after a short dry spell. While nothing new or groundbreaking, and certainly suffering from the usual shortcomings (thinly justified story, awkward dialogue, etc.), Alex Hunter is polished, low on bugs, and keen to give both casual and hardcore players a good experience without resorting to different play parameters. Environments are generic but nice, HO segments are run-of-the-mill but light on confusing clue names, and the puzzles, mostly the usual mix, include a few fresh but accessible offerings. Environmental interactions also tend to be logical and context-driven, which many games don't enforce. After allowing for the earlier list, the game has only two major flaws. One is simply that there is almost no practical difference between the difficulty settings - for the higher, hints and skips take longer and all "secret symbols" must be found to unlock the Bonus Room (the symbols are spoon-fed and the BR is kind of a joke anyway) - but serious players can simply ignore the included map and spurn hints and skips to increase the challenge. The other is that, whether finding hidden objects or scouring an environment, cursor placement to activate objects and interactions (inluding the usual hand and magnifying glass indicators) must be so exact that even pixel-scouring tactics failed to reveal them on a couple of occasions, forcing the use of the hint button. But overall this is a perfectly good and enjoyable adventure game.

First things first. This game is pretty good. It's pretty easy, but it's alright, and fans of the series will enjoy it.
That's not why I'm writing this review, though. I'm writing it because... there are some very interesting quirks to the PC version.
The less interesting error you'll encounter is, if you try to render it above 1080p, it won't work. That's not really such a big deal - I didn't expect it to work above 720, so whatever.
The more interesting bug is that the port does NOT include the music. See, the original release of the game read the music tracks from the disc and installed most of the rest to your drive. This one has a bypass so you can play it "without the disc."
But this means you will have NO music. At all.
Unless... well, you see, when I first played the game, I didn't realize I'd left a CD in my drive. So... instead of hearing the standard entry level music, I heard Smash Mouth's, "Holiday In My Head." I cracked up, because not only was it not meant to be playing, but... "Holiday In My Head." That is... the game.
This continued on every level for a while. Running past the grenades got me "Shoes 'n' Hats." After the second world, though, the music stopped entirely. The Smash Mouth CD only had so many tracks, after all. I bet if I'd put in my Sonic Adventure CD, it would have filled in all the blanks.
This port DOES have all the sound effects and textures, so it's not technically broken. And it plays really nice with a modern controller. But... look, I know some cats are against emulating. So just buy this. Now you own it, hooray! And go emulate the N64 version. It's okay, trust me.
If, however, you want the music to have nothing to do with the source game, OR if you already own the original disc, you might as well play this version. It really is a wonderful experience.

What. The Hell.
I won't say this game is badly made; far from it. It was brilliantly executed and well-produced. The environment and mechanics were made beautifully. It was excellent at turning expectations around and forcing players to think outside of the box in order to solve problems.
...But it quite frankly, on the whole, disgusted me.
It was ostensibly written as a commentary on the millenial generation. If it is an accurate one, my hope in the future of humanity has plummeted. It portrays an obscenely lost and egocentric attitude, with no idea what is going on somehow combined with the hubris of assuming control all of reality. It was a hopeless game without purpose or meaning behind it - it essentially formed its own straw man of nilihism, and bowed down before it as if it were to be admired.
The quality of an art piece is determined by 3 things: The clarity of its message, the content of its message, and the eloquence of its message.
The clarity of this game's message is laughable, unless it was trying to convey that confusion is the highest state to attain to - in which case its content was obscene, for that would be praising madness as a virtue.
The eloquence of the message was, admittedly, quite impressive... but not enough to compensate for the lack of quality in its content and clarity to me.
As such, I cannot recommend this game.

Scarred for life by this game. I'm really not into men who keep women in cages without their consent.
On a more serious note, my consensus: Definitely not the best visual novel I've played, but definitely not the worst. You can tell a lot of effort and polish had gone into this game, it's very well made and gorgeous to look at, even if the writing and characters fell flat for me. Considering how rare it is for games of any substance to be translated from Japanese, and how widely known and popular this game is I'd likely reccomend this to any otome/romance gamer... just know what you're getting into. II seem to be mostly alone in my opinion that it's cliche ridden in a bad way, and quite frustrating. The plot had a lot of potential, some of the characters did too, it just didn't hit any of the right notes for me. On top of that, there is a LOT of non-consenual/violent behaviour/groping/pinning/bad stuff, which is EXTREMELY BAD in a certain route, less present in the others but still definitely a factor. I can't stand this kind of behaviour glorified, not just in the 'yandere route' but in the others that are supposed to be far from that. There are otome games that handle yandere/violent characters in ways that make it interesting, this is not one of them.
However, there's a lot of content in this game, considering the price tag, and it's an absolute steal on sale. As aforementioned it'is not without it's flaws, quite stuck in standard character tropes and hindered by a frustratingly blank slate main character and cute-but-annoying-after-a-while sidekick. The appeal of the love interests is highly dependent on personal preference, it's not really a well rounded cast in my opinion. It's likely that one will appeal to you and the others will be 'meh'
, which takes away from the overall enjoyment of the game. The plot was interesting enough to pull me through, though I thought it was poorly handled, once I'd commited to it I didn't stop.
So, should you buy this game? I don't know. I really don't. It was a mixed bag, but if supporting it means other Japanese games potentially being translated? I don't know. Did I enjoy this game? To an extent, yes. As a guilty pleasure type thing, and I enjoyed deconstructing it and what makes it so popular (as an aspiring otome developer) but... I feel uneasy reccomending it due to the aforemention points.
If you do but this game, don't start with the diamond world, that's all I have to say.

I'd like to give Victoria 2 a positive review, but at this time, I just cannot bring myself to do so.
Positives of the game in my eyes:
-Economics are fantastic-If you like EU4, but want a deeper level of economics, then this game certainly fills that role perfectly.
-Colonization is fun-Pretty self explanitory here. Competing with other great powers for the rich coast of Africa is a fun contest of will and strength.
-Taking a nation from "civilized" to "Great Power" is amazing-I took Japan and made it into a great power, easily overpowering Spain and the USA in the conquest of China.
Negatives of the game in my eyes:
-Horrible amount of popup events-I understand that you get random events, sometimes negative and sometimes positive, but when you get the same dang event popping up fifty-seven times in twenty minutes, it makes for a lousy impression. I've heard that its due to some of the DLCs, but that's still no excuse for this to occur so often.
-Great powers gang up- You can be helping the smallest of nations with some small war, and suddenly you'll find yourself facing the UK and bloody every other great power on Earth for no other reason than the fact that you're at war. Others may find this realistic, I find it annoying, especially if I'm the one being attacked by the smaller nation.
-Literacy rate makes or breaks you-I realize that I do not yet quite understand the full concept of literacy in Victoria 2, but I hate that you can have a full education budget and dedicate all of your resources to try and build up the literate people, but it will still take you decades (and often longer) to go up a few percentage points.
-Unstable game-Pretty self explanitory. This game crashes every so often, though it the biggest complaint with this is that mods cause it to crash like a boss.
After all is said and done, do I regret buying this game? No, I certainly do not. However, I do think that you should ask yourself if you like grand strategy games and if you are willing to look past the flaws. It can be a really fun experiance, but you'll have to not get annoyed at the crashes or the endless popup events.

Perhaps one of the best 4X style games I have ever played, hands down.
To be quite honest, Civilization used to be my favorite game in the 4X category. I grew up playing that and the Age of Empires games. Unfortunately for my childhood memories, these games pale in comparison to the content, richness, and style that Endless Legend gives.
When I first saw this game on steam, I originally thought what most people thought: "Oh great, another Civilization rip-off." When I saw this was on-sale in some pack, I decided to purchase it just to see what it was. The moment I started the game, I was blown away. It runs better, it looks better, it plays better, there's more people playing it, and it has amazing support. Furthermore, if you have Games2Gether points, you can help shape the game itself (not that feedback doesn't, but the points system is pretty cool).
And finally, it's challenging. I STILL haven't been able to beat the AI on Endless mode yet, even though the hardest difficulty in Civ 5 is a cakewalk.
This game was worth the 29.99$ I spent for it in the pack, and I'd gladly spend 150$ flat for this game, with no add-ons (which, by the way, are amazing). It is that good, and I recommend this over any other 4X game, including Endless Space, another game by the same publisher.
I honestly have never been more impressed by a videogame than this one, and I have played a LOT of games.
Don't take just my word for it though, read all the other reviews, most will say the same thing. This game is amazing.

I am an avid 4x strategy game fan, and have played countless games in the genre. I never thought anything could dethrone Civ5, but Endless Legend has done exactly that. The game is beautiful if you a good PC, but still runs okay with low graphic settings on my original Surface Pro, and the interface works well on a touch screen. I love how the battles play out on the map so where you fight can be just as important as which units that are in the battle. On the topic of units, some people might not like this game's seemingly limited selection, but I think it actually works to its advantage. Each unit has distinct advantages and weaknesses beyond the typical rock-paper-scissors approach. In addition, individual units can also be upgraded with different armors and weapons which effect their effectiveness against different classes of units (e.g. Spears against mounted, swords against ranged, etcetera). Weapons and shields actually show on the units, too. Considering the level of customization each unit has, a larger variety of units would be overwhelming. The only legitimate complaint I can find with the game is that the AI is pretty easy, especially if you are a seasoned strategy game player. Over all, I think Endless Legend is the new king of 4x strategy

Reluctant thumbs up on this strange indie studio entry. Another reviewer mentioned that this game had some influences from The Stanley Parable, and I think that's the closest experience that players can find to this game. The difference for Only If is that the puzzles, such as they are, are a bit more rudimentary, or unpolished. Many solutions are hidden from the player until they explore their environment fully (sometimes even using disappearing objects or disappearing walls to do the job)
One scene in particular has the player pressing E repeatedly to keep from blacking out or falling into "darkness". But the player isn't given any instructions other than that. So I spent at least 10 tries of trying to explore my environment (as the game encouraged me to do all along) and ending up running head first into a blackout. Eventually I saw that spamming the button and running straight through one particular part seemed to be the only way to succeed at the scene. I'm glad I stuck with the game, because it has some stylish scenes and setpieces, but the frustration was close to souring the whole thing for me.
Story wise, the game tries for a very young, hip aesthetic, with snarky comments from the game's antagonist intended to make the player laugh as they're given ambiguous or frustrating instructions. After a couple of full playthroughs, I was honestly exhausted from all the wisecracks and reloads that the game threw at me, and glad it was finally over. But I enjoyed the genuine surprises the game threw at me as well, so I found it was worth playing, especially since I didn't have to pay for it.

Haven't bought Football Manager since 2013. I made a decision to never waste money on it again back then, as I simply didn't like the repetitive and frustrating direction the gameplay was being taken. The amount of injuries on FM games, regardless what training routine you use, is preposterous and should have been fixed years ago. Here I am again in 2016, still reporting that very problem. A problem that has plagued this franchise from day one. Playing the Beta version of 2017, it's the same old story. Players acting like children, injuries that kill any attempt you make at being successful. (They are relentless and unforgiving). Inexcusable. I can only assume the makers are taking the p*ss.
The tactics I find, are useless. I've tried at least five different formations and all have the same problem. Nothing happens but 'INCONSISTENCY'. Star players can't hit a barn door. (Try being Spurs manager - Kane won't score for me, Everyone gets injured all the time. It's a mess. An awful experience. A waste of electricity). Neither can the players ever sort their attitude out. As Juventus manager, I had to turn it off by October. Another awful, problematic squad, that wouldn't perform and were constantly injured.
You are bombarded with problems that detract from actual 'fun gameplay'. My players come across as whiney, spiteful creatures, who will do nothing for the shirt for very long. They can't be praised, because they then underperform. If you don't praise them, they underperform. (Wonderful!!! Lots of fun to be had here I see!).
The team talks are an assault on my Chi. It doesn't matter what you say, or what tone you say it, INCONSISTENCY and players underperforming is the result. Results and match events, are a continuous slap in the face, making you ask 'what did I say wrong now!???'. Every team talk and press conference is a lottery. What you think is a common sense statement, is actually a trick to ruin your team cohesion. This game is awful. It's actually been developed to make you feel harassed at something you love doing. It can't even be called a 'simulation', because the injuries and the behaviour of the players, is totally unrealistic and contrived to frustrate you.
In-game tactical instructions are limited and do NOTHING.
You can spend hours trying to figure out what role to give a player and never get it right.
Say something the game doesn't like, (99% of what you are given as a choice, ends up in disaster) and your whole squad will collapse. It's totally hit and miss.
Fiddle all you like if that's your thing, but you are either getting sacked, or the players will lose faith, or you will switch it off, because at that point, you will realise that you hate your life, that you wasted time on this game's BS and the fact you've wasted all that money on it again.
So my question is: What is this 'game'? A virtual reconstruction of what my hell would be like? When did 'games' become a bloody hindrance?
You also have that lame old problem, of players complaining about lack of play time, disrupting the squad, even though they've been playing. One minute they are playing well, (the only one in your team mind), then they complain for no reason and you've lost their form all season from that point too. You still can't tell players they are a disgrace and will never play for the club again. They just keep spiting you somehow and you can't do anything about it apart from fine them after a few warnings. (Warnings which do nothing). Anything sets them off. This game makes you feel like putting everyone on the transfer list and breaking your laptop. Every time I press 'continue', it hits me with another slap in the face. It's so convoluted and utterly infuriating nowadays, what's the point of this 'game' anymore? It has no point. It has ruined what everybody loved about football management games and churned out this totally unsatisfying rubbish year after year. But hey, as long as the facia is a bit different, they'll get away with charging you another forty quid.
Never again. Never again. This time the bridge will never be rebuilt.

Victoria II is one of the best strategy games I've ever played. It has indepth political simulation, a lot of atmosphere that gets you into the Victorian era, and a great diplomacy/warfare system.
The actual combat aspect isn't that in-depth, and is definently strategical over tactical. The economic system looks complex, but is actually a bit too simple. Kind of a neccisary evil, because the game is tracking about 130 million civilians and their needs and political aspirations.
Its like Democracy 3 as far as politics go, but its simple and sweet, Victoria 2 is a much better game in my opinion. Otherwise, it functions much like a shorter version of other Paradox grand strategy simulation titles, and the shortness here is a welcome addition. For example, you can raise a country  from the Artisan economy era to National Socialism in the course of an 8 hour play-through, whereas any one game of Crusader Kings 2 is about 90 hours long. As far as I'm concerned, this gives V2 much better replayability, as there's not a lot of comitment compared to other Paradox games.
I love taking small nations like Cuba or Hawaii and switching them to National Socialism or Communism, or watching the world scene progress through great wars, colonizing Africa, or stealing India away from the British. Still, it may seem too complex to the average player at first, mostly because the game doesn't do the best job of explaining itself, especially if you skip the tutorial. However, I actually recommend learning the game naturally, as a large nation like France. Go lazzae-faire economy for the first so you don't have to manage the economy (this is simple, too, but looks complex), and learn the game by conquering less advanced nations in Asia and Africa.

Try to imagine Obsidian's role-playing dialog system embedded into the console port of Diablo III.  In a nutshell, that's Dungeon Siege 3.
You'll notice that the majority of negative reviews on here can only be summed-up the way Machinima's Inside Gaming Daily recently described most haters' opinions. It goes something like, "I hate this pizza because it isn't a taco."  Granted, it isn't wise to change a franchise as much as Obsidian did here.  Many fans of DS1 and DS2 appear incapable of liking this game, and it seems a lot of them feel tricked out of their cash.  I'll mention their gripes here, however, to give a fair review, I don't want to just look at what DS3 *isn't*.  I want to review it based on its own merit. To be up front, I actually hated DS3 at first, but when I was looking for a co-op to play with my non-gamer wife, I took a second look at Dungeon Siege 3.  I found I had completely changed my perception of this game, because I changed my perception of its design choices, and it actually became one of my favorites of all time.
Dungeon Siege III is a gamepad-friendly isometric action RPG with local and online co-op.  While much more casual than its predecessors, there's still plenty of quests, hacking, slashing, shooting, magic, looting, upgrades, lore, and dialog - and when multiple players (online or off) are in a story conversation together, players can vote for their preferred responses to NPCs, albeit Player 1 has the final say.
There are four characters to choose from, and each delivers a different fighting style (melee, ranger, sniper, magician). Each character also has two "stances" to vary up their attack strengh, range, and/or speed.  Not to mention, the back story will also change, according to which hero you've selected.
Gone is the tactical pause.  Gone is the squad management.  Gone are the skill points you earn, specific to your fighting style.  Gone are the multiple skill trees for each character.  Each weapon and piece of armor you find can only be equipped by a specific character.  Obsidian has "streamlined" this game, effectively consolizing it.  This is the heart of Dungeon Siege 2 fans' complaints, besides multiplayer camera controls and multiplayer inventory management.  You now will be only upgrading a single skill tree for your character, which means close vs ranged combat will not award skill toward that specific stance. Instead of holding down on right-click to attack, you'll button-mash, and each press will be one swing/shot. Also annoying to some, even when you gain NPC followers, you will not be in charge of their tactics, nor their upgrades.
This game was developed by the same people who made South Park: The Stick of Truth, Fallout: New Vegas, Knights of the Old Republic 2, Neverwinter Nights 2, and Alpha Protocol.  I loved all of those games.  My point, they KNOW role-playing.  In my opinion, the story here is great.  If you don't have nostalgia stars in your eyes, it's easy to see that the voice acting here is by far superior to its predecessors.  Although the story is drastically shorter, it's certainly more focused.
All in all, I can tell you this:  if you have a friend or loved one you want to play an immersive, open-world action RPG with while sitting on the couch together, this is the game. You'll find a rich story, a simple skill tree, upgrades, dialog choices, and tons of loot.  It's one of the best (and few) couch co-ops that delivers a true RPG experience.  Plus, gamers of all experience levels can enjoy it together.

While I was able to try to craftfully master my character's moves, she was able to button-mash with a rifle-wielding hottie from a distance, and we made an excellent team! is a fun and challenging indie title by Rogue Snail.
The story is as follows: The Duck-Hunt Ducks have declared war on humanity, and their leader, Commander Duckin', have attacked a human colony on some stupid planet. It's up to a handful of handsomely rugged relic hunters with horrible cases of anime hair and their positively romantically named ship, the Spaceheart, to defeat them! Oh, and the Duck-Hunt Ducks have allied (read; forced into war-labour) with some space turtles, and they all have better guns than you. Have fun!
Players can take control of one of six available characters, each with a different stat balance and starting weapon. The player starts with access with Jammy, an all-rounded character with nothing interesting to offer AT ALL, and Punkyy, who specialises in melee and pistol combat like the edgelady she is. From there, Laff the Keyboard Warrior, By-You the 'Nade Spammer, Pinny the 420kg Blazer and Ace the Ace-Hole can all be unlocked though gameplay.
During gameplay, it is possible to obtain a substantial collection of 'more gun' to assist in gibbing thousands of ducks and turtles. Nine times outta ten, you get them from gibbing ducks and turtles. The controls are tight and innovative, and the game's focus is on dodging and using cover, rather than mowing through waves of enemies. The relics recovered from Commander Duckin''s forces actually grant bonuses to the player, and are a good incentive to become a completionist. The art style is pretty neat as well, and the music is pretty damn great. A few gripes of mine are with the fact that lobbed grenades have a locked toss distance, and using the scope doesn't constantly 'refresh,' I guess? Also, the images of the characters used in the menus are obviously sketches. Also, the game is pretty short in terms of levels, as there are only 4 zones, each with 3 levels, with a bossfight at the end of all of them. That said, the difficulty makes the game last for a fair while. Nothing major anyways.
