Pros:
-some puzzles are interesting
-hidden object scenes aren't too difficult
-the map is very helpful to tell you where to go next
-the use of inventory items isn't too weird or unpredictable
Cons:
-it would be very difficult (or sometimes impossible) to tell what to do next without constantly consulting the map.
-story is practically nonexistent
-artwork is cartoony and doesn't set any sort of atmosphere, but with the lack of story this isn't surprising
-some puzzles aren't really logic puzzles so much as brute force trial and error
The game includes three types of play:  hidden object scenes, messing around with objects in your inventory, and puzzles.  I play these sorts of games for the puzzles and consider the hidden object and inventory management as parts I just have to suffer through to get to the puzzles.  There is a fair variety in the types of puzzles, from jigsaw to sliders to logic, but some of them are less about thinking and more about making you try all the combinations until it works.
There will be several rooms open at any given time and you will have to keep going between them to complete the objectives.  At first this was very confusing because there might be 10 things in the rooms that you need to do and you might have 10 things in your inventory, but none of those objects helps with the immediate tasks.  There is little to no direction in the "story" to tell you what you should be working on solving next and which things you don't have the objects for yet.  Then, I realized the map always shows which rooms have activities that can be completed.  It's a cop-out to use the map like this instead of having a better written game where it would make sense what you are supposed to do next.
Along with not knowing what to do next, quite often a hidden object scene that you had previously completed will re-activate and have new things for you to find.  However, the game does not indicate in any way, except for the map, that you need to backtrack to that area.
If you can get it on sale, it can be some fun for the puzzles, but overall it is a poorly done game.

Alex Hunter is a surprisingly long hidden object game with little story, decent puzzles and a nice soundtrack. Although it never really surpasses the mediocre level, the sheer length alone makes it stand out of similar games.

Alex Hunter: Lord of the Mind is an average hidden object title in all aspects, except one: unlike most similar games it has a male protagonist.
Not that it really matters, since the story– a missing person investigation leading into a James Bond-like “stop the evil genius from taking over the world” scenario– takes up about 5-10 minutes of game time. It is nothing more than an excuse to use a Victorian visual theme, a very carefully designed and implemented, excellent visual theme.
The game is exceptionally long, thanks to the quite lengthy (although not particularly difficult) puzzles, the balanced hidden object scenes, and just the sheer number of places you can visit. It can easily clock over six hours even if one uses the map all the time to avoid the constant backtracking, making it an excellent choice if you want to have some game length for your money.

I want to give this game 5 stars, intellectually.  It had the good HINTs/STRATEGY GUIDE (bundled).  It had a MAP feature to speed travel and show you were the next actionable locations were.  It had the JOURNAL system that auto recorded all the clues you had seen elsewhere in the game.  It had BONUS CONTENT (i.e. "Secret Room", Wallpapers, Audio Tracks) which unlocked when you found enough of the secret mysterious symbols throughout the game.  It had a reasonable plot (for a Hidden Objs genre game), good atmosphere/feel, and the Hidden Objects puzzles threw a few Aha moments at me.
However, it felt like just before it hit excellence in most of those areas, it would fall slightly short, again and again.  It had a LOT of sliding piece puzzles, which I find personally annoying.  The plot didn't go far enough for me to get personally invested in it.  The arcade puzzles were interesting, but sloppily implimented ... so I'd have to replay because it was sometimes scoring hits as misses (shooting gallery), etc.  Overall it felt like things were being added from a master "to do list" of what games should have, instead of being organically grown out of the game itself.
Missing/Broken Feature(s):
* Achievements in Game (But no Steam Achievements)
* I wish it had Steam collectible Cards, too.
* Soundtracks in Extra Content section:  Only 1 of the tracks would play music (with LONG delay)

I enjoyed this game, it had a lot of potential back then...so much so in fact that I put some time and effort in answering a survey the devs sent out over a year ago. There were actually quite a lot of us who helped the devs identify all the current gameplay issues, and give them some feedback on how we who like the game to progress moving forward. The devs had made it well clear that they were prepared to put in the effort into creating new content for the game, and the community and the players believed them and supported them.
A little over a year later (after completing the survey), we finally hear back from the dev team with a laughable patch, stating the game is now in full release (with the price heavily knocked down).
Needless to say we all know what that means. The dev team has abandoned development on this game and has run away with the early access money from the players and most importantly, they did not deliver on their promise to the whole community.
I must say I'm baffled that Steam allows these developers to get away with charging full price on a game and failing to deliver: it’s a lack of respect on both the players and on steams’ standards.
Most importantly, it teaches us that we should never purchase a game in early access. Lesson learned then.
Do not purchase this game.

A game that showed a lot of promise during the Early Access days and had the potential to become one of the best, most immersive and most realistic hunting simulators, in the end failed horribly to deliver. What we have now is a game with minimal content, barely acceptable for a "full release", while ridden with so many bugs and glitches that they alone could easily ruin the experience for many. In the end, it somehow managed to become a game that was much better and a lot more fun to play during its Early Access days and as long as the developing team refuses to care, fix problems and add new content, even as DLC, I personally wish it could revert to that.
+ Large map, beautiful environment, realistic landscape
+ Good atmosphere, ambient sounds, day-night cycle and weather effects
+ The game gives a nice initial feeling and the first few times you get approached by a T-Rex can be pretty thrilling, but it gets old fast
+ Controls when trying to aim are clunky, but that actually adds to the realism
+ For a hunting simulator, I suppose it has a good variety of weapons
- The island may look beautiful at first, but once you've walked all over the map once, it all feels the same
- Camouflage used to matter during Early Access, now it's irrelevant. Hiding prone and motionless under bushes saved your life more than often back then, now most of the time it makes no difference
- Dinosaur AI, especially that of the T-Rex, has gotten worse and worse over the course of development. The T-Rex used to behave like a clueless animal when shot out of the blue, now it instantly locates your position and runs to you in a straight line, like a heat-seeking missile, stops and eats you without even wasting a second to look around for you. It doesn't get more unrealistic than that as in actuality, most of the time the animal wouldn't even be able to identify which direction it got wounded from
- Only five species, two of which share the same model in different scales
- All five species are aggressive, four of them being actual predators, the opposite of what you'd expect from a hunting session
- On top of that, supplies and ammunition are so scarce that it feels a lot more like a survival game than a hunting game. Hence why I always called it "
". The player is clearly the prey in this one
- The dinosaurs never eat, drink, sleep or interact with each other, killing the realism
- Hitboxes are and have always been a mess
- Dinosaurs may still attack you through concrete walls and thick trees, one of the major glitches that was addressed countless times but was never fixed
- Server issues and reports from players losing their entire inventories or never receiving the items purchased from the in-game after-death store are more frequent than one could imagine
... You can carry about 18 bullets for the .50 sniper rifle when you are in your underwear, but you can only carry about 15-16 if you put on pants and a shirt. Even less if you put on sunglasses and a hat!
... The character runs out of stamina after sprinting for a few dozen meters, while the dinosaurs can sprint to the ends of eternity without pause
... The character also has some sort of mental deficiency, as he/she suddenly becomes unable to throw a rock while crouching on one knee
... Watching a T-Rex walking up an almost vertical hillside practically defies description
Bugs, glitches and lack of content aside, it may be worth the purchase for its current price of €10 if you don't expect to be amazed, if you are curious and if you don't mind the expense and the indifference of the creators, as it will probably offer some good times, but let me remind you that the game cost €20 during Early Access. That alone says a lot.

Beat the Game is more of an animated music video that lasts shorter than it took to write this review, but it has astonishing animation and a player-controlled techno soundtrack.
I would almost call the title of ‘Beat the Game’ misleading, since this product hardly classifies as a game. It is more like a long and dialogue-free music video with stellar animation and an endless French style house/techno soundtrack (which is funny, since the creator is Turkish, the studio is American, and the music is Canadian).
Technically, there is gameplay, since we must hunt for music clips. Most of them only require us to scan distant scenery elements, but we also have to find some random items lying in the sand and bring them to other objects to complete the collection.
We use these clips for two things: creating our own soundtrack on the fly, which I consider the real main feature; and beating the final challenge, a short live show.
The only issue with this setup is that the playfield is extremely small and it is possible to do everything under 25 minutes. If you do not mind playing the price for this extended music clip though, then Beat the Game will not disappoint in its goals.

Beat The Game:
~~~~~~~~~~~~

Important News Flash for all hoverbike owners . . . in the last few weeks, the authority recorded an alarming number of accidents in the desert involving hoverbike riders and fridges! It has become a trend for people to drop their old fridges in the desert, and an even bigger trend for riders to smash their bikes into them at night due to poor visibility. And you, my friend Mistik, you missed the news flash and indeed rode into one tonight!
Beat The Game is an adventure / puzzle game where you play Mistik, a strange character who is dressed like a prison inmate and carries a holographic music mixer wherever he goes.
After the introduction cut-scene, where Mistik smashes his bike into the unidentified object, he will wake up in a surreal area. This area is basically where all the game will take place and you’ll probably familiarise yourself with it in the first ten to twenty minutes. The goal of this game is to collect all the sounds within the map, mix them to create great rhythms and put on a show at night using your music mixer to exit this section and win the game.
Mistik has another couple of instruments besides his music mixer. The first one is a sound scanner. By using this device, Mistik will be able to track sounds within the area. As soon as he identifies a sound, he will have to follow the sound with his scanner for five seconds to record it onto his mixer. There are twenty-four sounds in total to record in this game. Also, there are collectables lying on the ground for him to pick up, some of which will be needed to create new sounds.  Others will be used to activate a different device, such as the Laser Mark Object.
Graphically, Beat The game looks very good; the animations and cut-scenes are very well done. I really enjoyed mixing all the sounds together and creating smashing rhythms. In terms of controls, you can use your mouse and keyboard or your gamepad, which are all responsive. My biggest complaint is the length of the game. It will be finished within an hour to an hour and a half maximum. It would have been nice to have at least a few more levels with new sounds to elevate the game further. I really like the concept, artwork, and being a DJ for a while. However, I wanted more.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Nice artwork
-	Smooth animations and cut-scene
-	Easy to play for all ages
-	Fun to mix sounds and feel like a DJ
-	Fridges in the desert!
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No achievements or trading cards
-	Needs more content
-	Very short

The graphics and (perhaps) music are the redeeming factors of what can only be loosely referred to as a game. The developer, by his own admission, is an artist who decided to dabble at game design. You can mix your own electronic music while you play, using the sounds you record. There are only a couple of dozen of them but you can do something with them at least. This game is, by all means, unique. It has a lot it brings to the table that might be hard to find in other 4X games; customization of your soldiers armaments, a civilization construction system, an intuitive and easy to use interface, and a Sci-Fi touch to fantasy for its flavor and flair. It's a fun game if you're looking for an all-around solid game. Don't let its high-notes delude you however, the game's got a few bugs, it's a little iffy on its idea of Magic, and if you're looking for some familiar cliche's to build off of, you'd best look elsewhere. The game's basic premise seems mostly to stem from a unique attitude towards magic and fantasy, where the "Magic" in the system is treated both as MacGuffin and common currency. But don't worry! It's also life-blood of Lich-Ghost-Knights, and the source of emo-wizards rather potent magics. What the game lacks in familiar faces, it gains in some rather fun and new archetypes, such as the affor-mentioned wizards and knights, as well as "Dwarves" which are really just Troglodytes in the purest sense, Druids who think of themselves as elves, statues that are alive and religious, a race of mutant infectious bugs, and to bring it all home, you got nomads with giant beetles that feel exported from Morrowind. Not that that's a bad thing. It's about the most familiar flavor this game has, the rest of it is telling you "Welcome to something new."
At the end of the day, this game is fun. It has bugs though, and sometimes it's not exactly clear on what the quests require from you, but if you want a new flavor of 4X, give it a shot. When it's on sale. If you're going for full-price, I'd recommend first deciding if a Middle-fantasy-With-Science 4X is the flavor of game you want,

Good idea, but falls down in a couple of key places.
1) The loot variation is not nearly interesting enough, and the weapons are not different enough to matter.  It becomes just getting the biggest number, no thought to playstyle.
2) The actual game is very frustrating.  The enemies that use fast/hitscan laser weapons will do a warmup cycle that shows their thing warming up, and most of the ships will give some kind of indication that they're about to do their (very rapid) attack.  So, you want to keep your eyes predominantly on the playfield watching for incoming threats.   The *problem* is that the bullets and attacks tend to be very unpredictable, so you need to watch what's going on around the ship.  The experience of having to need to look in two places at once to avoid damage results in the experience of watching the playfield, only to have unpredictable bullet sprays and other ships run into yours, and then moving your eye over there and being hit by rapid attacks that you couldn't easily anticipate.
Good shooters are built on memorization of patterns.  Even randomized shooters like
(which I'd recommend instead of this game) give you enemies that are predictable, so you can take advantage of muscle memory.  This game is just flailing around with no pattern, so you never have anything to build off of.

Amaranthine is very nice little SHMUP.
It has pretty graphics, great soundtrack and simple, but fun gameplay.
Since it's SHMUP, it is played by shooting enemy ships and avoiding their bullets.
Controls are very simple, hold left button to shoot and move the mouse around to dodge bullets.
There are a lot of different enemies in Amaranthine and they are thrown at player randomly.
To make it less monotonous - if you find dodging hundreds of projectiles and turning enemies into explosions monotonous - there's few well made random events.
There's also neat spaceship upgrading system.
The spaceship can be equipped with three weapons, to be equipped weapons require energy, which can be increased by spending alloy - the currency of the game.
The alloy is obtained by destroying enemies and selling weapons.
Weapons are received from drops.
If I remember right, there are six weapon types and they come in three tiers - common, rare and legendary.
Higher tier weapons deal more damage.
Every weapon is unique, but it doesn't matter that much.
Still, it's fun to collect weapons.
Shield, that is spaceship's health, can also be upgraded.
Since it is possible to replay levels and keep upgrading the shield, that makes the game rather easy.
But that doesn't ruin the experience.
Story-wise, there are short skippable cutscenes in beginning and end of the game.
I find ending cutscene satisfying.
I'm glad I played Amaranthine.
I recommend buying it if you want few hours of a good time.
Bonus fact: Amaranthine means purplish-red or everlasting.

The Curious Expedition is not a bad game. It's one of those game those makes you wish there was a "meh" option, not because it is not fun (the first few playthroughs are pretty fun actually), but because its replayability really isn't as good as advertised.
1. First and foremost, the "rogue-like" aspect of the game is disappointing. Once you're done with the first few playthroughs, there's just nothing to be excited about. You've visited every location and know exactly what to expect from good and bad rolls everywhere. It's really just about scrambling the maps and changing the order in which you'll visit the same places.
2. Which leads to another issue: it sure is silly to pest against RNG in a game about rolling dice, but hell is it frustrating to lose just because the damn pyramid was in the one bit of the map you missed. Random map-generation was meant to create replayability, more often than not it just causes frustration . The result is, it feels like having a good strategy compared to your competitors won't be enough, you'll need that extra pinch of luck.
3. There just isn't enough difference between the explorers. Only a few stand out because of how much better than the others they are, either because of their traits or starting inventory. This does not incentivize you to do those extra challenges to unlock them all, most are just not worth the hassle.
4. The variance between the difficulty settings is pretty ridiculous. It ranges from easy to you'll only win if your rolls are amazing through the whole thing. That means that even if you do not mind the lack of novelty after the first few hours and just want to challenge yourself, there's just frustration at the end of the road.
5. Minor point - the music gets old pretty fast
The game has redeeming features: the narrative is well-written, there's great humor here and there, the graphics are pleasant - it does the most of these pixel graphics, and you do get used to it, and here again when there's still something new to explore in the game it is pretty fun and it definitely outweighs the frustration of losing to something you have absolutely no control over. But here I am, after 8 hours of play: I'm just bored of it, and kind of regret getting it but not really at the same time.
Take it when it's 50% off, it's great for a couple of hours.

This is a challenging optimization timing based puzzler with a bit of its own style. Several optimization puzzlers (SpaceChem, Infinifactory, Manufactoria) in this genre are very "big part", complex games where there are many possibilities for solutions.
This is a bit different. For most of the puzzles, the range of solutions is constrained - the constant grid size of 11x11 is used well without you noticing it at first. In addition, there is a limited amount of tools, also called 'action blocks', and the game exploits several of their traits including some subtle asymmetries. These combined not only means you won't have to think in such big quantities, nor will you forget how your solution works.
This is a style of programming puzzler I really enjoy and I've got a lot of time and fun out of it.
Update on negatives about the game, as well: The debugging is pretty poor - it is a very trial-and-error part of the game, though thankfully the mechanics are simple enough that it is not as bad as SpaceChem.

This game is well-made, quirky, and unique. The mechanism of finding and collecting sounds is fun to play, and the world that the developers have created is beautiful and surreal.
The obvious caveat with this game is that it is unlikely to take you more than an hour or so to complete. It's clear that the developers meant to make a much longer game; there are characters and objects that tie into future parts of the story that just don't exist. (Despite the 'to be continued', I don't expect the full game ever to see the light of day.)
It would be sad, though, to let that put you off completely. What is there of the game is well-realised and complete in itself -- the level that you play does lead you up to a satisfying end point. The mechanisms are fun, and I hugely enjoyed playing it.
My only real criticism, beyond the short length, is that there's little help in finding the sounds. They're mostly easy to discover, but I ended up spending the last twenty minutes or so wandering around trying to find the one missing sound. A hint system would have been helpful!
So, this is a beautiful, fun, and unique game. It's sad that it was cut short, but I'm happy to have played it and am glad that it was released rather than just dying in obscurity on a developer's hard drive. Don't buy it expecting the full story hinted in the level that you play, but enjoy it for what it is.

Rating 7.5/10
What is it?
Action RPG
The Good:
+Graphically the game is beautiful, but what really stands out is the use of color especially in regards to the characters skills. Every skill used is colorful and bright and makes the combat really stand out. Making a critical ht is satisfying because it really stands out.  It makes you wonder why other developers are so afraid of having color in their games.
+4 unique characters each with their own unique play style. Every character has 2 offensive stances used to either deal with single or groups of enemies and one defense stance. Each stance has 3 skills associated with it. Each skill has 2 way you can upgrade it, allowing you to customize how you want to develop your character. In addition each character has a passive skill tree further adding to your build. All of this leads to interesting builds.
+The game play mechanics are a bit more unique to this type of game. In order to use your abilities you need force and the only way to gain force is to attack your enemies. Defensive skills use power spheres which fill up as you take damage. All of this creates some unique game play elements and changes the way you play and develop your character. Dodging and blocking also play an important role in game play,
+You can always rely on Obsidian to craft a well thought out story.  The games side quests in some regards are even more interesting and creative than the main quest.  Books and lore are scattered around the world to further flesh out details if your into that sort of thing.
+Music/sound and voice acting are all top notch.
The Bad:
-If there is one aspect of an action rpg that you need to get right it's the loot. The loot has to be exciting, it has to make you want to kill enemies to discover new items, it should feel rewarding. This game has non of that. The loot in this game is boring. For the most part, loot just changes stats and more likely than not you will equip the loot that gives you the highest stats. A good loot system means the player has to make tough choices, this game doesn't do that.
-Multiplayer is all but dead meaning you are not going to get any achievements related to multiplayer. Even if you do play a multiplayer game you character progress is not saved if you join someone else's game when you go back to single player. How this even passed in today's time is mind boggling.
Conclusion
I really loved this game, I played it many times on 360 and will continue to play it here. This game gets a lot of things right in regards to the genre sadly it also gets things horribly wrong as well.  I love that each character is really unique and no two characters play the same. Hopefully we see Obsidian get to make another with more improvements.

THIS IS NOT A DUNGEON SIEGE GAME!!! This game is nothing compared to DSII, the gameplay and style are completly different. (I have not played the multiplayer and I probalby will not.) Your team building is completely limited to the constructs of  the preset game options, your  character class is permanetly set and you cannot stray in the slightest to develop a character to fit your design or fighting style like the incredible system in DSII. You can tell that Chris Taylor had really nothing to do with this game, the fact that he let it be produced is disheartening. The visuals are great dont get me wrong, but the camera is horrendous. It is always at an angle that makes you a bit nauseous, plus you cannot adjust it to see well at all. The target locking system is entirely automated, I have not found a way  to turn it off, so the enemy that you are targeting  is not the one  that you choose, completly eliminating any potential strategy in the battles. The story line is not too bad, a bit dry at times but overall it has been pretty decent. Alas the only real connection to the wonderful DSII is that a few of the names like Asunites are thrown in for good measure.
To anyone who is a fan of the DS series I WOULD NOT recommend this game. (I wish I had looked into the game further  before purchasing, but the idea of a new DS game I hit the  purchase button without hesitation.) But if you are looking for  a halfway decent loot based RPG then wait until it is on sale before you pick it up.

If you were looking for a worthy successor to the first two games, you won't find it here.  This feels nothing like it's predecessors.  That said, it isn't a purely horrible game, just not the sequel we were looking for and nothing amazing in its own right.
we get is pretty linear (which the others were somewhat, but a decent amount of ARPG exploration was introduced in the second game) with little to find off the beaten path.
is simple, as skill choice isn't immensely important and works out to about 1.5 builds per character type (so not much replayability within a character type).  In previous games, we had skill choice mixed with a variety of spell choices you could equip at leisure (but, still had particular types that were affected by the skills).
, a feature that was pretty much a signature of the Dungeon Siege series, has been reduced to 2 characters at a time (which, if memory serves, was at least 4 in the other games).  They have introduced some interaction between characters as well as their liking or disliking your choices, but not with much depth (I barely noticed it).
were actually really nice, especially on Anjali (who looks so awesome in archon form or with late-game armor, you feel a bit underwhelming as the other characters).  I gotta admit that.
was pretty fun too.  They've set up each character to have two types of combat stances, and switching between them can actually make for some versatile combat (and does allow you to make your build more interesting).
are somewhat varied.  You find a lot of class-specific stuff, though (actually, I think most of it was).  You find a decent amount, but don't upgrade them extremely often.  Some people like that, some people don't; up to you.
works but isn't extremely memorable.  That said, you see more if it and of your characters than in previous games.  So, better!
are pretty standard, but some do offer a degree of choice.  Again, not to a degree that makes it special, but it is a nice addition.
The game isn't horrible, or even bad.  I CAN recommend it, because it can be some good fun.  Just don't expect anything amazing and pretend this is called Journey Into Dungeons or something (and is not part of the Dungeon Siege series) and you should have a good time.  It does very little that is special, but doesn't do things that are overtly wrong either.  It is a solid experience, but I couldn't bring myself to replay it.

is a side-scrolling shoot 'em up consisting of you, a spaceship commander, blasting the metal brains out of enemy space vessels.
The premise is something along the lines of a distant frozen planet that has sent out a distress signal, and you having to investigate. There is a fairly brief explanation of this at the start which plays each time you start a new game. (I'll just add here as a tip: to skip the cutscene and get straight to the action, simply press the
button.) This brief explanation is perfect because it makes the story simple and unobtrusive, whilst at the same time giving the game a purpose.
Once you are ready to obliterate some enemy ships you will be plunged straight into the action. Each level is randomly generated to add more replayability to the the gameplay. This gameplay is a great lot of fun, consisting of you traveling through an endless amount of (surprisingly difficult) levels with a variety of enemies, weapons and environmental hazards. For many
, this would be the end of the list of gameplay features. However, Amaranthine has an interesting weapon upgrade/loot system. During each level you can collect alloys from the destroyed ships which you then use to upgrade your ship in between levels. You are also given the chance to collect weapons from other destroyed ships which you can then use to place one of the three weapon spots your ship has. I've seen some people complaining about the sensitivity of the mouse, however this sensitivity is required (especially in later levels) to perform precise manoeuvres.
The pixelated graphics suit the style of game and are pleasing to look at as well as the backgrounds, though they do start to get a bit monotonous. I would suggest that some different styled backgrounds be introduced.
Regarding music and sounds, one word:
. These sounds, both soothing and heart-pumping are the reason this game is tagged with
. Take a listen
.
The game is a great deal for the low price of $2.99. The cost is definitely not overpriced and respects the content of the game. This would be something that I couldn't excuse not buying in a sale.
Any other points regarding the game would be the lack of options. An ability to change the mouse sensitivity may stop the complaints coming through.
✔ An unobtrusive story
✔ Fun gameplay
✔ Great upgrade system
✔ Nice visuals
✔
music
✔ Low price
✘ Backgrounds can get monotonous
✘ Lack of options

Not a bad game at all. First, if you're on the fence about this from the screen shots, this isn't for you. This is a challenging puzzle game through and through.
If this sort of "use pieces to get things from points A to points Whatever" gameplay appeals to you, this is pretty fun, and is what you might expect. There is a demo, so you can decide if this game appeals to you.
Bear in mind, though, this game has a pretty steep difficulty cliff right out of the gate. I was having brief trouble with 1-star difficulty levels early, and a lot of the early levels will either require knowledge of pathfinding, or teach it the hard way to players. Even early manipulating blocks are presented with the "here's a new thing! Figure it out yourself" instruction. This is not a casual game.
This is, for those looking for a challenging puzzle game, a neat idea.
Graphics have a solid, consistent style. Music is actually pretty good, never mind for an indie puzzle game. I don't much care about these for a puzzle game, but they're both capable here. Controls are a bit clunky. If you are those who wants controls to work for your specific style, instead of being ok with dealing with a not-quite-super-intuitive interface, you might have some issues with constructing your solution at times. I personally didn't much have a problem with it, but I know some people who will very much like this game's concept might have issues with the interface.
Each puzzle after the brief tutorial is rough. And then, once you learn what the game is maybe expecting of you, challenging. And then, you'll come back to the game and solve something you struggled for almost a half hour with, a single puzzle, immediately, after time to sleep on or ruminate on the level. I've only gotten to the later parts of the first half of the main pack, but I can see this idea being the norm for this game. And "only" 65 or so levels becomes a complete, double-digit or so hour game when each level takes several minutes of thought, and possibly pencil and paper, to complete an individual level. And then, you can use what you've learned from that difficult level to beat more easily/accessably solved future levels. And the rare past level you chose to skip.
And this is a barometer for which I will judge harder puzzle games. I'm fine with learning the ropes for them, and once you do, this game becomes a game where you have a eureka moment randomly on a level and then beat said level reasonably quickly, after staring at it and trying hard for a while on with no progress.
The dev is also very receptive to the game's users, including being, in the past, willing to allow previous purchasers of the game elsewhere to get a Steam key for free when this was first put on Steam (From what I can tell from the game's discussions forum). I got this game during a sale several months after this went on Steam, but for smaller-scale games like this I like seeing how the dev(s) act with roadbumps in the release process. This game has, in the past, had a strong dev interest in its playerbase. I definitely consider this in my opinions, and this game passes with flying colors here.
And on that "graphics" front, the spray-painted "29" in the game's interface for the challenge mode is a subtle change that almost represents this puzzle game's strengths too perfectly from those who dedicate the time to complete this game. Originally, the challenge was to clear the game with 3,000 tiles covered, but because of the community, it was discovered that one could beat the game covering (as of now) exactly 2,900 tiles. It's worthy of optimisation; and that's pretty big for a game that's not super-big to achieve; an ultimate challenge that even the dev underestimated, to an extent.
I'm digging this. I might update this review as I play on, as I've not gotten past the first screen. But yea, this game is difficultly engaging for a puzzle game fan like me, almost to the point where I'm learning a bit about data structures (and am inspired to learn a bit about types of coding) from it.

TL,DR: A beautiful, well paced (with guardians expansion), and fun 4x strategy game.
Pros: beautiful graphics, interesting units and races, plenty of quests/victory conditions. Guardians expansion is an absolute must buy.
Cons: Combat system isn't very precise (Turn-based, units autotarget/act without user input if primary objective becomes unavailable mid-turn), some frustrating diplomatic situations (see below)
Overall score 8.5/10
Graphics: the asthelic is one of the best I've seen. All the races have unique units and there are plenty of minor factions. The depth of field creates a cool tilt shift effect that I enjoy. When you zoom all the way in, the units become slightly pixelated and the textures could be better. However the game looks beautiful and they clearly put a lot of time into graphic design.
Civiliations (9/10): Diverse. No two civilizations play the same. No two can be played the same effectively. They are both visually and tactically appealing. All possible aspects of each civilization are different. And if none of the civilizations meet your specific interests or playstyle, you can create your own. I wouldn't mind seeing more civilizations however
Units (8/10): Just as diverse as the civilizations. However, while the number of unique units is impressive, the number of unique units available to each factions is only 3. This is partly solved by the ability to absorb minor factions and create their units and the addition of the guardians in the expansion. Still, I find it a little depressing that each faction only has 3 units to call their own. You cannot produce the units of another civilization.
Additionally there are heroes that provide massive buffs to armies they lead or cities they manage. There are heroes for each civilization, and heroes from other civilizations can be bought in the marketplace. Heroes in general have a combat skill tree, economic skill tree, and a mixed combat/econ skill tree. Based on their civilization of origin and type (cavalry, flying, ranged, infantry) they have differing skills available.
The customization is introduced in the equipment section. Each unit/hero can equip armor, weapons, and utility add-ons. Strategic resources introduce equipment with more power and diverse abilities. This also alleviates the fact that each civilization only has 3 unique units. Overall I would say that the lack of unique units/per civilization is not a game-breaker.
Gameplay:
Combat (7/10)- The combat is weird man. It is turn-based and is very imprecise. There is no way to give units secondary actions or targets.  This leads to frustration when units perform actions that get them killed, or opens up a hole in your defensive lines. Other than that, the combat performs well. Terrain is paramount when choosing where to attack and defend. Making a beach landing means that your troops will be coming ashore two by two, effectively making them cannon-fodder for defening forces. Cities provide defensive bonuses, terrain can provide universal bonuses and factions-specific bonuses.
Pacing (9/10)- Relatively well-paced. There are small quests accessed by searching ruins, each civilization has their own quest line, and there are many victory conditions. The early game's fun comes in the form of exploring and expanding your empire. Towards the end, the victory conditions occasionally seem to drag-on.  I will have my cities maxed out and have ntohing left to do but either take over the world or wait 50 turns for the game to end. This doesn't always happen but when it does, it really takes the fun out of the game.
The guardians expansion enhances the pacing immensely by adding more quests to accomplish. I was never without something to do all the way up until I won. This is a must-buy.
Diplomacy (7/10)- Sufficiently functional. All the options you would expect are there (alliances, trade/research agreements, resources exchanges). There is no real political intrigue or ability to influence other civilizations aside from the roving clans. Occasionaly civilizations will do weird and stupid things with alliances and wars. Trade routes are present, but they are all auto created once the necessary structures are built. No religion system is present, although it could be argued that each civilization represents a religion.
Tech Tree (9/10)- Large tech tree with faction-specific techs. Some technologies and be acquired by performing quests. Each age has military, economic, industrial, scientific, and diplomatic technologies to research.
Multiplayer (9/10)- It works.
Overall this is an excellent 4x game. If you buy it, I highly recommend picking up the guardians expansion. The guardians expansion completes this game by making this game fun during an entire match. I repeat, buy the guardians expansion.

As far as I can tell
is not a finished product or at the very least, not a smooth experience. So the unique mechanic in the game is finding sounds for 8 step sequencer (basically you can play the game to your own soundtrack created from those sounds) Was the mechanic utilized intuitively? Not really. It is just kind of there as a sandbox tool and it did not create any worthwhile gameplay elements. Although I really enjoyed the aesthetic there are noticeable issues with camera lag and the flickering world. For $7 I expected a more refined experience considering 60-90 minute length.
If you ever tried composing music on PC you will find a familiar 8 step sequencer as the focus of this game (like a beat VST) Which is a really cool concept but the game does not incorporate it well into gameplay.For a game that is meant to be all about sound, there are significant audio problems. You can turn your own music on/off but there are other sounds around you. So music ends up overlapping and being annoying as a result. Maybe the music in the world should stop if you using the sequencer? Who listens to 2 songs at the same time. On top of that, some of the loops have a rather irritating sound quality. Also, most of the game has no voice acting except a useless menu announcer that only breaks the immersion of the game.
I really like the design in general. There are some amusing animated moments and the only stage has a very cool surreal environment. Now the problem is that I expected more stages. The game even tells you in the "Help" that completing a DJ part takes you to next stage (it takes you to the credits) Unfortunately, there are some visual glitches and frankly, the movement feels a bit bumpy. You can control the game with Point&Click, WASD or Analog. So at least they provided enough control options. It looks fine but if I was to justify the price based on animation quality alone it would have to be longer.
The game throws you into the level with too much going on at the same time. Things are happening and I am not sure why they are happening. You can find different items that automatically interact with objects around the level ( which is technically not a puzzle at that point ) I am not even sure if every item had a purpose. So I guess this game is closer to the interactive cartoon which would be fine if it was paced better. You meet few characters and there is not much interaction. The game has virtually no dialogue so I had no idea what is going on.

We published an article based on a demo of this game that we were able to play before release.
Here are some quotes from the article:
"[...] Beat the Game starts out with the player character riding across a desert on a hoverbike. The player is not told where he came from or where he is headed, but he ends up crashing, damaging his bike to the point that it no longer runs. Rather conveniently, he is stranded next to a Carbon Dioxide vending machine and decides to grab himself a can of Carbon Dioxide. Upon drinking it, he sees what is essentially a beholder floating in the sky and an elaborate red chair sitting upon a nearby sand dune. Upon sitting in the chair, what appears to be the roots of a tree spring forth from the ground and pull him into it. He later awakes in a room underground and thus the player’s true adventure into the game’s surreal world begins.
Beat the Game is played much like a standard point and click adventure, with one primary difference: players can move the camera and player character around freely. Players adventure around and interact with various objects, picking some up for later use as they go. Inventory management is simplified somewhat, in that items are automatically used when you come in contact with the objects that they are intended to be used with, but you are also given no indication of what items might be used with or where the objects that they are used with are located. I believe that the reason for the simplification is partially because the puzzles are more of a means to an end than anything significant, but I’ll get to that later.
[...]
Now, the reason that I say that the game’s puzzles are largely just a means to an end is that the game revolves almost entirely around music and the obtaining of various samples that are used in that music. The player has a Mixer, which holds the aforementioned samples. You can have one sample from each category active at any one time, or even just turn off all samples from a specific category. You can also modify each sample by changing its volume or changing the potency of various special effects, which usually just means some sort of echo effect. Once you are finished editing your current loop, it then plays in the background as you explore. It’s an extremely simple process that has enough depth to be enjoyable, but not so much that it will baffle the average user.
[...]
Despite the fact that I was only able to play for fifteen minutes, I am fairly sold on Beat the Game. Its unique world is brought to life with stunningly well realized and well animated characters of all sorts. It also manages to incorporate the creation of music in a way that is both user-friendly and actually relevant to the game’s core gameplay. I certainly look forward to playing more of it when I can and recommend that you keep an eye out for a chance to play it yourself."

To start off, I really want this game to succeed and become a big thing. And I truely appriciate all the work the developers have put into it. I am trying to enjoy this game. But in its current state, the game is just not fun.
1. There is way too much micromanaging.
I can barely get any time for my players to practice or stream because they are always needing something. Whether they are hungry, thirsty, or tired, it just isn't fun to have them run around the house, filling their needs, only for them to need to go to bed as soon as you are done. It also doesn't help that some players just end up "freezing" and won't do anything you tell them to. This game is not the Sims, and I didn't get this game to play the Sims. I just wanted to be the manager of an E-Sports team.
2. The map
The map for this game looks kinda ridiculous. I would rather just have real world locations and we can select where we want our team to be situated. It is much more relatable when I can recognize the world.
3. Mood
Mood is very difficult to keep up. It doesn't help that when mood is low, it is pretty much a vicious cycle, as you will lose more games, which in turn lowers the mood. This also goes hand in hand with players needs.
I actually enjoyed the game as PGM. It just bugged me that nothing I did would help because the games were random. I had all maxed out players and we would still get killed in the majors. But atleast it looked good, and it was a step in the right direction. I would have been fine with the same game with higher skill caps and less RNGness. But instead we got this. A whole revamp to the original idea. I don't want to build a gaming house. I don't want to take care of 5 individual players. I just want to train my team, become profitable, make a name for my team, and eventually become the best in the world. But in the game's current state, I think I would drive myself insane trying to accomplish that. One last note: I enjoyed the Counter-Strike-esque much better, but now I have a game in which I cannot relate to at all because it is nothing like a currently existing game.
My advice: ditch the whole needs thing, or make them decay MUCH MUCH slower. Change the ingame world to the real world. Rework mood: make it have less effect on the players, make it much harder to decrease.

Having fully completed this game, I now would say that the game was a disappointment.
It began on a path of mystery, where the "Voice" was our main form of exposition and the player needed to solve riddles and puzzles to further digress along the plot. However, as you get into the riddles of the white pawn (save the girl) they become more of a hallucinogen-like drug trip than a fantastical riddle/puzzle. The black pawn scenario (save yourself) reveals more about the plot outside of the riddles, while still giving puzzles and mazes for the player to solve. Although the black pawn scenario goes against most of our human nature in terms of choices, it is the better option for gameplay and plot.
The mechanics of the game are smooth and feel natural when playing. The proportion of objects is normal size, and doen't make the main character seem too small or too big for the world around him.
The idea behind the game is not new. I remember having the same feelings playing this game as I did playing Myst, an older, better and well planned puzzle/riddle game. The only difference with Only If is that I found myself constantly going online for playthroughs and solutions to the puzzles due to poorly designed hints and puzzle design.
The characters were interesting, and made me want to play the game to find out more about their stories, but there is a continuity error in the plot from the White Pawn and the Black Pawn. This needs to be fixed for the players who play the game for the achievements.
The achievements needed to be more vague, due to the fact that I found myself easily accomplishing the tasks neccessary to get them. It felt more like a numb agreement more than a hard earned success.
I hope to see this game developed further due to it's potential, but right now, it is not ready. If you want to play it, go ahead, but I would wait until the game is improved.

The only other game that I can compare this to is Zachtronic Industries' SpaceChem as both have gameplay that is very much like programming. In particular the Great Permutator's swap machine, randomiser, duplicator and what is effectively the equivalent of an if-statement make the whole game feel like a cross between some sort of esoteric programming language (an obscure language that exists purely for entertainment) and the kind of puzzle games that people used to make for handheld consoles, but with 16-bit console/retro PC graphics.

Very challenging puzzle game. I'd call it a programming puzzler, as it has the feel of hand-optimizing assembly language. You're sorting, adding delays etc. Highly recommended for the patient, deep thinker.

A permutation is a combination of objects in a specific order. This concept helps describe the overall objective of the game, to guide colored blocks down a transport puzzle to reach pre-determined destinations in specific order. A better name for the game, perhaps, could have been "Great Iterator", not because the grueling puzzles in this game often require trial&error problem-solving, but because they frequently must be constructed such that blocks loop through the puzzle several times, interacting with puzzle pieces multiple times until the puzzle’s conditions are met.
The puzzles can be solved with two different types of pieces. These are the conveyor, which move a block to the adjacent square in the direction in which it is drawn, and devices, modifier pieces that may change the block’s color, that have variable points of output, that collect blocks and releases them simultaneously when enough are inserted and so on. The puzzles require patience and lateral thinking. They are very difficult, particularly if you try to solve the puzzles in the fewest number of moves possible. With 50+15 boards and a built-in editor, Great Permutator has more than enough content to satisfy those who appreciate genuine challenge.

Great Permutator is real brain-burner puzzle game.  This game is a lot of fun but wow does it make you think.  It reminds me a lot of programming logic and such.  It's really fun, and you feel like a genius after solving almost any puzzle after the first couple easy ones.
EDIT: After some time I will add this:  The game is still really fun, but unlike games like spacechem or infinifactory, there are very limited amounts of solutions.  It's more of a find one or two unique solutions or it won't work, rather than let you solve it and try to optimize.  This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it does feel somewhat constrained.

Not only was I rewarded for applying the critical thinking skills that I already had, I learned about the limits of my intellect, and developed it at the same time.  Much like the jump from imperative programming to functional, even practiced puzzle gamers and critical thinkers will find themselves grappling to construct the strange loops of logic (ala Godel, Escher, Bach) required to rewrite the incorrect solutions the implied layouts provide.
Not only are many of the initial solutions challenging to reveal, players are encouraged to develop their score to compete with the best in every level, and shaving one tile off of a score can require a substantial shift.  I take pride in knowing that the majority of my solutions are tied for the best out there, and that by the time I reach completion (lord willin`), there will be haunting imperfections in my record, and intellectual arch-nemeses whose monikers I will scorn, but I will likely never meet.
Part of me fears I don't quite have the edge to pull it off.  Some puzzles I haven't solved genuinely hurt my feelings because I can't wrap my brain around why all the permutations I can deduce don't work.  I explore failed alterations that weren't even close to plausible after all.  At first I skipped a puzzle here and there, because I'd come back to it after doing something I could wrap my head around.  Now I can't proceed without solving one that already haunts me.
That is mastery in design.  That is why you owe it to yourself as a classy intellect to put this bad boy on your shelf and show the world what you've got.

The graphic detail is really great and the factions are interesting.  My giving it a thumbs down comes from a couple of key issues.  1. The research options aren't as tactically linked as Civ 5, it's hard to see how your choices are going to offer you any andvantages over your rivals. 2. The way you seige a city  is frustrating, especially if the random army of two, seiges your heavily fortified city with troops and all, halting your production, but no clear way to attack them with any advantage.  Maybe I'm missing something? 3.  The diplomacy part, just seems wrong, you end up having to commit way too much resources to get anything in return, allies switch on a turn for little reason. 4. likely my biggest issue with the game, and maybe it's because of the CIV brainwash, but you don't really exploit tiles in the same way.  You get the whole land mass, your cities have limited growth and yes you can extract resources and so forth, but you just don't have control over the individual hexes.  Just could never feel that my decisions after a 100 turns was driving me to any specific strategic victory.  Yet the AI was getting close to a victory somehow.

- Confusing game mechanics. The game tells you to 'press E'. You 'press E'. You live. A few steps ahead, the game again tells you to 'press E'. Eventually, you realise you actually have to turn around and run down a path that has appeared behind you, which you didn't notice because you were too busy pummeling your 'E' key through your desk. I don't believe in holding the player's hand constantly through any game, but this is not the way to establish a gameplay mechanic.

This is basically an indie puzzle game, built as a discoverable situation with no real guidance.  In other words, be prepared to die a lot.  You'll say "What the ffffffffff" in a lot of different ways, a lot of different times while playing through this game.
Initially, I almost gave up due to the button-mash-to-stay-alive thing that happens at the beginning and drove me a little nuts, not to mention a couple of programming objects failing to screen draw directions on occasion, but once I got beyond that, it was worth it.
This game is different, weird, and a bit heady (bordering on moments of pretentiousness).  In a world of sameness, it's refreshing to see a developer take a bit of risk, as well as listening to and hearing feedback from the community.
The big con you'll notice is that there's a terrible variance in the DRC (dynamic range compression).  In other words, it's REALLY REALLY quiet sometimes and nearly deafing at others.  I cranked the volume to catch dialog, only to have the floor shake because of audio some minutes later.  Had the developer though to simulate headphones for the character, it might've helped the experience quite a bit.  Especially given that the audio is intrinsic in puzzling solving and the experience.
The graphics, however, are pretty great considering it's free AND indie.  There are some really heavy atmospheric moments where I noticed that the music and vibe had increased my heart rate pretty effectively.  Awesomesauce.
Totally worth checking out and playing through.  Don't be discouraged.  Pop on some headphones (it makes it a bit easier) and be prepared to play with the volume a little.  And make sure your "what the fffff...?" is on standby.

Opinion is subject to change during development.
I expect to get more play time with Badass Hero, but I feel confident recommending it in its current Early Access state after 4 hours.
Badass Hero is a hard game, expect to die and restart plenty of times, but it does become easier little-by-little thanks to a permanent character progression system often found in other similar modern roguelikes.
My first dozen runs of Badass Hero were about getting acquainted with the controls, enemy types, and character progression system, all the while "oohing and aahing" at the wonderful comic book graphic style. Once I was comfortable controlling my badass, it opened up advanced platforming techniques like air dashing while wall-bouncing grenades and shooting at baddies.
After choosing a comic book (thematic set of levels) to play, each run had me discovering and equipping various weapons and armor pieces, found with both numerical random stats and special effects: rocket launchers that could freeze enemies, machine guns that could make enemies explode on death, and armor that made me invulnerable while air dashing, just to name a few. This item system aided in making each run feel fresh and surprising.
There are moments where the random level generation went against me, creating what felt like unfair, near-impossible to beat rooms, but with the right items, health pool, and skill, I felt there was still a sliver of chance. But the game is made to play over and over again.
Does the thought of finding a shotgun with piercing bullets and chance to ignite enemies excite you? Go on then, be a Badass Hero.

I tried this game because I love Renowned Explorers. Only the theme is similar, but otherwise they're totally different games. I know 3 hours probably isn't enough to write a review, but the bottom line is I regret buying this game and have no intention to continue playing it. It's simply not fun.
I have no issue with brutal difficulty, but the issue is not difficulty. It's that the game is not satisfactory. It feels like you win and lose largely because of randomness. And either way, it's simply not exciting. I also really love dice and I will say I do like the concept of the dice system, but combat is really not interesting at all. Again, it feels based more on randomness than strategy. Maybe if there were more dice, and  maybe bigger combos so that you want to hold dice more? But then it is just Yahtzee which isn't that interesting. I did like the system, but it feels incomplete.
Lastly, I very very much dislike that everything, time, hunger, fleeing, etc are all one system called Sanity. It makes no sense that eating increases sanity. The inventory limitations are awful as well and largely don't make sense. You can have a stack of 20 rations, but 1 extra hunk of meat takes up the same amount of space. Again, eating shouldn't increase 'sanity' it should increase 'hunger.' Walking should take up an amount of time for the day and use up Stamina. If it's going to be one meter, that's fine, but don't call it Sanity. It doesn't make sense.
If you like Oregon Trail type games that are brutal and unforgiving to a fault, this is for you. Otherwise don't expect a Renowned Explorers type of experience.

Curious Expedition is an excellent adventure with some really satisfying features. It's one of those games where you'll forever find yourself juggling your inventory and cursing with a clenched fist that you should of brought a shovel. It's a tough one to crack, but you will find yourself drawn to those little blank tiles where exposed map ought to be.
Once you've selected an adventurer (all of whom have different strengths) you'll set sail to 'the New World' in search of treasures and artifacts. Expeditions are limited only by the party members and inventory space, so the first couple of expeditions can feel very rushed, and you'll basically want to find yourself some new recruits immediately otherwise you won't be able to manage the tools you need for exploring as well as the precious treasures which make the expidition worth while. Not to mention the local fauna will almost certainly be inclined to try to eat you or chase you around the map. This, combined with secret caves, missing expeditions, native villages. cursed temples, mysterious traders and picturesque safe havens make for a very entertainning game that's different almost every time you play it.
Combat might make you do a little tilt of your head and a squint, but in a nutshell you need to use different dice combinations to perform a 'move'. These moves vary from attack, defense, status ailments and combinations of those three. You'll figure it out. The dice do a little shake to demonstarte that they are compatible.
I would love to see more people playing this game. It's an instant classic and is well worth it's price tag, steam sale or no.

From what I've seen, this game is considered terrible, to which I highly disagree. This game definitely doesn't pass as a Dungeon Siege game, the only thing that qualifies it is the lore that's in it (Which I think I gathered all but one piece of). It has many nerd-service moments, in which it refers back to the original game, and even some moments that refer to the second, but it's style is entirely different. I look at games for what they are, not what they should be. It's still a good game, full of great story-telling, and an alright Combat system. The Combat System could use a bit of work, and I would have liked some more companion interraction, but it was a different developer from the first two games, so first of all, you can't expect them to go all out like they would have. Second, people need to stop saying "It's not the same! It fails my professional inspection!" It was a bold move to go from a, well, I don't know what genre it is, but mostly mouse controlled, to a game that actually requires some thought into combat. The combat system is very situational, and quite challenging, I can say that in the last two games, the combat mostly depended on luck, and how geared out your characters were. This one depends on actual skill, with the gear of your characters... The learning curb is a bit off, seeing as how it went from disappointing cake-walk to frustrating fires of hell, but once you figure it out, it tends to be a rather well-thought-out system that actually levels up quite nice now that I think of it.
For those that couldn't pay attention to my horrible rant: It's not a Dungeon Siege game, though it has the lore of it. It's still a good game, for what it is. I highly recommend it. (Unless you're stuck on nostalgia rather than gameplay)

Having now played over 80 hours of Great Permutator and reaching #1 on the leaderboards, I feel like I should update the review, or actually, write a proper one.
Great Permutator is an unassuming game when you first see it, but turns out to be an extraordinary one as soon as you scratch the surface. The premise is simple enough - you have to transport red, blue and yellow blocks from the upper side of the screen to the bottom, using unlimited number of conveyor belts and a limited supply of special blocks, while fitting them all on a 11x11 board. However, after only a few levels you will find yourself scratching your head and wondering how to sort them properly.
And after that, the game grips your brain in its claws and never lets go. There are lots of levels that will make you think they're impossible, and make you feel oh-so-smart when you finally solve them.. that is, until you realise that getting it solved is just a beginning of the road.
Where the game shows its real greatness is the fact that every level has several different solutions. If you played many puzzle games, you know well enough that often a level has only correct solution, as devised by the author, and either you reach it or be stuck. Not in Great Permutator. Here you can solve the level by occupying 100+ tiles and be done with it. Or you can try to get an A+ solution. But while A+ solutions are good enough to get the achievement, they are not sufficient to snatch a good spot on the leaderboards.
Every level, apart from having a predefined (and known in advance) number of tiles you can occupy to get A+, has a world record, established by unknown player(s) and stored on the server. And reaching it is exponentially harder than reaching A+, to the point that as of now *nobody* found the best solutions to *all* levels at the same time. And even when someone does, there can still be some levels that can be solved in another, better, but yet unexplored way.
That said, I have little doubt that the game's author is a genius and I can't wait for more levels, as hinted by the now-empty "Add-ons" tab. Thank you for that GREAT game! ;-)

The old "review":

Recommended for puzzle game fans but don't expect it to hook you in as much as SpaceChem did.

I really enjoyed and recommend Victoria II with a few caveats. It won't appeal to everyone. Also each DLC expansion adds a different flavor and can make V2 feel like different game depending on which you load. This review is geared toward Heart of Darkness.
V2 is not CK2. I hate to define one Paradox game with reference to another, but there it is. Without cheating it will be difficult for any small nation to rise to a global power. It will be easy, however, for an existing global power to retain dominance. It can be fun to form Germany from a smaller power, split off Australia after colonization by Great Britain, or lock down trade in the East Indies as the Netherlands. Whatever you choose, you will need to focus on long-term goals because V2 mechanics favor gradual evolution over punctuated equilibria.
The real strategy is in economy management. Victoria II is more an economic simulator than strategy game. You can influence the world through clever commodity price manipulation, industrial production, and technology focus. You can always expand your empire through conquest, but the infamy system limits your ability to do so.
There are other mechanics to balance. Population (POP) nationality, class and occupation, and religion play a part. There are technology trees, diplomacy, colonization, political policies, and more. Everything, including the economy, influences and is influenced by these other mechanics. One shift can lead to dramatic other shifts over time, and it's interesting to watch how everything interacts. In most games you will notice the same story playing out with slight variations, and this can lead to boredom after a few runs.

Don't let the playtime fool you. I pirated this a long time ago (yeah, I know it's bad, but I eventually purchased it obviously), but i've played roughly over 300 hrs in this masterpiece.
This game goes extremely in depth with Economy and Diplomacy being the focus points. One can definitely get lost in all the sliders and diplomacy (still trying to get England to like me as #1 in the world)... but after a while you get a lot of what the game is trying to accomplish, and that is when your country will flourish.
Diplomacy:
This game uses a "sphere" system in which if you get a country into your sphere, you become the primary target in terms of trade (basically, you get all of the trade the country offers for a relatively cheap price). The game also uses a "Crisis" system in which when a Crisis Temperature in a region hits 100.. it's all out war with the belligerants that consist mostly of GP (Great Powers).
Speaking of GP... having a lot of GP's in your alliance as a weak nation is perfect (if you don't allow yourself to get sphered too quickly... i'm looking at you France). If you are a great power yourself, at the start of the game you're allowed only one GP, and if you're Prussia, you're basically screwed since France usually allies with Russia, and GB is willing to work with you at the beginning, then abandon you when you get too powerful... and then look to always declare war on you. Coming to think of it... resembles a lot like RL GB. All nations have a "Point System" that is divided into 3 values: "Military Power", "Prestige", and "Industrial Power".
Military Power: Points that dictate how much power your military has (takes into account technology, and number of Units/ and mobilized units)
Prestige: How well your country has done since the start of your campaign (Note: If you have a high Prestige, countries are willing to do deals with you much easier, and automatically generates "Sphere Points" to all countries.
Industrial Power: This is the most important part that will likely be the reason why you're rich, or why you're poor. The more Industry, the more money you can make from producing goods, and selling them.
Also, for Diplomacy... if you've ever played EU4 before this, then you are likely reminded of the "AE". Same applies here, but instead called Infamy. Infamy here however, will affect whether or not your allies will stay your allies... bare in mind when you go on a conquering spree xD. If you conquer too much too fast... you'll likely find yourself in a "Containment War" which basically means all the GP's that are not your allies will come crashing down on you (doesn't matter if you're focusing on the other regions of the world, so bare that in mind too).
Economy: If you were paying attention to your industry and pop (population) early in the game, you will almost always succeed in this. If you didn't go moblizing and losing all of your male populations, then there will always be men in factories (notice, when you mobilize, it's taking men out of the factories to fight in your war... so once the war is over, immediatly demobilize to get the survivors back to work).
My strategy every game is to take provinces from China very early in the game. That provides additional pop's, and if theres no work in China... your pop there will move to your mainland, which will fill up those factories really quick. Then you get a whole bunch of tax revenue aswell as extra men to fight in your wars.
There's a whole bunch of stuff I didn't include because I already burned my life into both this game, and EU4... theres more detailed stuff out there, but I hoped I convinced anyone reading this to purchase this game. Happy Blobbing!

*Whistles* This game has become a favorite of mine so I've got a lot of good to say about it- it does have some down falls, of course, but I didn't find anything to be game ruining.
POSITIVES
-The visuals are really, really gorgeous. All the backgrounds are well made and the character models have a lot of detail. The character models in general are gorgeous, the clothes seem to have a marble-like texture and the eyes stand out. They even move from pose to pose during dialogue and blink.
-The music keeps getting stuck in my head and is pleasant to listen to, there are quite a few different tracks to suit the different moods and they're also very well done.
-All of the routes are very different from one another, so playing a new route isn't a 'oh, this again' experience excluding the prologue. I haven't played many otome aside from free to plays, but the routes here seem to be very unique.
.
-Gosh, do I love the characters. Maybe they wont all be everyone's cup of tea
but I found most the characters to be interesting and likeable.
-Voice acting!!! I do love me some voice acting and Amnesia has it, professional voice acting even! I didn't find that any of the voice actors got annoying throughout my play, though I did find some voice actors to be better than others. Waka's voice actor specifically shone to me despite him being a side-characer.
-There were a few mysterys here and there- heck, one of the routes is essentailly a murder mystery without the murder. I found them enjoyable enough and finding out things bit by bit feels like putting together a puzzle.
-You can name your character whatever you want, which is nice.
-Choices you've already picked are highlighted green when you play through again.
NEGATIVES
-As gorgeous as the character models are if they don't move for a while or if your making a tough desicion it feels like they're staring into your soul. Also the necks look a bit weird, specifically Shin's.
-The same music tracks are used throughout ALL of the routes, so some of the more common everyday songs can be a bit boring after a while.
-...
-Cheesy dialogue at times. I suppose that's common in otome though.
-Rina, as I called her, doesn't have a voice. Maybe it's just me who's disappointed by that, but I found it a bit off-putting.
-I experienced quite a bit of lag while playing, nothing game breaking but enough to make switching between screens and menus a bit irking.
TIPS (some spoilers? maybe?)
-Don't start with the diamond world. Any of the other three routes would be good to start with but I feel that the Dimond world gives away too much for the other worlds and is too polarizing for a first route.
-Save at the end of the prologue when you're offered the choice of which world you want to go to, it saves time when you want to start a new route.
-The 'S' button is the shortcut to skip dialogue you've already read, which is useful for trying to get different endings in routes you've already completed.
-If you really want to wrap up the story you have to get the good ends in all four worlds
.

Pick your adventurer based on real-life characters and set off in search of fortune and fame through 6 Jules Verne inspired maps and perhaps the city will erect a statue in your honor touting you as one of the greatest adventurers to ever have lived!
PROS:
+ Choose from a slew of real-life adventurers such as Marie Curie, Nikola Tesla and Charles Darwin with their own stats, equipment and starting companions. A large portion can be unlocked through the game.
+ So many styles of play depending on who your main is... do you avoid combat altogether or become a beast slayer? Do you take down the slavers or trade for one of their slaves? How you do it is also a big question as well.
+ Many different selectable paths through randomly generated jungle, desert, arctic, dryland and prehistoric maps
+ A lot of strategy in what you bring with you before you leave on an expedition and what you trade to stay alive vs make fame/fortune when you get home.
+Chosing one of three perks after each expedition adds more strategy on top of everything else.
+ Have pack animals such as Donkeys (and Raptors) to carry your goods, train them to carry more or become mounts!
+ Amazing dice rolling combat system that allows for even more depth in what you want to do offensively/defensively
CONS
- No multiplayer so you can't play against friends
- If you do poorly on one map it is increasingly difficult to get back on your feet
I just fired this game up to play something for the night and I was in from the first map. The only way I can describe this is FTL-like strategy and gameplay set in a Jules Verne universe with board game mechanics.
You pick your main (all have different equipment and companions) and set off on your expedition. You can hire people along the way, trade for new equipment/weapons/goods, complete side quests and much more. You have to keep your "sanity meter" up or your crew will become dilusional and have a higher chance of something bad happening which is where the real "fun stuff" comes in. A nun I had hired turned into a cannibal and ate another member of my party... whhhaaaat?! Stealing goods from areas sets off traps and locals react to your actions as well so you don't get off free of charge.
The combat takes all of your characters dice and rolls them and you have to piece together certain "combos" that give you offensive or defensive attacks. This may sound crazy at first, but the strategy is unbelievable! Do you use the one dice to a regular attack for 1 damage into a precise attack for 3 damage or use it in a shield to protect you from 4 hits OR do you put it into a Feint attack which will stun multiple enemies... you can do multiple "combos" per turn so the strategy really becomes intense.
I caught on right away and played through one campaign that took me about 6 hours. It's definitely about the journey, not the destination. One of my characters, Tim Timers, left the group because he wasn't happy with our looting. Later on in that map he came back to apologize and join the group again. He stuck with me until the end and, on the final map stuck between an active volcano and a raptor when morale was getting really low, he came up with a speech that rallied everyone raising morale and we finished the map. No joke! It was amazing.
The only "negative" I could give the game is I wish there was multiplayer so I was playing against my friends rather than random AI bots, but this doesn't take away from the core of the game. It could only add another level on top of it.
Highly recommend this game for a good 6 hours or so of absolute fun!
