Warning: This game includes very upsetting scenarios (I'm looking at you, Toma). I would not let impressionable, young audiences play it.
I should start by saying that the reason I bought this game is because I watched the anime (which is based off this game) and I thought it would be interesting to see the different adaptations and interpretations. I think watching the anime can give you a good idea of what to expect in the most extreme paths (Diamond/Joker worlds).
In the game, each path leads to a full story, which makes it a lot easier to understand. The main character is still passive, which was the main complaint people had about the anime. Not every path leads to a healthy, happy relationship. I don't think anyone should play this game with the expectation of using it as reference for real life romance. That said, the CGs and voice acting are amazing. I also enjoyed the mini games, even if they're a bit buggy.
The general storyline/world building is not that great, but I didn't buy an otome game expecting to get the next Game of Thrones. What's important is the special scenes and those were really nicely written. I managed to laugh and be torn in quite a few of them.
My advice: if you want a mild, happy romance, this is not it (unless you stick to the clover world). Watch the anime first, then figure out if the themes are something you're ok with. If you are like me and enjoy comparing different adaptations of a single work, this might be an amusing game to analyze.

Relic Hunter Zero is a top down shooter in the same vein as Nuclear Throne thats been sprinkled with a tiny bit of Binding of Isaac's progression and unlocks. Despite being a freebie, this game ranks up there with some of the best top down shooters out there at the moment. And while seeming simple at first glance, the game actually has a lot more to it than first meets the eye. Each game mechanic that Rogue Snail chose to include in their (surprisingly free) game has multiple facets that add up quickly to create a well-polished, functional, and challenging skill-based shooter.
The gun play feels good, the sounds are strong, the screen shake adds to the impact, and the enemies fall when you'd expect them to, simply put: its visceral and satisfying. Each weapon has an effective range after which the damage falls off and enemies also take extra if hit in a certain place too, The damage indicators are nice and fit the flow of the game well. Grenades can travel over destructible cover to hit dangerous groups of enemies, and theres even an aim mode which lets you see further and increase your accuracy slightly. Ammo management is also a thing, rather than just having an infinitely firing weapon, each gun has its own magazine and reload times. You can use up whats in a mag and swap with a weapon on the ground without spending ammo from your ammo pools too. This can be a great way to stock pile early on and is surprisingly fun to swap weapons out all the time (but you dont need to!)
Movement mechanics seem fairly solid. You have stamina for sprint alongside a dash/dodge ability. The player is given everything they need to dodge, seek cover, return fire, and close the distance with the enemy if they want to get up close and personal with a shotgun or their fists. Beware though as melee also pulls from your stamina so you cant just dash in, hit and dash out. If i have -any- gripe at all its to say that using the keyboard and mouse, you can only seemingly dash in the 8 cardinal directions. Sprint and dash are bound to the same button which causes the accidental dash sometimes when you dont want it, or the inability to dash (because you end up sprinting instead.) But even with that said, the movement feels pretty good, even if it could use a bit of tweaking, an alternative key bind, and possibly an option to 'dash towards cursor' There is however a melee weapon that serves that function.
Each character has health and a rechargeable shield which can be upgraded slightly throughout the adventure. If your shield ever breaks though you will lose any boosted over-charge ability, so dont get complacent.. just rushing in and taking fire when you've got a big shield will lead to losing your shield powerups before you know it. Both your health and shield are determined by your choice of character and can be modified with relics that you unlock, as well as in-game pickups.
When it comes to unlocks you can unlock multiple characters, as well as guns, ammo, and relics to start the game with and make things easier. Like in Spelunky theres an unlockable level skip which can help you get back into the action a little more quickly if you find yourself too good for the early levels, and may put you at a slight disadvantage for increased challenge in the later ones. One thing that confused me at first was that the store not only sells you items for your current run, but if you buy an item it also unlocks for your next play through and you can start with it if desired.
The AI is even a decent challenge too. Enemy variety is moderate, Ive only seen a handful of types in the few hours that I've played but what is there is well placed when coupled with the variety of weapons they can use (and will occasionally drop when defeated.) Different enemy soldiers will fight together as a more effective group, and sometimes the enemy will even run away for cover if it needs to. The AI can even interact with itself on occasion which is a really nice touch that adds a bit more variety to the gameplay, can even be used to your advantage sometimes.
All in all the developers at Rogue Snail really hit a homerun with Relic Hunters Zero. The music didnt quite resonate with me fully on all of their tracks, but they nailed their gameplay mechanics in this title without any question. They even made it an open source project as well, meaning that we will likely see some great content mods come to this freebie because the ground work the Devs put in made for such an exceptional gaming experience. You can tell that the team put a lot of love and effort into creating their game; it shows in the influences taken from all over the genre being brought together in a way like we had not quite seen before.
Relic Hunters Zero might be a free to play game, but its more polished on launch than most of the paid titles we see on Steam these days. Imprisoned Light is a game where you choose one of 5 characters, kill enemies that are spawning constantly, and feed the crystals with souls you get from the enemies. The concept itself sounds decent, but the execution isn't really that great.
First of all, there is no tutorial. There's a how to play screen, but it feels like it's lazily put together. It's also kinda easy to overlook for the first time you're playing. When I played the game for the first time I didn't know what the crystals did, so I was really confused. It turns out you have to feed it with souls and protect it from enemies. If you don't do that in less than 100 seconds, a Grim Reaper appears and pretty much kills you. It's confusing and it leaves a bad first impression.
There's also a level up system. After killing certain number of enemies you can upgrade your health, attack power, mana, or speed. But it's not that useful when you think about it, since the difference it makes is pretty small. And the only difference between the characters is these 4 stats and their special moves. But it's better than nothing, I guess.
The game's also not addictive enough to keep you interested for a long time. Despite the game not being too easy (especially when compared to the older versions), you don't get that feeling makes you wanna continue when you die. That's probably because the game's pretty repetitive and the game doesn't really count your score or process, which also means you have to start over each time you die. That's not what I call good game design.
The graphics are okay. Backgrounds, (most) tiles, and some of the larger sprites look pretty decent, but the others look mediocre at best. Both the shapes and the shading of the sprites are pretty amateurish looking. The palette also lacks hueshifting which results with all colors looking pretty boring. The effects are also pretty bad. They are clashing with everything else and they are really pixelated looking. The UI looks decent at least, even though I feel like it could get a bit more polish. But overall, the graphics are just okay.
The music is probably the best part of the game. Despite sounding kinda generic they are pretty fun to listen. The sound effects are nothing special though, and some of them are REALLY loud compared to everything else.
There's also a Co-op mode. It's probably more fun than the single player mode, but since I don't have anyone to play with I can't really talk about it. But I doubt it would change my general opinion about the game at all.
Overall, it's an okay game. I would recommend it if it was free, but I can't recommend it right now because there isn't any reason to play it, even after all those updates. Yeah, there are new content and more polish but that doesn't mean the game's less flawed.
There are similar games on steam that play much better, just play them instead.

Don't be fooled by the screenshots: This game is a nice 16-bit attempt but, unfortunately, it's incredibly amateur.
The game has way too much going on in the graphics front. Colors are mishmashed and thrown together (why are background objects as bright as foreground ones), the environments have WAY too much clutter, sometimes it's hard to tell what is a platform or ground from the background, and at too many times there is foreground foliage that blocks too much of your view (If this is unintentional it's an amateur mistake, if it's intentional it is neither fun nor challenging). The cutscenes look awful as well.
The controls are sometimes awkward and ANY area involving pushing moveable crates onto water is a headache. Why doesn't the robot simply move along with the crate? Why do I need to manually move him along with it? Again, this isn't fun and it's a terribly cheap challenge. There is a level in stage two where you need to do this for an extended amount of time without any checkpoints and it is unbelieveably frustrating (I have actually quit the game since this area and do not intend to come back).
Apparently no one tested the levels for collision either as far too many levels with the jetpack allow to move behind walls or enviromental objects you're not supposed to, some of which trap you or kill you or all around mislead you.
It doesn't help that certain enemies come in different sizes and are not easily destroyed by your guns. This is most noticeable in the spider boss level where you simply cannot shoot the green enemies blocking your path because they're at an awkward height. This would have been easily fixed simply by not having the grenade attack hurt you ala Metroid. And while you have multiple weapons at your disposal almost none of them are very useful outside of the grenade.
And speaking of the spider boss, why is the boss level in the MIDDLE of the world? Why did the world just end a couple levels later when I went down a random sewer pipe? The pacing is just bizarre.
I wanted to like the game, and I realize it's probably a first attempt at making a game, but this is just too unfinished and poorly thought out for me to enjoy. This could have easily used more time in the kitchen, first attempt or not.

I played Terrian Saga: KR-17 for about half an hour so far.
The presentation of the game reminded me of a number of old 2D side scrolling games including Jazz Jackrabbit, Duke Nukem, commander Keen, megaman and Sonic.
You control a little robot and traverse through typical 2D platform levels populated with various enemies. You have your main blaster attack, a selection of items such as grenades, mines and a cruise missile. Occasionally you are given a jet pack so that you just fly around instead jumping.
I spent the first 5 minutes or so trying to figure out the controls. I got stuck at the very beginning because I didn't know what the jump button was or how to activate objects. I had go back to the main menu a couple of times and on returning to the game you cannot skip dialogue so it was a bit tedious. Also not all the controls are listed in the menu and I found that tutorial tips are easily missed or not clear. Anyway I eventually figured it out lol. Things turned to not be too bad. You really need to look where you are going to avoid hazards in this game, some are insta-death. I frequently died and had to start from the last checkpoint. But thankfully they are generously dispersed around each map. Controlling your cruise missile is basically like playing snake. It moves quite fast and easily clips into objects and explodes prematurely. The game has lot's typical platforming type of stuff e.g. jumping from one platform to another and avoiding dangers. I preferred using the jetpack to just fly most the time over jumping.
While the game is not really bad. I didn't feel that it was special and I don't really have any urge to play it more than I did. I didn't really feel engaged in the story and the game tends to have characteristics which are potentially annoying that you typically get with old side-scrollers. I would only recommend it to those with a passion for these kinds of retro 2D side-scrollers.

KR-17 is pretty obviously a retro-style platformer that harkens back to the good old days of the SNES. It plays very similarly to the 2D Duke Nukem Games or Megaman, but with some different twists. Really, if you like games from this genre, at $4- you can't really go wrong here. It won't knock your socks off, but it'll be a pretty good nostalgia trip.
Features:
* Gameplay is pretty generic, jumping shooting are standard faire.
* You have 4 extra attacks, plus a guided missile, largely for enemy destruction, but sometimes for puzzle solving. They're largely unecessary, but can be useful in certain cases. The guided rocket is a bit OP if you can manage to control it properly.
* The soundtrack is pretty solid, and while the songs can get repetitive, you won't be around a level long enough for it to get annoying.
* Most levels are pretty simple: the only goal is to reach the exit. Unfortunately, most levels require you to flip a bunch of switches, and it's pretty easy to miss one or two. Doesn't take much time to go back and find them, but its still a bit annoying.
* The controls are weird. Especially with the jetpack (you have to hold up on the right stick, and move horizontally with the left stick, otherwise you'll stop flying and probably die). Once you get used to that, it's pretty smooth.
* The enemies feel more like traps/obstacles than proper opponents, which isn't bad, but it does make them feel a little slapped down on the levels.

As I embarked upon my Curious Expedition, my spirits were lifted at the prospect of adventure and fame to be won. As the expedition entered its hundredth day, I found myself tired and slowly driven insane by these mysterious new lands. I sat beside the fire eating meat from the leg bone of my last companion, I reflected upon the choices that led me to this junction in my life and wondered if I would ever see society again.
The Curious Expedition is, at its heart, a text based rogue like adventure, and so story weighs in as the most important aspect of this game. It's set up like a choose your own adventure only rather than select an option and turn to that page, you select one of the two to four options usually available to you that either opens up other choices (be they dialogue, travel, trading, further exploration, or combat). The story constantly shifts and adapts to your choices and since each playthrough is also randomly generated, this leads to hundreds of story variables. It is unlikely that you will ever play through the exact same story twice.
So, what is the story then? The basis of The Curious Expedition is a competition between famous explorers and other historical personages.  Your end goal in every expedition is to find a lost golden pyramid, although you can also take on side quests such as to find a loved one or bring back specific artifacts. The winner is the explorer that gains the most fame from their various explorations through quickness of exploration, finding the pyramid, and so on. There is a number attached to that, and if you reach that number, you win the game. What happens through your journey is a personal account of your travels. So, for perspective, here is my in game journal from one ill-fated exploration (the developers weren't the best at using proper grammar or syntax, so you will see plenty such errors in this snippet):
The developers have set the game up in such a way that you can choose to read your expeditions as per the example above, and each expedition receives their own URL, to be held onto for eternity presumably. This was the one given to me for this playthrough. So, as you can see, the story you play through and later have transferred into a journal is completely subjective. The above represented a lot of the choices I made in that particular expedition.
I give this category the highest mark possible. 10 out of 10. Such diversity, humor, and fun all mixed into a tale of your own making.
The gameplay in Curious Expedition has a few different and interesting dynamics to it.
As I mentioned before, your choices come in the form of multiple text options. Once you have selected an option, you then see the results/consequences of said actions.
Sometimes, you gain standing with the local tribesmen, which is useful in finding henchmen, bartering for goods, being able to rest in their villages overnight, and so on. Conversely, losing standing with them can result in their unwillingness to help you, and sometimes even results in them trying to kill you. Other results include exploration, combat, and additional dialogue options which can result in cool things such as being offered treasure maps or being told the location of new lands to explore.
RNG is used in a couple ways here. RNG is represented by dice, of which there are several different types (combat, perception, defense, and so on). Dice are acquired by your specialties and the specialties of your expedition companions (and animals). Each time a decision is to be made which would result in dice rolls, your total available dice are put into play. For exploration, it is as simple as matching the required dice roll with your actual dice roll. Failure results in negative consequences (generally some horrific accident or the actual death of a companion). For combat, you roll, and then match dice combinations to garner a wide variety of results, from basic defense and attack, to special attacks, heightened defense, and so on.
Travel in Curious Expedition is essentially hex based, but instead of turns, your distance traveled is accounted for in sanity points. The further you travel, the more sanity points you consume. If you travel further  than your sanity meter allows, there are also extreme consequences, from injury to murder and even cannibalism.
Everything in The Curious Expedition is ultimately impacted by your sanity meter, your selection of equipment, the encumbrance of said equipment, and the companions you select to travel with you. The sanity meter is pretty simple. This function in similar fashion to health meters, except the further you travel, the more your meter drains. You can restore sanity by eating, drinking, resting, and by unlocking certain other events. Should you reach zero on your on your sanity counter, the results are as I described above.

Full review on the Indie Detective Review Series:
Simple, Beauty
This is a real gem. The pixelart graphics are well-executed, the gameplay is fluid and often demanding, and the reward system makes the 2-hour playthroughs worth repeating. Combining the best that exploration and squad managment games have to offer, this simple indie title has a lot of character. With exploratory flare echoing great authors of the era like Lovecraft, Verne, and Kipling, there is always something new and unexpected to stumble across. The combat system too has its charm, but also quirks. Character classes roll dice (think Fantasy Flight RPG mechanics) to assemble attack and defence combos, which take experimentation and frequently fall short of tackling even middling enemies. However not every member of your team needs to survive; all that matters is getting that rare loot home to Britain, for queen, country, and everlasting glory.

The cycles of winter/summer with legitimately terrifying roaming armies *daemons* that take your cities if you are not careful, makes the game a survival 4x game for the first quarter of the game.

I think it's time I write my first real review of a steam game--and I'm happy to make it this one.
Victoria II has a steep learning curve, but if you open yourself up: it's easy and addicting.
The attraction to Victoria II is not its asthetics, it's its offering to let you take on a whole new history.
Victoria II plops you into 1836, right before the crowning of Queen Victoria and at the height of the British Empire. The Hapsburg Monarchy still rules the Austrian Empire and Germany is still divided into many small states. The Tsars rule over the Russian Empire that still seeks its greatest extents and America is not even 100 years old.  France emerges from the Napoleonic wars in defeat but a new spring is just around the corner. The Ottoman Empire is the "sick man of Europe" but with the right leadership can embrace the new age with renewed vitality.
And even more nations await emergence: Japan, China, and of course the oncoming rush for Africa will change the face of the world.
Any nation is playable in Victoria II. Even more can be released or formed. Almost every game is different.
War isn't the focus here. Though it is an intriguing aspect.
What will draw you in: is the diplomacy.
Now that may sound boring but pay in mind the dynamics here. Although the great powers rule and may keep you in-check, playing as one (or better-yet, using them to your advantage to gain power) will keep you thrilled.
The Great powers of the time compete to influence other, smaller nations. Intricate webs of alliances and spheres can easily turn a localized conflict into a world war.
Crises over disputed territories can cause Great Powers to go at-odds, lobbying other powers to join their side in the tension-packed period where the world can drift into destructive war.
Later in the game, these can mean "great wars" were defeat can mean total decimation.
In fact, each country is only one war-gone-bad from collapse.
Compete to establish puppet states who will obey your every whim.
Sphere nations to earn off their industry and almost garantee their support.
Colonize the unsettled worlds of Africa, the Pacific, and North America.
Keep other nations from doing the same.
Also there are different civilization levels. Primitive, Uncivilized, partially civilized, and civilized. Depending on what stage your in impacts your ability to function as a state as your technology will be way behind, you won't be able to build industries, ect. until you "westernize" and join the world as a modern-style nation-state.
This alone can be fun as you struggle to survive in the old ways or fight against your own people who resist your attempts to change their very culture.
Warfare itself is more fleshed-out than initially realized. Your armies' ability to do recconassaince, perform sieges, and fight in battle is dependent upon their specilized unit makeup and perhaps too-often ignored: their generals.
An army of 80,000 draftees can be thrawted by a smaller, diverse professional army and an excellently-chosen general who can earn fame by winning battles which will in-turn provide greater bonuses.
Naval power is a MUST to establish yourself as a colonial power. Blockades can WRECK your trade. And just as with armies: diversity and excellent Admirals can win you the day.
Trade itself can be largely ignored and should be automated unless you feel otherwise inclined.
Politics within your own country can grab your attention.
The availible government types are:
Democracy
HM's Government
Prussian Constitutionalism
Absolute Monarchy
Proletarian Dictatorship
Fascist Dictatorship
Borgeouseis Dictatorship
Presidential Dictatorship.
To better understand this, the political party in power decides your trade policy, your tax policy, your military spending, how you treat minorities, ability to intervene/control factories and industry, and your upper house (legislative body) will decide what reforms you can impliment.
Democracies are governments where the party in power is elected and they guide policy until the next election.
HM's Government are the same but you have the ability to change the government in power (though reforms will require the appropriate members in said upper house).
Prussian Constitutionalism is this wierd grey-area between Absolute Monarchies and Democracies though usually have elections.
Absolute Monarchies have no elections (which by the way are totally annoying and only nudge public opinion especially in large countries) and can choose the ruling party.
Then come the dictatorships which are usually single-party.
THE BEST PART IS YOU GET DIFFERENT FLAGS DEPENDING ON YOUR GOVERNMENT
SOMETIMES DIFFERENT NAMES.
An example is Mexico who, if they have a monarch, will change to the Empire of Mexico.
The United Kingdom will change to Great Britain if a democracy or the People's Commonwealth if a proletarian dictatorship,
These will also cause flag changes.
Rebels will lobby for reform changes or even radical government change. Sometimes you might want them to win. There's nothing wrong with letting the generals plot a dictator's downfall.
Now finally mods which really can give a lot of replayability to this game.
Mods are relatively easy to get though are not taken from the steam workshop but from websites like Moddb.
These mods have infinite potential offering different timelines, scenerios, new nations, new flags, new alternate timelines.
Some even add events to the more minor nations to make them more dynamic to play.
OH
ONE MORE THING
Multiplayer IS possible, don't worry. And trust me, it's awesome with friends.
You can coordinate to carve up continents for your empires.
You can plot against each-other. A great game is Austria and Prussia competing for dominance.
Here's how we do it:
Download Hamachi which will allow you to create a network your friends can connect to.
They will use the Hamachi-provided IP address the host of the network has to connect to your game.
It's advised to put the game to save often. We do half-years.
Make sure you verify the integrity of your game cache every time you play together. And close out of the game entirely if someone crashes and do so again just to be sure.
You MUST have the same version to operate.
If you want to load saves, the host (and only the host) needs to disable their firewalls.
another thing: the Host should host the hamachi network AND the multiplayer game.
We haven't tried mods yet.
To conclude this review, make sure you invest into this game (and hope someday for another Paradox game that picks up where this one leaves off--1939 or somewhere around that era). It may seem overwhelming at first, but attack and google around if you're lost. Usually you can find a forum post where they have your question or you can start your own.
Find friends to join the game with you.
Take pictures. f12.

Amnesia memories is one of the few visual novels which I have completed. Often I’d start one but would end up losing interest half way through the novel but amnesia memories held my interest throughout the majority of the story.
I have to admit that the initial plot is average and is something that comes up quite often. As it centres around a girl who has amnesia and sets out to remember her past without letting others suspect her of her memory loss. It has a mystery plot with a twist
At that point it will start to make sense and it eventually comes to a nice conclusion.
Characters- you have your cliché love interests, the tsundere, the emotionless smart guy, the playboy, the yandere and the…I’ll leave the last guys personality up in the air, as he’s my favourite character and it’s best to discover what he’s like as you progress through the story. Furthermore each hero is unique and different enough to keep you interested. Side characters such as Mine and the manager seem to have a different personality depending on the route which keeps you guessing there motive and whether they want to hurt you or befriend you.
The soundtrack and voice acting is superb.
At times their may have been moments where I wanted to scream at the heroine
but I endured through them so I could get to the Joker route and get the good ending in that, I did not regret it one bit.
Overall I recommend this visual novel to those who are fans of the genre, want to get into visual novels or simply want something more and better than its anime adaption.

so, first review! hopefully i can be of some help ;w;
10/10
1) gorgeous art and stunning CGs [which are also very plentiful! if i'm not wrong there are about 30 per route for the first four, so that alone is about 120...i can't speak for the hidden route, but i can't imagine much changes]
2) original premise and good storywriting; a predetermined boyfriend is definitely a change!
3) unique love interests who do have their flaws [perhaps some of them a little too much!] but are, in general, a refreshing change from the lovey-dovey, completely perfect boys found in other otomes
4) beautiful soundtrack and voice acting
5) great atmosphere and it's very easy to get very connected to the characters/situation
1) lack of english voice acting; personally this didn't bother me as i normally play in japanese either way, but i know that some people prefer english voice acting
2) the parameter system [affection/trust/suspicion and doubt in a certain route] is not ever really explained in the game, which can be kind of confusing
3) the game can be kind of slow to progress and a few days often go by without much happening
4) some of the characters are
problematic [though this won't bother everyone]
5) super minor, but the air hockey game is super duper hard to play due to lag; if you're one for getting all achievements in a game, this will probably be a bit annoying for you! [tip: disabling all sounds before playing air hockey usually lessens the lag a little, but it's still far from ideal]
overall, i really had to struggle to come up with cons for this game;
is quite possibly one of the most unique, well written otomes i've ever played and really sets the bar quite high for those to follow. the characters are all very well written, their development is shown very clearly and they really do feel much more human than a lot of the love interests in other VNs; to boot, the artwork, OST and voice acting is astounding. a real sense of mystery and tension can be felt in this game and i wholeheartedly recommend to those considering playing to buy it because you won't be disappointed; before long you'll find yourself falling in love with this comical, memorable cast.

Only If is a first-person puzzle/adventure/exploration/3D platformer game developed by indie developer Creability. You play Anthony, a young kid who wakes up after a party. After awakening, things quickly become… weird.
The core of Only If is to make your way through a series of rooms by solving puzzles. I love puzzle games and was expecting something like Gone Home or The Stanley Parable. It didn’t live up to expectation (I will get to that later), but I will say that Only If had a few new ideas that I really enjoyed. I also generally liked the ambience of the game, which was a great combination of creepy and pretty.
But… Unfortunately, the game is also filled with bugs and difficult controls. Some of the puzzles require trial and error which in combination with unskippable dialogue and cutscenes makes the experience some times tedious. I am also missing subtitles as many of the puzzle hints are given in difficult-to-hear one-time dialogue.
The difficult controls really manifest themselves in one of the later levels, which for some reason turns into a loooong platformer. I consider myself pretty good at these types of things, but I still kept bumping into edges and falling to my death, having to restart again and again.
I also have few nice things to say about the storyline. I liked it at the beginning, but the plot twists were strange and juvenile, and I would have much rather liked no explanation at all instead of the story that we got. Also a warning for the sensitive: There is a lot of swearing and adult themes baked into the story.
Even though I can’t recommend this game I am looking forward to seeing the next game by this developer. After all, I liked the general idea of Only If so with some more time and polish the next game they produce may be a hit.
(Update: They made a new game which is really cool - OLDTV ! )
Only If is free on Steam so you may still want to give it a go. Otherwise if you want to play a game similar to this I recommend The Stanley Parable instead.

Here's the thing, plain and simple. Most people are deterred by DLCs, but the fact of the matter is, this game was released almost 6 years ago. This is how modern games should work; Buy a game for 60 dollars, and then the developers work on it for multiple years. This confers a certain amount of learning curve retainment. Once you have the DLCs, the game is transformed into aneffective kingdom micro manager. So, the game doesn't cost $40 to be any good, it costs $240 once you've bought the DLCs. Which brings me to Paradox's business practices and its dis-respect for the gaming community. You know - their customers.
If making a game which is really only any good with hundreds of dollars of DLCs isn't bad enough, then charging twice for the privilege is something entirely new. As I said, my original version was purchased through GG. They ported the game to Steam and Paradox provided activation keys for the base game. According to GG they didn't provide them for the DLC's. As I said, the game is really only enjoyable with the DLCs. Paradox should be ashamed of such blatant double charging, but of course they're not - they just 'can't go into it any further.
So in short the base game is barely OK.  With the DLCs its playable, but massively overpriced. Paradox's business practices are shameful.

Oh my god these negative reviews!
Here's a summary of them for you:
1) No Chinese!

Before I go any further, let me remind you at this point in time everyone is playing the BETA version of the game. There will be crashes, there will be bugs. Most of them will probably be fixed on release day. If these bugs are what is putting you off buying, then hold off until release and check back then.
With that out of the way:
You have to approach the FM series like you would FIFA: Each year is an evolution, not a revolution.
Except, where FIFA upgrades their graphics each year to make it look shiny and new, most of FM's improvements come under the hood. The match engine, even in the beta, is a distinct improvement over last year's, with fullbacks no longer dominating match ratings and awards. If you want the football simulator with the most realistic match engine, this is it.
Is the game worth the purchase price? Well that depends on how much you're paying and how much value you want for that price. If you're outside the UK and don't want to hedge your bets on a Steam refund, I strongly suggest shopping around online for the best price in pounds, and buying that way. The exchange rates are favourable for pretty much everyone else. I bought it for 29.99 GBP, which converted to NZ$52 including exchange fees, a saving of 42% over the standard Steam price of NZ$89.99 in New Zealand.
I've already clocked up over 50 hours, so that's a dollar an hour, and that will only get better.
Bottom line: If you are looking for a good football sim, have about 30 GBP of local currency to spend, and don't speak only chinese (you're reading this so that's not an issue), then buy this game.

There aren't many games where I'd find it fun to be forced to eat my scout dog in order to get to the golden pyramid only to find out that I needed a moonstone in order to enter, and I'm forced to escape in a hot air balloon, thus blowing my chances of winning.  Or where my donkey eats a healing mushroom that inadvertently causes him to dance around spouting gibberish and turn cannibalistic so that I wake up one morning and my interpreter is gone. But these are the sorts of things I've come to expect in this game, and I've learned to take it in stride and try again. In the meantime, it's been great for some laughs and stretching my thinking. You definitely learn the hard way in this game, and some things (like the aforementioned moonstone) might have been better explained and thus prepared for, but trips to the wiki are making things somewhat clearer. Combat was pretty inscrutable at first even with the tutorial, but eventually I was able to puzzle out enough to do pretty well, and it's in keeping with how the game forces you to evolve your tactics as it throws you random curveballs. Sure, there's repetitive aspects, but that's how you get to use what you've learned, and at the same time there is an astounding amount of variety in the details that keeps things fresh. Like now I know that when I desecrate a certain shrine and unleash a huge flood that sweeps me into an impassable mountain range, I damn well better have some dynamite with me to blow a passage out or I'm screwed. So yeah, it can be frustrating, but you can't stay mad too long 'cause it's all kind of charming and funny as well.

I played for about 7 hours as of this writing, and that covered 4 games, which included about 15-ish expeditions, and I got to the point that I feel like I've seemn all the variations. The events become overly familiar, and the character's special abilities don't have a clear an obvious enough effect to make playing with each of them a differnt experience.
The game looks like it would have the kind of replay that you see in something like FTL, but there is simply not enough variety to create that kind of experience.
The 'moral' decisions are always the same: "Do what's good fro the natives or do what's good for your expedition?" and that gets a bit stale. In general the theme of the game is a bit trite.
If you're only looking for about 5-10 hours of play for these neat mechanics, then go for it. But, overall, I'm going to mark this one not recommended because it doesn't live up to its potential as a replayable adventure.

There are many moments like this where it feels like a little more time could have made for a much less frustrating experience. text:
My Steam career lives and breathes roguelikes. I never played Rogue, but the current sea of indie titles leveraging the content-efficiency and replayability of roguelike structure has washed up some truly brillian RNG experiences for me. No big-budge, cinematic masterpiece setpiece could possibly compare to my last crusader, at -100 Sanity and teetering on Death's Door just steps from the finish line, finally succumbing to dysetnery. I love roguelikes.
The Curious Expedition seems to take its main inspiration from early 20th-century Mighty Whitey colonial adventure pulp, and then pumps it through the low-res but high-quality filter of SCUMM-engine point-and-click adventures many players of this game will have grown up on. Manage your inventory space and your party's loyalty in order to unlock each Expedition's MacGuffin, in hopes of getting home before your 4 rivals to claim high-score glory in your homeland. Curious Expedition is naively charming, seemingly just cartoonishly aware of the groteque historical violence most colonial explorers inflicted on the lands they explored -- the game has you abducting aboriginals and rending landscapes in the jingoistic pursuit of plundered artifacts and desecrated altars. I don't expect every little game to make bold statements about social justice, but the rich fictional writing is there, and it seems a swell opportunity to satirically examine the mighty whitey paradigm has been missed entirely.
The game play rather sloppily, in terms of player decision impact. Fail states are extremely predictable and can rarely be avoided. This is common in roguelikes, where tragic failure is presumed. But in Curious Expedition, there is little stress in watching your party slowly decay. The different characters (including JIM ♥♥♥♥ING STERLING, SON) feel samey, talk samey, and it is hard to feel attached to them. Expedition failure happens suddenly; usually one catastrophe will chain-react into others until your leader is left alone and eventually succumbs to a final insanity event. Maybe content updates  can alleviate this, but it seems baked into the game that taking a wrong turn on an empty map can screw you so badly you'd never have had the resosurces to backtrack to the other side before losing your party. I like that the diary narration actually contains game-relevant information rather than just flavour. But losses in this game are quite rarely a learning experience.
Curious Expedition was beginning to excite me in its first 2 hours, but I rapidly smashed into its skill and content ceilings after that, and at 5 hours of play, I do not expect to return to the game without significant design or content updates. After a few hours of experience, it is plain to see that the player doesn't have too much to contribute to Curious Expedition's quaint systems. This game rides on its aesthetic excellence, its quirky humour, and a general, high-school D&D "See what happens" approach, but as a more serious diversion, I found it lacking.

I really wanted to like this game.
Grutte Pier was a pretty cool guy, and the games art style looks pretty nice.
For the most part the game manages to be a reasonably fun, simplistic RPG, with a few skills and a couple of upgrades.
There is a lot of back tracking around with no real distinguishing landmarks and only a slightly inadequate minimap to steer by,  which while not very fun is at least bearable. With music or a podcast of course because in the first 10 minutes or so of playing the single bland music track gets annoying, and with no voiced characters there is no reason not to mute it.
All of this could be forgiven were it not for the occasional stealth sections. These sections are not overly hard by themselves, but they only serve to highlight the clunkier parts of games design, which can generally be ignored in the combat parts. First of all there is no clear indicator of guard sightlines, they have small circles of light from their lamps, and look in different directions, but with mostly tight paths to move down, it can be frustrating to work out exactly how close you can squeeze past. Thirdly there are no checkpoints, so while the section itself is not difficult per say, if you take a wrong turn because you can't always tell where a road will go based on the minimap, is easy to fail and have to start all over again. Secondly, the clunky movement system and poor pathing of the player character are mostly ignored except for during a stealth section in a tight maze. There are only so many times you can get stuck on a barrel because of the clunky movement and get caught by a guard while Pier runs on the spot before you start to wonder what the point of it is.
There is also a slight narrative dissonance that I found annoying, where you can kill 20 men at once with a single power attack, and take on waves of 30 or so soldiers at once, only for your character to say "oh no soldiers are patrolling, better be careful" and have to sneak past. If the sections were optional or only really game before you get a sword I would mostly not mind, but the clear artificial nature only makes them more annoying.
The thing that really pushed me over the edge into a negative review is a section where you have to get to town in 5 minutes. First you fight or run through a group of enemies, then a stealth section, then  another fight, then another stealth section. Then another combat section. all on a timer. It's a 2 hour story (up to 4 if you aim to find all the chests) split into 9 tiny chapters. It's very simple in its combat mechanics- a regular attack and a strong attack, there are 6 different 'styles' of attack you can purchase and apparently you can switch between them but I wasn't able to with the default or custom key bindings. The movement and attacks are the same key (left click) which is an obvious terrible idea, making the combat clunky and awkward. There are stealth sections thrown in that seem out of place and frustrating, as well as timed sections that aim (and fail) to provide some sense of urgency.  The story plays out through awkward conversations that fall prey to the 'nobody talks like that' writing style. There is no manual saving, and I constantly had an issue with the character getting stuck after opening chests causing me to have to quit and restart a level.
The art style is beautiful and I love the environment, however the game as a whole just feels unfinished and more like it should be a part of something more. Given that it's based on an already existing story that makes sense, but it just doesn't translate to a game format.
Not sure how historically accurate it was for Pier to be smashing crates all around Friesland, but it sure is fun.

The story of a European man trying to defend his home meanwhile fending off the foreign hordes. Somehow still relevant in 2017 huh?
The only reason I am giving this a thumbs up is that it was 75% off when I got it and that is the price about it deserves.
It should have been a visual novel instead of a game because the story it tells is cool (nothing special or extravagant about it though, typical hero story) but the controls and playing aspects are terrible. The whole game takes place in like three areas and there is  a lot of backtracking, almost every chapter. I hate backtracking.
Controls are about point and click pathfinding (which is also terrible) and right and left clicks for two different attacks. Since there is no more to the fighting mechanics it really gets dull and bland very hastily. I finished the last two chapters with just running through the enemies instead of fighting them since it made not sense or was not fun at all for me. There is a stealth mechanic from PS1 era of games and really is easy and mundane. There is also no voice acting and cutscenes are just frames (yet I have to agree that I enjoyed the artstyle).
All in all if you want a game with an interesting story with twists and turns or a game where is enjoyable fighting and bringing something new to the table, stay away. If you want a cute looking visual novel that will take you about two hours to finish it at the cost of your mouse buttons, by any means purchase. Enjoy...I guess?

I'm a long time 4x veteran, starting from Civ 1. 10 hours into Endless Legend, and I must say the game is amazing. Deep, complex and intewoven systems affecting each other, very asymmetric factions, nicely integrated faction-specific story and gorgeous graphics. I haven't seen any bugs yet. What more could you expect?

Endless Legend does so many new things with the 4X genre and it does them exceedingly well. Here's a short list. And don't take my word for it, you can see this stuff in countless, nay endless, reviews:
-Beautiful map inspired by the opening to Game of Thrones. Best map in strategy gaming? Surely a contender. It's crack to the map lover/model builder/graphics head.
-Factions are unique. Can't declare war with one. Feed off the slain with another. A third makes pillars and casts spells based on pain. Another can force peace on opponents. Their play is unique, and how they fit together to form the world is compelling.
-New fangled take on the tech tree that really works and doesn't shoehorn you down avenues of research.
-The integration of quests and other rpg elements that link to a deep lore in a way not done before. It's good writing.
If they got just one or two of these things really right, EL would deserve a spot in your library. They do all four with finesse and polish. Then theres the different approach to regional management and settling, the unique combat system that I really enjoy, the immersive story elements, and the ways that fighting can take place even in the absence of all out war, which empire builders have sorely needed.
For all these changes, Endless Legend is definitely a 4x game. You plant cities, explore the terrain looking for treasure but also questing for adventure - as the minor civs have villages that issue quests that provide rewards, allocate workers, grow your research and economy, confront other civs, make nice or make war.
Something about the world really sucks you in. There is funny mix of sci fi and fantasy elements. I am not a particular fantasy fan, but the lore and the world really feels inhabited and compelling.
There have been a number of good 4x games that have come out recently. My point here is you: can't go wrong with this one.

Look, straight up it's not a bad game, but I can't in good conscience recommend it for $9. The concept is great (the story is based on a real historical figure) but the game overall just feels a bit unfinished.
There are only two buttons for combat: quick and strong attack. There are no combos, no dodge feature, not even a way to block. It could have used a little more depth to the fights. As it is now you just stand in front of some enemies and mash the attack button to take them out, that's about it. It feels a little sluggish as well, like there's a delay between and after attacks that leaves you open to getting hit that is very hard to avoid. You do get the option to buy six new strong attacks (3 for your fists, 3 for when you get a sword), but it doesn't add any strategy, you're still just slamming your weapon/fists around to take out more guys at once. Also there is no EXP system, levels, or inventory. To heal you just avoid combat for a few seconds and your health and stamina will automatically refill.
I know this was somebody's dream to make this game and I really respect that so I won't slam the game for not having Dark Souls levels of depth, but it just feels like something is missing. I got this on a bundle sale for about a dollar, so if it's on sale, sure, have a go at it. I enjoyed my time with it. It's only about a 3 hour game and I got every achievement for it except two in that time as well. It's very easy, which is actually nice since at the time I wanted a relaxing short game, not some 20 hour epic, but the core of the gameplay just needs to be expanded upon. Right now it just amounts to follow the dot on your minimap to talk to someone or fight some guys, and as explained the combat is really bare bones. On the other hand I did learn of the existence of Pier and read the Wikipedia article on him so that's cool I learned some new history from this game. I'm sorry for the negative review, but when you can get something like Sleeping Dogs on sale for $4.50 that has way more exciting combat I can't justify spending $9 for this.

The Curious Expedition is a fun strategy exploration game set in the age of colonial exploration. The game is meant to be bite sized in nature, and each expedition will only take you an hour or so max. Full games consist 6 such expeditions, with your chosen expedition leader and your progress saved after each return home. This way you can do one snack sized sortie into the wilds, or go whole Frank Buck and do a whole career in on sitting. After your sixth and final sortie,  your explorer will reitire to enjoy the fame and fortune (or poverty and infamy) they have earned bravely taming unconqured wilderness. After that you are ready to begin anew.
Each expedition the map of the deep, dark unknown lands are randomly generated. Before you set out on your career, you will begin by picking an explorer from amongst famous historical and fictional figures. Only a few are available at the start, with more being unlocked as you make more progress and meet certain conditions. All have their own strengths and weaknesses, as well as their starting equipment and followers. The followers that are accompany you are many and useful, such as guides, warriors and translators. Each has their own strengths and weaknesses that vary from person to person. Maybe your translator is great at building up reputation with the locals but suffers from claustrophobia and won't enter dark places? You may even find new companions as you travel and they can all level up as you experience successes and failures, becoming more useful as time goes on.
How far you can travel on the map is limited by a sanity meter which is lost by travelling, especially through rougher terrain,  but can it be restored by eating rations or resting at friendly locations. The types of places you can encounter are many and varied and you can never be sure what to expect from one random map to the next: Caves hidden behind waterfalls, ancient ruins filled with riches, friendly tribes, the abandoned camps of failed missions, dangerous volcanoes that spread fire across the land, or the fabled golden pyramid, your ultimate goal. Given the random nature of events that can occur in these places, no journey is likely to play out the same way twice.
As said, the main goal of each outing is finding the golden pyramid, but there are plenty of other lost artifacts to find along the way and you will have to balance out the wealth and glory you will gain from obtaining (translation: Stealing them from sacred sites) them with the potential anger you will cause among the natives for desecrating their holy places. If you cause too much anger  the natives may be unwilling to shelter or feed you, or even become actively hostile and attack you. Combat can and will occur, sometimes with the natives you've managed to annoy, sometimes with the hostle wildlife. Dont be afraid to flee if you have to, a tough fight can leave you as a corpse for a future expedition to find.
I always find each adventure is a blast and I never know what to expect. Balancing sanity, health, and native relations against the potentional  wealth and glory is a real act of  reward vs disastrous failure.
Upon returning to England, your wealth and glory are tallied and you will gain a new perk for your next trek. After 6 treks your results are tallied with other members of the explorerers guild and whoever has the most will be declared the greatest explorerer of all time. Over repeat adventures you will unlock new explorers and companions from history and fiction. Maybe H.P.Lovecraft will come with you this time around or maybe you expedition leader will be Charles Dawrin? It's all a lot of fun and it's short play time and huge variety of events mean that it really bears repeat playthroughs.
The graphics are done in a really pleasant pixel style and the music and sound effects are also good and help set the mood. Your followers will add interesting flavour text at each location, sometimes superstitious nonesense (maybe), sometimes sound advice you might want to listen to. They aren't hugely detailed, being quite tiny, but the artists still manage to fill them with life and character. Do pay attention to what they say, each character has loyalty and annoying or angering them can turn them against you. It adds another layer to the balancing you have to do to succceed in your expedition.
One note: Don't let my short play time dissuade you, while I have only recently acquired the full Steam version, I played the free beta for hours. It also needs to be mentioned that the full release game is MUCH better all round, with vastly improved gameplay, a huge slew of new events, and even better, a recent free expansion that adds artic expeditions. With the devs promising more to come in future days, the time has never looked bighter to don your monocle and jodpers and set off for lands unknown. Tally ho old chap, let's see what's out there!

*Note: This is a copy of the review I posted on Wildlife 2*
Okay I'm gonna say it... this game is better than Zoo Tycoon 2
*Immediately changes name and goes into hiding to avoid assassination from the ZT2 mafia*
Before I explain why let me say that I spent countless hours growing up playing ZT complete collection and ZT2 complete collection, and for this comparison I'm referring to Wildlife Park 2 + all expansion packs and DLCs
Things I like better about WP2:
1. Animal designs are so much more realistic than in ZT2, and many are unbelievable adorable because of it (the otters!!!)
2. Animal's needs and behaviors are more realistic (i.e. needing it to be hotter or colder, interacting with the natural parts of their environment for food, water, shelter, and entertainment)
3. More animal and plant species to choose from (including oddities that can only be achieved through breeding and certain species that have color options when you purchase them)
4. Zoo IS NOT set up on a grid system which allows more design options.
5. Environmental challenges such as weather changes and temperature challenges
6. You don't have to make a zoo, ZT2 made you have a zoo entrance and guests would show up and complain no matter what you did. WP2 gives you the option to make a zoo, nature preserve, farm, ranch, animal shelter, or just a natural environment for the animals to exist in.
Things I like better about ZT2:
1. Terraforming controls are much more user friendly in ZT, however those in WP2 are more realistic in terms of how one would actually landscape and form lakes and deep water tanks
2. The sorting system, WP2 has no sorting system for anything and that can be overwhelming before you know where everything is and tedious once you do.
3. Staff didn't need their own individual buildings, nor did they have a limited range
Really in the end it all comes down to what you are looking for in a zoo game. In my case, I wanted realistic animals more than anything and a wide variety of them on top of that. However, if you want a more user friendly, child safe (I've seen multiple posts in the discussion boards from parents who aren't pleased with the realistic mating in WP2) zoo game, then perhaps ZT2 is better for you.

What I Like: Bought this not realizing it was only DLC. What I like is that, despite it only being DLC, it's a standalone game too, you can play it without needing the base game installed.
What I Dislike: The game teases you with what you can find in other expansions. In some campaigns you're allowed to mess around and play with animals from other expansions (Which is pretty neat tbh, and not really a downside), however, this confused me once I went into freeplay and was only left with "some" of the marine animals. All others are locked, the game does not tell me why and I cannot find any information online as to why. I understand why the base game animals are not there, but when I have unlimited cash in freeplay there is no reason why all the marine animals are not available.
Overall, this is a good game. At times it felt like it was trying too hard to be a zoo tycoon copy. While this game does play like a ripoff of the more major title, some parts of it are done way better (better quality animal appearences, more realistic animal interactions, the ability to choose the color you want on certain animals, guests require doctors when animals hurt them) but other features it falls short (instructions are never clear, sometimes frustratingly so, random parts of other expansions are "thrown in" as a tease but leave you more confused than in want of more (I spent 2 hours trying to figure out what to do with the researcher until I realized he couldn't do anything in my game), and controls take some getting used.)
Despite the bad sides, this is an incredible competitor to Zoo Tycoon 2 and I believe if they had polished it a little more and made it more player friendly, it could have been more popular than the ever nostalgic ZT2.
Reccommended for anyone seeking an alternative to Zoo Tycoon.

Well, what an interesting game.
I, like many recent reviews in here, aquired this through humble bundle. Unlike many of those reviews, however, I actually like the game. I think much of the love that's already here comes from long - time EA purchasers, who have seen the game since inception, and many 1st timers (aka humble bundle'rs) who have just come into this game for the first time and are seeing it with fresh eyes.
I think that the complaints from them come from the RNG nature of procedural generation, possibly. And the game throws a few twists at you as well; I will admit, I am not a fan of the last level; using all my resources to get to the edge of a map that them makes me traverse the whole map again; epecially as i literally walked 1 tile next to 2 of those damned switches on my first trip around the map. I understand that it's there to ramp up the challenge, but I think that it is a bad mechanic, and the difficulty should be in the severity of the terrain, rarity of resources, and threat level of encounters (animal attacks). Raptors chasing you over the map is 'fun'. I think that they should be faster and keep overtaking you until you kill them/are defeated, for instance.
The packing / carry mechanic needs work, and doesn't do a very good job of explaining what's makeing you over-laden.
Maybe this should be getting posted in a balancing/issues forum.

I backed Cross of the Dutchman on Kickstarter, but it failed to meet its goal. So when I saw it on sale on Steam I had to pick it up. I was happy to see that they managed to get something out despite not having the funding they wanted.
But my excitement about the game stops there. Simply producing something does not make it good.
This game looks like it's a clone of the Torchlight engine, but with all the features removed. There is only a single weapon and one normal attack: namely, melee with a sword. A handful of related abilities make up everything else you can do. Suffice it to say that combat is a repetitive chore. Most of the enemies are identical, and the only real challenge comes from their numbers if they manage to swarm you while an ability is cooling down.
Beyond that, the only mechanic in the game is stealth, and it's a great lesson in how not to design stealth. There's also an artifical timer you have to beat during the stealth sections, which only makes it worse. That timer is very small, hidden in a corner, and never called out, so it's easy to miss the first few times.
There's really no inventory, leveling, or skill tree to mention. I expected that a game like this would have those things in depth. But it's incredibly shallow.
On top of all that, the story is a bore.
I wish there were something to love here, but there's simply not.
There is a better version of this game possible - it was contingent on securing funding to flesh it out.

All meat and no filler with this action adventure based on folk legend.
Cross of the Dutchman is short, but effective, with a fast-paced story and enough new techniques to avoid the grind. Learning and gameplay are seamlessly woven to give you mastery of combat by the end. The narrative delivers a healthy emotive range from sarcasm to sentiment, with animated cinematic interludes to connect each chapter.
The visuals complete the immersive setting, with music that matches but never intrudes. The small but open world effectively drives the plot between key locations, with just the right amount of exploration to savor the art but not feel bored.
Although playable, the controls felt imprecise at times and could be frustrating if the game were much longer. The game also included far too many achievements (few of which required any deviation from the main arc).
Enjoyable up to the end, Cross of the Dutchman is worth the play.

Let me start by saying that I hate writing a negative review, especially since this game is a Dutch game (and as a proud Dutchman, you should always support the things that originate in the Netherlands). But I just can't give this game a positive review.

My main issue and the reason why I (fully triggered, frustrated and tilted) threw my controller out of the window was the combat system. It is just so f***ing bad... Here a list which things I found frustrating:
- Your character will hit air most of the time because you cant properly place your character in a good line with the enemies
- There is no indicator for cooldown on your secondary (more powerful) attack
- Moving is clunky (especially with mouse) and especially bad in combat (see reason 1)
- There is no easy way to swich between secondary attacks
And then there is the autosave feature. I got send back way too far back because of dying/getting caught that I just became even more triggered and decided to stop playing and write this review.
So in conclusion, I feel bad for giving this game the thumbs down, but because of the bad combat system I cannot in good conciousness recommend this game.

Mystery Expedition: Prisoners of Ice , is a HOPA* game, developed by Lazy Turtle Games and published by Tri Synergy Inc.
*HOPA - Hidden Object Puzzle Adventure.
They're somewhat dated but still overall good. The visuals can be adjusted in the option menu.
I want to mentioned that the audio for this game is well done even if it's simplistic and somewhat repetitive. The audio can be adjusted in the option menu as well.
There are only two difficulty game modes to choose from: Easy, Expert and Adventure (Custom.)
Notebook has three sections: Cutscenes, Notes and Map.
The inventory panel has the option of locking in place to make it stationary.
All of the game's hidden object scenes consists of traditional word lists with some or no interaction.
Most of the game's puzzles are fairly easy to solve without having the need to skip any of them.
There is a unique feature in the game. Igloo with a pet penguin. Collecting coins that are found throughout the game. Coins are used to buy certain items for the penguin but they don't come cheap. Relics are displayed on the icy shelf behind the penguin.
There are ten different relic collectibles to find throughout the game.
There are eighteen different beyond object (morphing) to find throughout the game as well.
There twenty-eight different achievements to earn from playing the game. Only three achievements are tied to hidden object scenes, puzzles and completing the game. The remainder of the achievements are tied to finding all of the changing and relic items in the game.
Final thoughts, I've found this game enjoyable to certain extend. The replay value for this game is low. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

For this great game you don the hat of explorer in an “Indiana Jones”-esque tale of discovery.  I thoroughly enjoyed the progress of the story and the interactive character’s who play their part in your progress.  I liked the option of being able to alter the hidden object scenes into jigsaw puzzles to solve instead.  I did find it frustrating at one point when I had to pause play and return at a later date and was unsure of the next task. I insisted on using the hint option which kept instructing me to a situation that I did not possess the tools to solve at that point.  Thankfully I attended all previous scenes and found the tool and task to be completed.  I was also a little disappointed in needing to specifically orientate a tool within a scene before it was recognized as the appropriate activity.  I had presented the tool multiple times within the scene and had it be rejected.  I was blown away by the injected realism of the crew interactive scenes.  By making those scenes realistic it made the game and the story line more believable and there the gamer became more invested in the outcome.  I also loved the way history and culture was injected into the story.  The history, beliefs and traditions of the Inuit people give the story line and game a link between the tangible history of an ancient culture and the mystery surrounding it.
I recommend Mystery Expedition: Prisoners of Ice to fans of hidden object fans. The story is the high point here.

I don't normally write reviews, but this visual novel has left an exceptional impression on me. Since this game is nothing but story, I'll try to keep it spoiler-free.
(Side-note: This visual novel has an anime! It's crap compared to the game though, so I don't recommend that)
Overall Positive Features:
Story - This is the most important part of the game, so respectfully it's the best part. There are five arcs to this game, each pertaining to one of the five main male characters. Even if you aren't the biggest fan of the main male character to the arc, the heroine's relationship to him is generally not the only focus of the story, so it's still enjoyable.
Japanese Voice-acting - the voice acting work of this game is well-done; character voices fit the personalities appropriately, and nobody sounds like an emotionless brick unless they're supposed to.
Character art and CGs - The design of the characters and the CGs are really nice in my opinion- even if you're really stingy about art, the designs are at the very least tolerable.
Music - The soundtrack of this game is fantastic and fits the mood extremely well. The song for the opening movie also has a lot of hype, I love it.
Things You May Find Iffy:
Orion - Orion is a character that is with you throughout the entire game and provides commentary on what's happening around you for the majority of the game. He's also extremely important to the plot, so even if you don't like him, you're stuck with him. Personally I like Orion, but his constant presence can be annoying to players. Since you can't 'disable' him, it can ruin the game for you if you don't like him.
Background Art - I'll level with you. There's only like three or four colors along with some gradient in them most of the time, excluding white. I personally don't mind this since it allows me to focus on the characters in front of me rather than being distracted by a super-detailed background, but you may find it a bit too washed-out for your taste (check the screenshots on the store page to see if you like it or not).
Bonus:
Endings - This game has A LOT of endings. Every arc has at least four endings: The good ending, the normal ending, and at least two bad endings, with a total of 26 endings.
Memories & Extras - Okay, so at some point, you will unlock the item "Memories" for the main menu. The Memories are little bonus scenes where the heroine spends time with that character at some point during the story. Next, there's the item "Extras" which you also unlock at some point for the main menu. These are basically silent thoughts from the main male of a particular arc. And by silent, I mean there isn't any voice acting, it's pretty much just pure reading.
CG Voice Clips: As you unlock CGs, you can review them in the gallery, which is pretty standard. Certain CGs (that is, CGs with a little red rose in the corner of the preview) will play voice clips when you ctrl + left click certain areas with about five different voice clips to each CG (this includes alternate versions of that CG, by the way). While it's a nice feature, looking for these things becomes a clicking hunt as there is no indication that you can actually click there (and for shorter voice clips, you're sometimes supposed to click on an area multiple times).
Mini-Games: Okay, now this is kind of silly, but this game has it's own version of rock-paper-scissors and air hockey. Rock-paper-scissors got turned into a reflex game where you have to "attack" if you win so you get a point, or "defend" if you lose so they don't get a point. Air hockey is, well, air hockey. You can play against the five main guys as kind of varying levels of difficulty, and you get an achievement for beating them all. The moral of this story is that if you're getting frustrated at one of the guys, you can just beat them at air hockey and rock-paper-scissors.
My Final Thoughts:
Overall I think this game is fantastic and while it's definitely not an experience meant for everybody (the heroine having a romantic relationship with one of five guys should have made that obvious) I personally believe that the story is enjoyable to anyone who enjoys romance (I do suggest however that if you're not of the intended audience you should just look up a walkthrough of this game, and again, don't even bother with the anime).

When life gives you lemons, do you throw them at your friends? Maybe at a wall instead? Or....perhaps, do you squeeze the juice out and make lemonade? The possibilities are pretty much endless. Excuse me for my silly segue, but in an odd way Amnesia: Memories reminds us that life is full of possibilities - so, which will you take?
Amnesia (no, not the horror game that exploded in popularity on YouTube a few years back!) is a Japanese visual novel developed and published by Idea Factory under their "Otomate" brand. Now, if you're not familiar with the term "otome", that usually refers to visual novels with a female main character that dates males. If you don't recognize the term "visual novel", it's basically what it sounds like: a novel of sorts with accompanying visuals.
The gameplay in Amnesia involves choices quite often, so it's more of a choose your own adventure sort of deal instead of just walls of text. Personally, I really liked this approach because the game has a lot of endings (20+), especially bad ones. The differences between "good" and "normal" endings are usually somewhat minor, but the difference between a "good" and a "bad" ending is huge - usually bad endings result in death, I was really surprised to see this from a visual novel, especially one about dating pretty dudes. Sure, a lot of the bad endings are silly, but some of them were genuinely creepy. The dark aspects hiding under the game's innocent front were a little surprising to say the least.
What truly surprised me though was the game's characters, especially the main 5 "dateable" guys. At the start of the game, you're given a choice between 4 worlds (Heart, Spade, Clover, Diamond), each of which has a main dude to focus on. Sure, in most of the worlds nearly all of the main cast is present (which includes coworkers, occasionally family members, and the extra friend or two), but clearly the male lead is what the game wants you to focus on. However, nearly all of the characters in this game are pretty interesting, from the bizarre manager at work to the mysterious Ukyo, the 5th unlockable "true ending" guy. There were a few exceptions, but I think that all comes down to personal preference in the end. Personally I didn't care for Shin or Ikki's routes much, while Kent (my favorite), Toma, and Ukyo all had pretty interesting routes with some nice twists and turns along the way.
I loved Kent's route in particular because it was great to see him develop as a character along the way; he goes from being a serious, rational, analytical type of person with seemingly no emotions to someone who is very sweet and caring. Most of the main dudes also develop along their routes, but just to clarify - it doesn't ever really feel like the game is overly mushy-gushy or stereotypical for visual novels. The dialogue is cleverly written and it helps to make the experience quite enjoyable.
Well, mostly at least. There was one character in particular that bugged me to no end: Orion. "Who the hell is that?" you might ask. Well, he's the little guy who caused you to have amnesia in the first place. He's a spirit that follows you around everywhere, and I think he seriously could have been handled a bit better. Orion
to state the obvious, and he does so at every occasion. I think the entire game's length could be shrunk by an hour or two if Orion talked less honestly, though some of his dialogue is pretty important so I think he's still a fairly worthwhile addition to the cast.
Despite that gripe though, I really enjoyed my time with Amnesia. The visuals are lovely and the music is a good mix between emotionally stirring melodies and casual background tunes. Whether you're a secret anime boyfriend harem lover, a fan of visual novels, or even just someone that enjoys solid writing, I think Amnesia is certainly a great experience.
Amnesia: Memories isn't perfect, but it's pretty damn excellent. For fans of otome (girls x guys) visual novels, anime, or just reading in general, this is an absolutely great game that shouldn't be missed!
Oh, and Kent is the best. Your favorite is the worst.

Wow, this game was so worth it. Watch the trailer. If you don't want to buy the game after that... don't. The trailer is what hooked me; its not action-packed, dramatic, or even cinematic. It's literally just a narrator telling a short story that can happen in literally any game of Crusader Kings II: and that is what makes it such an awesome game. The stories this game creates are like no other. Your dynasty can get wiped out by disease in your 10 minutes, or rise to fame and glory because one emperor really loved you. Usually its somewhere in between.
Dynasty conflicts and disputes over tiny bits of land can last centuries, creating ripple affects across the world. While you develop your dynasty and nation the rest of the world goes on and each country aims for its own goals; you may find the AI accomplishing more impressive feats than you some games. Oh; and the game is incredibly historically accurate. You'll learn a lot of history on accident without even realizing it. Definitely makes you understand feudal-society way better.
The game isn't perfect; it has a ton of DLC. In my opinion most are worth it, though. This game has been out a looong time and is definitely not a money machine. Just be careful with your spending and buy DLC if they look really fun (again, most are!). None are required for anything I described in this review however, nor any of the main trailers.
If you love sandbox games, medieval history, political/diplomacy games, or just role-playing this game is definitely for you!
P.S. I know Paradox has come under fire for a lot of random things, mostly their DLC policy. While they do have a ton of DLC, none were lacking in content that I've purchased. (though I do spend a good amount of time considering my DLC purchases) CK2 can definitely be amazing without any DLC at all, so don't let that put you off this game. I can't speak for any of their other policies but this game is definitely worth the money.
