I installed this when I saw it would be free-to-play for this weekend, started playing it around 10:30 on Friday night.
8/10, would accidentally stay up till dawn again.
As RTS games go, this isn't my favorite (I prefer Total War, Company of Heroes, and Sins of a Solar Empire) but it's good. EVERYTHING is turn-based, with battles limited to 6 rounds. The only things I actually disliked about this game were unit creation and building construction being combined into 1 stream, and that stream being annoyingly slow at normal game speed. The speed actually wouldn't bother me much if they had known to not cross the streams.
The music and visuals are great. Total War games, which don't even try to pretend their turn-based world maps are anything more than a frame for cinematic, large-scale, real-time battles, but you spend the majority of your time in this game on the world map, and the world map is gorgeous. Even the battles are fought on a zoomed-in version of it, with both sides deploying on terrain features around the tile the armies actually met on. It's something to consider carefully when attacking or trying to set a trap.
All 9 factions are pretty unique, with their own play styles and interesting backstories (except for two that I can't find out the differences between in the free weekend version, maybe one is DLC). In this regard it's closer to Sins of a Solar Empire, with each faction having its own take on a small set of standard unit types, than to Total War where there are dozens of common units and each faction has better versions of a couple. For example, two of the human factions are steampunk-Viking descendants of the crews of a stranded starfleet (sadly, neither's royal family's surname is Shepard); their infantry are power-armored crossbowmen with shields and a point-blank-shot damage bonus, while their "cavalry" are footsoldiers with jump-jet-equipped power-armor that renders horses obsolete, and their monster is a steampunk mech.
Overall, this game is totally worth it if you like 4x, but don't need it to be all or even mostly about war. It's actually a nice change of pace.

Take Civilization 5, add a pinch of World of Warcraft, some Fallout, and a dash of steampunk.  Shake and cook until it is truly unique from other settings.  Play it on a planet like Pandora but even more fantastic, on a map from Game of Thrones. This is a GREAT GAME, easily better than Civ5, Civ Beyond Earth, Warlock: MotA, or others of its ilk... except for a few glaring frustrations.
TL;DR: Combat, Options menu, and alerts need fixing before it will actually be better than the above where my friends and I will actually buy it.
What needs fixing: combat: GREAT IDEA to have a mini turn based battle on the map when a battle starts, using the surrounding terrain.  I LOVE THIS!  What I don't like is the near control ofver units.  The interface allows you to move, or attack and move, but not move and choose who you will attack.  You are a tease!  This is a silly flaw.  The way it is, it is frustrating, and I cannot recommend anyone playing it out.  It is frustrating to lose your units solely because you don't have the control over them that you almost provide.  It is almost better to just auto calculate each battle.  Whatever your design philosophy might be, why don't you ALLOW YOUR PLAYERS THE OPTION of having full control of both movement and attack during a battle?  Make it a box you click in the options menu.  Speaking of which...
Options menu:
Why wouldn't you provide the option of faster combats, notifications, alerts for the player, and other things wile the player is in the middle of a game?  Even if you have to restart the client, I had to stop playing a campaign just because I wanted to change the animation speed of combat from slow to fast.  It was just taking too long for me to get through a combat.  Again, I enjoy the combat, mostly, but to only allow that option under advanced settings at the start of a game, and then not in the options menu during it is a silly, frustrating oversight.
Alerts:
When running all the cities and armies for an empire, you might forget about a request for new policies or to assign new build orders.  Endless Legend does not stop you from ending your turn if you have not dealt with important issues like this.  This is a PROBLEM.  Learn from Civ5 and do not allow the turn to end unless the player deals with issues like this.  Unless your scheme is to make a deceptively great game that makes people throw their computers against the wall.  If they do, it should be because of frustrations in game, not because of frustrations with the interface.  I actually lost hundreds of resources because I hit "end turn" when I missed a little box that would have told me it was time for the every 20th turn policy review, thus not allowing me to select perks for my empire for the next 20 turns.  That is stupid.
Do I recommend this game?  Not yet.
If they could take lessons from Civ5 about how it does business regarding game options and probably multiplayer( didn't get to test that out, too busy trying the other Endless games), it could be the BEST of its kind.  It has a truly unique and deep story, for each civilization, which each plays differently.  I couldn't play a game to completion for just a few hours in a 2 day free weekend, so I don't know how each victory condition balances against each other.  I like that they made the single city challenge a viable option for multiplayer against those who don't like it in the form of the Cultists faction.  I like that the setting is so refreshingly new.  This is not a Tolkien LotR fantasy, though a few elements survive. I like the writing (I only found one typo in the Drakken intro/story quest).  It could probably use more wonders to build, but maybe that is part of that DLC.  I already own Civ5 and Warlock:MotA, and for me to buy this it has to be dramatically better than those.  It is, if it fixes the issues with its interface.

This is one of the worst, buggiest games I have played in years.  Most buggy games seem to be somewhat forgivable because they have fun elements, but this game had absolutely none.  The game is incredibly linear (occasionally there is a single path branching off the main path, but these are rare and short).  The camera angle is terrible on the PC - I find myself fighting 50% of my enemies off screen.  I routinely cast fire jackal just so that it can show me what direction my enemies are.  Your characters are tightly tethered together so that all battles feel like three-legged races.  If you try to move right while your buddy is moving left, too bad!  The both of you will end up struggling to move but going nowhere while the big boss rains damage down upon you.  This sense of being joined at the hip continues even when just trying to maneuver through the dungeon.  Because of the terrible mechanism for moving about (on the pc), one of you will likely get stuck on a door jam or stair banister.  When this happens, you will not be able to move to walk around the obstacle because your buddy will likely have already traveled too far.  They then have to come back to get you!
Battles can be especially frustrating as you find yourself mashing keys over and over again just to make some effect take place.  This leads to a strange bug that occurs occasionally in battle for the fighter characters and almost routinely for spell casting characters.  Normally, when casting a spell, a button is pressed and while that button is held down the cursor becomes a blue glowing ball that you are supposed to use to aim the spell.  When you release the key press, the spell is cast and your cursor returns.  At least, that's how it is supposed to work.  Routinely in battle our spell caster would get slaughtered because releasing the key press didn't cast the spell - instead the blue glowing ball whizzes around the battle field and until it decides to go away on its own the spell caster cannot move at all.  But don't think that playing the fighter characters will be much better.  Because you have to spin the camera in order to aim at your enemy, I routinely find myself attacking thin air while someone beats me from behind during the 5 seconds it takes to do a 180.  Theoretically this can be solved by placing your cursor precisely on your enemy, but I find that near impossible while a group of enemies swarms me.  There finally came a point where I realized that I had not enjoyed a single moment of this game and decided to never play it again (despite reaching what I think is the final battle).

Awesomenauts is an extremely addictive and fun game, It takes the style of an old platforming game and converts it into a modern day masterpeice, The graphics in the game are eyepleasing with some humour added in aswell, The music for the game is overwhelmingly good, each character has its own theme with a remix included, giving each character its own uniqueness and awesomenautess. The gameplay of the game is addictive and fun.  You must defeat the other 3 players by destroying their core on the other side of the map from yours, You must get past at least 2 Turrents to get to the core, The turrents will constantly fire at you once in range so you music use your Droids to use as sheilds to get through the turrents, the enemy has the exact same gameplay mechanics though meaning that you must intertwine with the droids to get through, Each map features its own Neutral Creature and danger/help Neutral creatures will drop the currency used to purchase upgrades Solar (Along with Droids) and health. The dangers/helps can include various things like a worm that is activated on the press of the button above it, and anything above the worm will be eaten. There is also more environmental things like flames coming out, blocking an area. They even host competitions on Awesomenauts for prizes in real money, so you can even make a living ( not really ) playing this game! The replay value is outstanding as you basicly play 3v3, constantly but it can get boring after a while.
Overall i give this game a 7.8/10 It is very fun to play when bored/wanting to play it. The game is aestheticly pleasing and sounding and the gameplay is very fun.

Summary: I enjoyed this game and feel I've gotten my money's worth ($11).
Read: This is a rogue-like game.  It means you are expected to die and try again.  You can play well and make smart decisions and yet still lose.  In fact you probably will.  But games are short and you just start a new one.
This a decent game.  The music is well done.  The art work is good.  The writing is good.  The gameplay is engaging and it's terribly fun to run away from vicious hyenas or a raging forest fire.  Exploring the landmarks and finding out what they contain is exciting.  The combat is balanced yet challenging and requires you to make strategic choices about your battle readiness. You can flee if you can't handle a fight but there are consequences.
I ran into two problems.  Problem 1:  A lack of content.  At 10 hours in I've seen everything multiple times.  Most scenarios have a variety of ways they can play out based on your party composition, abilities/effects, inventory or karma with the natives.  But I haven't been surprised in a while and how many times can scaling a cliff to reach a temple be interesting?  You either have climbing gear, a rope or nothing.  It's a choice, sure, but I've seen the same cliff and choice a dozen times now.
Problem 2:  Inventory management isn't fun in this game.  There are a lot of things you're going to want to take with you, but your inventory is dismally small.  This is by design as you have to be strategic about your choices.  Ok great, so it's a jungle map and you'll need machetes for jungle tiles and ropes for swamp tiles.  You need torches to enter caves.  You also may need climbing gear, shovels, med kits, whiskey, extra bullets, etc.  You have limited slots, and each item stack takes up one slot.  One shovel or ten shovels is the same.  And a major aspect of winning is finding treasure, which also takes a slot for each unique item.  Very quickly you have to start choosing what you should drop.
What's the point of planning a trip out when you immediately have to start ditching your carefully chosen resources?  Then, you can buy a variety of powerups at merchants on the map.  Except you never want to part with your vital resources, plus how you possibly know which powerup you will need in the future?  You don't have room to take them on a whim!  So ultimately you only buy things when you have a dire need, and purchased dearly with something else you needed.
Remember those machetes you brought with you?  You burn one every jungle tile you pass through (without there's a steep penalty).  You can only buy 10 before starting the map, and you typically won't see them for sale again.  If you do, lord knows it'll be a hard choice what to buy them with.
The one thing that would make this inventory management all worthwhile is if there were unique event choices depending on what you had on you.  And there are.  For like five things, which you will see over and over.  You want to climb a cliff?  Do you have a rope, or climbing gear.  You want to enter a cave?  Do you have a torch?
Complaint #3:  This game is random, except for one thing that annoyed me.  Before leaving for a trip you are given a bonus quest.  One is to find a kill a hyena name Snuffaluffages or whatever and return with his hide.  It's a always a hyena and it's always Snuffaluffages.  Would it have been so hard to randomize the creature and it's name?  Another is to find a deserter name Konrad and bring him back to face justice.  It's always Konrad, and he always chooses to fight you rather than go back.
I'm sorry to complain so much because this game is fun and I'm about to go play some more.  10 hours and I've only made it to the final expedition once, and died.  I'd like to beat on normal at least once.

I have to say that this is the only 4x strategy game that I have really gotten into, and it is seriously worth it!
Here's the shortened version:
pros:
- different races to play as that actually give a lot of diverse gameplay options
- each race has its own (interesting) quest-line and (vibrant) history
- quests really give you a purpose and a bit of story to drive you forward and keep you engaged with your faction.
- combat system takes the best of Civ V and Total War to create a really fun system!
- seasons!
- relatively simple interface (you probably need to play the tutorial to fully understand it though)
- customise your army units
- very sassy AI!
- beautiful graphics
cons:
- you can't see exactly how strong an enemy is before you attack (at least, i havent found a way yet)
- tutorial is quite heavy, but also worth it so....
- cities are a little hard to see clearly as there is a lot of stuff going on...
- it is a little buggy and often crashes when I play multiplayer, but not enough to deter me from the game!
The long version:
What I like most about this game is the sense of real diversity between each 'culture/races/people'. They each have very specific and drastically different ways of playing them. For example you have a race that is a cult - they can't build extra cities so conquering by force is useless, so instead of soldiers they have preachers who spread their influence and 'take over' other players' settlements through spreading their cult. Another clan is basically vermin zombies who don't even have the option of diplomacy - all they can do is attack other players and eat them or turn their enemies into zombies which they can then control. Or a third one is a bunch of metal armours with souls inside them so they don't require any food resources! There is much more than that but they all have advantages and disadvantages that are really well balanced and truly FEEL different and diverse!
On top of that the combat system is really interesting.
First of all, each race only gets 4 different base units. That's it. But wait for it..... you get to customise them! As you level them up you get access to tier 2, 3 etc items like armour, weapons, and jewelery which all give you different stats which means you can create different units tailored to your own style of play or needs. For example I'm playing with the woodsland people (not their official name) and i have access only to archers at first. But I have created 2 different types of archers through this system - some are better at fighting infantry units whereas my second class is stronger against flying units. And now I also spent a while upgrading all my unit designs so that I can manufacture better units. There aren't THAT many different options, but there are enough to make it diverse and you can have a lot of fun with it. I also just like the ability to upgrade your units instead of simply receiving new units and you don't really know what they do. This way, I really am getting to know my army for once.
Secondly, it's not like in Civ V where your units throw javelins from one hexagon to another hexagon or something like that. In battle you have your little units and they each take up 1 square, so you can control each of them individually, at first you need to decide where to place them (they get advantages or disadvantages based on terrain) and then you decide which enemies they attack. It's the same basic concept as in total war, but with less units and turn-based. You're also able to see the stats of your opponents and so can strategise pretty nicely without it taking forever or being overly complicated.
The only down side is that you can't really tell the strength of an enemy army until you have engaged in battle with it (which has meant that 1 and a half of my armies has been accidentally wiped out because of that. But i think that is mostly because i had only archers. Because i didn't have access to anything else at that point because i was focusing on production instead of armies.)
Finally, quests. I haven't play that many 4x strategy games but I haven't seen quests like these before. And I love them. I tend to play mostly RPGs because I like story and my main concern with 4x games such as Civ V was that I didn't really care about my people. But not in Endless Legend. Oh no. The quests and bits of story you get gives you motivation and a purpose and that is what is keeping me playing this game! And I don't even have time for it! It feels like there is a story happening - you're not just developing your community for nothing, you've got a purpose and i love that!
Basically, it's complex, but simple enough to understand - just the way i like my games.

Updating my review to reflect the fact that I have now finished the game.
The negative reception to this game was a bit surprising to me at first. The game couldn't be that bad, could it? Well, after playing I can safely say, yes. Yes it is that bad.
The opening pre-rendered cutscene almost had me fooled into thinking this game would be a cool, fast paced action thriller adventure. Those hopes were quickly dashed by the first in-game cutscene.
Here's a full list of everything wrong wth this game:
-The characters move WAY too slowly
-The animation is stiff, cheap, and clearly cutting corners. (At one point, I swear to god, one of the characters walked straight through another character. Not like the models just overlapped, one character moved DIRECTLY through another character model. HOW do you ♥♥♥♥ up animation that badly?)
-The voice actors cannot convey emotion for crap, not helped by the lack of facial animation.
-The game is very dialogue-heavy, making cutscenes take FOREVER to go through. Metal Gear Solid 2, eat your heart out.
-The direction you are given in game is either blatantly obvious ("I'm going to go over there now" probably means you have to go over there) or too vague.
-The interface sucks. It should not be this difficult to open your inventory in a point and click game.
-The story is repetitive and ultimately leads nowhere. How the hell do you make a trip to Paris seem boring?
-Every single character in this game is a cardboard cutout with no unique traits.
-The sound design is terrible. I had to turn on subtitles to even understand half of the rambling dialogue because the characters never speak above a whisper and the music is cranked up to 11 by default..
-The game REPEATEDLY crashed on me while I was trying to finish it, so I had to pause and save the game after everything I did just in case the game decided to randomly stop working on me.
At the very least, the game was short by Point and click standards. Even with all the crashes, sections where I got hopelessly lost or stuck because of some minor detail, and the endless stream of dialogue, I was able to finish the game in about seven hours.
If you are intrigued by the mystery  and want to know where it leads, just look up the Wikipedia page and save yourself the disappointment. Stay away from this game.

I would NOT recommend Victoria II, however...
I WOULD recommend Victoria II if you have the two major DLCs, "A House Divided" (AHD) and "Heart of Darkness" (HOD).
Even with these, Victoria II is still a bit of a mess - but fortunately not the huge steaming♥♥♥♥♥♥pile that the vanilla game is.
Seriously, for all Vicky's flashy stastics, historical nerd porn, and awesome technology tree, it has MAJOR flaws, and I mean pretty ♥♥♥♥ing major flaws.
I'm surprised certain design elements got past the final stages of development for this game. And, furthermore, considering HOD is essential for at least slightly realistic battles and therefore more fair wars, HOD is a paid patch.
There is a big problem with feedback. One of your provinces is being sieged? Good luck finding out which one it is in your massive global empire. Oh, and that unit finished that siege eight months ago. Oh, suddenly we're losing money. Oops, forgot to upgrade that colonization effort to a protectorate and now somebody else has taken it.
Even with HOD, the colonization mechanics are still rubbish at best. There is no real historical accuracy at all. Now, I know it's a game where you're supposed to create your own history, and that's fine, but why the ♥♥♥♥ is Russia colonizing Ethiopia?
The diplomacy system is S H I T E. It's simply awful. The diplomacy points system makes little to no sense for the era and the 'Very Unlikely/Unlikely/Maybe/Likely/Very Likely' system is terrible.
But the worst aspect of this game are your allies. They are pointless.
Playing as Portugal (which in EUIV is a fun, challenging nation to play and has an interesting history in the Victorian era), I sent an alliance offer to Britain. hey accepted with 'Likely'. The Netherlands almost immediately declares war on me and Britain ♥♥♥♥s off like a little ♥♥♥♥♥.
Not only would this NEVER HAPPEN in real life considering Britain and Portugal have been allies since the late 1300s, but also because they are both enemies of the Dutch in this time period.
And guess what? Suddenly France, Spain, every man and his dog are at war with me. Not fair. I lost all my colonies in Africa and lost Douros to the bloody Spanish.
That sucks. The AI really hates you in this game. No joke. I think it genuinley hates the player.
Something I will praise is the economy system and the factory/industry mechanic, which are both unique and well done. War itself, if balanced, is actually pretty fun and managing the politcal system is rewarding and captivating.
But, this game is outdated and mostly broken. I would say you should wait until those Swedish ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s at Paradox release Victoria III, or buy EUIV if it's on sale.
Despite it's flaws, Victoria II can be fun if played with both of the major DLCs and a lot of patience. Oh, and maybe some cheats because sometimes the game is so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I feel like I need to send it to a mental hospital.

Cross of the Dutchman is a subpar ARPG, and in an already weak genre like ARPGs, it's pretty down there. Actually, can I even call it an ARPG beyond the simplistic clicky gameplay? You don't build your character, you don't get experience and you don't level. The most you do is spend money to increase your health or unlock new moves.
"Filler" is the name of the game, as quest markers take you from point A, to point B, to point C, to point A again, then back to point B, then point A for some reason, then point C which opens up point D, etc. The only content outside of the bad main quest is just combing over the same maps to find treasure chests filled with gold. That's it. You don't find new weapons, hell, you don't even have armor. Calling this game barebones would be an insult to bones that dogs chew.
So what do you all actually do? Well. You point and click to your next destination as pointed out by your mini map, then get in some fights. Seldomly, you do some annoying stealth missions. All you really need to do here is just hug the walls. With that, I just described everything you'll be doing. You don't have puzzles to solve, you don't have side quests, there's no caves of monsters or beasts. There's not even stupid crafting or dialogue choices.
I have to ask: Why build these villages to be as big as they are anyway from a game design standpoint? I'm not gonna be doing anything else beyond the stupid fetch quests. So why make it harder for people to play your game by having towns with pointless NPCs that just clutter everything? It's rare you can talk to anybody in town that isn't either a store keep or part of the quest you're already on.
The combat has a strange stiffness to it. Where I would think a guy using his meaty fists would be really satisfying, I found myself more frustrated when he refused to continue his combo. There's just something wrong with the combat, and I couldn't put my foot on it until I unlocked this forward kick ability. Unlike in Diablo when you click something and your character does it on the thing you clicked, Dutchman has an oddity where Pier will just refuse to line it up. His uppercut works fine for the most part, but his kick just sometimes will refuse to aim at enemies - which proved to be the only frustrating moment of the combat until I just outright stopped using the kick, as the rest of the game is in fact a cake walk. I don't even know who this game will challenge. Children? People with one arm would have no trouble with this, even with the few keyboard commands this game has.
There's also two types of enemies: Footmen and archers.
Exciting.
The biggest sin when it comes to the lack of variety that this game commits, is just not having the little things like inventory management like health potions (because the game has regenerating health instead) or a real progression to the gameplay outside of getting a sword at one point.
The story cribs a few things from the legend of Robin Hood, like forming your band of merrymen or the bridge fight between Robin and Little John, but as is, it's only serviceable, but lacks personality outside of its cinematics, which depending on your taste for Tumblr art, could really turn you off. (Which at certain points, I thought the cutsey comedic art felt incredibly out of place.) I won't spoil anything, but like many origin stories, it comes to an abrupt end before anything really interesting happens, or letting you get that proper resolution. What little there is between characters is the usual RPG back and forth
Oh, and did I mention this games REALLY short? Even despite all of the repetitive gameplay, and going over the same maps over, and OVER again, they really couldn't figure out how to lengthen it. It's not that I wanted this to be longer, it's just shocking that there's so little to do outside of the main quest. Even ARPGs know how to jerk you around.
My final time (except for the trading cards idling) was 2.2 hrs and I was THIIIIIIIIIIS close to being able to get a refund, which I might have been able to if I paid a little more attention and didn't fail the stealth stuff as much as I did. (I actually can't get a refund anyway because I got it from an indie game bundle.) Maybe you're the chosen one that can beat it and refund it... but I wouldn't risk it. The game is just... bleh.

Don't play this game with too critical an eye for detail, because you will almost immediately see small issues that will add up over time. It's an incredibly flat world, and one has to labor to understand the lore, setting, characters etc. The Characters are incredibly flat; after finishing a phenomenal Nihon Falcom game recently where I can name you umpteen number of memorable NPCs, Oblivion has thousands of cardboard cut-out characters, with Friar Martin as the one exception. The settings are as forgettable and unoriginal as any other RPG. For example, depictions of Hell are always intriguing in games, but Oblivion's depiction is as uninspired as ever. No sense of dread here! The music is solid throughout. Jeremy Soule always delivers.
Really make sure there is something specific that you know you will get out of this game before purchasing it. I kinda impulsively bought it on sale, then looked up reviews, then played it, then kinda regretted buying it.
It's not bad. It only fulfills either your expectations or your nostalgia, but doesn't surpass either. Believe me, I've played more endearing games published back in 2007.

Some context; I've played the non-steam version of this game since release. I've logged around 3300 hours into it.

To begin, this game has one of the best soundtracks known to man. Jeremy Soule's performance in this game is astonishing. The music moulds the environment to create a human touch to every area that you enter. The obscure details and quests that this game has to offer is what weaves a unique player experience. By creating a dynamic experience for each playthrough, you will learn that you know nothing about the intricacies of this game. The only downside I can think to this game is that without the Oblivion Character Overhaul, the faces look ugly as hell.

Dungeon Siege III is an action R.P.G. developed by Obsidian Entertainment and published by Square Enix. For centuries Legionnaires have protected the nation of Ehb until they were betrayed and all but driven to the brink of extinction. Years later, now that evil has returned to Ehb the people turn to the few remaining Legionnaires for the protection of the past. As an heir to the Legion will you accept this plea for help? Dungeon Siege III is the latest entry in the beloved long running classic roleplaying series from Square Enix. It is worth nothing though that this title is quite different from the previous games in the series.
At the start of the game you choose one of four different character classes and set off on an adventure to take back the nation of Ehb from an evil force that has gained control of the land and declared war on all of the former protectors of Ehb known as Legionnairies. Dungeon Siege III has all the elements of a traditional roleplaying game with you, the player, gaining experience points through combat, various tasks, completing quests and discovering lore. You can use these points to upgrade your chosen characters abilities to your particular style of play through a fairly diversified skill tree. There is also a great amount of loot to be collected in the form of weapons, armor and trinkets that can be accquired through combat, exploration and different merchants scattered throughout the land. Choosing the right weapons and items for your character as well as for your companion are vital to your survival as the narrative plays out. Even though the plot in this game is a story that has been portrayed many times before, I was really entertained with the way it was presented in Dungeon Siege III and thoroughly enjoyed the adventure from start to finish.
Graphically I think this game is beautiful, it's played in a isometric top-down view much like "Diablo" and the "Baldur's Gate" titles. From the dense Rukkenvahl Forest, through the beautifully cobbled streets of Stonebridge to the mines of Glitterdelve and beyond, the environments of Ehb are varied and full of the little details that one looks for in games of this type. The title also uses a gorgeous color palette and blends in depth of field effects quite nicely both during gameplay and cutscene dialog. The sound quality is exceptional whether it's the sound of combat, dialog or just ambient background noises as you travel across the land. Also of note is the terrific musical score which is quite memorable in this game. There are a couple of tracks that I would really like to own but sadly the soundtrack to this title is not available anywhere and believe me I checked. To summarize, I really like R.P.G.'s that take you on a quest to a wide variety of locations and Dungeon Siege III excels at this while providing quite a visual feast for the eyes.
I really enjoyed my first playthrough of Dungeon Siege III despite some problems with the camera angles at times during combat. The story was intriguing, the combat was alot of fun, the characters and lore was quite interesting as well. Each of the four available characters have vastly different styles of combat so the replayability of this title is high. I plan to go back and play again with each of the other characters at some point. Though I have to admit that for some strange reason I remember downloading and playing the demo of this game right before it launched a few years ago and I did not like it. I can only believe that is because of my gaming habits having changed around that time and me moving more towards R.P.G.'s like "The Elder Scrolls" and "Kingdoms Of Amalur" and away from the old-school roleplaying games that first captured my interest in the genre to begin with. I don't know...all I can say now is that this is indeed a great game despite all the HATE that it constantly receives and is RECOMMENDED for roleplaying gamers.

I decided to check out this game after being viewing a few episodes of the anime of the same name. I'd found the art style beautiful but the main character flat. The game, I feel, is somewhat better than the anime, but not without it's flaws. The story is filled with anime/Hime cliches. Finally finished~ After over 60 hours, I got to witness every single ending this game has to offer and all the extra content.
I went into this game having already watched the anime, so I'm already used to the heroine being a very passive type, as well as some quirks of the other characters (I'm looking at you, Toma). So I don't really have any complaints in that regard.
Amnesia is a fantastic mystery-oriented, somewhat dark romance dating sim. You play as a heroine who wakes up with amnesia and you must try to hide your amnesia. This concept works really well because you as the player don't have any idea what's going on with the heroine's life. All the characters have their own charm and they're not stereotypical or flat. The UI is super smooth, the art is gorgeous, the music suits the mood and doesn't get too repetitive, and the voice acting...-it's really good. I got this game on sale and I felt like it was a great catch. This game made me question my choices and I actually learned a bit more about myself and how I would react in certain touchy situations.
Individual route reviews! Characters completed so far: CONTAINS SPOILERS
Toma was the first one I chose, and yeah, many people find his to be the most shocking route. In fact, I got the bad end as my first playthrough, ahaha. I find it diificult to like or dislike him. I...am aware of the fact that's he not quite right in the head, but...I'm ashamed to say that I really like Toma. Since he's not real, he's not a threat to my well-being. Although if he were real then I'd stay far away. But I was beside myself with mixed emotions when I did the happy end. Toma is a really pitiful character, his pain makes me feel sorry for him and I wish I could help him, so I guess the happy end did work out for me in the end, although some people might disagree. Overall, I actually like Toma (though a part of me is fighting it).
the second character I decided to play. He has a really harsh personality, and he's younger than you, which makes him act even more harsh and independent because he wants to be on equal footing with you. He's pretty much the opposite of Toma; bitter on the outside, sweet on the inside. He does have a lot of swoon-worthy qualities, such as his sense of honor and his sudden kisses, and his bass playing in secret so he could surprise you and join your band, and he's also very human because he does have his weaknesses. It's easy to see why he's the featured character for the game. I remember his happy end made me cry because it was really sweet. Personally, his harsh personality isn't my type but he's a pretty likeable character.
by far the biggest surprise for me. He is introduced as a very stoic graduate student who loves to disagree and argue with you. He's also very blunt and can say insensitive things. BUT. Kent is a very innocent and sweet character (once you get to know him later, of course). Having no experience in romance, he's extremely cute and honest. I do find his personality rather rare if not unrealistic. I absolutely loved his happy end (and I got it on my first try too). If you thought Shin's happy end was sweet, Kent's happy end was ten times as sweet. He's also the only one (I know, so far) that knows and believes Orion.
this is your playboy character. He's surrounded by fangirls and I initially thought it would be similar to Toma's route, but nope. The bullying was way worse in Toma's route. Ikki really isn't my type. He's sincere with you, so it's a matter of getting your character to trust Ikki. There were some quirks in Ikki's personality that I was surprised by...like how fragile he actually is (but not as fragile as Toma). He's also not very perceptive, unlike Shin and Toma who were super sharp and figured out you had amnesia on day 1 (Ikki finds out on the last day...gg). I thought the story would delve deeper into why Ikki wanted you to fall in love with him within 3 months (I thought it had something to do with breaking the spell put on his eyes, but I guess not). Overall, I found that it was pretty enjoyable, he's a smooth talker but I can never put much value on his words and I had a hard time seeing a logical progression of feelings. It could be just me, though.
poor crybaby Ukyo, I cried too.
After all that, I can't decide who I liked best. I know Ikki comes in last (sorry Ikki fans), just because he wasn't my type. If you had to twist my arm and make me choose, I'll probably go for Toma...even though he's disliked for various reasons. ^^
Some minor complaints I have is that some scenarios aren't really consistent. It seems like only the good end route is the route that's completely consistent, while in the other routes the game seems to forget some details based on the choices you make. I also am not too fond of rereading the same text 4 times to get all the endings since there isn't too much variation in the story except for the end, but most VNs are like that. I also don't like rereading the prologue 50 times because it really doesn't add to the reading experience each time, I'd suggest adding a skip option for the prologue so the player can just get on with it.  It also bothers me that the lip flap movements don't sync up with the voice acting, especially when the speech is being dragged out (I'm looking at you, Toma's seiyuu), but it's easy to ignore if you're reading the text most of the time. I really love the character art, but when the characters look surprised, they actually look like they're terrified...but these are all pretty minor flaws.
Overall, this game is fantastic and I would definitely recommend playing if you're into dark romance dating sims!

This is going to read like an editorial so consider yourselves warned.
People, I am upset. You know why? This is a good game and it doesn't get the credit it deserves. First I would like to address some criticisms that this game receives and then I will give my personal review.
When I read that this game crashed constantly, I decided I still wanted to give it a go. The story sounded very original and I liked what I saw from the store page. I played this on Windows 7. Did the game crash? Yes. 3 times in over 6 hours of game play. People, a Fallout game can do that. This is a game meant for an older OS and it says so right on the page. I never had the game crash on the major sections that are commonly complained about in the discussions section, and my game never crashed during or after a cutscene.
To help with not having to lose a lot of ground due to a probable crash, I autosaved after going to each new location. This game gets slack for not having an autosave option. To manually save takes seconds, and to see this as a negative is failing to understand when this game came out. Autosave after every checkpoint is still fairly new, and takes away responsibility from the player. Who remembers memory cards, or finding the typewriter and hoping to have ink ribbon? ;) All in all, having to manually save should not be a shot against this game.
Now that I have gotten that off my chest, here is the review. I loved it. The opening cinematic is beautiful and action packed. The music is right out of a spy-action thriller movie. Then we meet our characters. This is where it gets interesting because they are a group of likeable criminals. The voice acting is well done and the bonds are felt between the characters, especially as the plot thickens. You primarily play as Cathryn, the leader of the three thieves. There will be times when you will change who you control, since each plays their own role in a heist. You also play as the international police officer who is investigating a murder and is on their trail. Are their art thefts and the political murders linked? Well, that would be telling.
This game is more like an interactive movie than a point and click game. But its a good movie. The puzzles are much more down to earth and not outlandish like in P&C games of the 90's. There are certain minigames such as hacking security, or finding ones way through the Parisian catacombs; Each security hack is different so it isn't the same tired formula. Sometimes its hacking lasers; or its cameras; or its amusements rides, and they all have different methods. Also, they are skippable! After so much time has passed and you find that you are stumped, you can skip it and continue with the game. I found myself stumped 1 out of 5 minigames and found them to be a fun addition to the game. While the game isn't hard, I wasn't bored with the easy gameplay. The story kept the game going. I think that is what the developers had in mind: Don't get bogged down by puzzles or furious over minigames--keep the story going.
Now the technical aspects. The cut scenes are of noticeably better quality than the in game graphics, but I think that should be expected. I believe that the game looks good. The sound may need a bit of toggling. If you have everything at full volume, you will hear this great soundtrack and hardly any vocals. Although if you opt for subtitles you can read everything but then you'll miss the great voice work. I found I had to turn down the music and turn the voices on all the way to get a good balance, but this may depend on your sound setup. The music is awesome! I felt like I was in a spy-thriller-espionage movie! It was great. Also, all the dialogue and cutscenes are skippable by pressing Esc., so that IF your game does crash, you don't have to suffer through lots of dialogue and cutscenes.
Now I really want to talk about what I love the most. The story is good but the themes are what seperates this one from all the others. Moral relativism is something I haven't seen explored so fully in a P&C game as in this game. These characters feel very real. They are good people who do something wrong for all the right reasons. They sometimes doubt if they are doing the right thing. They fight, they argue, they cover each other. The officer you play as is atrocious, but he follows his leads, even if ordered not to. These characters have ideaologies and they face situations that make them question what they think, especially Cathryn. She is young and very idealistic. Mild spoiler ahead, but I believe it necessary. Near the end of the game Cathryn has dinner with the main villain. The villain stays in the shadows for most of the game, but it does make sense in the plot. When Cathryn is invited by him personally to dine, it is done in a very civil manner. She goes to his house and he is the perfect host. No torture sequence, no being locked up. Just a dinner in which a very confused Cathryn tries to find out who this person is. How could this perfectly charming host be this horrible person? He calmly tells her about himself-his history, his family, his hope to reconnect with his daughter someday, and yes, the things he felt necessary to do for his people and country. What is scary is that from his point of view, he is justified. His logic makes sense. I don't want to give anything else away, but that dinner sequence was amazing: an older antagonist trying to enlighten a young idealistic protagonist and challenge everything she has ever believed. Charisma in the hands of evil is a very dangerous thing.
Now the ending: It worked. It ties up all the loose ends and even leaves room for a sequel, which it could take or leave.
I really liked this game. I feel bad for the slack that it has gotten. It's P&C lite, and more of an interactive movie, but its a great one. If you can operate it on a older OS system, again Win7 worked fine for the most part, I seriously suggest you try it. If you are hesitant, wait for a sale, but don't pass this one up.

First of all I'm not a person who normally enjoys point and click adventures as I find them rather slow developing and cumbersome story wise and this game is by no means any different. Also I agree with those who highlight that there are a string of nasty game crashes which most people will get to experience especially in the Paris/catacomb region. While there is an inbuilt crash reporter in game, one would wonder if this actually works since those crashes have been existent since the games release back in 2010. So how does one report a bug if the bug is actually the bug reporter? Any ideas? Email the developer you say. Good idea! One problem though, the German Developer known as 'House of Tales' doesn't seem to exist anymore, at least there is no easy to find web site to contact him on. Hence the answer so far is to simply save game constantly and reload after crash and work through the matter that way.
The game is a simple point and click adventure dressed up to look like a movie rip off like 'Entrapment' with a cheeky wink here and there to the James Bond Franchise especially to its evil character lore’s. You play various parts of a trio group who have vowed to make the world a better place by stealing expensive works of art from the rich and then give the proceeds to charity by selling them on the black market, earning this trio a Robin Hood image.
While the game eventually explores this notion more in depth exposing the blaring weakness behind the group’s logic, it also explores a whole range of loose end stories. For one thing the members of your group may have independent hidden motives that you are not aware of, the estranged relationship between a member of your group called Cathryn and her father may have more to it than what she is admitting and finally the paranoia and the sickness of a comrade who paints illegal copies for you, may have more foundation in truth than make-believe.
You also spasmodically get to witness and be involved in the investigation of international police who is investigating a bizarre string of deaths regarding political figures and how there seems to be a nonsensical art stealing connection behind it all.
The game after treating your eyes to a sexy animation at the beginning quickly falls flat thanks to a slow informative development which at the time really seems to be going nowhere. You really don't get too appreciate that ALL things in this game are relevant till the very end when the villain invites you back into his lair so that he can tell you about his entire diabolical plot. While this comically reminds us of Albert Broccoli’s James Bond formula, they really do a decent job of this in game and it really does make sense for once why the villain would invite you in and why the villain would want to tell you everything. In fact maybe Albert Broccoli could take out a pen and paper and make a note here and there for upcoming Bond movies.
However unlike Bond movies the down side is that the concluding animation is nowhere near as sexy as what the game begins with and with the constant build up to a final big explosion, it eventually falls flat with a small fizzle display which wouldn't even raise an eyebrow to Michael Bay.
So why do I wave an Olympic sized thumbs up in the faces of angered customers and glaringly bad design choices?
Well for one thing I really appreciate how they tie in all the loose ends at the end. It’s an idea they chose to follow which I haven't seen in any other form of media. You see the person the trio is working for is a genocidal maniac whose belief system is expressed in a secret room in his mansion which I can only describe as 'messed up'. It’s the uniqueness of the story itself and the way it is presented that I have a deep respect for. It didn't just feel like I was playing a cheaply made rip off. There was just more to it than that. In fact his back story was so real that I had to do a quick google search after playing this game to see if Elengi of Surinawa was in fact a real person or not. He isn't, but you can easily see how he could have been.
Secondly while the beginning is seriously missing a musical score to get you in the mood, when it does eventually cut in, it really does make you feel that you’re a part of the heist. Accompanied with this is the fact that the voice dubbing was pretty flawless in my books. I could easily envision the characters being that way and saying the things they did. Granted the stereotypes were frustrating especially with Mike. In fact I have never seen a more annoying game character in game than this one. His constant guffawing’s of his own greatness was enough for me to wish that the other two would pick him up by the ankles and use his head as a toilet brush. He is seriously more annoying than Jar Jar Binks in Star wars. Mike the most annoying and out of character in any medium I have ever seen, would probably be more in character and give George Lucas a wet dream if he was to appear in an Alien pub covered in fur. It’s just something you have to experience to BELIEVE. However on the flip side Mike does have one of the best lines in the game. It's the very last line he does with the villain. Classic!
While they spend 5 days to steal one painting and 10 days to steal another, the title '15 days' has a double meaning as revealed at the end and kind of leaves the story open to an upcoming sequel. If they do make a sequel and I hope they do, I really hope that they finish that one off with a sexier animation than what they begin the game with. Something that would make Manga people fall to the floor and do obeisance too. Also if you hint to an explosion in the end, don't give me a fizzle. I want a BANG. I want a Kaboom which would rupture my ear drums and wake up Godzilla at the same time and finally any chance you can kill Mike? How about we call the sequel '15 days to die'? Mike gets sick and Cathryn's forced to get that baseball bat with barbwire out of the closet.
In final a really unique story idea which nicely ties up all loose ends at the conclusion. A game which at several parts both grabs a gamers interest and loses it just as quickly. A game which has one of the most annoying game characters I have ever witnessed now placed on my hit list. A game with its current crashing issues is simply not worth the price they are asking, but is worth at least a gander when it does go on sale and if you’re a point and click enthusiast.

CK 2, as a grand strategy game, is one of a kind.  Play as a ruler (count, duke, king, or emperor level) and work your way up or across to cover the known world in your favorite color.  Oh what's that?  Your ambitious brother just murdered you when you didn't have an heir?  Time to play as your inbred murderer with a stewardship skill of 0.  Oh you didn't know he sucked so bad? Forgot to tell you that being inbred makes you sterile and you have no more heirs to continue the game.  He dead now you have to start over.
Now you notice that your brother wants to kill you in a completely different game.  You imprison him and his friends that were in a faction with him.  You are satisfied by the stability of your realm and to quote your spymaster "tortured some folks."  What's that?  You didn't know you released them after torturing them?  Executing makes their relatives angry and now more vassals that were not angry with you are now angry with you?  By the gods!  Look there! There's another faction to replace you with an inbred infant (you did not have sexual relations with your sister of course ;)).  It is unfortunate for me to notify you that this inbred infant is you.  You are the last of your dynasty and has no correlation with your execution of all your kin beforehand.  No correlation at all.  Good work, you lost again but now you learned that allies are always important.  Having sexual relations with your relative is also important.  Learn you must practice you will.
Past adventures aside, the base game will play like a demo for the dlcs but if you want to buy the dlcs remember that someone with all the expansions can host a game for you and other store fronts have less expensive alternatives than Steam to purchase them if you wish.  Also, each time a major expansion comes around the corner the game and dlcs are heavily discounted before releasing the new expansion.
If you are worried you would not like the game then ponder as to if you like in-depth strategies to begin with.  There are many ways to fail in this game but many ways to succeed and sometimes luck can really go a long way.  Watch some videos from your favorite strategy Youtube channel or maybe try new channels.  Try Youtube channels like quill18, Yogscast, Paradox (they stream their own game as well), Arumba, etc (just a few as an example).  If you get bored of Europe, India, Africa and Central Asia then try a mod.  Play in Warhammer Fantasy's world, or A Song of Ice & Fire (Game of Thrones), or Middle Earth (Lord of the Rings).  A lot of blood (from paper cuts), sweat and tears went into this game and if you experience the game you will notice it; however, do not just use the reviews of this game to sway you and make an informed purchase based on what you would like for your experience.
I still recommend it.  I mean I don't put these amount of hours in a game I hate.  The tutorial is just that hard.

I really wanted to like this game, but it's not very fun. Even with the supposed balancing of the latest expansion, it's impossible to play even on the lowest difficulty and win. There's far too much random nonsense that can even make a map impossible to complete, and it reflects a fundamental lack of adequate playtesting to make sure that sort of thing doesn't happen. It's not cool or impressive, it's just regrettable and leads to quitting the game...which at least is an option in this; it doesn't go the extra level of douchiness most roguelikes do and disallow quitting without saving.
But it's also not a very good game. The map doesn't scroll when the cursor hits a border, and it often centers on the worst and most inconvenient possible places. It doesn't work with the scroll wheel as it's supposed to, and the -/+ dynamic relies on a number pad for convenience, which my keyboard doesn't have, so it's useless to me. The tutorial, additionally, is completely unfinishable thanks to poor quality control. It's like this really wasn't adequately playtested and reached 1.0 without paying attention to the development period.
It's a cute visual aesthetic, and I really wish I could give this a better review, but I can't imagine anyone really wasting their time on it and being happy they did. Even at the lowest difficulty, it's a remarkably unforgiving game, and I in turn can't forgive that. If you give players the option, here's an idea: actually make it as casual as you lead them on to believe it is. Even if that involves hand-holding, you do it. You do it, because not everyone is SUPER HARDCORE and wants to be punished for playing a game.
It's probably my fault for thinking that eventually, I'll find a roguelike game that actually delivers on its promise of fun. Instead, I feel overwhelmingly like the sentiment is a plague on games in general, and I would like to see the excitement of procedural generation applied to far more interesting and deserving concepts.

Well, I played that incredibly short demo that came with other Humongous games, but that was it until I decided to purchase the full game on sale and give it a try. I had a good time playing it (though I wish I could have experienced it as a kid.)
Freddi Fish 1 was Humongous' first game to use hand-drawn animation instead of pixel art, so that's something I admire it for, but that and its age (pre-Windows 95) mean that it isn't as refined or advanced as its sequels, though I like the retro charm it has. The animation and art are generally pretty good. The weak point is probably Freddi and Luther, who look very different here than in later games. They're drawn differently on most screens, usually looking okay, but sometimes very awkward or even terrible (Luther, especially, can look atrocious on some screens.)
One thing about this game is that it has a sort of sober atmosphere. The music, which is excellent by the way, has some very somber tracks and the graphics tend to be rather dark and muted. The game's premise is also serious: you're on a mission to prevent mass starvation. Of course, there's plenty of bright, cheery characters and fun, colorful animations, so it's not a dark or depression game, but it's definitely the most somber Freddi Fish game. The game also has villains (two bumbling Mafia sharks and the Squidfather) and I hate these characters. A Godfather parody could work in Spy Fox, but it's totally out of place in this series. I can't for the life of me understand why they reused these same villains for Freddi Fish 2.
Overall, this is a good though dated children's game and if you want to introduced a child to this series, I'd recommend starting with this one.

I have to say that this is the only 4x strategy game that I have really gotten into, and it is seriously worth it!
Here's the shortened version:
pros:
- different races to play as that actually give a lot of diverse gameplay options
- each race has its own (interesting) quest-line and (vibrant) history
- quests really give you a purpose and a bit of story to drive you forward and keep you engaged with your faction.
- combat system takes the best of Civ V and Total War to create a really fun system!
- seasons!
- relatively simple interface (you probably need to play the tutorial to fully understand it though)
- customise your army units
- very sassy AI!
- beautiful graphics
cons:
- you can't see exactly how strong an enemy is before you attack (at least, i havent found a way yet)
- tutorial is quite heavy, but also worth it so....
- cities are a little hard to see clearly as there is a lot of stuff going on...
- it is a little buggy and often crashes when I play multiplayer, but not enough to deter me from the game!
The long version:
What I like most about this game is the sense of real diversity between each 'culture/races/people'. They each have very specific and drastically different ways of playing them. For example you have a race that is a cult - they can't build extra cities so conquering by force is useless, so instead of soldiers they have preachers who spread their influence and 'take over' other players' settlements through spreading their cult. Another clan is basically vermin zombies who don't even have the option of diplomacy - all they can do is attack other players and eat them or turn their enemies into zombies which they can then control. Or a third one is a bunch of metal armours with souls inside them so they don't require any food resources! There is much more than that but they all have advantages and disadvantages that are really well balanced and truly FEEL different and diverse!
On top of that the combat system is really interesting.
First of all, each race only gets 4 different base units. That's it. But wait for it..... you get to customise them! As you level them up you get access to tier 2, 3 etc items like armour, weapons, and jewelery which all give you different stats which means you can create different units tailored to your own style of play or needs. For example I'm playing with the woodsland people (not their official name) and i have access only to archers at first. But I have created 2 different types of archers through this system - some are better at fighting infantry units whereas my second class is stronger against flying units. And now I also spent a while upgrading all my unit designs so that I can manufacture better units. There aren't THAT many different options, but there are enough to make it diverse and you can have a lot of fun with it. I also just like the ability to upgrade your units instead of simply receiving new units and you don't really know what they do. This way, I really am getting to know my army for once.
Secondly, it's not like in Civ V where your units throw javelins from one hexagon to another hexagon or something like that. In battle you have your little units and they each take up 1 square, so you can control each of them individually, at first you need to decide where to place them (they get advantages or disadvantages based on terrain) and then you decide which enemies they attack. It's the same basic concept as in total war, but with less units and turn-based. You're also able to see the stats of your opponents and so can strategise pretty nicely without it taking forever or being overly complicated.
The only down side is that you can't really tell the strength of an enemy army until you have engaged in battle with it (which has meant that 1 and a half of my armies has been accidentally wiped out because of that. But i think that is mostly because i had only archers. Because i didn't have access to anything else at that point because i was focusing on production instead of armies.)
Finally, quests. I haven't play that many 4x strategy games but I haven't seen quests like these before. And I love them. I tend to play mostly RPGs because I like story and my main concern with 4x games such as Civ V was that I didn't really care about my people. But not in Endless Legend. Oh no. The quests and bits of story you get gives you motivation and a purpose and that is what is keeping me playing this game! And I don't even have time for it! It feels like there is a story happening - you're not just developing your community for nothing, you've got a purpose and i love that!
Basically, it's complex, but simple enough to understand - just the way i like my games.

Awesomenauts is in the MOBA genre (much like DOTA 2, Blizzard All-Stars. or League of Legends), but I feel like it stands out because it is a lighter, more casual game in a genre which is dominated by the aforementioned hardcore games.
Everything has been simplified; 3 players per team (instead of the standard 5), generally there are only 2 lanes, and each character only has two abilities and a unique standard attack. Instead of having both experience and gold, there is only one currency in Awesomenauts, called Solar, which functions as both. Upgrades for your characters 2 abilities and their general stats (speed, max health, health regen, etc.) can then be purchased with Solar. This upgrade system is nowhere near as complex as the item system in standard MOBAs and thus no predetermined "item build" is needed to be competitive.
There is also much less micromanagement needed in Awesomenauts than a standard MOBA. There are no couriers or manually-controlled summoned units. The vast majority of abilities are just aiming with the mouse and one or two button presses. Also, "Last-hitting", a MOBA tactic where you want to get the killing blow on non-player enemy units, is in Awesomenauts but not last-hitting is less punishing than many MOBAs like DOTA 2. Last-hitting an enemy gives you their Solar directly, but if don't, the Solar simply drops on the ground where you can still pick it up if you get to the spot where they died before anyone else. As such, I feel that last-hitting is less important in Awesomenauts than some other MOBA games, which I personally like.
I like Awesomenauts because I feel like being competitive doesn't require any pre-planning; it is very "pick up and go". If you find the item purchasing process in standard MOBAs to be tedious or overwhelming, or you are trying to introduce the MOBA genre to someone new, young, or just a casual gamer then I would highly recommend Awesomenauts.

Amnesia: Memories is a visual novel that combines beautiful art with some of the best storytelling I've seen in a game in a long time. Do not confuse it with a Horror game of nearly the same name, because rather than leave you fearful, this title has the potential to leave you with a tremendous sense of awe, and almost sadness; not that the story is sad, but that it is over and you will never again experience it as you did that first time.
I 100%’d this game, something I almost never do, simply because I HAD to see all the endings, and the thought of being done with this game was more than I could handle. It is voiced (a big plus vs. other otomes) and keeps the story moving without burdening you with excessive side jobs to grind likeability stats.
I'll attempt to keep this as spoiler free as possible, but if you don't want to risk it, I will say this: get this game. This is the first game I have purchased where I wish I had spent MORE on it. I got this game on sale for $7, and I've seen it go under $5. It is worth full price. If you see it on sale, do not hesitate, grab it. This is a beautiful, smart and joyful game any visual novel fan should experience. Use one of the guides, I recommend Pie-inator’s, to help you get to each of the endings and enjoy.
Possible Spoilers Below
Amensia: Memories is about a girl who loses her memory when as stray spirit collides with her head. Whoops. Now, instead of any sense of self, she has a friendly little guide by the name of Orion to help her get through life and figure out who she is, and who she can trust. After a brief introduction to Orion, you’ll pick your world, meaning, pick your guy.
The first choice is Shin. Shin’s path is a good mystery. He’s a pretty typical tsundere, and your childhood friend. His best quality is that he understands the MC and will do absolutely anything to help and protect her. This path’s main function is to introduce you to the cast of characters that will play important roles as you continue your journey to understand the truth about this world you have stepped into.
Next up is Toma. If you didn’t think there is a little something wrong, and dark, about your situation while playing Shin’s path, you will understand it now. Toma’s path is not overly unique for otome’s and visual novels, but it’s pretty twisted. Orion’s interaction with your character takes it to the next level, especially if you’re going for the happy ending. It’s pretty great making bizarre choices in a game and having someone actually call you out on it.
Next up is Ikki, a playboy type who you think you have all figured out the moment you meet him. But this is the path where you begin to realize this world has some really strange things going on, far beyond the normal. Ikki’s path is very sweet and really turns all of your assumptions about the character around. By the end, you’ll probably have a little crush on Ikki, and that’s ok.
The forth path is Kent, a character who has mostly sat in the background in the previous paths. He is quiet and intelligent, and a bit harsh. As you begin this path, both you, Orion, and the MC wonder how it is that you are actually dating this guy. Your relationship is pretty rocky, to say the least. But the further you go down this path, the more and more Kent’s true character comes out. This is probably the most romantic path, and ends in such a sweet way that you may find yourself falling for this adorable nerd.
Along the way, as mentioned, you’ll also be interacting with Orion. His presence up until this point is pretty much a mystery, though if you’ve been paying attention you’ve started to get some clues as to what’s going on. His company really elevates the entire experience so far through his adorable reactions and unwavering support of the MC.
If you’ve gone this far, you have also met the strangest character in the cast, Ukyo, and buckle up, because now that you’ve completed the other four guys’ paths, Ukyo’s is now available to you. This is where the story goes from strong to unreal. Ukyo’s path is the story of the world, the overarching plot that ties all other paths together and explains exactly what happened to the MC. It is heartbreaking and beautiful and very well may have you in tears by the end. Not to mention Ukyo’s path has a grand total of NINE different endings.
Walking the path with Ukyo is dangerous and confusing, but leads to one of the biggest payoffs I have ever experienced in a game. It takes some time to get to this path, but to not experience this path is to not experience the game.
Overall this game is breathtaking, with beautiful art, fantastic music and an out of this world story. It is a SMART story, and doesn’t talk down to the player, but rather challenges you to accept unbelievable circumstances as truths. It is not your typical otome. There is a depth to this world that you would expect out of a big triple-A RPG, not a casual visual novel. It is a must have for any visual novel fan.

Ragnarok Online RE:START is an almost-from-scratch re-release of the original Ragnarok Online servers that were released in Korea in 2002. International versions saw release later on and at one time Ragnarok Online had over 15 active official servers at once. This spawned a bunch of unofficial “Private Servers” that were community run and had no association with the official servers.
Ragnarok Online is an MMO based around Norse mythology. The story-line in my opinion is very indirect and nearly non-existent. You can play the entire game without realizing there is some sort of background to what world you’re in, but I suppose very few people play MMOs for the storytelling. Aside from that, this is your almost typical run-of-the-mill MMO with stats, skills, classes, and endgame content in two different flavors, PVP and PVM.
In this game, you have two levels. Base levels, which is the general gauge of your power and is directly related to the amount of stat points you have available. The second set of levels is your Job level, which is directly related to your class and skill spread. In this game, at the max level, you will not be able to get every skill, and thus you are required to plan how you would like to play your character somewhat in advance. The max levels in this game are the Base Level of 99 and the Job Level at 50 (novices cap at 10). Your Job Level will reset every time you advance in class progression.
As mentioned earlier, the two different flavors of endgame content are in the form of PvP and PvM. In Player vs Player, you have War of Emperium, which is a prestigious Guild vs Guild event that occurs once a week. Guilds lay claim to castles in specific cities and defend them from other guilds. Guilds that successfully do so have access to powerful and prestigious items the longer they hold these castles. For Player vs Monster, there are fabled monsters, called MVPs of varying powers. Certain classes and builds can solo-kill these monsters, while others require a coordinated effort. Since RE:START is a rebuilding of a server (that in theory will eventually catch up in updates to the current elder servers), there may eventually be an Endless Tower (MVP Gauntlet) and WoE v2.
Enough of the formal introductions, let's see the good, the bad, and the score.
: The game has a relatively unique art-style. It’s a 3D environment with 2D sprites and hand-drawn character art. The game’s graphics may seem aged, but they bear some aesthetic beauty.
: While the graphics seem aged, the sounds themselves are perpetually timeless. The sound effects and accompanying map music are very fitting, well-made, and can be enjoyed in-game, or out.
: On the flip side, the game is a great social game. This game however, is pretty terrible if you prefer to be by yourself 100% of the time. If that’s your style, you may not enjoy this game. As for myself and my playgroup, we enjoy playing this game and is one game that we can all play without much acquiescence, which leads to the next point.
: The game certainly has a surface-level where most people can enjoy the game for what it is; and then there’s the deep-end of the pool where people follow optimized build paths, equipment, and strategies. People can choose to play at whatever level they like and the game offers some slight forgiveness if you choose unwisely.
Because this game is very aged with some well-vetted players, I consulted the community forums for some opinions on what they believe is wrong with this server.
: The game has a premium currency at two levels: Kafra Points (KP) and Silvervine (SV). One KP is roughly equivalent to one cent USD. KP can buy anything from the cash-shop without limitation, including SV. KP is not tradable. SV can be traded for the in-server currency (Zeny) and gives the ability to Free-2-Play (F2P) players to buy cash-shop items with Zeny. The price between SV and Zeny fluctuate. Some players believe that KP and SV have too much influence over this server, while thankfully not directly being Pay-2-Win (P2W).
: Community members believe that the members of the operating company, Warp Portal (WP) either don’t respond to hard-hitting comments, or cherry-pick the ones they do respond to, leaving a lot of controversial topics untouched and left to fester. They do interact on different occasions, from different levels of staff, but not on all the appropriate topics.
: There’s a very popular item, called War of Emperium Potions. While they have the name, they can be used outside of WoE freely. They cost 5 Kafra Points, which is equivalent to 5 cents USD. They heal for more health than other NPC-offered potions and weigh less than their alternatives. While there is a specific player-made range of potions that are better, these WoE Pots have influenced the server heavily. There was also a bug that impacted all server consumables by placing them at their intended healing values, but WoE Pots were reverted to their previous inflated restoration values while others were left; this was due to the fact that some players had spent real money on WoE Pots, and to leave them in this nerfed state would have caused some serious community backlash. More on this topic is covered in my video.
: The server is riddled with bots. There have been many efforts in making bots’ lives more difficult, and some have succeeded. When I originally started playing, there were roughly 8,000 players on the server, and about 4k-5k of them were expected to be bots. Over the time, the Game Moderation (GM) team has removed a lot of these bots. The server now sits at about 4k active players, and the players project that about half of these accounts, at least, are bots. WP is actively removing bots and discussing alternatives, but as of the time of this review, the bots have had a major impact on the economy and player experience.
: Some other popular topics were that the managing staff seem to have no intentional direction with the server, each new patch causes some sort of game-changing bug to pop up (ie; consumables bug), and that it is possible for players to modify client-sided information that will impact server-sided play (on a small, but noticeable scale).
For those who are unfamiliar with my channel, my scoring is a little less-than-traditional, but still relatively simple. I rate five categories from 0 to 2; 2 is great, 0 is terrible. The four categories are as below reviews, with the last being a "
" category. This category allows me to grade games based on criteria that some games have that others won't. For example, I wouldn't try and grade this game off of it’s amazing storyline.

I've played RO since before the days of renewal and trans classes. RE:Start sounded like a great idea in concept. But the execution and community... well... both aren't there.
First off, keep in mind Ragnarok Online is an OLD game. Everything about it feels like an old MMO because it is one. So if you're not into classic gaming, I'd stay away from RO in general.
This version of RO would've been ideal for me. I liked the balance of classes pre 3-1/3-2. I liked idea of working with a community to level, joining a guild for War of the Emperium, and becoming a part of the game's player-run economic system. Sadly, none of those aspects of the old RO I knew are here.
First, there is hardly no community. Most of the player characters I ran into were bots. I MAYBE saw an actual player for every 15 bots I ran into. With that said, the bots and few players lacked any kind of MMO etiquette, not hesitating to kill-steal from you or mob-train you. Speaking to other players is like speaking to a rock. I didn't encounter many people who spoke English, so it made my MMO experience feel rather isolated and empty.
Another huge problem I had was the gold sellers. For the life of me, I can't figure out why Gravity can't get rid of them and ban them - outside of the fact that they just don't care. Any time you go into a city, you WILL be spammed by gold sellers in public chat, private messages, and even in the in-game mailing system. I've even been spammed while leveling in the field! They're relentless and absolutely detrimental to the game economics.
On the plus side, the leveling cruve is easier than old-school RO. And in the beginning, you will get plenty of help and resrouces to ensure you get off to a good start.
All in all, Gravity had a good idea, with super bad execution. I longed for some nostalgia from my college days of playing RO. But this experience was not at all what I looked for. The bad community, bots, and gold sellers sully this game and its a shame the few players and Gravity doesn't do anything to better it. I'd find another free game to play unless you don't mind getting spammed or soloing in RO
