Victoria 2 is probably one of the best but most complicated strategy games ever made. The sheer scale and scope of it will blow your mind if you haven't played a Paradox game before (actually it still will even if you have). But once you start to understand its systems and the time period, your mind will really be expanded. The politics system and the economics alone are more detailed, realistic and complex than anything outside of a high-level supercomputer simulation (and certainly more so then any other game I know of).
It is daunting to learn the complexity of this game, but fortunately you don't really need to master all the systems in order to be able to play fairly well (you can get-by without understanding everything). And the more you play the more you'll master it and, like I said, by the time you've done that you will literally be a smarter person. The game's mechanics are complex enough that you cannot really predict the outcome of things in the long run (like which countries will come to dominate), because it's all based on complex systems interactive with other complex systems to create the ultimate complexity. Which does a good job of simulating human history,
The vanilla game is good, but it gets much better with mods. Of which there are lots. There's tweak mods, overhaul mods, alternate history mods, etc. But the one I would recommend for both improved gameplay and improved realism is POP Demand Mod (it's probably the closest you'll get to actually directing history).
This is a game where you take a nation from the 19th century, very much into the 20th. You can industrialise as an advanced European colonial power, or start as a primitive country (like say China or Japan) and if you play right, you can race ahead and catch up and even overtake the Europeans. By the end of a game you're likely to be in a very interesting world, with Monarchies, Democracies, Fascist and Communist states fighting it out in world wars. You will never have the same end-game world in more than one playthrough, so you're creating alternate history as you go.
If you're into hardcore strategy and/or history, then you've got to experience this game.

This is in my opinion a decent hack and slash title that imitates Diablo with a limited consequence system. For example, you get to make decisions such as letting someone live and that may benefit you or not later on.
While I could complete the game on medium with a keyboard, a controller would have been far better as I rarely used the block function anyway.
What the game has going for it is a nice colour palette, satisfying combat and a deep system to customise your character's skills and equipment rules. I also love is that there is next to no time for loading between areas and thankfully this game doesn't bother with a checkpoint system.
Where it falls is that the character's aren't that interesting. I played as Anjali who is a fire being of some kind. Yet her dialogue options were just dull. Now there are some funny lines from some of the characters so you will get a jolt of humour or two.
Also the AI of your partner can be annoying at times as you have no control over it. When your character gets knocked out, your partner can you revive you. Now you'd think that your partner would make it their priority to get you back on your feet. Wrong. Some times they will but sometimes they'll just mess about, doing their thing until either they finally come over or they die. Furthermore, if there's 4 characters, why can you only have 1 partner. Surely the mission to save the world (yup, no points for plot originality) would be better served with 4 peeps rather than 2.
Finding your objective can also be tricky, especially with multiple levels of height in areas. Then there's the inventory system which while ok could be worked better. It takes time to get all 3 other partners but you can start getting their stuff from the get go. Stuff that only 1 person can use. Carrying it seems like a waste of space so there will be a ruthless amount of selling to be done.
On the whole my experience with this game was positive. As mentioned above there's tons of loot, good enemy variety, interesting enemy variety and the world comes across as having depth. Eventually I will try a second character so replayability as well.

Very nice adventure game from 2010, but it is quite different from current flagships of genre like Deponia, Syberia and even The New Beginning. You know what we gamers lack? Interesting stories that are not Fantasy, Sci Fi or take place in the US. Cross of the Dutchman COULD have been that. A story about strife with a European medieval hero.
Instead we got not even a generic ARPG, we got THIS...Let me tell you what Cross of the Dutchman "features":
- An overworld map, a small one, but large enough to be annoying, since you'll be revisiting the same areas over and over again getting from point A to B back to A
- Clunky animations, seriously, nothing in this game is well animated
- Oversaturated colours (personal annoyance)
- A hideous combat system that consists of mashing A on your controller and occasionally tapping B for your special attack, which either destroys whole swathes of enemies or just hits 1
- A very bland and foreseeable story
- Shallow characters
- A crappy and arbitrary stealth system
- Lots of crates to break, which will respawn, but not contain any more gold
- A boring upgrade system
Alright, so the story is about a revolution, it's depicted in boring stills without any voice acting. The game lacks that completely. In the end the story was so boring and forgettable I half-skipped all the dialogue. It's cringy and feels like a 10 year old wrote it. Very generic. So, basically you run around the map from one quest point to the next, building your little revolution. Of course you ALWAYS have to take detours, because the direct route is mysteriously blocked. You're smashing crates for gold, which is fine. What is not fine is those same crates respawning after you've already smashed them, because they contain no more gold. You need that gold to purchase upgrades like +health and stamina as well as special attacks. To be honest, the former are mandatory upgrades, the latter are unimportant, your basic ability is more than enough.
Between running around, smashing crates and reading boring dialogue you have to fight HORDES of enemies at times. They swarm you really easily. As I said the combat consists of mashing auto attack, which executes a 3 hit combo if you want to. Press B whenever your stamina is full to unleas a potentially devastating attack...or miss completely. Seriously the same attack patterns netted me either a whole bunch of enemies or just 1. The combat could not be any less challenging. There is no dodging, no blocking, no positioning, archers will just stand there and shoot you point blank, you can't avoid attacks and sometimes your attacks simply miss the target. This isn't helped by the fact, that you're going to be spending more than half of the game without a WEAPON. Yes, this is an ARPG and you do not have a damn weapon. You only get that later on, when the game is almost over and frankly the only thing that changes is that your attacks have a bit of an AOE effect.
The last bit is the stealth part. Luckily this only happens twice in the game...the first time it's even believable, the second time is just arbitrary frustration (the only part of the game where I repeatedly failed). You have to dodge soldiers at night who carry lintels. Whether they can see you or not seems to be entirely up to chance. Sometimes I was walking right in front of them or beside them, other times I was spotted 10 meters away. Very annoying, since there is no manual saving and the checkpoints can be a ♥♥♥♥♥ at times. The second stealth sequence is so pointless, since you're killing everything in your way until suddenly you have to avoid any enemies, only to be killing them again a few meters later. Makes no bloody sense.
I don't know why people rate this game so highly, it's got NOTHING. It's (thankfully) only 2 hours of your time or less, if you happen to not die. What you could have done here is a story about a farmer who leads a revolution and loses everything in the process, a depiction of a righteous man going down a dark path, a "hero" organising a revolution. This is a short story and a badly executed one at that, with forgettable characters and an ending that was entirely foreseeable. Just, I don't know, I got it for a very low price, but even for that I feel cheated. Steer clear imho.

If you are expecting an experience like Torchlight or some other ARPG with random levels, you would be disappointed. It tells a tale that is based on reality between the Saxons and the Frisians. I found the pacing to be okay, but I somehow knew that it would be short when it introduced chapters. It is extremely linear to the point that you could have just removed the game and still have told the story. I guess the gameplay was only there to break up the other story-telling bits. My guess is this game could be completed in about 30-45 minutes or less if the cutscenes were skipped as well as simply going from A to B.

This game caught my attention for several reasons. Firstly, is was an ARPG with controller support, so that meant that I had to give it a chance. I've enjoyed gaming for years, but I really do prefer to game with a controller, so that was an absolute plus for me. I was also fascinated by the historical fantasy aspect of this game, so I was pleased to find during gameplay that this concept was maintained throughout with clothing and architecture.
The soundtrack was good, and the graphics were very vivid and colorful. The one thing I have to say about this, though, is that the color saturation seemed a bit off to me. I must have walked past the carrot patch a dozen times during the prologue, because they looked like beets to me, and I noticed that "ruddy" color scheme throughout. I'm unsure if this was intentional, but it was definitely noticeable.
Mechanically, the game is sound, but there is room for improvement. I felt like, at times, there was a bit of lag or delay between button presses and action on the screen, specifically with combat. That does improve later on with the addition of the sword, but the delay coupled with the lack of auto-aim made combat unimpressive and a bit more of a challenge than it probably should have been.
I liked the health, stamina, and combat upgrades, but gold is scarce in the game, so if you intend to obtain the achievement for having 1,000 gold, it's best to do that before purchasing upgrades. In my case, I hadn't reviewed the achievement guide beforehand, so I'm stuck at the end of the game with little to do but start a new game for that achievement. That brings me to replayability. If I didn't intend to replay for the purpose of attaining my last 3 achievements, I probably wouldn't feel the desire to revisit this game.  That fact leads me to address the pricing. I feel like the price point could be lowered a bit. I wanted this game very badly, so I paid full price for it, but I'd feel a bit better about that if there was more content, or greater replayability. Since that's not the case, this might be a game you'd want to pick up on sale. In my opinion, even a dollar or two off of the full price would be a fair deal.
Also a positive are the number of destructibles and the looting aspect in the form of gold. While I wish that gold was of greater occurrence during the game, it is possible to attain all upgrades if you enjoy smashing destructibles and looting chests, like I do. What I would like to see improved, though, is layout. The gaming environment is relatively small, with a lot of backtracking or revisiting of areas as the game progresses. This world has tremendous opportunity for expansion, so hopefully, we'll get to see that in a future update.
Story and character development are also areas that can be improved. There's not much to the characters or the story, and a lot of the dialogue between characters seems to have been inserted as filler, as if the developers felt that something was needed but didn't quite know what, or didn't have the time/budget to do what they really wanted.
The game can easily be played from start to finish in an afternoon, and it comes with a lot of very attainable achievements. This will likely become my first "perfect" game, so if that is something that interests you, you might consider this when deciding if this is a game for you.
Overall, it's a perfectly enjoyable game with some unique elements. I'd encourage achievement hunters and ARPG fans to give this a try. I'd also encourage the developers to either revisit Cross of the Dutchman in the form of content updates or publish a sequel. I would definitely consider their next publication.
Edit 9/14/2016: I've played through this game twice now, and I wanted to add a little something to my review. While, from strictly a gamer's point of view, I still think that this game would benefit from some polishing and additonal content, I have to say that I have great admiration for the developers undertaking the challenge of an illustrated history lesson in video game format. I can imagine that the devs may have felt that, while considerable creative license has obviously been exorcised, they were attempting to balance history and historical fiction, entertainment with the limited information available about the real "Great Pierre." I have to admit that as much I love history, I was unaware of Pierre until this game. It's fascinating to me that he made such an impact in Dutch history and even somewhat to world history. Whether or not he was really the 7ft giant of a man wielding a 7ft sword in battle, the reputation was hard-earned. I now understand why Pierre came to be known as the Cross of the Dutchman.

TCE is one of the best games in its class, a Roguelike-inspired strategy/adventure game that will leave you wanting more. Easy enough to beat several times in one day if you're dedicated, yet hard enough to make every victory feel like you clawed your way to it from the depths of hades.
If you're looking at this game and you're even half sure you want it, get it. If looking at it fills with you a warm and gooey sense of longing for the hours spent huddled around CRT monitors taking turns playing The Oregon Trail, buy it. Even if you're a more modern gamer, but you're a fan of FTL, Caves of Qud, the Binding of Isaac, or similar, buy it.
Need more convincing? Read on.
Sometimes when a game developers look back to the past for inspiration, the results may drip with nostalgia but ultimately come out uninspiring. At other times, however, a game can look back and learn from both the past and the present to create something truly special.
This is one of those latter games, the ones that make us remember why we still like pixel graphics well into the 21st century.
The Curious Expedition is a delightfully fun exploration game set in a very "Pulp Action" Historical Fantasy setting. Think Indiana Jones, or the works of Jules Verne. You control one explorer plus a handful of companions (usually 4) as they trek through uncharted wildernesses in several flavors, always looking for a Golden Pyramid. Along the way way you'll meet native tribes, encounter wild animals, explore caves, investigate ancient shrines, and more. You will need to survive six such expeditions, each one longer and harder, but with greater rewards than the last, in order to finish the game. In order to "win" the game you will have to, on top of that, be the most famous explorder in the world, and there are four other explorers working hard to take that title from you.
What makes The Curious Expedition shine is the way it perfectly captures the 90s adventure game feel, without falling prey to being so obsessed with a bygone era of gaming that they can't make significant improvements on the model. The strong Roguelike influences give the game more replayability than most older adventure games (some of which are really only good for one playtrhough), and both the interface and the mechanics are a breath of fresh air.
One fair complaint about the game is that it is a bit of a one-trick pony. If you are looking for a deep sense of accomplishment such as filling up particular collections of rare artifacts will provide, you may not be happy here. This isn't a game about, long-term goals, it's about short-term survival and short-medium-term treasure hunting. Instead of the long term approach, The Curious Expedition instead opts to give you a fairly digestible experience, one in which a winning game can be finished in under 3 hours without breaking a sweat.
The end result is that, each game, when played well, ends up feeling like solving a good puzzle. If you think of TCE as being almost like Sudoku rather than trying to think of it as a game primarily about exploration, you may find yourself very satisfied. That's not to say there isn't still plenty of theme, however, the game is rich with little surpries that will continue to delight you many hours in. What utlimately makes the puzzle worth coming back to though is the complexity of it. There are so many variables, so many ways to solve the problem of how to survive six expeditions while staying the most famous, so many possibilities hidden within the map generation, ready to delight and baffle you.
All in all, The Curious Expedition is a delightful game about making hard choices and then either cheering at the results or laughing because you can't believe how wrong things went. It's a game about being too broke to afford enough food for your expedition and then lucking your way into enough supplies to get you through. Then on your next expedition, you stock up on tools and supplies, burn through them all like they're water in the desert, and die with the pyramid in sight.
Still not sure? Maybe some information about where The Curious Expedition is headed will push you over the edge:
The recent Arctic update has proven to be the breath of fresh air the game needed, and the new challenges and rewards of arctic environments are incredibly fun. The fact that the development team has made it clear that they would like to produce more new content on a similar scale is very exciting. The game is already a great value that will entertain you for many hours, so any expansion of content is only going to increase the longevity of a game I can already see myself playing for a long time.
On the note of improvements, the fact that modding is also a planned feature is huge. TCE's fantastic framework opened up for anyone to modify will create infinite possibilites for adventure.
I paid full price for this game and I don't regret it, so even if you're still unsure at least think about getting it on sale. It's worth it! Now if you'll excuse me, I have a final expedition to finish with a pack of dogs and dinosaurs to accompany me. Plus one unfortunate former journalist turned into a unspeakable monstrosity. Just a normal day in The Curious Expedition!

So, I love map/adventure games, and a while back I got the game "Renowned Explorers". That game was pretty fun but I quickly explored all of the maps within four or five play throughs and dropped it.
However, this isn't a renowned explorers review, this is a curious expedition review. And my gosh, I only dropped this game for a bit AFTER I unlocked all of the characters and played it a ton of different expeditions. This game is extremely fun. I absolutely love this game. I could write a huge paragraph about what's great about it, but for your sake, here's the key pros and cons:
Pro:
The maps are always randomly generated to the point that no map looks the same (or they all start looking the same lol).
The varity of characters and their abilities add in a great mix of challenges. There are also a varity of hidden characters that are arguably more fun than the normal characters.
The battle system is sweet and simple. Works very well for what it needs to do without overpowering the game.
The writing is charming.
The art style is beautiful and timeless.
The game difficulties are creative and add different challenges instead of just uping the chance of bad events or something.
There's a lot of good strategy involved, but it can also be played stupidly and straight forward without needing to over think everything.
Very replayable.
Perma-death works really well. A lot of time perma-death is very annoying and just makes you frustrated that you lost all of your progress. However, this isn't the case in The Curious Expedition.
Unlockable characters acts as a fun side challenge in many ways. They're pretty fun to unlock, and then you can challenge yourself to beat the game on all of them.
Music is really good actually. I also like how it changes tone based on your sanity.
Pet Dinosaurs.
(Insert here whatever I forgot :P)
Now for the important part to you review readers the Cons:
Music cuts out sometimes, which isn't a huge problem, just a little weird.
Huge amount of luck within this game. To be honest, this never bothered me too much, and you can swade your outcomes based on strategy but if you play kind of like "I want to explore everything" like I do, you tend to have the worst of luck because your sanity drains really low very fast and then terrible things happen. I kind of wish easy mode would maybe lower the sanity drain of travels automatically or something.
The chasing mechanic of the enemies is kind of awkward.
Although the text is clever, there isn't a giant amount of varity in events. They're all very short so this never really bothered me too much, but it might bother anyone who wants more of a story.
Huge lack of varity in missions. There's only like five or six of them. I would have liked a tavern or something you could visit and receive more mission options. Maybe some really low paying small ones or something or at least a few more interesting ones. I suppose they were limited in what they could do without having a bunch of carbon copy missions, but they could program special events for the missions or something. That being said, the missions that are in the game are all really clever.
Dinosaurs are usually the last area to explore :(
What the heck is the point of loyality? I have yet to find the loyality bar or meter for my crew members and it's never really effected me too much past my members becoming alocholics and then becoming angry and ditching me at the end of the expedition.
Anyway overall I think this game is really fun though, I don't think any of the cons really hindered game play. Totally worth picking up if you want it.

Endless Legend is a hexigrid turn based strategy game set in a randomly generated medieval fantasy world that has you making alliances, declaring war and peace with other nations. If it sounds familiar, that's because it is, but there's the promise of turn based battles rather than bumping your units into enemy units. However, its little more than you watching these battles play out on the hexigrid. The entire game amounts to little more than watching a gorgeous painting dry. Its a true time sink for anyone into the genre, but after spending 12 hours into it, I didn't start to "enjoy" Endless Legend until about six hours in once I had mastered certain nuances.
The game is like several others in the genre, you'll make settlements in regions and grow the settlements and chose their development. Then over time, they'll amass industry, science, food and "dust" or the game's currency. Industry gets things done quicker and I wish I had paid attention during the tutorial to know that. Science researches upgrades faster. Food keeps your citizens alive and dust pays for a lot of things. Each settlement will have a default yield of all four resources, including a fifth and that's influence that every so often you'll get to unlock more things that can be upgraded. If you'd like a higher yield, you need to balance your town's populous to put effort into each of the five. Its little more than clicking and dragging an icon from one grid cell to another. These citizens are never seen, its like a statistic that you have control over.
Now that everyone is up to speed on these genre as a whole, you'll use these settlements to generate units. You can speed up any process by spending dust to get it done on the next turn. The nation / faction you select will determine the units you can use. Everything from dragons, to ogres, archers to knights and so on. The game breaks down into three different class types, infantry (melee), ranged and support. You can combine units on the world map into an army, so six units into an army, but then the icing on these little cupcakes are heroes, which you can buy for around 2,000 dust. The heroes are tougher than units, but they can still be killed. When they're killed they respawn after a battle with little health. If they're injured, they're disabled for a few battles and you can assign only one hero per army.
You'll move your armies around and engage in battles or attack settlements. That's when the army separates back into units. As a general you've moved your armies, and now its up to them to fight on the hexigrid. Before hopping into battle, you've got a choice, manual, spectate or auto. Auto will just tell you what happened, who died, who survived. Spectate will watch the turn based battle play out for a total of six phases. So each unit goes once and that's a phase. If you select manual, at the start of each phase, you'll get to point each of your units at an enemy to attack. Then they'll do what it takes to carry out your order. If they can't do it by the end of their turn, they fall back on your choice of either offense, defense or stand their ground. So if you want an infantry to attack a supporter way in the back, but they just can't reach them in this turn, they'll move as far as they can, and attack someone else instead if you have them set to offense.
If a unit is attacked, they'll defend or attack back right then and there, but that counts as their turn. Your units have all sorts of abilities, defense, offense and stats. Your units use the abilities, you don't. You're sitting there watching the whole thing play out up to six phases. After six, if there is no decisive winner its considered a draw and its back to the world map! During the battles, if you have other nearby armies, they'll join the fray as time goes on, so if there's an army two spaces away on the world map, they'll join the battle in phase three. It definitely makes things interesting.
Another thing that's interesting is troops from each unit will fall dead, but that doesn't mean they'll be any less effective. So if there are six archers in one unit, five of them are dead, that lone archer can deal as much damage as the six of them. The amount of troops per unit is only a visual aide.
So you're not just conquering your enemies, you're winning battles or at least your units are. You'll build boats to get them from place to place, or just walk them. When capturing settlements, you've got a choice, attack or siege. Siege will cut off their resources and weaken them for your attack.
Attacking settlements can be difficult to the point that it made me think there was some sort of a glitch. You can keep attacking an enemy and see the damage indicator telling you that you've done 45 damage, but their health doesn't go down. This is the effect of being within city walls or even around a settlement in general.  You'll need to keep attacking them knowing that at some point their health will finally go down. Its a strange hidden mechanic with no reference that they're safely fortified. Settlements also come with extra militia in a garrison. If you can't capture a settlement on that turn, the militia will regenerate.
Conquering a new settlement will mean its people will hate you, but you can just arrange some morale boosters to be built. You'll also need to fix whatever problems the settlement has. A few of the cities that I had taken over had food shortages, so I had to reassign the populous from dust (gold) harvesting to food harvesting. The game will warn you if your people are about to starve so you can fix it. In fact the game notifies you of far too much with prompts that you'll need to open. These processes have been done, these units have leveled up, this hero needs you to select their perk.
Heroes have perks, just like you as a nation have upgrades. To be honest, there was far too many upgrades and perks that my mind went numb and I just started randomly selecting things. Some of the upgrades boost your harvests. Other upgrades unlock new units. As for the heroes, they'll unlock skills and passive buffs, but again nothing felt like a game changer especially when you have such little control.
One interesting facet is the seasonal change. There aren't four seasons, no; here there are just the two. Summer and winter. The winter makes travel slow and starves your people, so if you don't have enough food stored up from the summer months, you might have to pull everyone off of other duties and assign them to food harvesting. It really forces you to use things that most wouldn't even think about when playing.
Like most games of this nature, when you start, you can list a lot of specifics such as world size, climate, how many nations and difficulty. You can select random for most of them and hop into a new game generated just for you! The rival nations will watch your actions. If they feel threatened they can declare war or even offer a truce with some rewards if you're about to curb stomp them back down the hole they came out of. Its interesting seeing nation leaders so happy to trade with you or say hey we have common friends, let's be allies! No one asked to travel through my land though and that's usually a good sign that they're about to wage war on you and make a play for a city. There are neutral minor factions too that you'll need to either murder, bribe or negotiate with.
I spent twelve hours staring at a beautiful painting and at some point I started auto skipping the battles. I discovered that an easy crushing victory on spectate turns into a draw when auto battling. You're almost forced to watch these slow battles play out and that's just part of Endless Legend. Even if it weren't for the battles, the game is dull, but still gorgeous to look at with beautiful music.  I'm not even sure that I can recommend it to fans of the genre, just because you've played this before, but its now time consuming with these battles you have no control over.

I feel like I need to blame the source more than Traveller's Tales this time, since the Lego Ninjago story itself is pretty mediocre and so is the world it exists in. The game has its fair share of Lego game issues, namely tons of glitches and absolutely no polish, but it's still fun to blast around Lego pieces as a squad of Ninjas.
But there's other issues, like the audio balancing being terrible no matter what I change my settings to, the game severely lagging every time it saves, and the game shoving your screen with unbelievable amounts of clutter for the bajillion popups that appear. Anytime you get a new unlock, anytime there's a small cutscene, or anytime anything happens at all the game wrenches control of your character and spends way too much time explaining how to complete the objective.
There also don't seem to be normal levels, instead every level is part of the overworld that you can freely walk through once you beat a level... I guess it's fine for a game like this, it's a little similar to City Undercover, but it still feels lazy. This isn't a very long game either, as the main story is probably closer to three hours while most lego games are 4-5 hours (my time is almost 7 because I had it minimized for a while by accident).
Other minor annoyances, like every Ninja having exactly the same moves with just a different look to them, and every enemy (even skeletons) having exactly the same "oof" noises when they get hit starts to grind on you.
But this is a Lego game, and if you liked the movie or just want another stack of easy-to-gain achievements then it's hard to beat. Much like the Lego Ninjago movie though, I can't recommend this game.

NOTE: The time displayed for my Victoria II playtime is actually incorrect; I've played far more than 50 hours (Steam playtime at the time of this writing). Unfortunately, I originally purchased this on the Gamestop PC App (because bargain-hunting) and Gamestop didn't offer Steam keys for it until a while after my purchase. In any case, here's the review.
Victoria II is one of my favorite Paradox strategy games. It holds the distinction of being the oldest game which I continue to play, even if that is tied to its current lack of a sequel. Why, other than that, is this the game that I still play? It's hard to say, but I think that it captures its time period very well. When you build an empire in Europa Universalis, there are time periods when you have a strong sense of historical belonging, but that can't last throughout the whole game. The same can be said for Crusader Kings, which now has a ridiculously expanded timeline thanks to DLC. Victoria, on the other hand, is the Victorian Era encapsulated. Whether you dominate your foes on the mainland or "discover" vast swaths of land in Africa and the Pacific, you feel like a Victorian leader. It's a tremendous time period to experience, and an even more tremendous time to be a European Power, or an up-and-coming uncivilized nation like Japan (which will pretty much become a Great Power whether you help it or not). I reccomend it to all strategy game fans: it's probably my favorite Paradox game... subjectively speaking.

EDIT: Wanted to say, I bought this game based soley off the screen shots. I just read some reviews. Had no idea this was a true story. You'd never know that through the game's story telling. Also, I'm calling the game an ARPG bc there's Action and Hack n Slash with character development. You buy your level ups. Sounds like an ARPG to me.
When I saw this game in the store I was very eager to play it. It has an art style I like, ARPG's are a personal favorite of mine, and controller compatible. Unfortunately, bad game design has turned what should have been a great game into something that is marginally playable. My advice would be to stay away.
This is a fundamental of game design. Esp ARPG's. Cross of the Dutchman has mountains of dialogue. So much so, you'll spend more time reading poorly written dialogue than playing the game. There is no story telling by gameplay. If you skip all the dialogue you won't know what's going on or what to do next many times.
It's fine by me that your character has no customization, but loot is really where this game fails. Loot drops are what makes ARPG's great. There is no loot in this game. As a matter of fact, this guy uses his bare hands to kill soldiers. He's constantly looking for a weapon, but no one has any to spare.
This game has you going over the same maps multiple times. When you go into a new map region parts will be blocked off. You'll have to come to the blocked off parts later in the story so be prepared to traverse every region 5 or 6 times.
There are barrels and boxes you can break to get coins (bc tropes are real people!). You go over the region and try to hunt down all the breakables for coinage. The next time you arrive in that region, all the barrels are there again. However, the ones you broke previously have no coins in them. So you have to go over a region 5 or 6 times as small pieces of that region unlock through story told only in dialogue and there is no way to know which barrels are full of moneys and which ones are not. Other than having eidetic memory, you're just boned.
It's for these reasons I do not recommend this game.

Dungeon Siege III is an Action RPG that seamlessly blends intuitive fast-paced gameplay, a robust RPG system featuring a large selection of abilities, loot galore and the depth of story Square-Enix and Obsidian Entertainment are known for creating. Players will be able to adventure by themselves, on the couch with friends, or online in a fully multiplayer experience.

More arcade-style action than I was expecting, this is still a pretty fun action/RPG. I don't know if the co-op is any good (the game seems to tout that as one of its main features), as I only played single-player.
A pretty polished game overall, with enough depth to the combat to keep the otherwise-mindless slaughter of enemies interesting. The boss fights can be a little gimmicky, but that's true for damned near every hack-n-slash action game these days.

Dungeon Siege III is definitely a Dungeon Siege game. Like its predecessors, it blends action-RPG gameplay with the character development of a more traditional RPG. However, the gameplay in Dungeon Siege III is bland, and the combat is dull and repetitive. Maybe it gets better, but I lost interest pretty quickly. It's a sort of console-friendly Dungeon Siege.
The storyline seems to expect you to be playing Co-op with friends, and maybe that would add variety to the fights. But solo, it's really difficult to stay interested, when most of what you're doing is mowing down wave after wave of enemies in the same way, over and over, and you make your way from point A to point B.
This is an uninspired game, not worthy of your time.

Crusader Kings 2 (CK2) is a middle ages dynastic simulation game. In it you play a historically accurate noble family. You don't play a nation or a specific figure from history. You play the dynasty. So long as your dynasty survives, your game continues. There are no victory conditions. You can't really lose unless your dynasty ends. There are no rules. Intrigue, romance, conquest, and more are your tools to keep your dynasty alive and in power. Your primary aim is to keep your vassals happy and your reputation relatively unstained. It is the closest approximation of what medieval court life was like and illustrates the difficulty nobles at the time had with keeping their vassals happy and their dynastic aims alive.
If the notion of playing a drama and relationship sim appeals, this game is definitely for you. Its complete with all the backstabbing and romantic drama one would expect in a real court. If you are looking for a combat game, well, this game is definitely not for you. It does have combat and such things, but these are really a side show to the real game. Expansion and conquest are important, but take a backseat to the drama and intrigue.
This is a game that will suck dozens, if not hundreds of hours from your life. Its fantastic.

I've never written a review for any game before, but I find that there are far to few fair reviews of the game.
First if you're a first time buyer, do not be scared of buying the game despite it's negative reviews. The game certainly has a steep learning curve for beginners, and it might never have been steeper, because of the new more realistic interactions with the agents, where they can demand release clauses for your wonderkids which makes it harder to just look up 20 wonderkids and buy them and then become a powerhouse 3 seasons in, as well as the improvement in manager AI where opponents will adapt and exploit your weaknesses.
This really isn't a game for those that want it all to be easy.  But if you're here you have a passion for football or soccer, you want to unearth the next Neymar perhaps? Find the new Ronaldo, get the new Buffon, or lift the Champions League trofee.  You may never do it, you may do it, it takes work, scouting and most of all time, there is nothing that guarantees instant results.   Quite frankly the game is more a scouting tool than a game almost, which should tell you that this is the most realistic and the best football manager game out there.
If you're an avid football manager gamer, temper your expectations. This game is mostly based on FM16 which was a good step forward from FM15, despite it's problems.   With every iteration of Football Manager there are some people that want fifa level match engines, face it, it's not something we will ever get, because that's not the kind of game this is.  We have the mandatory updated database, injuries are still a woe, just as in real life, and is simulated pretty realisticly, and if you look around at the avarage injuries a team has at all times, you will find they have quite a few at all times, so don't complain about it, you're not entitled to have an injury free first team, and there are quite a few ways to reduce the amount of injuries one get.
The game is more streamlined, you have far easier access to all your necessary information, and backroom information goes straight to your inbox.   The game now runs on 64 bit, which makes it run far smoother,  if you have a 64 bit computer, which I have to assume you do.  Social feed is an gimick that has arrived in this iteration of the game, and looks to be something that Sports Interactive might build on in the future, which is a nice detail that adds in the immersion until they run out of original twitter posts and you get tired of seeing the same old where you have three reactions to the match.  As for the match engine, it still has problems, but rome wasn't built in a day, right, or 3 years, which is about the time we've had the same engine,  being upgraded and slowly fixed last three years.  And as I told first time buyers above, injuries are a part of the game, and if they are an issue, it's your own fault and not the game's.
Now, I urge you to buy the game if you have a passion for football, and would like the most realistic simulation of managing a football team.  If you just want a game.. and you stumbled on this, then you should not, cause it's not just a game, it's a way of life, and as life demands alot this game does too.

I have spent more time playing Oblivion than I have any other game in my Steam library to date. In total, my time spent with Oblivion is roughly 175 hours. I bought the game back in April and just now finished it today. I completed every quest that made its way into my journal and have explored every village, city, cave, fort, ruin, and landmark along the way. I finished the main quest, the faction quest-lines, the Knights of the Nine expansion, and the Shivering Isles expansion to completion. There are likely a handful of quests with which I never met their quest-givers, but all-in-all, I consider myself to have fully experienced all Oblivion has to offer.
Here are some quick pros and cons to summarize my experiences with Oblivion:
Despite Oblivion's issues, I still had a lot of fun playing it. One of my favorite memories include becoming a vampire around 25 hours in and not finding a cure until nearly 50 hours later! That was a wild ride! As for the two expansions, I enjoyed those as well. The Knights of the Nine was a bit slow to get started, but once it did, I found myself totally absorbed in the story and quests, and ultimately had a great time (and obtained some sweet loot to boot). Likewise, I found the Shivering Isles expansion to be a blast to play. The Isles' quests, characters, and scenarios are some of the best that Oblivion has to offer. I might even go so far as to say that the Shivering Isles itself is a better game than the base game!
All-in-all, I thoroughly enjoyed Oblivion. If you like other entries in The Elder Scrolls franchise, or just like exploring interesting worlds, then I highly recommend giving Oblivion a go!

Travel back to a time where there were plenty parts of the world that were undiscovered and groups of explorers wanted to make a name for themselves by discovering all that was unknown while at the same time gaining fame and riches. The name of the game is The Curious Expedition, developed by Maschinen-Mensch, and what I've just described to you is the foundation of this exact game.
You will get to choose one of the world famous explorers to be your leader and then it is up to you to hire the correct crew, make sure you have enough for supplies, upgrade characters and your pack mule, and of course thrust yourself into the unknown. Each adventure you go on will have a randomly generated map to navigate through, your ultimate goal is to reach the golden pyramid hidden somewhere on the map, but you will also have missions that you will need to accomplish first.
Up to this point this game probably sounds pretty easy, well let me dispel that myth right here and right now. You see that as you travel you're going to use up supplies sometimes its machetes, water, climbing gear, torches, or it might just be the groups sanity. That last one is the reason why this game becomes extraordinarily tricky. You will have to be very aware of the group's sanity, if it zeroes out there are some detrimental effects that can occur. There is one more curve ball for you too, there are times where your group members might try to commit mutiny, attack another member, become a raging alcoholic, succumb to a disease, or just run off in the dead of night. This game will throw things at you from every direction.
If you successfully navigate your way through an expedition you will get the choice what to do with the artifacts that you have discovered on your most recent journey. Do you give them to the museum and see a boost in fame, or do you sell them so that you have more capital to work with? There is one thing that I will warn you of and that is that no matter what you only have a limited inventory to work with, so you're going to have to balance your prizes with your supplies that you need to get back home.
This was a very interesting game, and it definitely took me a couple attempts to figure out how to really get into the game, but once I was in I got hooked. Sure, I had some blow up moments of getting attacked and watching everyone die, sure there were times where I took an artifact from a temple and the entire land started to change and basically doomed my expedition, and sure there were times where I thought to myself "if only I had one more inventory slot". The thing is that there's challenge in this game, every decision can definitely make or break you, or hell it might just make you fly by your competition.
The graphics are old school, they take me back to the 80s art style of PC games. Now that's not to say that that's a bad thing, I actually think that this style choice actually works really well with the game. The game was set in the past, there's something to the theme and feel of the game that really shouts that this is the correct art style.
So here's the deal, this game isn't going to be for everyone, but if you are looking for something a little different, where challenge can be high or low in a matter of seconds, where there is truly unknown lands, treasures, and dangers to every expedition, I think you're going to like this game. This game gets an 8.7 out of 10.

This game is highly inventive and full of playful details and things to discover. Although dated, particularly in the graphics department, it is still a fantastic treat and like a true adventure game it always rewards exploration in small ways. The replay value is also increased by the fact that the items you need to solve the game have randomised locations. The game is frequently funny, and despite most of the humour being aimed at children it is still a game that adults can enjoy and crack a smile at.
My least favourite aspect: The cutscenes. They have a tendency to get dull, and while Freddi and Luther are both decently developed, the side characters are not that interesting. This is, of course, coming from a grown-up's perspective; children will no doubt be able to enjoy them more.
All in all, this is an excellent and entertaining game that might not immediately catch your attention, due to the old graphics and sound as well as the unassuming presentation, but when it does you could easily be stuck for hours, just clicking at everything on the screen until another unexpected animation flies across the screen. Definitely recommended.

As a Diablo-eque hack & slasher, Dungeon Siege III is far from the usual fare you've come to expect from Obsidian. While the game is fairly linear, where forks in the main path usually means loot chests or side missions, choices being reflected in the epilogue was a nice touch and a welcomed addition.
Instead of building a party, you only control 1 character with 1 other character deployed as an AI companion. Combat involves mixing up the 9 skills, and their empowered variety; the stances switching and constant dodging reminded me a little of Bastion's combat.
The game is pretty and practically glitch-free. It is a shame that the beautiful character models were rarely showcased as the dialogue camera never panned over to your character, other than in the DLC. Other mild annoyances are the slow-ish walk speed and restrictive camera pitch.
One feature they did retain from the Dungeon Siege brand was the huge continuous world. It's quite amazing how the lack of loading screens can add to the enjoyment of a game.
All in all, I can understand why Dungeon Siege fans condemn it and others bemoan its "console dumb-down". Dungeon Siege III seems to suffer from the recent trend of being a decent game but also a "bad" entry in a franchise, however it should still be an enjoyable distraction for a budget price.
NOTE: probably best played on a gamepad

In a world lacking good visual novels (especially otomes) Amnesia's gorgeous art, well written routes and length of play make it stand out. The Japanese voice acting is stellar and there is a considerable amount of humour in the game as well. There are lots of other reviews that do an excellent job of pointing out the highlights of this game, so I would just like to address any concerns on the negative ones.
As someone who has played many Japanese visual novels, read manga and watched anime, I can unfortunately attest to the fact that Japanese r.ape culture is surprisingly (or not?) bad. Part of the reason why I have trouble playing Japanese made visual novels is because of the♥♥♥♥♥♥culture (*cough*The Second Reproduction*cough). Off the top of my head, I can think of a few in the game that I've seen many other times in Japanese VNs/anime/manga: "Only I can see you in a swimsuit", "If you let me into your room alone, it's your fault if I do something to you", "All men care only about sex", "I can't trust you alone with another man", or literally anything that Toma says. Now, the sad truth is that this is not something that is necessarily problematic with the visual novel—it's simple ignorance apparent in many Japanese visual novels. I would recommend trying to look past this in order to enjoy the visual novel. I think Toma's path is very well-written, but as a woman (or as anyone, really) it's terrifying. What's even more terrifying is that some people who played that path actually enjoyed it! The path is disgusting in the sense that it's a tragic reality (perhaps not as extreme as what Toma did) that many people in abusive relationships face, and the fact that the game romanticizes it is awful.
However! Toma's path does not ruin the rest of the paths for me. In fact, it makes Shin's all the more satisfying. I still think it's worth playing because it provides lots of background information and is has the ability to make me keep reading, like how those nasty zit-popping videos I can't tear my eyes from. (Also, you need to play Toma's path in order to get the final path, soooo…)
I understand how this might frustrate some people who either i) don't play many visual novels or ii) are used to badass protagonists with a zinger around every corner. Admittedly, I enjoy badass protagonists, but the protagonist we're given is recovering from amnesia and is in a very vulnerable position. Hers is the personality to stay calm in extraordinary circumstances—that doesn't make her boring. I found it interesting to see her 'original' personality form, as well as new bits from her interacting with the world differently. The guys comment on it as well, and at the end of the game it's almost startling when the protagonist speaks for herself (to represent the memories coming back) in a way that removes choice from the player. It's only at the end that we (the protagonist, Orion, and us the player) see the protagonist's true personality.
Overall, I would give this game a big thumbs up. The♥♥♥♥♥♥culture is very cringe-worthy, and if you have had experiences with abusive relationships and/or sexual assault, I would steer clear of Toma's route. I did buy the game on sale (90% off!) and I'm not sure if I would buy it for $33—but then, when have I ever spent that much money on a game? My route preference was: Shin, Ikki, Kent, Ukyo… Waka, Orion, Sawa, Mine, Rika… uh, the heroine? The apartment, maybe. Oh, and Toma.

Cross of the Dutchman is an action RPG based on the “true story of the folk legend” of Pier Gerlofs Donia. Is it historically accurate? I don’t know. Does it follow the legend? I also don’t know, I had not really heard of the tale until I played the game. I do know, however, that the game is rather short. And it couldn’t be otherwise, for as it follows the story of Pier, it has a clear beginning and clear end.
The game has the looks of a rather typical RPG, but it lacks all the extra customization of one. Even comparing it to rather linear games, this one is particularly so. It was clearly geared to tell a somewhat interactive story more than it was to be a full on game. The maps are average, the quests are not atypical of RPGs, even if they do follow the story, and there’s nothing overly challenging in it (except maybe when it lagged on me during mob areas). Was it fun to play? Yes, but it had nothing to make it stand out except that it’s based on that story… There are no skill trees, though you purchase ‘upgrades’ for your skills and switch between them, there are upgrades for health and such, but little else worth mentioning.
The graphics are simple but nice. I wasn’t particularly fond of most of the cartoony art style (though I did like the general art), but it wasn’t bad either, and effort was clearly put into it to portray it as accurately to the time and area as possible. The music and sounds were pleasing enough, and overall the game ran fairly nicely; the only time I encountered problems being during a couple sections in which there were too many enemies and it lagged some on my computer.
Controls are simple (mostly you’ll only be using the mouse), but I found the obstacle-avoidance a bit sketchy. Combat (which is quite basic skill-spamming) was a bit clunky as well, because it’s difficult to aim your hits properly and often times you’d end up hitting air repeatedly. Cross also had some slightly interesting stealth-like areas (though the game doesn’t offer an actual stealth engine); it wasn’t too hard to get through them (but it was annoying to get caught) and made for a bit of a variation, which was rather nice. Just don’t expect it’ll be full on take-cover type of stealth.
The story itself was good, though as I mentioned before I can’t really compare it with the real story/folk legend. The dialogue was rather poor, however, sometimes I felt like it was trying too hard to be funny.
All in all Cross of Dutchman is a nice, simple game. It was easy to grab, play for a bit up to another checkpoint, and then go do something else, so I think it’s a good game for casual players as well as for those who will want to sit through all 4ish hours of gameplay in one go. However, it doesn’t go beyond average, and I don’t think it’ll be satisfactory for people who don’t care about the story, which is the strongest point of the game.
Yes, but I wouldn’t expect too much out of it.

An action/adventure/brawler game in which you control a farmer named Pier on multiple quests to stop brigands and soldiers from causing havoc.
Controller support is in the game as well as K/M, I played using K/M and the first thing I noticed was that I had to click where I wanted to move my character, WASD would had been a better option for me since I have a small twitch in my right hand. It was still playable but it felt like I had less control of where I wanted Pier to go and I did manage to run into barriers instead of going into the opening.
The story of the game is based on real life events that happened around the 1600s which aroused my curiosity.
The gameplay isn`t anything revolutionary but it gets the job done, you talk to a few people, you get a quest, you venture out and do the objectives and return to the quest giver to progress.
Since I do first look at games mostly, I didn`t see any progression of abilities or items management, I.E. weapons.
I did like that there are chest hidden around and that it is 1 of the achievement in the game (No coin, no War: Loot all chests), that can help prolong the time you stay and play the game.
I`ll be returning to the game to play more of it for sure and maybe even try to get all 31 achievements.
Story is good, mechanics could be a little better but I think it is a good little game that you will enjoy.

Unlike other grand strategy games where you lead a country or a race, here you are a character that leads a dynasty that in turn rules lands and armies. Yes, there is a good part where you move armies and deal with warfare; but there is also a part where you spend way too much time deciding on a wife, or whether to try and murder your imbecile son that is about to inherit all your title. Yep, this game also has an RPG side; all characters in the game have different stats and there are well over 200 traits to give life to endless stories and scenarios. You have a lot of freedom in a way which allows you to do tons of things, but without help from other characters, most will just take very long or lead to failure. Here you also have to manage your relations, with your vassals, with the liege, with your foes, with your family, with your council, and more. Nothing is easy but also nothing is impossible, and like in real life, money does wonders but can’t buy everything. The game definitely has a lot of depth yet nothing is overly complicated. I’m sorry if I seem vague but if I get into details (like the legal system), this review will be ten times as long and might spoil some things that maybe you’ll want to discover by yourself. The soundtrack is one of the best I ever heard, but this is a common theme from Paradox games. The graphics are very nice but they can do with some improvements (such as the desert terrain).

I hoped to be able to play something somewhere between Portal and The Stanley Parable, two games that I loved deeply. But 'Only If' can't be compared to them in any way.
'Only If' personify mediocrity, and for all I've heard and read, the only feeling it can give a player expecting a semblance of quality in gameplay or in plot is a raw disappointement.
'Only If' is tedious to play, even with a simple walk-through to actually explain what the game expected of me.
I didn't stop after the three first levels because the game was too hard a challenge, but because there was simply no point in going on. So I used the keywords to skip annoying levels, which turned out to be each single oneI would advise to check the ending with the eponimous keyword if you quickly want to get an idea of the plot. Because there isn't that much to spoil anyway, and it may save you precious minutes of your life which you could use to replay the Staneley Parable, Portal, Quantum Condrum, Q.U.B.E., or even Vitrium.
I am not sure whether 'Only If' is still in beta—that would explain why there are no option menu at all to toogle sound or fullscreen while in a run.
I'm not going to criticuze the absence of proper save/load system, since the keywords system is the only think that allowed me to keep sane by skipping the lousy parts until the end to get an opinion on the game as a whole.
The good things : nothing to pay, decent graphics, good audio quality.
Now, the painful :
- Loud, lousy, long-winded dialgues.
- A lot of profanity that doesn't add anything to the characters or experience.
- The concepts of subtelty, clevernes or finesse are zeroing from the very beginning to the ending.
- And that means that metaphors and symbolism are touched awkwardly, and most things are pointlessly surrealist.
- A loose plot-line with, in the role of the evil mastermind, a burlesque antagonist who show the IQ of a clamp and thinks his simplistic and heavy kind of humour very clever.
- A pace that tries to be original, and just gives the feeling to be testing something in alpha stage.
- The Gameplay of a repetitive, nebulous, bleak thriller.
- To my surprise, I found the ending even worse than the game iself. Especially the pace. The way they handled the music in an attempt to create humor with the /final revelation/ is as exasperating as a bad movie blockbuster.
Conclusion : I must admit that I have played worse games than 'Only If' here, still, I can't help but feel like I've wasted more marbles on it than what it was worth.

Though Morrowind was my introduction to the Elder Scrolls series, it was Oblivion that made me love the series -- not that Morrowind is bad, it's fantastic, but I only had access to it on my friend's Xbox... anyway, I digress. Oblivion is still a great game, but it does have its fair share of issues.
Trying not to spoil anything, the main plotline goes in an interesting direction, though I think they might have missed their mark with it. Instead of feeling like an integral part in the story, you end up feeling more like a bystander of the events that unfold and that's not a particularly enthralling situation.
Gameplay-wise, going from Morrowind to Oblivion, a lot of mechanics have been simplified, for better or worse is subjective in some instances I feel. For example, several actions such as combat and spellcasting no longer operate under RNG, so you don't miss point-blank strikes on enenies and cannot fail to cast a spell. Combat in general can get a bit monotonous, as spellcasting is pretty still pretty tedious if you focus on several types of spells. Melee combat is largely just pressing attack until the enemy stops moving, but since enemies scale to your level, it's always a bit of a chore to kill anything.
Yeah, level scaling. This is one of the largest problems in Oblivion. In an attempt to make the game stay balanced regardless of where you were, they inadvertently created a large imbalance. This is because the way enemies scale isn't related to how your skills or attributes grow, but your overall level. For (a personal) example, if you're an Acrobat and you end up leveling Sneak to 100 at the very start of the game and expend your level ups without multipliers, every enemy will scale accordingly. You might find bandits wearing Elven or Glass equipment while you're stuck with your tutorial area dagger and dying from one hit. You end up having to plan how and when to level up to avoid this issue. There are, however, certain mods that address this issue, allowing for a more casual approach without being so severely punished.
Another commonly criticised problem is that a lot of dungeons and caverns were actually automatically generated, making several areas look almost -- if not completely -- identical to each other.
The game is also extremely buggy, but it's Bethesda, so that's not news. You might want to save often though, since Oblivion likes to crash with no warning sometimes. Usually the only "warning" it might give is a sudden drop in frames which usually indicates that a crash to desktop is not far away. As for other bugs, you might want to look at the Unofficial Oblivion Patch online, which fixes a variety of bugs from minor to major.
Before I finish this ranty review, I have to add that the Shivering Isles expansion is my favorite Elder Scrolls expansion out of all of them. The new strange world you have to explore and the antics of Sheogorath are great fun.
In short, I still consider Oblivion a great game, but your mileage may vary. There are tons of mods out there too.
If you get past the potato faces, it's a very complete game full of quests and locations to explore. It keeps you engaged for a long time. The expansion is out of this world.
Of course this is a great game! I would love to see this remastered for the new consoles though. It'll happen one of these days!

One of the greatest RPGs every made; the detail of the world, quests, and characters is incredible, even now. I've played hundreds of hours on the xbox 360 version of this and decided to buy it for PC many years later, It's just as good as I remember it being. There are a few things worth mentioning for those who have never played Oblivion before however.
- The game is awkward and buggy, NPCs have very unatural and absurd conversations. People will introduce a new topic every sentence and ignore what the other person is saying. The phenomon has spawned a variety of YouTube memes; just search for "Oblivion NPC conversations" and you'll get the idea. Additionally, strange bugs like enemies charging into walls, guards killing each other by accident, tripping over skeletons, and so on are quite common.
- The graphics are obviously old. That isn't to say they're bad, the game is by no means unacceptable, but be aware that all characters look like they're made of cheddar cheese. The landscapes however still look very good, especially for being a game from 2006.
- The combat, while far less aggrevating than Morrowind, is still clunky. Swords feel like chopsticks and arrows have a range as if they were made of lead. Magic is also less fluid than Skyrim, but it does not take up a hand slot, it is an independant ability activated with C.
- The levelling system can be very irritating. Enemies level with you, which means you never really feel like you're getting any better. A goblin will always feel as difficult to kill as it was in the beginning of the game, enemies get better as you do. I'm sure theres a mod somewhere to disable this, I haven't looked because I don't care much.
- Finally, the only major issue is performance (and even this is quite petty). With an RX 480, maxed out with HDR and MLAA (AMD settings) at 1080p, I average around 120-144 fps outside. However, the framerate does sometimes dip severely to 60 fps in cities and chaotic combat, such as the battle of Kvatch.
In conclusion, Oblivion is definitely worth the money, I can't think of many reasons why anybody wouldn't want to play it. If you like any of the other Elder Scrolls games, Oblivion is no different. Oblivion is a special game because it captures a feeling of freedom that few other games have been able to. There are so many unique quests such as entering a painted world, spying for a paranoid elf, fighting as an arena combatant, assasinating targets for an evil cult etc.

a game about picking a explorer and then exploring distant lands. during wich you engage in combat, loot shrines and temples, and interact with various settlements. your meant to finnish six expeditions without perishing along the way. at the start of each expedition you receive a quest or challenge which you may accept for the chance of earning more funds. before every expedition starting from the second one you may also recruit party members or use your available funds to purchase equipment like machetes, rope and climbing gear that reduce the cost of movement or chocolate and whiskey which regain sanity. after each successful expedition you get to chose one of either three or five perks which grant some small benefit without any downside. unlike some of the perks your explorer can have which possibly might have a negative effect. your funds are only in use here, at the docks. the exploration is handled much like a board game, tough it does utilize mechanics that wouldnt really be doable in a physical board game. instead of limiting your movement to a dice role or a set value as in monopoly or the finnish boardgame "Afrikan tähti". the movement here is limited by visibility, so you can only go as far as you can see. movement is also limited by another factor, sanity. as you move trough the desolate, dark and claustrophobic jungles your party's sanity will start to waver. this culminates in them running into the jungles or developing some colorful quirks such as bipolar, pyromaniac or claustrophobia. it is also possible that these quirks be present from the start where you recruit them in the docks, or in some cases, village. these quirks can also include racist, sexist or alcoholic. only one of these actually seem to have much of an impact tough. that's alcoholism. this is a trait your gonna wanna avoid since it forces you to regularly supply your party with whiskey or suffer decreased loyalty. the combat is a dice based affair. you have three base classes of dice, each with two sides and then some special dices. the base classes are support, attack and defense. as previously mentioned there are two of each. you then use all of these different dice in order to puzzle together combos which either deal damage to the opposition, put up a defense towards the incoming counter attack or both. you can also achieve trough certain combos special effects such as poisoning or bleeding. both of which i feel are self-explanatory. the special dices i mentioned are rare cases where certain kind of party members have unique dices. like the shaman which have dices that can heal your party or animal party members which all have there own set of dices. tough those usually boil down to less useful variants of the attack dice. there are also some items which materialize in the combat as dices with special combos attached to them. these are guns and spears. they do a lot to spice up the combat immensely and for later expeditions are almost mandatory in order to fight of raptors and large numbers of giant crabs and gorillas. all in all its a fairly fun system, very simple to grasp. it doesnt have much in the way of complexity and can at times be frustrating or borderline rage inducing since much is based on dice rolling. in other words luck based. so many times my expedition was sunk by bad rolls. sometimes a bad dice role would force me too flee combat, and fleeing had such disastrous consequences that it snowballed into failure. the interactions with settlement that i mentioned early on is comprised of trading, recruiting and regaining sanity. peppered trough the maps are two types of settlements. missions and villages. the missions have storage rooms in which you can dump valuable loot in too free up some inventory space. they also allow you to rest for a price or for free if you have a missionary in your party. resting is a way of trading time for sanity. you may also trade with missions. the villages function mostly the same. they allow you to rest, tarde, but however lack a storage room. instead of that they allow you to recruit new party members within the expedition itself. since these are locals they will hesitate to follow you after the expedition tough. frustratingly enough this is based on a dice role. the other things with villages is also the fact that there is a bar which governs your reputation with the locals. blowing up mountains, looting sacred temples and ruins or resting in their village will decrease their liking towards you. to improve their liking towards you you can do quest related to the village itself or trough certain perks. while resting in villages there can also occur random events which, depending on your choice, may decrease or increase their liking towards you. in the late game there is also a third kind of settlement, slave camps. these ones allow you to sell party members or buy new ones. they also furfill the the basic tarde function. these differences do vary it a bit since missions and villages aren't the same. otherwise the settlement part of the game would lack in the way of variety. all the villages are the same and even share the same reputation bar. now to the big one, explorers. these ones are what separates your different playtrough the most since there is a large selection of them to chose by. especially if you count the secret ones, then the amount of available explorers just gets staright out stupidly large. every explorer has a starting set of party members, perks and items. this most drastically changes the early game and not so much the late game where you most likely will have lost old party members and picked up new ones. you will also use up items and aquire new stuff.most explorer perks can also be gained. so by the late game the explorers all become slightly indistinguishable from each other. the secret ones include more obscure explorers which dont fit into the time period the game chooses to portray. the 19th century. these also include joke ones such as pewdiepie. the explorers are blank slates devoid of personality. it makes it easy to put yourself in the role of an explorer and makes it feel like your journey. it feels personal so you'll remember all the funny/tragic misfortunes you experience. its nice how all the party members that survive all the way trough gets a bit of closure in the form of a short message that tells you how they lived happily ever after. the framework for the expeditions are that there is a competition of who is the greatest explorer. the winner gets a statue. so you need to complete the expeditions and make it back with tons of loot for fame. the explore with the most fame wins! during your playtroughs you will however be creating your own personal stories of how you found an egg that hatched into a raptor. you'll then get stories about how you almost lost him to a gorilla and how you later tragically ate him in order to not go mad. this is where the game shines. it allows for enough randomness that each quirky event will feel personal. Oh, and the games point of the excess of European imperialism in the way you completely devastate the native land in the name of petty glory is funny and clever. im gonna throw in a complaint and that is that a pacifist playtrough is not fun or really viable on harder difficulties. the abundance of enemies and how maps and mechanics dont allow for a lot of mobility means you a lot of times cant avoid combat. the randomly generated maps do for the most part a great jobs of making believable locations with sensible located villages. altough later in the game where volcanos become more common it can lead to times where you have to do great, exhaustivly lenghty leeps of faith into a area covered by closely packed volcanos. all around its a fun game. the sessions are relativley short whitin that 1-2hour sweet spot. the combat is good enough and the exploration is additive. the high difficulty make it replayable, as do the amount of explorers

I didn't really know anything about Ninjago until the movie appeared on my radar, so by no means should the game be considered to be just for Ninjago fans, it improves the tried-and-true LEGO game formula considerably on every front, as far as LEGO games go it's very ambitious on innovating which you wouldn't really expect from a movie tie-in game especially because it succeeds to improve.
Platforming is more flowing, character progression and ability unlocks is engaging, combat adds a reward for good execution in world and in challenge dojos, tying the combo meter to stud multiplier for example should become a standard in all future LEGO games. Visuals do a better job than ever before making the world feel like LEGO even in the natural environments because for the first time plants, rocks and textures match their real-life scale and are not oddly miniaturized. Lego Ninjago The Movie is a good game with not much content. Some mechanics from the first game are removed, and some new mechanics are added. Overall, the game is fun, and typical of Lego games, funny and collectibles fest.
The changes:
1. Red Bricks in this game is replaced by 8 Ancient Scripts, there is no multiplier stud, the highest multiplier stud in this game is x2, the rest is invicibility, stud magnet, dancing step, etc.
2. No multiplier stud, how do you get lots of studs to buy things? Well, first, you dont need to buy anything in this game, each characters are unlocked after you finish certain task in the exploration or by challenging dojos. Stud multiplier can be gotten in the new battle system, which is one of the good things in this Lego Ninjago. The battle system is revamped with several flashy moves with kung-fuish names like Sky Dragon, Dancing Rabbit, etc. And each moves can have lots of combos if you do it correctly, the higher your combo, the bigger your stud multiplier will be, with max x20.
3. Skill system, when you progress into certain parts of the story, you will get Ninjuity Tokens, you can use this tokens to unlock skills from 6 different kung-fu styles, from Dragon, Master, Rabbit, Tiger, etc. Each skills add more damage, more times to your combo, add effect to certain battle moves, etc.
4. No minikits, this can be a bummer or a blessing for some people. No minikits means, less replay value and shorter playing time, especially when the game is already short.
5. In each stage, you dont have to collect certain amounts of studs to get "True (insert something here)" status anymore, instead you will get a bar of True Ninja which represents your Ninja level, and this can be gotten from exploring the world, playing stages, or challenging dojo. Everytime you reach new leve, you will unlock body parts to be used in the character creator.
6. Dojo is another new additions in this game, each stage has one or two dojo(s) you can challenge, after clearing the dojo, you will unlock gold brick and new characters to play (new characters are unlocked if you reach the gold rank). Dojo also the fastest way to grind your True Ninja level.
7. No Free Play, after you finish a stage, you can explore all the place you visited in the stage in the open world exploration.
8. You are ninjagos, each ninjago is a master of an element, and the puzzles in this game involves using the required elements and certain character's abilities, not much changes here.
9. No vehicles/mounts, this is one of the bad (at least for me), walking around is not cool in Lego Ninjago, but fortunately, there is a character who has the the ability to walk fast by holding B button, and you can got him in one of the dojos.
10. I finished the game in 7 hours more or less, and got 100% in 16-17 hours. Lego Ninjago is the shortest Lego games I have ever player.
Conclusion: I recommend this game, but it doesn't worth full price guys, wait for a deep deep sale. I had fun while playing this, but it was a short fun, it's like a one night stand, fast, fun, but memorable. But in one night stand, you might unlocked the girl permanently, but this game, you won't come back to play this after you finish it.
