Another Lego game, and another game based off of a movie. And this one is pretty good all things considered. I'll be listing off various things about this game that I liked/ didn't like, and the features that it does and doesn't have, so chances are I'll hopefully answer any questions one may have about this game before buying it. So let's begin.
The story: If you've seen the movie, you've pretty much seen the game. It even uses clips from the movie in place of cutscenes, which works to some degree but I'll touch on that later. As such, the main story follows that of the film, and while it does leave some things out, it also places a lot in. For instance, you get a lot more character with Jay when you play as him and Lloyd in the second act. And it makes the film just a little bit weaker in comparison, and I kinda like that, as I mentioned before, it gives him a bit more character. There are other scenes like that, but sadly not many.
Voice work: I'll be honest when I say I really don't know to much about this department, and have never really reviewed it before, but if you're expecting Michael Pena to be voicing Kai in this, then you're gonna be dissapointed, because as far as I know, none of the voice actors from the film appear in this game. The actors that do appear in this game try their best to imitate their film portyals and of which they do to a certain extent. You can clearly see (hear?) this in Garmadon, whenever he say's La-Loyd. It just doesn't feel right, and the fact that they're using clips from the actual film and having these actors "dub" over it just feels wrong. And after seeing the movie (twice) and then playing the game and recalling how the voices should sound, it just feels like a piece was missing from the instructions. (I'm sorry, I had to make a pun.) Regardless of who is voicing them though, they still do an alright job pulling off the characters and making them enjoyable to play as. Also don't expect anyone to say anything when in free-roam, that's been left out sadly.
Controls: If you've played past Lego titles on the PC, then this one should really feel no different. Keys are awkward and layout is pretty much the same. If you use a controller (XBox like I do) then you'll probably have a much better time with this game. Some mechanics from past Lego games have been implemented such as the dodge ability (RT and LT on a controller) that allow you to evade enemy attacks and instead of pre-determined moves like in Avengers, you now have several attack styles to use, such as the Rushing Boar (tap X on controller and use L-thumbstick towards an enemy) and the Skyward Dragon, which allow you to raise your combo meter even higher than in past games. And the more you raise your meter, then bigger multiplier for studs you'll get. The place you really see this come to frutition is in the arenas, which I'll talk about later.
Levels: I could've talked about this when talking about the story, but it didn't fit in in any way that felt right, so I decided to just make it a seperate topic. Reason is is because in truth, there are no levels. And by that, I mean there are no story-exlusive stages where you're dragged out of the map, and placed into a different one. The chapter you play is also the map you play on. Kinda like Assassin's Creed. And what this does is it effectlivly makes the environment you play in much more memorable, which is kinda neat in a way, esspecially with the Docks. The big downside to this, and one that might hurt some opinions on the game, is that there are no longer any Mini-kits or True-___ collectibles. (i.e. True Jedi for Lego Star Wars) In place of the True-___ stud meter is a simple level up bar that fills up with the Lego studs that you collect, and while still called True-Ninja bar, it only serves as a level up gauge that once leveled up, unlocks some customization parts. There are no replacements for the Mini-kits, which has been a long time staple for the Lego games, but given how they made the actual maps the levels themselves, I can kinda see why they did it. Apart from that though, there really is no limit to what you can do inside of a story mode mission so long as you have the right character. Granted you can't accept side-quests while in a story because you can't, but you can go out of your way in the story to collect a Gold Brick, pick up Red Brick, or even snatch up a mini-figure bag (Yes, bag. They're like blind bags now and it's really cool.) And mind that everything you unlock is free, which kinda negates having a True-Ninja bar in the first place. The only things studs are used for are for Tornado of Creation Builds, which do cost a shiney stud when first playing, but other than that, you don't use studs at all. There are some side-levels, called Dojo's, where you'll be required to gain a certain amount of studs to unlock all 3 characters, but those are pretty easy to get. The Dojo's themselves are also pretty nice, taking place outside of the map in a themed area and have you going up against some of the show's main villians.
Graphics: It's a Lego game. They look like Legos. But the game does look really good, blending Legos and real-world environments to make it believable.
Arenas: Basically the multiplayer part of the game aside from normal 2-player co-op, Arenas do what Battle Mode did back in the day of Lego Star Wars: The Complete Saga. Only now it can hold up to four players. And while there are only 3 modes, Samurai Showdown, Mystic Bounty, and Ulitmate Ultimate Weapon. Samurai is basically capture the flag, and the more flags you hold, the slower you go until you can get them to your base. Mystic is an orb collecting mode, with various orbs scattered throughout the map that vary in points. UUW is where you hold onto the UUW and earn points. Whoever holds onto it the longest wins. For all games, it's really who gets the most points wins, and they're fairly easy, against the ai bots that is. At the moment, there are only 3 maps, and I don't know if there will be more for I don't even know if there will be dlc for this game. But the maps are based in Ninjago City, the Uncrossable Jungle, and the Unclimbable Mountain, each being the same in each mode. There are also items that can be used to your advantage in each, but none are exclusive to a map, Now these modes are most definatly fun, as I find myself going back to them just to see what I can do, and I would totally like to see this area be expanded upon should there be dlc released.
Character List: Probably the only other disapointing thing about this game is the lack of characters. While it does feature main characters from the show such as Kai in his Season 2 outfit and Pythor, it only features just about one of each character, which is a shame because of all the great outfits that the Ninja wore throughout the seasons along with upgraded color schemes that some villians got as well. At present, there are a total of 101 characters, not including the custom ones, and a locked character that has yet to be revealed, even at 100%. And there are some characters that I would have loved to play as such as Season 5 Cole in his Ghost form, or the Titanium Ninja, and some characters such as Classic Zane and Cole could've really benifitted from using their classic weapons instead of their movie counterparts gear. Should they release dlc in the future, I will hope that it includes more of their outfits and more gear, just to add to the overall.
Customization: As with pretty much all Lego games, you can customize your character pretty much however you want. I will say though, the department sadly feels lacking. I was limited to what color of what hair I could use (not a lot of blonde options) and not many things look good with each other.
Overall, I would say go and get it. On PC at least, as it is a fairly small game compared to past ones, and for $40, I think it's a fair price. Hope this helps anyone who's looking to buy this game.

This played like a blend of Diablo 3 and Dragon Age. It is a pretty standard RPG - build yourself up, save the world, sort of deal. The graphics are lovely, and visually pleasing, but most of the world is standard fair (but very well done). I really enjoyed the combat, except for the camera mechanics. They know how to make worthy boss fights too, and keep the difficulty at a good level. Most bosses took a few tries to get past, a few were smooth, and several took many attempts. The length of boss fights was plenty long - it felt like a BOSS fight since you'd be battling for 5-15mins, instead of blasting them down super fast. Normal mode kept me on my toes, but wasn't gruesomely painful - which is how I like normal modes. I think the weakest point is the character development, for there really isn't much. There are a few fun phrases, but nothing to make you glom onto the characters and love them as you would in Dragon Age.  7.5/10, would recommend to RPG adventure fans easily.

A flawed game unlike the other Dungeon Siege titles, or most other Obsidian games either. I don't know how fun I'd describe it as? It's... it's actually MASSIVELY bland. And pretty short. And one of the systems I enjoyed most was apparently only in the game because I bought the DLC, so that's another half-strike.
I don't know whether to praise or damn this game. It's seriously some kind of limbo-state. Very controller-centric action RPG gameplay, probably one of the worst co-op setups I've seen in ages off of consoles (only the host keeps gear/save data/XP! ♥♥♥♥ you, other guy! don't go trying to bring your character up in here!), but then it adapts some of my favorite quirks of the genre (story choices and actions in-game giving you perma-perks to stats, controllable evolutions of skills, solid amount of customization for your characters within their roles).
If you buy this: buy it with the Treasures of the Sun DLC. You may as well - the game's a bit short, and TotS gives you some cool new toys and a rather fun new region. Just know going in that the game is not amazing by any standards. On the other hand, it doesn't really ♥♥♥♥ UP anywhere that I can point out, either.
I still don't know how the hell I feel about this, and I've been debating it with myself for about a week now as I played it to completion.

Dungeon Siege III is a great game, but it simply isn't a Dungeon Siege anymore. The gameplay mechanics are very, very simplified compared to original Dungeon Siege, or even a Dungeon Siege 2. Nevertheles, it is a great, solid, rather simplistic RPG with beautiful graphics and engaging gameplay, but do not expect almost anything you've used to in previous installments.
Very good and interesting story line. Decent gameplay. Not a whole lot of re-play value however.

This game feels awfully similar to Dragon Age II while playing it, though it is a LOT harder. The similarities to Dragon Age II also means that Dungeon Siege III doesn't play even remotely similarly to the previous two DS titles. It's an extremely good game if you can live with the high difficulty level, and because it is so different to the first two DS titles, it is not essential that you play those two games before this one.

I ended up having to replay the last bit cause I missed one of the achievements which kept me from getting the fully-win-the-game achievement. At some point I hope to play the other three characters, but I really liked Anjali so it might be a hard change.
There are quite a few interesting aspects in the game that I enjoyed. The skill selection process, for one, as well as the essences to add boosts to your character by way of weapons and armor. The multiplayer is certainly not the greatest, it would be if it didn't have a tethered camera. There is a way around this, but I am not desperate enough for a multiplayer to deal with adjusting the game by way of editing files.
So all in all, I would suggest buying this game to play solo. If you want it for the multiplayer aspect, I think I should say to skip it.

As a longtime player of Football Manager and Championship Manager before it I have grown increasingly frustrated at the direction the series has been taking. A game called Football Manager should be first and foremost about football, yet every year all the time and effort seems to have been spent on dealing with player contracts and the media. I'm not saying these shouldn't be in the game, but they should be low priority. This year sees the introduction of a social feed, where you get to see tweets from your teams most clueless and repetitive fans, and a player promise system, which ruined game for me, but more on that later.
Tactics, something I think should be a high priority, remain incredibly limited, with the ability to issue only vague instructions. There's no way to instruct your players to press hard immediately after losing the ball, but then fall back into formation, no way to tell a player to drift out to both wings like Alan Ball did in the '66 Wold Cup, no way to tell your right winger to cross early and our left winger to look for the overlap. The team width instruction I find baffling. Am I setting up my width for when my team have the ball, or when they don't? I definately don't want the same width instruction for both scenarios, and I can't think of a team which do. Coaching is equally simplistic and vague. Previous versions of the game, going back a fair few years, allowed much more nuanced instructions. Bring back the arrows!
Now the promise system. Five of my players became unhappy, because I hadn't kept my promise to strengthe the squad. This suprised me because 1. I had strengthened the squad, and 2. I never promised to strengthen the squad. It's possible that the team's previous manager had made that promise to them, but I did not. Having five players unhappy at me, for something I didn't do, has caused me to give up on this game.
What I hoped for is that the games existing mechanics would be improved. What the devs did is leave them unchanged and introduce new mechanics which don't even work well. I imagine if the devs for this game were to make Christmas dinner they'd spend all their time preparing sprouts, chuck a turkey in the oven as an afterthought, and not bother with roast potatoes at all. Not for the first time Football Manager has left me disappointed.

Cross of the Dutchman is a third-person brawler/hack-n-slash set in the sixteenth century, dealing with the start of the rebellion of Greate Pier, a historical giant from Frisia who fought against the Saxons, Burgundians, and Hollanders.
The game is told without voice acting, story progression occurs through in-game dialogue and cartoon cutscenes. The story ends after his first great victory, so before he became a pirate/bandit captain.
Graphics are colorful and beautiful, they really portray the mediaeval Frisia in a good way. Environments are detailed and very nicely crafted. All characters appearing in the game wear realistic depictions of 16th century clothing and the main cast is instantly recognisable. A nice touch is that Greate Pier is indeed a full head taller than most others, as he is described to have been.
Sound is well done with good soundeffects and a very nice fitting score. At the end during the big battles it is very cinematic.
Combat is limited to a two button affair: normal attack and special attack, which takes stamina. Through upgrades (8 in total) you can learn new special attacks and each has its special purpose, although I mainly stuck with the circle attack. There is no strategy to combat other than hitting the enemy as much as you can and running away from dogpiling. Don't expect Arkham-style brawling here.
As long as the game is combat or exploring, it's fun. However, there are lengthy stealth sections where upon getting caught the level resets, where you cannot attack at all and have to avoid the light radius of patrolling soldiers. Getting caught means the level resets, which in the final stealth section can cost you five minutes of replaying across several areas. They are the only real bad part of the game, and unfortunately not skippable.
The game will take about three hours to complete, or four if you want to collect all the Points of Interest and hidden chests. Achievements almost all unlock during normal gameplay and with one exception, can all be gotten even after the fact. The exception is an achievement for having 1000 gold: if you buy upgrades too soon, you can lock yourself out of this one so beware.
Overall this gets a recommendation. The game is not expensive and is definitely fun to play through. You're not just getting a good brawler, you're also getting a nice peek into a Frisian historical hero.

I preordered this game , lured by the promise of an action adventure rpg with delightful graphics and based on historical events.
NOTE: Some of the points in this review are based on my expirience playing with a XBOX 360 controller
In reality however , the game just did not deliver. Firstly the combat is borderline passable, had it been a little worse , I would have categorized it as awful. You have one fast attack -bound to the A button on a standard 360 controller , which is ok I guess if X which is usually bound for attack wasnt bound to draw/holster sword. And then you have your heavy/special attack that uses stamina. Thats it. No block , no dodge , no roll or anything of that kind. I get that Pier is supposed to be this huge muscly Dutchman , but making him able to roll away from incoming blade and arrow attacks wouldn't have made him less believable. Would have made the otherwise sluggish combat much more dynamic too.
Then you have the game world. "Small" pretty much sums it up. Oh , dont worry tho , it wont feel as small as it is , because you will revisit every location 10000 times. Walking. At the pace of a turtle with late stages of arthritis. Yep , no sprint button as well. Pier is waaay too manly to move faster than "I sort of need to pee , but don't want anyone to notice " speed.  And while we are on the topic of movement speed the totally unnecessary stealth segments limit your speed even further. When I say stealth I mean this in the loosest sense possible.
Upgrades are almost non existent , you only have 2 stamina and 2 health upgrades , and 6 total special attacks WHICH YOU CANT BUY PAST CHAPTER 7!!! Thanks game , I finally have enough gold to buy the strongest attacks and all of a sudden all the merchants die or disappear.
Length wise the game is pretty short , maybe 3 hours or so. Its not really even long enough to drop all of its cards , so Im alt+tabbing it atm to get my cards. This is not necessairly a bad thing, it would have become really frustrating had it been more than 5 hours long with the same amount of content. Replayability is non existent , as achievements are pretty easy to get and you cant really play it any differently than your original playtrough (well maybe you could buy stronger attacks before chapter 8 or something)
Mandatory pros / ways to make the game better list : Music is really nice and fitting. Art style is ok too and was one of the reasons I preordered. Story is ok , although it lacks some depth , maybe throw in some dialog options in and some characters may die in different scenarios. Combat would have been a lot better with a roll or block mechanic. Bigger map would have been nice, maybe put in a mountain/snowy area where Pier could save on of his kids from wolves. Being able to spring outside of combat would have been nice.
TL;DR: Game has potential but needs some serious tweaking.

However, it simply is to short. This game offers to tale the tail of this giant midievil warrior who weilded a giant sword and slew hundreds of man in battle. He stormed across the battlefield, avenging his family and killing these forces who had invaded his country and taken everything from himself, and the men who fought with him. He created a massive personal navy and became a midieval pirate lord, plundering and raiding ships, all the while defending a country he loved. He goes from place to place attacking these invaders who have now taken over towns and cities. He kills many and makes the land run red. As his life begins to come to an end hei pauses for a moment to think about what he has done, after fighting for so long. He sees that around, left in his wake, is untold death and distruction and this man stops fighting. He disbands his crew (some more forcefully then others) and convinces them, through conversation or by steel, that they need to stop fighting. After finally stopping his blood shed, he hangs up his sword, takes off his armor, and finally sits down and builds a new farm. He lives a simple like until he dies one year later. And this is what you can find on wikipedia for gods sake.
Peir Gerlof bacame a monster to fight monsters and he let this monster he had create run wild until he finally put it down, in favor of being a peaceful man. And if this story was what you wanted to be told then you get the first part of it. You get chapter 1 of the story in this game, not the whole story.
I wanted the whole story and it wasn't delived, thus I can't say that this game can get my vote.

Modern day MMORPGs :  " Please bring these 3 apples to an old grandma on the other side of the village. You will receive 5000 gold, full gear and a pet dragon at the completion".
Ragnarok Online Re:Start : "Here's a knife and some potions. Good luck dying"
Ragnarok Online RE:Start is a wonderful, charming game that can be extremely brutal. It is not for everyone by any means. You will find yourself pouring over forums and calculators, trying to figure out the optimal build for your character, only to find out that someone did something completely unconventional with exactly the same class but with much better results. So you'll try again and experiment. And then you will meet your first friendly merchant or a helpful priest, you'll get that first equipment or a card drop and suddenly everything will start getting easier and you'll want to start collecting different weapons for different size/element/race monsters and locations. Or you'll spend your days sitting in Prontera and chatting with random newbie players much like yourself.  And that is when you'll realize that you're having way more fun than you expected.
P.S. Disregard the negative reviews with the connection and lagging issues. It's being worked on and at this moment the server is much more stable. For people with micro-stutters, type  /skip in game. It'll drop frames and should improve the movement substantially.

Well, here we go with another Steam sale and another sh**-load of games purchased that I'll spend forever trying to beat and turn a regular review, for no other reason than my own personal satisfaction.
So, you know, I'm living the dream.
I decided to pick up Freddi Fish this sale, since I had finally gotten around to beating Pajama Sam and Spy Fox, and I already played the pretty stale experience titled "Putt Putt Joins the Parade". I mean, what the hell? Let's just play all the Humongous games!
Freddi Fish has you playing as the titular character, who is a young aspiring fish detective out to help people with their various problems. In this first entry, all the fish in the ocean are literally DYING. I'd say those are some pretty low stakes to set for your first game.
Your grandma had all the fish's supply of kelp (a bit foolish, if you ask me), and it was unfortunately stolen by sharks who would leave clues behind in bottles out in the open for anyone to find. So, the game has you both trying to help fix whatever random problems a fish might have gotten into (trapped in a cage, living in a bright shell, or... using a mandolin as a crutch), as well as tracking down the bottles throughout the ocean floor. It's a nice combination between following clues and solving simple puzzles, that gives the game better flow than something like Putt Putt.
What I don't like, however, is the process you have to go through in order to get said bottles. This is still one of the older Humongous games where you can't skip the transition animation between screens, and the puzzles are so simple that the game gets really... really... really dull after a while. It's not unbearable, but it doesn't help the game for being fun, or at least memorable.
The game also seems to have a bit of a lazy HUD, where Freddi and Luther will actually swim in front of their inventory list on certain screens, as if it's a part of the background. And the aesthetic has me... mixed, at best. I love the backgrounds. The hand-painted screens look wonderful, but all the cartoony, bright fish that swim in it don't fit. Like, at all.
It's a similar complaint I had with 2015's refuse-worthy children's film "The Good Dinosaur". They both have wonderful backgrounds, but the characters that inhabit them are a big contrast from it. I think the backgrounds in this game would be better for a point-and-click horror game for a diver slowly losing oxygen than needs to find his lost submarine. A lot of the backgrounds are dark, intimidating, or ominous in some ways that gave me more of an isolated and suffocating feeling than the feeling of playing a simple kids adventure.
Of course, the voice acting is pretty "meh". Freddi and Luther are fine, but with the rest of the characters, it's pretty hit-and-miss. Some memorably terrible voices would be Fiddler Crab, the dumb shark, and the hermit crab. They just sound too overly-cartoonish or just flat-out bad to listen to.
And the game's story is pretty weak. You get some kelp to save all the fish in the sea, but the fact that no one cares about the potential starvation, or that the only political impact is just the king being mildly concerned about their ENTIRE FOOD SUPPLY GONE MISSING, seems a little odd to me. I mean, if America lost all of it's supply on food, would the President start a press conference, and open with, "Well, citizens of America, it seems we have lost all of our food supplies. Don't worry about it, though! There's these two kids that told me they'd find it. So... just go about your own business."
And some of the fish are inanely stupid, getting stuck in incredibly simple problems. Seriously, Fiddler Crab. How the f*** did you get stuck in that f***ing cage. It's not a crab trap. That is a simple locking cage. Did you accidentally lock yourself in there? In your own cage? And Luther is such a hindrance as a sidekick, it really feels like Freddi is the one going around and fixing everyone's incredibly simple problems, instead of them just going out and actually finding the solutions themselves, if they could just move their g****** legs.
Yes, this is a children's game. I know people like to the throw out the "But it's for kids!" argument whenever you call something from children's entertainment sh***y, but I pull no punches and I use no excuses for my criticism. If I didn't like something in a game, I didn't f***ing like it. It doesn't matter if it's "just a kid's game" or "just an action game", and I need to get over myself. It's that mentality that lets horrible entertaiment like Transformers run rampant in the film industry.
Slight rant aside, Freddi Fish is an honestly bad game. It's story was certainly lacking, especially with the tacked-on moral at the end, it's artstyle clashes, and it's puzzles are far too simple (even for its intended audience). It just felt very devoid of anything unique as a kid's edutainment game. I won't come back and play this game anytime soon. I'm giving Freddi Fish and The Case of the Missing Kelp Seeds, a 3/10.

Victoria 2 is another RTS with a pause game from the fine folks at Paradox Interactive and set during the height of European colonial and Imperial power. Typically when you hear 'RTS' the first thing that pops into your mind are games like Command&Conquer and other simple 'point, click ,conquer' games where your simple goal is to win the war by any means or casualties necessary. Nothing wrong with that, but if that is the kind of strategy you enjoy you should stay far, far away from the far more realistic perspective that Victoria II offers.
Typically Paradox games are never the same (though their somewhat simplistic map and interface might lead some to think they are just the same game in different period), with Crusader Kings series focusing on dynastic ambition, Europa Univeralis on amassing a massive Empire and Hearts of Iron on winning the World Wars. Victoria 2 falls into that golden sweet spot between Europa Universalis and Hearts of Iron where the history is already written. Some things are quite likely to happen no matter what you do: such as the Germanies being united by either Prussia, Austria or Bavaria. Liberalism will also gain strength around the world and the USA will emerge as a Great Power without peer.
Other things though? Not quite so certain. You can easily cripple even the largest powerhouse such as the United Kingdom with an illtimed or ill-fought war that leads to hundreds of thousands of your precious Pops dying out; in essence crippling your industry and dooming you to a waiting game where you hope to recussitate your lagging economy.
Thankfully the game has a deep, and I mean DEEP economy system which you can spend hours or even days simply trying to manipulate to become an economic powerhouse without peer. Some games are actually simply put games where you try to maximize your economic potential and gain a toehold in the global market and they can be just as fun and rewarding... or even more so than a traditional warfare approach.
I could go onto rant about the depth, beauty and awesomness of Victoria II, but I figure I should sum this up somehow:
+Incredibly deep and complex.
+Lots of replay value.
-Unpolished gem.
-Graphics can be a turn off for some.

Dungeon Siege 3 is, IMO, 3/5 stars. The original Dungeon Siege franchise used to be a party based, hack/slash game that focused on highly customizable character and party selections;  however, the latest installment was a blatant clone of the Diablo franchise, without the strengths that Diablo has. While it is still a strong installment, it does not live up to the expectations or any of the potential that the release had.
The main problem is that the game play was far easier than any prior Dungeon Siege or Diablo game, and only had a few difficult parts.  While the character's health was generally low and you can only define Katarina as "squishy," the dodging function was exceptionally overpowered.  Once I got a good tempo while playing Katarina, I spent more time dodging than anything else. Due to the game's auto-target system, it was exceptionally easy to dodge, dodge, face in the general direction of your target, shoot, dodge.  While this removed most, if not all, of the difficulty of the game, it added a level of difficulty created by the pure frustration of changing targets.  Once the game selected a target, it was usually counter productive to attempt to change to a more desirable target than it was to simply kill all the least desirable targets to get to your intended target.
The second issue was that the story was completely unengaging.
The UI was cumbersome, and counterintuitive.
Finally, the exact way stats affected your character were never defined, leaving the power gamer in me screaming for satisfaction.
It's a clear step-down from the original Dungeon Sieges in almost every way, but it is very similar to the Diablo franchise now. The original Dungeon Sieges were hack/slashes, but were party based and unique enough to stand apart.  If you don't have some other game to occupy your time, DS3 is an awesome game. However, don't go in expecting something comparable to DS 1 or 2. Expect another Diablo clone and while it is a pretty good clone, no clone is comparable to the original.

More and more, I am starting to realize that the creators of these games have forgotten what makes a challenge fun.  It is that it is possible to succeed.  Even when you don't, you knew it was possible.  Not so in Endless Legend.  I played the game for many hours.  It is a total waste of time.  You think in the beginning you have a chance as you are busy planning how you will allocate your resources.  However, it only devolves in to an endless chore because no matter what you do, there is never enough production to allow you to make progeress against the AI.  The people who create this game think that they are being creative when they simply make it so that if you can do a lot of research, you can't build.  If you can build, you can't do a lot of research.  Then they create the game so that, in order to stand a chance, you must be able to do a lot of both, but they make that scenario impossible.  So you endlessly spin your wheels until you find yourself in yet another chore.  Yipee, just what I wanted in a game...a chore.  What you need for a fun game is to establish some type of successful balance that makes the game winnable.  In this game you cannot.  If you work on one thing, something else will cause you to lose the game.  I'm done with this game....I'd rather clean my house...at least I know it is possible to succeed.

The game is like every other LEGO game except more focused around combat, which isn't a bad thing at all. I find the game as a whole to be fun and action packed, but it does have it's downsides.
Fighting on the Green Dragon Mech/Lightning Jet is a bit clunky (or maybe it's just not my thing). Voice acting for characters like Garmadon and Cole just don't seem to exactly click, especially during the cutscenes. Other than that voice acting is fine. As well as in certain locations, like the Beach, their isn't strong consistency. However this problem is very minor but would still fall under cons. The price is a bit overpriced, it's more like $30-37, but you can always refund
There are so many things I like about the game and it will have me hooked for a while. Combat is fun with the so many different options, so many ways to explore your environment, and also purpose to revisit levels as characters you unlock later in the game. This also helps to just relive the game in a new way, making sure it doesn't get old. I love how this theme is very consistent throughout LEGO games, and it's really enjoyable.
However the game will not make sense if you haven't seen the movie and/or the show. Also side note about the movie: certain parts of the movie will not make sense if you haven't seen the show. Especially how Garmadon became the way he is because the explaination he gave in the movie doesn't do it justice. Anyway, there are a lot of pros to this game and I find everything about the game enjoyable besides the cons I mentioned, but you can easily pass over those (besides the aerial-combat one, that one bothers me a bit).
Anyway, I say the game is totally worth it. It may be a bit pricey, but I assure you it's worth it. That's the only way I can say it. I thought it was pricey at first, and now i'm praising it in this review. After all, you can get a refund if you don't like it. It's totally worth a shot.
Overall, it's a great martial arts tribute in a LEGO game. I would recommend it to anyone, even those new or unfamiliar with LEGO games and to those who are new to Ninjago/ the Ninjago Movie.

If Steam had a neutral rating, I would have given it Cross of the Dutchman. Cross of the Dutchman is not a bad game but it is a very average game. The game doesn't do anything particularly wrong but it doesn't really stand out in any way either.
I liked the theme of the game since it is always nice to actually play a game in a different setting for once. The story is not bad despite only a few of the characters being memorable.
The combat is solid but lacks a lot of depth. The game is essentially a button masher. The game does not include a block or dodge button so you pretty much just attack and run away from enemies. I got a little tired of the combat towards the middle of the game but the last couple of missions are pretty good. The game kind of feels like a long fetch quest though as you go back and forth between cities fighting enemies.
Unless you want to find all of the treasure chests or get all of the achievements the game will only take around three hours to complete. That is mostly due to the fact that the game is not particularly difficult.
At full price I don't think Cross of the Dutchman is worth it. If you like beat 'em ups/hack 'n slash games you could still get some enjoyment out of the game and I would recommend it to you if you can get it on sale.
Note: I received a free review copy of Cross of the Dutchman.

A pretty competent isometric brawler with good looking art. You are a farmer whose village is under attack by Saxon soldiers, who serve as cannon fodder for your fists/sword. The plot is fairly bare bones, and about 15 minutes of my time in the first hour was spent finding boxes to smash for coins.
There's also a stealth segment in the first hour, which was mercifully very short and simple. I hope they don't make that a regular thing. There are only checkpoint saves, whereas I would have preferred the ability to save anywhere.
The combat is fairly simple with only 2 inputs: Left Click (normal attack) and Right Click (Special attack). You can buy alternate special attack, health upgrades etc are certain points in the game. However, large groups of enemies can stun lock you which makes it near impossible to get out of a bad situation, which is a significant drawback here.
This is one of the cases where my review would be a sideways thumb, but since Steam doesn't allow that I'll say: get this game if you're looking for a simple brawler with a light story.
NOTE:
(a) The screenshots on the store page made me think this was an action RPG like Torchlight, which it is not. However, that is not necessarily a bad thing, just different.
(b) I recieved a key from the developer for review purposes.
(c) I'll update this review as I keep playing. Hopefully I enjoy it enough to give it a thumbs up eventually!

: Cross of the Dutchman
: Action, Adventure, Indie
: Triangle Studios
: Triangle Studios
: 10 Sep, 2015
"Cross of the Dutchman is an action adventure game based on the true story of the folk legend 'Pier Gerlofs Donia'. The story takes place in medieval Western Europe, in the province of Frisia, near the turn of the 16th century."
The story itself is good, and I really like the fact that it follows a little piece of history of someone who  became legend, and it's great you get to see from this stylised perspective some of the things he did and achieved. What they say is actually correct, at least from what I already know of it. If I could ever teach history I would want it this way! It's a lot more interactive compared to just being told, since you follow the character and you do something you enjoy which is playing a game. It's not heavy on the detail but it's accurate and gives you enough to enjoy it.
Obviously things are exaggerated for game purposes. But that just makes it more entertaining than just getting it from a book – and it may make you interested enough to look up the full history for yourself!
The story (as told like this) follows the tale of a very manly farmer with a very loud and manly voice whose farm is attacked by some very nasty Saxons who just don't leave him in peace, when all he wants to do is work on his farm and live a simple life. I would tell more about the story but I don't want to spoil the adventure you'll be embarking on. But you probably get the impression that Pier is very manly. You will be impressed by it.
The graphics are cartoonist and polished, making it more interesting to play following this distinctive art style. It doesn't lag for me, the gameplay is smooth and responsive, and it all works well with the atmosphere of the game, the feel of medieval style Holland and how Pier interacts with his environment and his enemies. There is not a great deal of variation in the visuals (Like the grass and trees and roads) but it's not needed for this game. Also, Pier is very manly in the way he punches and kicks and destroys containers.
Everything's with the mouse, and you can basically do everything in the game like this, you don't need to use a keyboard. I didn't try out to see if the keyboard was viable since the mouse is enough to get you where you want. You can mis-click if there's a barrel next to a person or if you're trying to reach a obscured area. Sometimes you will also start punching or hacking in a random direction against an enemy  when they start swarming you, but that's probably because you're clicking like crazy, and because Pier likes to finish off his manly moves before changing direction.
The sound is great, it fits in with the scene you're playing, like: Pier's farm, when and you're fighting, where you're sneaking, and what you're doing. Pier also has very manly shouts which makes you want to break open all the barrels and chests just so you can hear it. And kill all the enemies even on timed missions.
I really liked this game, I was excited to start playing it and I wasn't disappointed by what I experienced. The sound and graphics and story makes this a great game to learn history from Friesland. It's an amazing experience that went to game. It's great that it can be accurate without getting boring!
In fact one of the only things that bothered me was the re-spawning of the chests and barrels, because the re-spawned ones don't have any loot, and if I missed one I would have no way of knowing short of staying in the scene and kicking everything open again. But that's ok. Pier is very manly. AND YOU CAN KEEP SMASHING BARRELS AS MUCH AS YOU WANT. RARGH!
I cannot recommend this game enough. Its full of learning material, with a cool story, good gameplay and amazing music. It’s an overall good experience, and truelly amazing to have.

Ho boy do I have fond memories of this game! Back in 1996, my parents bought me this classic point-and-click when I was 2 years old. Suffice to say, it isn't all that fantastic as a game, but it is still a great way to kill time. The game features a goldfish named Freddi, and a green guppy, Luther, as they embark on a quest to find her grandmother's treasure chest. This game's art style is very colorful and wacky, while the backdrops illuminate under the shimmering ocean surface. The music definitely gives me that summer vibe as Freddi visits various locations such as a beach, a junkyard, and even a king's castle. There are loads of things to click on in the back ground and foreground. Since this is a game for very small audiences I can imagine that this serves as a simulator for waving one's keys. Aside from that the character's dialogue is very tounge and cheek. I forgot how amusing those mafia sharks were in the cutscenes. The game even has section dedicated to teaching mathematics, which is probably the reason I'm so good with math now! All in all, Freddi Fish is a cute, fun exploration game, but would not recommend to an audience who never grew up with any of these games. For the kiddies and for those who have fond memories, this one's a real treat as it is loaded with various things to do, despite it being a game that will last a couple of hours maximum.

Many games are repetitive, but what helps The Curious Expedition stand out is the witty flavor text and the wide variety of unlockable characters.  No two PCs play the same way, even though they all have to abide by the mechanics in some form.  Now sure, one could say that about any RPG, but one rarely sees a game that really brings out the vibe of 'I'm on a safari in a very dangerous land, full of people who get very miffed when I wreck local wildlife and ancient Gods who will try to kill me as I steal treasure from under their noses.'
Or perhaps it's the ultimate "Colonial Era Adventurer Simulator" of our time?
At any rate yes combat is a major setback in this game, and yet one can learn the ropes.  In short:  Spears, my friend.  Spears have been a historically significant weapon among countless civilizations and for good reason.  Those pointy sticks can and will save your rear when combined with the proper dice against the various hostile fauna you will encounter.
I've been playing this game since it was still in Early Access, and the various features the devs added over time really helped enhance the experience.  All in all, even if it rubs you the wrong way I for one doubt that you'd completely regret your time spent with this game!

This was my first Paradox game.  Well, technically the demo of this was my first Paradox game - a demo in which I put in about 100 hours (even though you could only play as the US).
Victoria II has aged pretty well, although it is not as new as Crusader Kings II or EU IV.  There's a bit of a steep learning curve, but you don't need to know everything to start having fun with the game (and it's not *as* bad as some games).  The game is fairly balanced and bug-free - at least for a grand strategy game with a horrifyingly elaborate economy and political system (how about modeling everybody in the whole wide world for 100 years? Yes, it's that horrifying).  Both expansions are recommended - this was before the switch to modular DLCs, and both expansions are BIG changes and expansions to game mechanics.
You can play as any nation in the world from 1836 to 1936, an era of colonization, unprecedented technological change, and a lot of geopolitical bureaucratising.  If slowly going Bismark over diplomatic struggles, exploiting crises to launch terrible world wars, or carving out continents for economic and political sway appeals to you - this is your game.

I just grabbed this game for a fun little romp, but I can already see hours of my time going into it.
This game is excellent. It looks like your typical top-down shooter indie game, but it's so much more.
Around a half hour in I realized that I kept dying to the minor enemies in around stage two, and that was when I realized how much this game has to offer. If you plan on running in and firing away into crowds like you do in every other top down shooter, you won't make it far in this game. Long reload times, relative ammo scarcity, and strong standard enemies mean you have to put a reasonable amount of thought into each encounter.
It's not a strategy game by any means, but I regularly find myself looking at the latest cluster of enemies and quickly planning my shots in the back of my head before I go in, as to leave the best chance of making it out alive. However, it doesn't require so much thought that you spend any time waiting, thinking of what to do. All it requires is that you're actively aware, and that's really fantastic. The game trusts that you'll learn how the weapons, mechanics, and enemies function, in order to really master the game. It's also not the grueling challenge that you see many games that require that understanding become. Relic Hunters Zero is a happy medium between the difficult game that asks you to master, and the fun shoot-em-up romp we've come to expect from a game of it's style.
In summary, Relic Hunters Zero is a great way to spend some time if you want a top-down shooter with a little more substance. 10/10.
P.S. I'm hoping the fact that it's open source will lead to lots of additional content in the future.

Where does one begin with Just Deserts...
We'll most likely telling you that the game is a sham. But that's probably going down the rabbit hole too fast, so I'll have to back up a bit, and start at the beginning of my experience with this game.
I was in a Discord call with some friends a few years ago. We were sifting through random tags on Steam, and telling each other about all of our crazy finds. Incidentally, that was the same day that I found VA-11 HALL-A, an experience of infinitely higher quality that I briefly touched on in another review. At first glace, I though Just Deserts could have potential. It had the same anime appeal that drew me into a lot of unadvised purchases, and the trailers displayed it as a light novel dating simulator. Upon playing the game I found it to be a jumbled mess with no focus, switching genre and pacing on a whim, trying to endear you to the girls with visual novel sections, while leaving room for the time management system and bare bones RPG gameplay.
It's a classic case of the bait and switch. It may not be intentional by the developers, but the fact is that because there are so many elements to this game, it never fully succeeds in one single aspect. The visual novel had great potential, with an interesting premise and funny situations between the girls and our defacto romantic visual novel protagonist. The complexity of the characters increases as you get to know them, but not to the extent of other visual novels that are worth your time. Character progression is cut short, and the only reason I can assume why is because there were other aspects of the game that got the attention.
The 1/3 of this game that is an RPG feels like it could be replicated in RPG maker without much difficulty. You attack the aliens, and then they attack you. If you die, you lose. If they die, you win. There are a series of upgrades that make your numbers bigger in exchange for money, which is obtained by killing aliens. It's the tride and true RPG gameplay loop that has worked since Final Fantasy. Unfortunately, a 30 year old concept isn't going to cut it in a modern RPG, and I feel something more engaging or intereting could have been made if more time had been invested in designing it. Are you starting to notice a pattern here?
The time management aspect is also nothing to write home about. You have a limited amount of time to date the girls and uncover the mystery of the alien invasion. If you spend your time wisely, you can get a fair bit of each done on your first playthrough. There's nothing wrong with it per se, but it still does nothing to break the mold.
A lesson we can all learn from Just Desert's mistake, is that truly great games don't balance more than two major aspects. Huniepop, a game marketing in the same vein as Just Deserts, is a Puzzle Dating Sym. Persona 5 is a Time Management RPG. Pyre is a Visual Novel Action game. These games are focused and accomplish what they set out to do. Why would Persona bog itself down with another aspect? Why isn't Persona also a Puzzle game? To put it simply, it would detract from the main focus, and lower the overall quality.
The main focus's in Just Deserts are the girls. They're designed well and written with a fun group dynamic in mind. In the visual novel sections, you can tell these girls have been working and living together for a long time, and all collectively enjoy poking fun at the beta-male protagonist as a group. Unfortunately, they are only the sugar coating on top a mile high cake of unnecessity.
If you're a big enough weeb to be even slightly interested in this game like I was, buy Huniepop. It's an overall better game with just as much appeal. Plus, you actually get to see anime tiddies in that game.

I'll be honest, I didn't expect much from this game. So, I'm not disappointed. It's just very painfully average.
Writing is pretty bad. Lots of inner monologuing that is supposed to be funny, but ultimately is cringy at best. Lots of "..." and "Uhm...", that are there just to artificially prolong gameplay. The story itself is very rushed. As if the author knew where he wants to start and finish, but had absolutely no idea what to put in the middle. If you take away all the grinding, unskippable animations and constant "...", you could probably finish the story in an hour. Some routes and characters seem like an afterthought, way less developed than the others.
There are no dialogue choices. At all.
There is gameplay in this game. I wish there was not. It's very simplistic and repetitive. The enemies are unimaginative cubes and spheres.
The dating sim elements are dumbed down to "buy # of items she wants you to buy, then go and farm for more money". With time restriction of 28 in-game days this is just annoying.
UI is terrible and settings are minimal. Can't speed up or skip animations (which makes already tedious combat all the more slow and frustrating), can't set the transparency of the text box, can't set the speed of text itself. No separate audio slider for voices.
The art is inconsistent. Character sprites are amazing. Backgrounds are ok. CG are... 50/50. It's as if they had two different artists who drew for this game. And one of them was sloppy and didn't know anatomy at all.
Music is just there. It's not memorable, nor is it distracting.
Voice acting is... sigh... it's for the most part incredibly amateurish. Eve and Jen are fine. Great even. Especially Jen, her voice acting was on-point, very emotional. Great job. Cecile and Yumi are... acceptable... but Cornelia can, in my opinion, safely nominate for the worst voice actress in history of gaming. Zero emotions (and no, not because her character is unemotional) and bad sound quality. It's as if we're back in 90s.
They remind me of Honey Pop. But when in HP it was so bad it was funny, here it's just so bad that it's... bad.
Overall, it's not the worst visual novel that I have ever played. But then again, I have played some serious♥♥♥♥♥♥that I don't even want to remember. This game was just unsatisfying. It's cheap, and if you like visual novels, you may give it a go to kill a bit of time. Maybe you'll find it amusing. But if you LOVE visual novels, then stay away from this. It's just not worth it.

Quickie:
Having to greatly tone down the ambitions and scope of your game due to a lack of funds must be agonizing. This is exactly what happened to Triangle Studios with Cross of the Dutchman, a game about the Frisian hero Pier Gerlofs Donia, and it shows.
It's a playable adventure game with some hack & slash and very rare stealth elements. Playable being the keyword.
Nothings actually "good" or well made, but there isn't anything really bad in here either. It's bland.
I did, however, enjoyed my time with the game. Full disclosure; being from The Netherlands and having Frisian relatives might have helped with that. A historically themed game set in Frisia sounded amazing.
The historical part is ultimately the most disappointing part about the game, though. You'll get to see the tale about how a simple farmer became the legendary "Grutte Pier" told in a mostly lighthearted and really straightforward manner. I'd have loved to have seen some more detailed information about the Saxons, live in Frysia during that time-period and so on. Even if it where just simple codex entries. But unfortunately, there's nothing like that to be found. That might just be my inner geek speaking, though.
The environments are pretty and the sound-design is fantastic. But Pier himself...
He's a large pile of rather dumb powermuscles.
Or atleast, that's how the game portrays him, and I doubt it's what the developers where going for. I like the lighthearted form of story-telling, but it isn't handled very well, lacks any kind of character development and hurts the whole game in the process.
The game itself is a four to five hour affair wherein you'll punch some soldiers, search for treasure chests, do some light sneaking and participate in a whole lot of backtracking.
The combat's...fine. Basic, but it works. You'll get some special abilities early on and you can fully rely on using the heaviest one and your standard punches to defeat your enemies. Sneaking around is a bit annoying. All of a sudden the player can't attack guards he fought just a couple of moment ago and get's instantly killed when spotted. It's short, easy and only happens twice, so it's not a big deal.
The amount of back-tracking is, however, a very big deal. Somewhere at the start of the game, Pier makes a joke about feeling like an errand boy, and that never goes away. There are just a small number of area's you can visit and you'll be running between them so many times it get's very repetitive. And then it ends.
There's nothing in the way of side-activities, beside searching for some hidden treasure chests. They're...treasure chests.
Finished the game with every chest opened without any issues.
The game feels like a well-polished idea. It might know what it wants to achieve, but clearly isn't able to do that on it's budget. Everything is just...there.
It's a game. It's playable. It exists.
And that's more then I thought would happen after the Kickstarter failed.
I'm glad it's here and enjoyed my time with it, but I can't possibly recommend it.

This is a special game, and even though I absolutely love the artstyle and the historical relevance of it, there are a few things that make me cringe.
Let's start with the good!
-Faithful to the real thing
I believe this game has done a great job at capturing the historical "mood" of its setting, from the art style to the face's drawings, to the behaviours themselves!
-Amazing Art
Not much to say here, but I really think the art direction in this game is quite good!
Then, the bad!
-Tried and True "Coward mechanics"
Perhaps it wasn't the goal of this game to innovate, but the initial fetch quests, as much as I love the little gimmick here and there, are way too cheesy!
Extra Credits, a Youtube channel about games, has talked about this, and so have many others.
Just because a game is acceptable it does not make it good.
-Lazy Dialogue(50/50)
I am quite divided in this part, as for every line of witty dialogue I see there is an overly "Cheesy RPG" line that is overused, but overall, I think the devs could have done a better job with this, as sometimes it really does draw away from the mood.
And now, the ugly part where we take the good and the bad, put it all in a blender, and out comes the ugly, the conclusion!
Overall, even with its flaws and assortment of bugs, overused mechanics and failed RPG style(that was corrected by the devs, so kudos to them on that), the amazing MUSIC(I forgot to mention that!), the Art style and the mood really set this game apart, leading me to recommend it.

Pier e la sua famiglia volevano vivere in santa pace, in una piccola cittadina, ma un giorno tutto cambiò..
Così Pier forma un gruppo di difensori formati da agricoltori, per fermare gli oppressori.
Gli atti che troveremo nel gioco sono inerenti alla Leggenda di Pier, conosciuto anche per la "Croce Olandese".
Storia, narrata e spiegata in modo accurato.
Diverse combinazioni di mosse
Dialoghi divertenti
Stile Artistico

I love the concept, but this game suffers from funtropy- where devs come up with a brilliant idea, put all their heart into it for the first half then just lose direction and add more and more zany or unnecessary content or "wouldn't it be cool if" features that end up ruining what made the original idea great.
What I love about the game:
> The way it captures that 19th- early 20th era of exploration and imperialism
> The randomness, procedural map generation, and the rouge-like qualities
> The graphical style, it fits the game for what it is
> The combat, which is straight forward but interesting (dice based but with a twist)
> The "casual game" style- I can start a game and be done in an hour or so, not too demanding timewise
> Unlocking new characters to play with
What I dislike:
> No save function and winner takes it all- you have 1 life and if you die you lose. Period. No top scores/top attempts here, if you die on the last, toughest level, your previous one hour of gameplay has been meaningless
> Dinosaurs, magic, aliens, dimensional teleportation, and Universe-ending events which clashes completely with the 19th century theme and completely rips you out of the immersion successfully created by other parts of the game
> The music becomes intolerable after a short while, and is extremely loud at times (win screens)
> A lot of linearity regarding special missions, and general game choices become repetitive quickly
> The row of depressing "if only's" and "why did they's" that you figure out while playing the last few games you ever will
In summary:
> Another "GREAT potential" game
> Devs should follow Einstein's adage, "perfection is not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing more to take away"
That said:
> It is hard to bring myself to not recommend this game considering the price I paid (which was way cheaper than it is now), stricly because of the "fun per dollar" ratio- expect to play it through a bunch of times, but once you've figured it out you will get bored and annoyed and never touch it again. Unless they address the issues. But devs always move on once the money starts flowing.

For those of us who were playing the Elder Scrolls before the release of Skyrim, we know just how groundbreaking this game was. It had graphics and a game engine that were far beyond its time. For those who have not played this fantastic game, it offers a world that is nearly 50% larger than Skyrim. The guild questlines in Oblivion are also far more lengthy and interesting than those in Skyrim. There are 199 quests and over 350 discoverable locations in Oblivion. Don't get me wrong; I love Skyrim and I think that it's a better made game than Oblivion. Oblivion is perhaps less immersive than Skyrim, but it certainly makes up for it with hundreds of NPCs with whom you can interact with. Oblivion simply offers so much content and was so influential in the genre, that I would hate to see it fall by the wayside because new-generation gamers were dispelled by the older, more cartoonish graphics. The sheer amount of things to do in Oblivion is staggering, far more than is offered in Skyrim, in my opinion. Also, the amount of playtime that you can get from the DLCs for such a low price is a fantastic deal. Any fan of Skyrim who has never played this game ought to buy it and see where Skyrim falls short in certain areas and realise why Skyrim is one of the best games ever created in its own right. Oblivion is a complete game that will exeed expectations and it will continue to stay relevant for years to come.

Freddi Fish, an intrepid and inquisitive young fish, pays a visit to her grandma's house. While there, she learns that her grandma's kelp seeds have been stolen! Freddi sets out with her best friend Luther to find the culprits and restore the seeds to their rightful owner.
FFaTCotMKS is a point and click game designed for younger children. The resulting gameplay is simplistic but intuitive. Puzzles tend to fall into the
category, which is fine. I completed the game in about 40 minutes, but I expect it to take a bit longer if you choose to explore the areas more thoroughly. I liked it, though it may not be enjoyable for everyone. It is very easy, after all.
Freddi is a very brave and conscientious role model for children. She pays proper respect to her elders and does her best to set things right. I found it very difficult to be interested in Luther, however. He barely helps beyond asking meaningless questions and is seemingly only after the kelp seeds for his own benefit (despite being reprimanded by Freddi several times). However, his antics make him an interesting foil to Freddi and her grounded disposition. Still, he felt unnecessary and I personally didn't like having him around.
The side characters give the game an atmospheric quality that I enjoyed as a child and continue to enjoy as an adult. Their colorful personalities are memorable beyond the confines of their limited time on screen. Interactions with them are simple and genuine, and an enjoyable aspect of the experience. I chuckled a few times at the villains' dialogue, especially.
FFaTCotMKS takes place underwater. It appears to be the ocean, but it could be a sea or some other large body of water, as it is never explicitly stated.
I liked the variety inherent in the different environments. The world is well populated and immersive, and there are a TON of things to click on in every screen of the game. Colorful little creatures bounce around, a starfish teaches you basic math, pearls shine and an opera fish performs a solo. It's worth exploring every inch just to see what crazy thing will happen next! These fun little events are synonymous with Humongous Entertainment's early point and click offerings, and they help bring the world to life.
The game has a very charming, almost handdrawn look to it (forgive me if the art actually IS handdrawn, I'm not very proficient at spotting the difference). The graphics are endearing and vibrant while simultaneously giving off the look of a cartoon. It's fun to look at and even runs in widescreen!
Character designs themselves aren't incredibly impressive, but their personalities more than make up for any obvious deficiencies.
The music is serviceable and ambient, but not very memorable. The sound effects, on the other hand, are abuzz with life. You'll recognize many reused sound effects if you've played any other Humongous Entertainment games, and I guarantee they'll put a smile on your face.
I wholeheartedly recommend Freddi Fish and the Case of the Missing Kelp Seeds. It's chock-full of educational and humorous content for younger minds. It looks and feels like an interactive animated television show, it has a strong identity and an altruistic endgame, but, most of all, it does exactly what it sets out to do: provide a meaningful experience. I think it's definitely worth a buy, though I'd recommend purchasing a reduced price. 7 dollars might be too much to some people for the amount of content you're provided.

Did you enjoy Dungeon Siege 1 or 2? Do you like action rpg's like Diablo or Torchlight?  Or you even enjoyed the D&D lite Bauldur's Gate version for console? If you answered yes to any of these questions then don't buy this game.
What DS3 does is a disgrace to aRPG's. What's so strange is it from Obsidian, one of my favorite developers. How they messed this up so badly is beyond my comprehension. Let me point out a few of the flaws.
CONTROLS - In all aRPG's the left mouse button moves your character around, attacks enemies that are highlighted, and picks up loot. In DS3 the left mouse is the attack key only. It's basically what most games have set as shift+attack since when you press it you stop what you're doing and preform an attack no matter if there's an enemy or not. Moving is the right mouse button. The move button does not attack at all. Picking up items is the 'E' key. Yup, they took one simplistic function and divided it into 3 buttons that will confuse and frustrate you. That's just one example of how badly they messed up the control scheme here.
CHARACTER - Character development should be an important aspect of any RPG. You are presented with 4 different characters to choose from, all with different abilities, and a decent back story. So in the beginning you're thining you'll be able to develop and grow this person. Nope. Firstly, you are not allowed to zoom in on your character for a close-up look. When you get new weapons and armor their apperance changes, but you can never really get the feel of how much more badass you are. Combine that with the worst inventory management system I've seen in 10 or more years. You are never allowed to view your character in an inventory screen and see good your new loot looks. And if that wasn't enough, when you interact with other characters in the game you are only ever shown the other person's face. Basically once you choose your avatar, and begin the game, you will never be allowed to relate to them again. Match that with a talent tree that doesn't give you a choice as to what to develop. You are forced to unock all abilities in each tier.
GRAPHICS - There is one major problem here. Peoples eyes look like they are dead. Everyone's eyes in this game is slightly whited out and it seriously feels like they are the eyes of the deceased. Also a problem is the UI. I mentioned some of it with the inventory, but the UI is just bad all around. Not to mention your characters abilities icons aren't very good. They don't do a good job at representing what each ability does.
SAVE POINTS - Really!? Save points in a game!? It's the 21st century is there anyway we could have just moved past this? Was it in Square Enix's contract to publish this game it had to have Save Points instead of an auto-save feature, check points, manual save? Oh, and when you do save; instead of just selecting the save slot, you must first select the save slot you want and then you have to actually go to the bottom of the screen and press the save button. An unnecessary step and only further points out the bad programing decisions that were made in this games development.
MULTIPLAYER - Last but certainly not least is MP. You do not bring your avatar into a MP session. You are only allowed to play as one of the Hosts NPC buddies. This turned out to be a very solid hack/slash/loot game.  You can choose from 4 solidly different characters.  The combat starts fairly simple (mash attach, use 1 or 2 abilities), but it gets more complex in a really rewarding way.  Each character has 2 combat stances, and each stance has 3 abilities that you get as you level up, plus 3 defensive abilities.  Each ability can also be mastered to unlock a more powerful version of that ability.  You get to distribute a few meaningful upgrades each time you level up.  The entire game was bug free for me in single player.  The graphics were really nice, and the plot was pretty solid (although as with most fantasy games I said "huh?!" a couple times).  The looting is good, the inventory and quest systems are good.  The game isn't incredibly long, but for me that was good.  It was about 9 hours for the single player and it really felt like an epic journey.  A few sidequests, but it wasn't bogged down with them.  As I ramble on, I realize that the bottom line for me was "this game was pretty awesome."   I am also a couple hours into the co-op.  Only the person hosting gets to save their character, but as long as you play with the same person, you'll both get to keep your stuff.  Co-op is mostly smooth, but since you have to both be on the same screen, sometimes your partner running off, gets you trapped in a corner.
A surprisingly good game. I picked it up on sale, but I could recommend it at it's current price.

Thinking of the MOBA it might sounds like a plodding war of attrition with particular hero characters between traditional battle roles, like tank, healer, ranged, and damage dealer. The game is simple, each team have to push against waves of human players or their AI sidekicks (if less player); whichever bunch gets through the other side first takes home the win. Turret situations, summon spots bring forth extra help, and concealed ways permit players to flank their enemies. Awesomenauts fabricates an intricate layer of system around a no frills 2D center, and this is the place attentive players will find brilliant strategies.
Each character has a unique set of skills, consisting of a free-use weapon and two special actions. As the player acquires Solar, they can return to their base to heal and spend the Solar on various upgrades to these skill sets or core statistics such as movement speed and health. For each of four areas: the two special skills, their free weapon, and general statistics, the player can selected to buy up to three of six available improvements, with some improvements which can be bought multiple times with benefits stacked.

Cross of the Dutchman is an action adventure game based on the true story of the folk legend 'Pier Gerlofs Donia'.
While the game doesn't have very complicated or interesting combat (Only a normal hit and a special attack without any dodge/block mechanics integrated into the combat).
The game did strike me as having an appealing aesthetic and the questing was fun to do even if some of the logic behind doing tasks seemed flawed.

A fine hack-and-slash that is a little bogged down by some clunky and slightly awkward combat, with a tad too much chaff and filler that will have you running back and forth along unnecessarily twisting roads. The art style may or may not be your thing. If you want to see more, check out my thoughts in the review video below:

Triangle Studios
Action Adventure
$8.99
GTX 650 2GB OC Edition, Core i3 4130 3.4 Ghz at 1920x1080 Res.
Cross of the Dutchman's story takes place in the Netherlands in the 16th century. In the game you play as Pier Gerolfs Donia, a big muscular guy, who is the village's defender in his battle with the Saxon oppressors along with a few other people he meets along the way. The game is based on a true story, and the story itself is told through the game, but it's told in a very linear fashion. Overall there are 9 chapters, each lasting around 15-20 minutes. You don't really connect with any of the character, your wife and 2 kids just feel like people who are there to push the story along, I never got to know them or to actually talk with them because almost all the dialouge was just for the story. There are no side quests and there isn't much to do other than going through the story.
The artstlye in this game is very cartoon like and hand drawn. I personally loved the artstyle of the game in every way. It really reminded me of Beseige's artstyle. I loved this game's cutscene art more than anything, I thought it all looked great, everything fit in so nicely and it all just looked very atmospheric and colourful overall.
The gameplay in Cross of the Dutchman was very basic, you used the mouse for pretty much everything, including movement and fighting and occasionally holding shift to make sure you don't run off during combat. Now while this did work for most of the game, it was really basic. You hold down shift and spam LMB to do normal attacks and RMB ocassionally to do your special attacks. There were only a few enemie types and most of them felt varied but only either charged at you with a sword or shot you with a bow and arrow. There are also stealth sections in the game, which I found to be overused and not done very well, the AI was super predictable and could only see in a really small cone of view making the stealth sections the easiest part of the game. Most of the game is really just walk around and hack and slash. The gameplay and combat overall weren't that bad, just very, very basic.
The soundtrack for the game is wonderful. It makes the game feel more atmospheric and it really fit in well almost all of the time. General sound effects were also good.
The whole map of the game consists of about 5 areas, mostly towns and are all quiet similar. There are also other routes you can go with through the map to find hidden chests and such. So exploration = rewards which is something I always love to see, even though there isn't a whole lot to explore.
Now here is where the game had a lot of problems, the performance was really bad for me, I tried everything and even when I turned the graphics all the way down the game still had stutter and kept dropping to well below 20 fps. I tried to fix it in every possible way I could think of but without any real graphical settings other than "Low. Medium. and High" I couldn't do much about it. I did a few benchmarks and honestly my CPU stayed at avererage tempatures, so did my graphics card even at high settings but the framrate still stayed between 20 - 40. The game also took up 4 whole gigabytes of ram which is crazy for a game like this. This does seem to be a problem only I was having but just something to watch out for.
Overall I rate Cross of the Dutchman a
I had a hard time scoring this game and I did want to give it a positive score but the negatives just overtook the positives.

First, if you’d like to see gameplay footage and a bit of review, check out my video here:
If you’d rather do that whole reading thing, well, keep reading.
If you like exploration, pressing your luck and a bit of difficulty/rogue-like gameplay with a boardgamey feel, then you’ll probably dig this retro-style game.
When I was growing up, I played a lot of Apple games in school as part of an after school computer literacy program. The ones that always interested me the most were the ones geared toward exploration. Yeah, they were trying to be educational but pfft it’s a game, come on. My favorite was based off of Lewis and Clark’s expedition.
The Curious Expedition gives that great old-school game vibe while still being its own thing. The basic gameplay revolves around going on six expeditions, trying to best other explorers. You gain fame for completing a successful expedition as well as donating cool things you find to the museum after an expedition.
At its heart, this is really a press your luck game; you have limited resources (and sanity) to accomplish your goals. You’ll have to weigh whether it’s worth exploring more of the map and risking horrific failure or just finding the damn golden pyramid.
Mechanically, the game is very sound. Since traveling around costs time and sanity you really have to make a plan on how you’re going to tackle a map. Add to that the fact that you can only carry so much and your crew has varying abilities and you get a lot of interesting decisions; do you carry that treasure worth fat loot or do you need that sanity regaining whiskey?
Combat is definitely worth a special mention; it’s great. It’s all dice based and has a very Yahtzee feel to it. Essentially you get 3 re-rolls to get the outcomes you’re looking for and different combinations of dice do different things. It’s both surprisingly tactical and often times tense.
There’s also a pretty good variety of locations/events and a TON of different items you’ll find as you play; I’ve put in about 13 hours as of this review and still have many things I haven’t seen. That being said, some people would argue there’s not really a lot of replayability. You get different explorers to play as and different biomes to explore, but essentially the gameplay is always the same; go to an area, explore, find loot, get home. Personally, I think there’s more than enough to enjoy for quite a while. You may even want to load it up from time to time just for the hell of it.
Besides, there are some genuinely cool surprises you can find. On one expedition, I found an egg and kept it in my inventory. Eventually it hatched and it was a raptor. A FREAKING RAPTOR. He carried stuff and tore things up. Awesome. Not to mention the cataclysmic events that occur when you defile a temple…always entertaining (and sometimes game ending).
Aesthetically, we have pixel graphics and a bit tune soundtrack. Honestly, I’m not usually a fan of this. I’m 34. I grew up with games that had to be made that way and they pushed the technology. I find retro-style graphics/games are usually just trying to tug at your nostalgia more than anything else and that it doesn’t usually fit the product. This is thankfully the exception to that; it really FEELS like an old-school game I could have grown up playing as opposed to a slapped on decision and the game is definitely better for it.
Overall, definitely recommend this game if you dig exploration and rogue-like gameplay with a boardgamey feel. I did get it on sale but I’d say it’s worth the $15 price tag for the amount of fun you can squeeze on it. Good luck out there fellow explorers!
