Your best laid plans end up in tatters due to an character's unfortunate death or a sudden invasion, and you try to scrape the crumbles as best you can to try and go on, a few decades and some lucky breaks later you are able to accomplish what you set out to and maybe even more. These kind of things make this game the best strategy game period, it's not all playing the systems with some RNG thrown in, the world of CK2 feels alive, it reacts to you and you have to react to it, and the myriad of ways in which you can do things means it never gets boring.
The way it really stands out to other strategy games it you never get to a point where you achieve absolute domination over the rest of the players/nations, as each successive character you play as will have to make or manage to consolidate their own power base, even if you're in a super mighty empire that you managed to forge generations ago; or you can try to do something you haven't like conquer a distant kingdomn and abdicate your old one to a family member and spread your dynasty elsewhere, or convert your realm to a new heresy and fight your previous coreligionaries to make the heresy the new 'one true religion', etc.
The variety of starts and mechanics for the different religions and government types only adds to the replayability and while most require additional DLC to play as, I find the base European christian starts just as fun and varied as any other. I'm 1000 hours of play time in and I've yet to try over half the religions and regions.

Why is Oblivion so good? Simple. Its superior story, characters, guild questlines, and true adherence to the genre of action-RPG.
Compare it to a game like Skyrim and the differences become clear:
It has far better, story driven quests - I don't recall a single brainless fetch quest.
It has a perfect split between action and RPG - unlike Skyrim, which is not an RPG at all but an action game.
It has some of the best guild quests, as each guild has something unique to offer - especially if you space out your advancement in joined guilds throughout your entire playthrough.
It has some of the greatest DLC of all time - DLC which can increase your playtime by around 80 hours.
And it has some of the most atmospheric and superb music found anywhere in gaming.
Now unfortunately, due to Oblivion's ancient release date (exaggeration), the graphics have aged some - mainly in the character department - so I would definitely recommend downloading some mods (for improved character faces download the Oblivion Character Overhaul V2). Other than that, downloading other graphics mods or quality of life mods, Oblivion represents one of the best experiences a human can have in open world gaming. Buy it.

First of all: This is a very one-sided review. I maybe oversee some negetive things of this game because i love it so much and had so many wonderful hours playing it.
If you like/don't mind these "8bit graphics/style" and you like the theme of the age of adventures and exploration of a new world you will love this game!
Sometimes I stay at the titlescreen for a minute just because its so wonderful designed.
It has so much Charme. It really fits the age the game is about.
It looks like I am a real fanboy yes I am. Its like this game really hit my heart.
I cant really tell why. I think the artdesign and the athmosphere of this game gives me flashbacks. Flashbacks of "good old times" of computergames... flashbacks of me when i was a child and how i imagined how it would feel to be a adventurer and explorer.
And i have to say i like Rogue-Likes in general. And I love to write my own stories with Rogue-Like games. In that point i really like the "Report" feature after an expedition, where it looks like a real Diary of an Explorer. You wont use this feature every time but i like to click it when i had a real great or/and exciting expedition. Just to enjoy to read once more what has happend.
(First i thought this was a "Early Access Player Feedback report" button)
I cant stop tell how much i love the athmosphere. For example the short sound when your ship arrived at the world and a new expedition starts. The music/backgroundsounds of every place/event.
Yes for others this maybe not important or only "small details". I love these details.
And I like it that all/most of it feels new designed and not "I have heard/had that sound/music/athmo from that and that game before."
The sounds/background music fits so well to the events/stories that are being told.
Maybe this text doesnt help many people because its so onsided positive comment.
But at this time i really had to say/write this.
So once again: If you like/dont mind 8 Bit graphics and you like the theme of Adventure/Exploration of the new world and especially if you like rogue-like games i totally recommend to buy this game. For the few Euros/Dollars it costs it gives you many hours of joy!

Amnesia: Memories is a bit different, than it's namesake from Frictional Games. Good for me, because I'm a loser when it comes to horror games. Travelling in a world filled with beautiful, thoughtful yet stubborn men was an experience I was happy to have.
The thing is, almost all of the men seem to be too unrealistic for my taste. There're many personality disorders, anime stereotypes: you have your tsunderes, overly self-confident guys and everything you can imagine. Considering that this is a "date simulator" - it's completely understandable, that the game developers have wanted to make the guys appeal more desireable and mysterious. The game itself can carry on the story pretty well, but when it comes to your playable character - everything seems to fall apart.
Our protagonist, you, doesn't really have any type of thoughts - besides this mysterious Orion-bugboy, who says everything you supposedly think out loud to you. You won't have any monologue by yourself throughout the whole story - Orion will be the one to take care of that. To be honest that was a bit of a disappointment for me.
Otherwise, the game is fun and you get emerged into the story pretty quickly.
PROS of this game are...
+ The graphics are beautiful and I really like the voice actors in this one
+ You've got a variety of supporting characters with pretty interesting personalities. So you don't always have to talk to the guys.
+ Every milieu is kind of connected and you get to see the different roles of the people on different storylines. This makes everything more interesting and surprising.
+ The game shows which options you have already chosen, in case you decide to play one "world" again.
+ You also get fun mini games and screenshots, linked to your actual gameplay.
CONS of this game are...
- The characters aren't really that original and some of them aren't even good looking. (To me, at least)
- The achievements are easy, but it's very difficult to know how to get the good endings. I've only managed to get two bad and "average" ending.
- Some of the parts are the same (obviously) and it kind of boring.
- The storylines aren't that long, so if you're a fast reader - you'll get through of them quickly.
+/- You don't get to choose your gender.
My overall experience was fine. I liked the game, it's fun and it's a great way to kill time. I actually had a little crush on one of the main characters, so I think it worked out for me quite well. It's worth the money, so don't be afraid to get it.

It allowed me for an emotional connection with the main character. The fighting was not too hard but satisfying. And the story was tragic but sweet. Though my thought at the end of the story was:
The world is artisticly made, it feels very dutch, with small wooden towns and old large farms. It was easy to navigate and you could easily remember what was where. The crowded village population made the game feel really alive.
The world was quite small, only about 6 areas to explore. You'll visit each place 3 times over till the end of the story. And it feels a bit tiring because you keep clearing the same area over and over. Without side quests it was basicly walking from point to point.
The story was very well written and allowed for an emotional connection with the character. The flow of events seem to logicly follow each other. A farmer with temper and courage grew tired of oppression but went in over his head. And things slowly start to escalate the wrong way. The harder he seem to fight the bigger his misfortune. Then i come to my main critic:
It was not finished! Our hero fought through all the trouble and held fast, trying to save everyone but ends up loosing his loved ones. This should be the turning point of the story. Where our hero bursts in a rage of hate and revenge and kills every single saxon as long as he has breath in his longs. But then the story stops, it just ends. Leaving me watch the credits with unsatisfied feelings of hate and revenge and no where to express them.
Simple but effective! There was not much complexity to the gameplay, you basicly walk around and slash every enemy you encounter. Which is not a bad thing since this is an Adventure game. Good balance of the amount of money you found which limits speed of upgrading.
It was quite easy. A little more variation in enemys, some bosses or maybe a little puzzle here and there wouldn't do harm. I got almost all my achievements on the first run and with the lack of side quests, makes this little replay value.
Good story setup. Emotional connection. Simple but effective gameplay. Beatiful art. And an overall nice feeling.
Story feels unfinished. Lack of side quests. Little variation. Small world. Easy gameplay.
For a game that has been in production for 6 years, it seems more could have been made. But since this is the companies first full adventure game, and had to do various remakes before release, i'll be forgiving and looking forward till their next project.

Cross of the Dutchman is a story-driven game based off a real folk legend.
The game is quite simple, so don't expect any heavy RPG elements.
The combat is very plain. You have a quick attack button that you can mash constantly, or a special attack which can kill multiple enemies at once, and throw them into a ragdoll mess. It's glorious. Although there's not much to the combat, I find it quite satisfying.
There are multiple areas in the map that allow for a little exploration and to collect chests of money.
The game also has occasional stealth sections. They aren't too hard, as you just need to avoid people with lanterns. Although they don't provide much challenge, they're a nice change of pace from the rest of the game.
Overall, it's a pretty relaxed game. Don't come into it expecting the best fighting mechanics, or RPG elements. The game's main attraction is that it takes you through an interesting story.

This brings me back to being a little kid, going with my little brother to the library, getting DVDs of Dragon Ball and playing Humongous Entertainment games on the computers. While the game can be completed in only an hour, It's one of the most nostalgic hours of my life. But, a review isn't based on nostalgia alone. Let us talk about the actual game.
Story wise, Grandma Grouper has lost her Kelp Seeds, which she shares to feed all undersea life. You are Freddi, and with the help of your best friend, Luther, you are tasked with finding the lost 'treasure'. But watch out! The Squid Father and his shark goons are also after the seeds! Talking to, helping, and interacting with the undersea life is the only way to reach your goal, but you better hurry!
While a simple kids story, this game does it exceptionally well. I never once felt interaction was forced. Everyone seemed to know Freddi in some way or another, but that doesn't de-value the interaction. While I did beat the game, I didn't obtain enough sea-urchins to enter the undersea volcano, which will send me back one day to find out its mysteries.
The game plays as you would expect a point-and-click game to play. While you move around the world, you are set to be in one area, while finding things around the world to interact with. It plays fantastically, but at times, the object you are looking for may be too well hidden, and blends into the background a little too easily.

with the game. While some people are voiced decently (The Eel, Stingray, Pirate), others seem like a very odd choice. The game starts off with a single pioneer. You are basically forced to Primal Eden at gunpoint to help the Expansion Galaxies eradicate dinosaurs on the planet. If you die your close relatives volunteer to pick up where you left off.
Once on the planet for the first time, you have nothing more than a machete, settlers mate and clothes with no camo value at all. The game is an open world first-person shooter. You can find weapons or buy them if you are a high enough rank.
When you kill one of the  five dinosaurs on the planet. You use your settlers mate to harvest it. There are rare dinosaurs as well that drop special weapons that is later purchasable through the In game market when you die. From the harvests you gain G, that is used to purchase these weapons and equipment.
There are these settlements throughout Primal Eden that offer crates of weapons, equipment, and ammo. Certain settlements offer special weapons that are extremely expensive in the in-game market. Like the .50 cal rifle that is only found in one location and only spawns one per server.
Hosting a game is a bit difficult to setup. The game has a fair amount of bugs. You will have to open ports 42303 and 27015 in order to host. The game has no dedicated servers and what this means is your PC will become a server basically. You may still get the port error code message even if your ports are forwarded correctly. Your game may crash with other errors as well.
If you're into open world  survival horror first person shooters where you can hunt dinosaurs or other players. Then I highly recommend this game. It has its fair share of bugs, but the games direction is something unique and different

Endless Legend seems to think it's a semi-interactive movie being rendered in real time, where every move of a unit results in beautiful gradual reveals of new lands as the grey fog of war rolls away in a manner that is wonderfully polished, but also rather slow. Similarly in battle, you can watch as each of the six little figures in your army draws their bow, nocks an arrow, and goes through an irritatingly long firing animation. Then a number indicating the amount of damage doesn't just appear, oh no, it has to rise up and glow and pulse. Practically everything in this game glows or pulses. Even the borders have pulse animations. Buy this game if you love beautiful graphics and have lots of time to spare to appreciate the loving detail with which every last object has been crafted. Buy it if you can't decide whether you want to play a game or browse a graphic designer's portfolio. But don't buy it if you want an interface that responds faster than a sleepy teenager on a Saturday morning, because you're likely to get sick of how long it takes to go through the most basic actions of a strategy game which thinks every individual unit deserves treatment worthy of an RPG protagonist.
The interface is also dubious in more ways than just the overdone graphics. Early in my playing, I wondered what the "next unit" key was - a common feature of most similar games which ought by now to be standard - so that having exhausted one unit's movement points, I would be able to move the next without having to search for it on the map. Tapping a few guesses like "n" and "Tab", which did nothing, I then attempted to press F1 to look up the hotkeys, but still nothing happened. Fumbling around a bit more, I found that hitting the Escape button presented me with an "archives" button on that menu, unhelpfully labeled "an assemblage of wisdom".
Did you think this might be the help function? It's not. It's a link to an Endless Legend wiki, which isn't even hosted on a professional site, but on the free and ad-infested Wikia network. I'm not sure what exactly lies behind this outsourcing of documentation to the userbase, but among the possibilities are laziness, sloppiness, and crippling overspecialization where everyone was working on the graphics.
As I write, the Wikia for Endless Legend does not have a page describing the hotkeys.

Amnesia is one of those games that I heard about years ago and became desperate to play because of the art quality. It was a very highly received title in Japan as well.
Based on other otome I've played, I think this is... sort of junk food. Lots of people like it, but that doesn't make it good. Even from a graphic novel standpoint, it's not especially well put together. That said, if you like the premise and you like the fetishes the routes offer, of course you'll overlook these flaws. I'm the same way with other games.
My first issue was that you have to choose a route at the start of the game. There's no 'let's get to know the characters' thing before you choose a route, which is why I preferred when this sort of mechanic was used in Nameless.
As others said, you have a passive heroine. Normally, this would be ok, since most otome heroines are self-insert anyway, but she is notable among the genre for her debilitating lack of agency. Based on dialogue which hints at your pre-amnesiac self, it seems that you were a bit of a selfish, needy and demanding person before. The guys generally express a sort of relief with this new, placid 'you'. So, basically, the guys like you because you're pretty, regardless of how you act. There's not even the pretense of personality here and for me, that their standards are so shallow makes me like the bachelors way less. I can't even say it's misogynistic either, since your heroine also doesn't have much reason to like these characters besides their looks.
You get a good ending if you're agreeable, a bad ending if you're not. You start the routes essentially already in a relationship, so for me, that already negates one of the most engaging aspects of these sorts of games.
Both the characters and the storyline are borderline satire. The smart guy's shtick is that he's like a computer; the 'big bro' shtick is that he's crazy obsessed with you, but seems normal; the crazy guy is laughing maniacally one second and remorseful and moe the next; the story keeps making excuses as to why you can't just do the reasonable thing for the sake of pursuing romantic interests. One step more and this game would have gone into Hatoful Boyfriend territory with the ludicrous nature of it all.
In total, the game caters to the fetish of 'helplessness', which has seen growing popularity in both Japan and North America. Basically, you have determined love interests (no need to search), in pre-selected routes (no risk of not getting guy), where you have no memory (not accountable for past errors or responsibilities) which is caused by a supernatural force (no concerns over actual medical problems), who takes responsibility over not just your memory, but your relationship status (no need for hard decisions) and your boyfriend(s) routinely put in you in a position where 'they will take care of everything' and restrict your agency. There's segments in all the routes which basically have your heroine wait in her room for days at a time, with occasional visits from one of the bachelors.
For me, there are other English otome that did most of the elements presented in Amnesia much better. It's a shallow game that caters to the right niches. I don't condemn it for that - I just wish it had catered to mine!

From the description and screenshots, this sounded like an interesting game, with potential for deep meaning, mystery and creepiness. It's also been tagged "horror" for reasons that escape me but as that was user-defined, I won't blame the creators. However, the game did still disappoint. I'm glad it's free. I wouldn't want to have spent money on this.
The recurring thought I had while playing this, which is its main problem, is that throughout, it feels like it's trying to be deep and mysterious, when there clearly is no deep and mysterious message behind any of it. You have something acting pretentious while it's obvious that it's nothing more than an action/comedy, which isn't particularly exciting or funny but is tedious due to the "artsy" or "suspenseful" parts.
My dislike for the game grew a lot stronger when our protagonist used a homophobic slur. It was already hard to find any reason to care for the generic "party hard YOLO" youth that he seemed to be, nor for the elusive "Sam" character, who was the same generic character only in female form. It strengthened the feeling that the creators are not at all out to make an artsy, creative statement, so why is it constantly acting like they are? I also have to question the decision to make what seems like a branching path, only to force the player to take both in one playthrough anyway. It makes the antagonist's comments on your decision rather empty.
I'm keeping this spoiler-free, so I won't specify the details of the ending but it was about as trite as I expected following all the tedious "puzzles", the sort-of out of place "action scenes"(I say sort-of since the game is only artsy at face value) and frustrating platforming stage that feels the need to glorify drugs for some reason. Oh and if you spy a certain achievement name before getting to the ending, the "twist" isn't exactly shocking. Although it does raise some questions as to why they made that particular joke about the "twist." Seems kind of, how do I put it, ♥♥♥♥ed up? But honestly I wasn't amused, shocked or appalled by the ending. It was rather fitting for a game that in the end just felt pointless.

I dare say cast away any negative reviews of this game as once one figures out the intricacies of the puzzles in this game they should see that virtually all negative reviews are simply lack of understanding the game mechanics. Only If is primarily a suspense puzzle game. The puzzle pieces come in many different forms and once in order, the gameplay will offer a very enjoyable experience.
The game is part story mode, part puzzle, part strategy, part suspense, a dash of skill and totally mind bending. ...Did I mention puzzle...This game is wrapped in puzzles to solve! Dust off the old brain cap, as there are hints and signs(that literally fall on you in some cases) throughout the story to instruct the player as to what order to progress through the story. Failure to do so will lead one astray so pay attention to the dialogue, pay attention to the signs and be ready to put your character control skills to the test.
Did I mention dusting off the old brain cap...There are no hand-holding tutorials here but, everything one needs to know in order to progress is given in the order one needs to know. I recommend having a pencil and paper handy to take notes along the way, especially if one needs to exit the game before completion as in the nostalgic spirit of games of yesteryear, the player will need to type in the name of the level last played.
There is strong language in this game. However, even to those whom are easily offended by language, the syntax the language is used in this game is perfectly fitting to the atmosphere and frankly, this game would not hold the suspense and atmosphere it has without the current choice in character dialogue. I give personal kudos to the game designers and studio in their choice of character dialogue. Too many game designers and game studios hold back on appropriate language syntax for the game atmosphere they are trying to create and as a result there are a lot of watered down less than par games on the market. Again, I give kudos to the game designers and studio for their choice in dialogue as it really does create the suspense and atmosphere this game requires.
The only downside to this game at time of this writing has nothing to do with the gameplay at all. The problem: Integration with Steam achievements is slightly broken. So long as the player does not "shift-tab" away from the game window the achievements appear to work just fine. As I understand there is something with how the Steam overlay for the Steam community integrates with the game that is bugged and causes the achievements to not register upon completion. Although this is something that should certainly be fixed, the fix is quite simple. The fix is to use Steams ability to verify the integrity of a games local files. The process takes about a thirty seconds. Afterwords all one needs to do is restart the game and go unlock any missing achievements. This game is not alone in this matter, there are numerous other games that have the same issue with achievements not working for the same reason.
All in all I really enjoyed this game and feel all one needs is a little patience, and desire to puzzle solve in order to see the beauty in game mechanics "Only If" provides.
Thank you to the game designers and game studio for making Only If available on Steam! For a first game effort the result was absolutely genius!
Thanks for taking the time to read my review. I hope my review is found helpful by the community and if so, please consider giving this review a thumbs up.
Now go immerse yourself in a great suspense puzzler!

If you're the type to ignore bad game design in exchange for a nostalgia trip, then sure you would like this if you loved the old RO... It's not the same, though.
First of all, if you hated Renewal, you may not be so happy because the beginner area looks exactly like in Renewal, and the UI as well. There's also quests just like in Renewal, from the beginner area. I'm not sure about the skill mechanics, to be honest, but someone did say it was Renewal mechanics. That renewal stuff doesn't bug me compared to the other things, though.
In my case, I did play RO when it was P2P up to today, so it was somewhat nostalgic for me, but even moreso annoying and reminded me of how flawed the game design is/was. Right when you enter, you can see there's a hidden NPC called "Bulletin Board" and the model or sprite for the board isn't even there, so it's invisible. This tells me that they really did not put effort into the beginner experience and neglected to fix things that are obvious bugs in plain sight. There's also bad grammar and spelling.
The beginner area has Steel Chonchon monsters which by the way, will kill you in one hit as a novice. I think they maybe wanted to combat against mass litter by adding these monsters(?), but instead it causes frustration for anyone who wants to loot their items from monsters, because they'll zoom right up and steal everything from under your mouse cursor. This makes it much harder for those wanting to become a merchant, which costs money to do. It's even worse when there's not tons of people around to constantly distract those stupid flies with their own loot, but then you want to be in the areas with less people due to inevitable KSing in crowded areas... so that was a bad experience for me.
There are also many flaws of the old game's design that are overlooked due to blind nostalgia, which would likely be huge turn-offs for those who have not played RO before.
For example some of the job change quests, namely the thief.
In order to become a thief, you first need to go through a maze in the pyramids in order to talk to the job change NPC. Sounds simple, until you realize you can't do this without having a higher level escort you or being extremely lucky. If you get hit twice by the aggressive and fast bats in there, you're dead and have to start all over again. They spawn way too fast even after they die, so you really are gambling to do this alone, unless you over-level, which is extremely time-consuming as a Novice. So much for the game pushing the "independant lone wolf" personality on aspiring thieves who will have to suck up to a superior in order to get the job done, which contradicts the job quiz they give you before you leave the beginner area and all of the thief job's descriptions.
So, if you REALLY want the nostalgic experience, I think you're better off trying a "Classic" RO private server.
And if you don't want to deal with the annoying job change quests, just about any private server with a job change NPC or custom job change quests.
Although it's not too common, I've played private servers which have better game design, quests, and story in the end. These would be much more up to standards with beginners who don't have rose-tinted glasses stuck on their face.

Ragnarok RE:START, a version of a game (released in 2002) that has withstood the test of time. Millions of people have entered the world of Rune Midgard through officially sanctuned servers and the multitude (and never ending supply) of private servers. It has inspiried mini-games, sequels, and inspired other games. (Ragnarok Online, to Ragnarok 2 (after it's second attempt at life), Tree of Life, Journey, etc.) It's a game that has been released in many different languages.
---------------------------
The question remains, what is Ragnarok RE:START and why is it different than Ragnarok Online?
---------------------------
Well, I can answer that for you. The style of server that RE:START operates is one that is a mix of the original mechanics and the revised "Renewal" mechanics. It is a mesh of two different worlds of game mechanics and content. This is known as "Revo-Classic." While keeping some of the Renewal content, such as Achievements, and mixing it with classic EXP Tables and monster HP pools.  This mesh of "old and new" has brought to light a healthy and cohesive version of the game that players (old and new) can enjoy together. Be prepared though. You have difficult challenges laid out before you that you must endure to be at the top of the food chain, be it PVP, MVP, or WoE.
ALSO! It's a restart of the story. We are starting the game over with Episode 1, the beginning. Through monthly updates that will progress the game up to the latest episode, we as players will be granted the opportunity to experience the evolution of this time-tested game from the start. The Re:start.
What this also includes is class releases. Endgame classes upon launch are currently Knight, Hunter, Blacksmith, Priest, Assassin, and Wizard. We currently do not know the release dates for the secondary classes to the starting line-up, but what we do know is that the third tier classes won't be available any time soon (High Priest, Creator, etc.). Nor will the Renewal classes (Rune Knight, Warlock, etc.). We have no ETA for the other classes, either (Gunslinger, Ninja, or Taekwon.). But, we can expect to see them as time passes.
---------------------------
So, what's my review?
---------------------------
I've been playing this for almost two weeks now(Headstart and pre-Steam launch), and being someone that has played Ragnarok Online from the early days where the game was actually a subscription based title, I can confidently say that this version of the game has rekindled my love for it. I have never hated Ragnarok Online, nor it's grindy /GRINDY/ gameplay. I'm probably in a minority when I say that I thoroughly enjoy the grind. It's brought a new outlook upon the game as a whole. You level faster than you did back in the old days, but slower than you would on Renewal (or so it feels to me). There's a rebalance of experience where you can hit job 50 relatively quickly. The flipside of making it easier to obtain is that the grind to 99 slows at the highest of levels. Drop rates are similar to classic, where you can spend several days farming a (for example) a Pupa Card and only see one.
The grind is a turnoff for a lot of players, as most gamers these days typically want to be rewarded for their efforts early one. There's nothing wrong with that, and I can relate to it. However, when you get involved with Ragnarok Online Classic and Re:start, you have to expect the grind and understand how challenging it can be.
If you can make it passed the extensive grind, Ragnarok Re:start is a lot of fun. Partying with up to 11 other people (for a total of 12 person parties) and sharing experience amongst everyone is one of the things that I throroughly enjoy. You don't have to be apart of an expert team to succeed either. There are challenges at the higher levels that do require some coordination, but if you party with people through the first half of your experience, you learn tricks and skills that will help you succeed. No doubt you will also meet people who share similar interests and others who quickly become friends.
The community in Ragnarok has always been a big draw for me. In hindsight, RO has always been a social game. Guilds, groups of friends, parties. They are all vital aspects when you enter the world of Rune Midgard.
While some things that I particularly enjoy are currently not available, like War of Emperium (Guild vs Guild castle seige gameplay) and classes like Rogue, I am able to find other ways to find delight in my day-to-day routine. Preparing for WoE (which is soon to come out) isn't a bad way to play.
---------------------------
Pros
---------------------------
+ A new way to experience an ever-evolving game.
+ Social Gameplay
+ Challenging & Rewarding. (Nothin' feels as good as when that card drops, man.)
+ Class Diversity
+ Re-balancing
+ Non-gamebreaking Cash shop
+ Story Progression
+ Active Support Staff, whom respond and take into consideration the playerbase's voice/opinions.
+ Excellent Community.
+ Potato Computers can run it.
+ Graphics. (Yes, this is in both Pros and Cons.)
---------------------------
Cons
---------------------------
+ Bots. They're forever going to be an issue.
+ Lag. I personally don't experience it a lot, but it is there.
+ Learning Curve. This is fixed with tools like, Ragi.al, Re:Start Spawn locations map, and
+ Grindy.  /VERY/ grindy. Be prepared. You've been warned.
+ /CURRENT/ End-Game limited to MVP Farming. This will be fixed as WoE and new Episodes roll out.
+ Graphics. I put this here tenatively, as I enjoy the 2D/3D style. However, it's very early 2000 design and the game has never experienced a graphical overhaul. If you don't mind sprites and stylized 3D enviroments, you're good.
